findings.finding_value: M01-A is called "Reverential Fear / Fear of God as Governing Orientation." The name signals three things: (1) "reverential" — the fear is morally and relationally appropriate, not merely visceral; (2) "fear of God" — the fear is directed, relational, and object-specific; (3) "governing orientation" — the fear is not an episodic event but a sustained inner disposition that governs the whole person. The name accurately captures the dominant characteristic of the sub-group's 364 verses: a settled, life-shaping reverence toward God.

M01-B is called "Acute Fear and Alarm." "Acute" signals the episodic, situationally-triggered character — the fear arises at a moment and addresses a specific stimulus. "Alarm" adds the reactive, involuntary dimension. The name distinguishes B sharply from A: where A is chronic and orienting, B is acute and responsive.

M01-C is called "Terror as Overwhelming Force." The name signals the distinctive structural feature: the terror is not primarily a state of the human inner person but a force acting upon or through the inner person. It has agency, direction, and overwhelming intensity.

M01-D is called "Dismay and Inner Collapse." "Dismay" signals sudden disruption of inner coherence; "inner collapse" signals the disintegration of the functional capacity to act, think, or speak. The name points to the end-state of the characteristic, not its trigger.

M01-E is called "Trembling / Fear Made Somatic." The compound name signals both the physical register (trembling) and its inner ground (fear). "Made somatic" captures the direction: inner fear expressing through the body, not bodily sensation generating the fear-emotion.

M01-F is called "Anticipatory Dread and Anxiety." "Anticipatory" is the defining modifier — the fear precedes its object rather than responding to a present threat. "Dread" signals intensity; "anxiety" signals the more diffuse, chronic form. Both dimensions are evidenced in the VCG corpus.

M01-G is called "Timidity and Cowardly Shrinking." "Timidity" signals a disposition-level weakness; "cowardly shrinking" names the evaluative dimension — this is not merely fear being present but fear evaluated as a moral-volitional failure. The name carries the evaluative charge of the sub-group's evidence.

The cluster is called "Fear, Dread and Terror" — a three-part name that signals the full semantic range from measured inner orientation (fear) through intensified anticipatory pressure (dread) to overwhelming assault (terror). The name correctly implies that the cluster spans a spectrum rather than a single uniform experience.

The cluster is named "Anger, Wrath and Indignation." The name signals three distinct registers within one essential phenomenon: (1) anger as the broad category of the reactive morally-charged inner state; (2) wrath, implying the heavier judicial and covenantal register — settled, purposeful, and consequential; (3) indignation, implying the more principled and sustained moral-displeasure register. The name correctly signals that this cluster is not a simple single phenomenon but a family of related states sharing a common root in moral reactive passion.

The programme names this cluster Grief, Sorrow and Mourning. The name signals three distinct but overlapping realities. Grief names the inner state itself — the inner-being weight of loss and its effect on the person. Sorrow names the settled condition of one who carries that weight — grief as a sustained inner disposition rather than merely an acute event. Mourning names the structured outward form grief takes — the act, the ritual, the communal practice through which inner grief is given social shape. The conjunction of all three in the name signals that the cluster encompasses not just one of these but the full arc from inner state through to outward expression and social form.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic is called Exultation. The name signals three things: (1) intensity — exultation is a heightened inner state, not a mild positivity; (2) directionality — exultation is always toward an object worthy of the surging response; (3) triumph — the term carries the sense of victory and vindication, appropriate to the primary register of the evidence where exultation follows divine rescue (Psa 9:14; 35:9; Isa 25:9; 61:10; Hab 3:18). The name also distinguishes this characteristic from Joy (participatory rejoicing) and Gladness (warm inner brightness) by naming the upward surge rather than the sustained warmth or engaged participation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The characteristic is called Joy. The name signals: (1) **Active engagement** — joy is participatory; it rejoices *in* something; it is directed and engaged, not a passive inner warmth; (2) **Inner-being scope** — the name is a recognisable inner-being state, distinct from Exultation (which surges), Gladness (which is warm and diffuse), and Pleasure (which is receptive). Joy as a name names the whole person's active rejoicing capacity; (3) **Communal resonance** — unlike Exultation (which is more individually intense), Joy has a communal dimension built into its common usage — one "rejoices with" others, and the commanded feast-joy of Deuteronomy is inherently social. The name correctly orients the enquiry toward an active, participatory, engageable inner state.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The characteristic is called Suffering-Joy. The hyphenated name signals: (1) **Paradox** — the name holds two apparently contradictory states together as a single inner-being reality, not as a compromise between them; (2) **Directionality** — "Suffering" precedes "Joy" in the name, indicating that suffering is the context within which Joy arises; (3) **Distinctness from Joy and Gladness** — the name signals that this is neither Joy (which rejoices in what is good) nor Gladness (which is the warm inner state of one whose circumstances are assessed as good) but a third positive inner-being state that specifically arises through suffering. The name correctly orients the enquiry toward a paradoxical inner capacity, not a surface emotion.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic is called Gladness. The name signals: (1) **Settled warmth** — gladness is a positively-coloured inner condition rather than an active surge (Exultation) or engaged participation (Joy); (2) **Cognitive-evaluative dimension** — gladness includes the soul's recognition that something is good, which the name captures by its diffuse, non-directed quality (one is glad rather than exulting at something); (3) **Inner condition rather than inner act** — the name points to a state rather than an event; the glad person inhabits gladness rather than performing it. The two sub-groups (M04-L and M04-O) fill the name: M04-L contributes the evaluative-cognitive face (the assessment that things are good); M04-O contributes the circumstantial-experiential face (the warm inner response to what is recognised as good). Together they name the settled, bright inner condition of a person or community that has accurately assessed and is responding to genuine goodness.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic is called Delight. The name signals: (1) **Object-focus** — Delight is always delight *in* something or someone; the name implies a specific treasured object that the inner person rests in and returns to; (2) **Receptive orientation** — unlike Exultation (active upward surge) or Joy (participatory engagement), Delight implies a resting, returning, orienting movement toward the beloved object; (3) **Affective-volitional integration** — the name in English carries both the emotional quality (it feels pleasurable) and the volitional quality (one chooses to delight, one finds and returns to what delights); this dual quality is exactly what the corpus confirms — M04-G is the affective face and M04-H is the volitional face; (4) **Scope across good and evil** — English "delight" can apply to both legitimate and illegitimate objects, which is consistent with M04-P's corrupt-delight register.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic is called Pleasure. The name signals: (1) **Receptive quality** — Pleasure names what is received and felt, not what is generated or directed; it is the soul's positive receptive response to what is pleasant; (2) **Agreeableness** — the name implies a felt quality of fit or agreeableness between the inner person and the object; (3) **Less directional than Delight** — Delight is always toward a specific treasured object; Pleasure is more ambient, received from surroundings, persons, and circumstances rather than focused on a single treasured object; (4) **Less active than Joy** — Pleasure is the inner being at ease in what is agreeable rather than actively exulting or rejoicing.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic is called Wonder. The name signals: (1) **Arrested quality** — Wonder names an inner state that is stilled rather than surging; the person in Wonder is arrested by what they encounter, not actively exulting; (2) **Receptive-perceptive** — Wonder is specifically a response to encounter, not an initiation; the inner being encounters something beyond itself and Wonder is the result; (3) **Breadth of register** — the single word "Wonder" covers the positive (marvelling at God's deeds), the cognitive (encountering the incomprehensible), and the negative (appalling dark astonishment); the name's breadth is a programmatic signal that the characteristic spans all three; (4) **Distinctness** — the name distinguishes this from Exultation (which surges), Joy (which participates), Gladness (which settles in the good), Delight (which rests in the beloved), and Pleasure (which receives the agreeable).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The seven names form a deliberately differentiated lexical set that maps the cluster's inner-being territory with precision. Three pairs and one unique: (1) **The surge-and-settle pair**: Exultation (Char 1 — active upward surge, triumphal, directed at God's glory) and Gladness (Char 3 — settled warm cognitive brightness, diffuse, evaluative). These are the poles of the cluster's positive-affect range: the upward active and the settled receptive; (2) **The participation-and-receptivity pair**: Joy (Char 2 — active participatory engagement, communal) and Pleasure (Char 5 — receptive agreeableness, ambient). Joy engages; Pleasure receives; (3) **The object-and-cognition pair**: Delight (Char 4 — specific object-focused treasuring, volitional) and Wonder (Char 6 — cognitive encounter with what exceeds comprehension, arrested). Delight settles into the object; Wonder is arrested by what cannot be contained in an object; (4) **The unique**: Suffering-Joy (Char 7 — hyphenated, paradox-naming) is uniquely named as a compound, signalling that it is a characteristic that holds two apparently opposed inner states as one. This naming is itself analytically significant: Suffering-Joy is the only characteristic that requires two nouns to name its essential paradoxical structure. Together the seven names signal the cluster's range: active-directed inner states (Exultation, Joy, Delight), receptive-ambient states (Pleasure, Gladness), cognitive-perceptive states (Gladness, Wonder), and the paradoxical-transcendent state (Suffering-Joy).

**[CHAR-1]** E — "Shame as experienced inner state." The name's three components are all analytically load-bearing: "shame" names the emotion/condition; "as experienced" marks it as a phenomenological reality — the felt inward event, not a moral verdict assigned from outside; "inner state" locates it constitutionally within the person, not merely in their reputation or social standing. The name explicitly distinguishes this characteristic from M07's other characteristics (enforced humiliation = M07-D; relational worth-denial = M07-E; shamefulness as moral judgment = M07-F). The CHAR-1 name signals that what is under investigation is the inner life of the person who feels shame — not what others think of them, not the moral quality of what they did, but the collapse of dignity, confidence, and standing that they experience.

**[CHAR-2]** E — "Humiliation as enforced abasement": "humiliation" names the characteristic experience; "as enforced" specifies the mechanism (done to the person by another agent — military defeat, social demotion, divine judgment); "abasement" names the direction (downward movement of standing). The name distinguishes CHAR-2 from CHAR-1 (felt inner experience without specifying enforcement) and locates it in socially enacted, divinely executed, or circumstantially produced downward movement of standing.

**[CHAR-3]** E — "Dishonour as relational worth-denial." The name is precise: "dishonour" names the specific register (stripping of honour/worth); "as relational" specifies the operational field (it always operates between persons or between person and God); "worth-denial" names the mechanism (what is being denied is the worth the other person actually has). The name distinguishes CHAR-3 from CHAR-1 (felt inner shame) and CHAR-2 (enforced downward movement of standing): dishonour is specifically a relational act of worth-misassignment.

**[CHAR-4]** E — "Shamefulness as moral-evaluative judgment." The name's structure: "shamefulness" names the quality being evaluated (the condition of being shameful, as distinct from the experience of shame); "as moral-evaluative judgment" specifies the operation — this is the conscience's assessment rather than a felt experience. The name distinguishes CHAR-4 from CHAR-1 (the felt inner experience of shame) by locating it in the evaluative rather than the experiential register: CHAR-4 is what conscience says about conduct or objects, not what the person feels in response to their own exposure.

**[CHAR-5]** E — "Shame produced by contempt and rejection." The name identifies: (1) the characteristic experience ("shame"); (2) its specific mechanism ("produced by contempt and rejection" — not by guilt, not by social demotion, but by the attitude of contemptuous dismissal or active rejection directed at the person). The name positions CHAR-5 as the received face of the contempt-shame dynamic whose source-side (contempt-projection) is M06's territory. CHAR-5 holds what the person experiences when contempt is directed at them.

**[CHAR-6]** E — "Innocence as structural counter to shame." The name has three components: "innocence" names the inner moral state (blameless conscience, clean will, hands free of deliberate wrongdoing); "as structural counter" identifies the function (not merely adjacent to shame but constitutively opposed to it — the inner state that makes guilt-shame structurally impossible or practically protects against it); "to shame" names the characteristic it counters (specifically guilt-shame, the M07-C register of shame before God). The name positions CHAR-6 as the positive inner-moral condition that CHAR-1's guilt-shame register presupposes the absence of.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Reading the six names together, a precise inner taxonomy emerges. "Shame as experienced inner state" (Char 1) establishes the primary phenomenological register — the felt inner event. "Humiliation as enforced abasement" (Char 2) names the mechanism by which shame's outer form is produced. "Dishonour as relational worth-denial" (Char 3) names the relational act that violates the person's worth. "Shamefulness as moral-evaluative judgment" (Char 4) names the evaluative-qualitative dimension — the conscience's naming of what is shameful. "Shame produced by contempt and rejection" (Char 5) names the specific contempt-mechanism and its product. "Innocence as structural counter to shame" (Char 6) names the positive moral condition that the other five presuppose and oppose. Together the six names constitute a systematic map: the experience (Char 1), the mechanism (Char 2), the relational act (Char 3), the evaluative quality (Char 4), the contempt-source (Char 5), and the protective counter (Char 6). No name is redundant; each covers a genuinely distinct dimension of the same shame-field.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The programme name is "Arrogant self-elevation." The name encodes three essential elements that the verse evidence directly substantiates. First, the direction: elevation — an upward movement, rooted in the spatial metaphor running through the Hebrew vocabulary (rum — to be high/to rise; ga.on — rising grandeur; ga.vah — to exalt/rise proudly) and the Greek (huperēfanos — appearing above; hupsēlos — high). Second, the agent: self — the inner person as the one doing the lifting, not receiving it from outside or from God; Psa 75:6 (vc=34301, M08-A4-VCG-05) — "not from the east or from the west... comes lifting up" — names the illegitimacy of self-directed elevation. Third, the mode: arrogant — the elevation is illicit, claimed rather than given, competing with what belongs to God alone. The name already distinguishes CHAR-1 from legitimate dignified standing (which the evidence is silent on as CHAR-1) and from God's genuine exaltation (M22, set aside at Phase 5.5).

**[CHAR-2]** E — The programme name is "Presumptuous defiance." The name encodes two essential elements: (a) defiance — the characteristic is directed against an external authority (divinely-established limits, appointed persons, revealed commands); and (b) presumptuous — the will acts beyond what it has been authorised to claim, assuming a right or freedom it does not possess. The name distinguishes CHAR-2 from simple disobedience (which might be reluctant or passive) and from CHAR-1 (elevated self-regard): CHAR-2 is the active, forceful, deliberate assertion of the self against a specific known limit. The Hebrew root zid (boiling, seething) is directly encoded in "presumptuous" — the characteristic is not cool calculation but a will that boils over, as Deu 1:43 (vc=34123, M08-B-VCG-01) evidences: Israel "acted presumptuously and went up into the hill country" despite God's explicit prohibition.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The programme name is "Boasting and self-display." The compound name encodes two registers: "boasting" names the speech-act dimension (the verbal assertion of one's own worth, achievement, or credentials — kauchaomai/ha.lal), and "self-display" names the visible/social presentation dimension (the public making-known of the self as worthy — alazoneia, alazōn). The name signals that CHAR-3 is constitutively public and external: unlike CHAR-1 (inner dispositional elevation) or CHAR-2 (volitional transgressive act), CHAR-3 moves into speech and social visibility. Jam 4:16 (vc=33886, M08-C-VCG-01): "you boast in your arrogance" — the arrogance (CHAR-1 substrate) finding verbal expression in boasting (CHAR-3).

**[CHAR-4]** E — The programme name is "Vain conceit." "Conceit" names the cognitive register — a false mental conception of the self; "vain" names the emptiness of that conception — inflated without actual substance, as fusioō (to puff up) names the condition of being swollen beyond one's actual content. The name precisely targets CHAR-4's defining feature: a mind that has constructed an inaccurate, inflated picture of itself. The name distinguishes CHAR-4 from CHAR-1 (dispositional self-elevation), CHAR-2 (volitional transgression), and CHAR-3 (verbal self-display) — CHAR-4 is the inner cognitive form of pride. Rom 12:3 (vc=60866, M08-D-VCG-02): "do not think of yourself more highly than you ought" — huperfroneō names precisely this: thinking (froneō) above (huper) what is warranted.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The programme name is "Pride of power and position." The name encodes the specific medium through which this form of pride operates: "power" names structural force (military might, physical strength, national capacity — the ga.on proud-might register), and "position" names social and material standing (wealth, fortified height, authority). Together they distinguish CHAR-5 from CHAR-1 (dispositional elevation), CHAR-2 (volitional defiance), CHAR-3 (verbal boasting), and CHAR-4 (cognitive conceit) — CHAR-5 is the structural-power register of pride. Lev 26:19 (vc=33982, M08-E-VCG-01): "the pride of your power" — the compound phrase is native to the evidence itself.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The five names encode five distinct registers of the same underlying disorder, and reading them together reveals a taxonomy of pride's expressions. "Arrogant self-elevation" (CHAR-1) names the dispositional-directional register — the inner upward movement of the self. "Presumptuous defiance" (CHAR-2) names the volitional-authority register — the will acting beyond its authorised limits. "Boasting and self-display" (CHAR-3) names the communicative-social register — the inner elevation moving into speech and visible self-assertion. "Vain conceit" (CHAR-4) names the cognitive-epistemic register — the mind's false self-picture. "Pride of power and position" (CHAR-5) names the structural-medium register — pride expressed through and sustained by received structural goods. The cluster-synthesis finding from the five names together: M08 is not a cluster of a single vice with varying intensities — it is a cluster that maps pride across the full range of inner-being faculties (disposition, will, communication, cognition, structural stewardship) and the full range of human existence (inner posture, transgressive act, public speech, self-knowledge, relationship to power).

**[CHAR-2]** E — The characteristic is named Submission. The name signals an essentially relational and directional structure: to submit is to place oneself under (sub-mittere) — to position the self in relation to a legitimate authority. The name implies both an agent (the one who submits) and a recipient (the authority submitted to), confirming that this is a constitutively relational characteristic that cannot operate in isolation. The name also implies an act: submission is done, not merely possessed — though as the evidence shows, it becomes a disposition through repetition and formation.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic is named Contrition. The name derives from the Latin conterere (to grind, crush, wear down) — signalling that this is the inner state of being ground down or broken, not merely softened. The name signals an acute, physically-resonant inner reality: the crushed spirit (Psa34:18 — "crushed in spirit"), the broken heart (Psa34:18 — "brokenhearted"), the contrite spirit (Isa57:15). The name thus immediately conveys the severity and intensity of the inner state — not mild regret but genuine interior breaking before moral reality.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic is named Meekness and Gentleness. The name is compound, signalling that two related but distinct inner-being qualities are carried together: meekness (the inner capacity for governed strength — the will that does not deploy force inappropriately) and gentleness (the calibrated, compassionate quality of engagement with others in their weakness or need). The compound name reflects the two-term evidence corpus: metriopatheō (Heb5:2 — be gentle, deal measuredly with the erring) and okneō (Act9:38 — absence of hesitation, immediate volitional responsiveness). Neither term alone names both qualities; together they constitute the characteristic's dual nature.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic is named Dignity. The name signals a quality of inherent worth expressed in composed, grounded comportment — the person who has dignity carries themselves with settled moral seriousness that does not require external validation or self-promotion. The name points toward the inner-grounded nature of the quality: dignity is not conferred by status or performance but is the expression of settled inner worth. In the semnotēs corpus (1Ti2:2; 1Ti3:4; Tit2:7), the name signals a quality of the character that shapes how the person inhabits their role and relationships — weightily, seriously, without self-displaying performance.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic is named Willing-heartedness. The compound name signals both its constitutional location (the heart) and its constitutive quality (willing — freely-moved, uncoerced). The name points immediately toward the inner source of the characteristic: it is not willing-ness in general but willing-ness that originates in the heart as the integrating centre of the person. The name also signals the absence of compulsion as constitutive: willing-heartedness is specifically the quality of the heart that moves freely rather than under external pressure. Exo35:5 — "whoever is of a generous/willing heart" — and Psa51:12 — "a willing spirit" — together show the two constitutional locations (heart, spirit) that the compound name encompasses.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic is named Humility. The name signals a fundamentally relational orientation: to be humble is to be in a certain posture relative to God and to others — not a self-enclosed state but a positioned one. The name encompasses both the willed act of self-lowering (M09-A — the voluntary disposition) and the experienced state of being low (M09-B — the condition register), indicating that humility in Scripture names both what the person does and what the person finds themselves to be. The Hebrew terms tsa.na and tsa.nu.a (walking humbly, the humble) and ka.na (humbling, being humbled) carry relational direction built into their structure — humbling is always humbling *before* someone. The Greek tapeinos/tapeinofrosunē/tapeinoō family's root (tapeinos — low, base, not elevated) signals that the characteristic is defined by position: the person places themselves or finds themselves below their natural or claimed standing.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The six names together reveal the cluster's organising logic. Three names signal relational direction: *Humility* (before God and others, downward), *Submission* (toward legitimate authority, under), *Willing-heartedness* (toward God, freely). Two names signal character quality: *Dignity* (settled inner gravity, non-assertive), *Meekness and Gentleness* (calibrated restraint and readiness, other-directed). One name signals an inner state: *Contrition* (crushed, broken, before God's holiness). The cluster-level reading: M09's names cluster around two axes — (a) *how the person is positioned relative to others* (Humility, Submission, Contrition — all naming postures-before), and (b) *what quality the person brings to social and relational existence* (Dignity, Meekness, Willing-heartedness — naming the character of the person in relation). The compound name Meekness and Gentleness is the only two-term name in the cluster, confirming its structurally composite character. All six names exclude self-assertion and self-promotion as constitutive elements — the names are the lexical index of the cluster's governing theme.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Wilful sinning." The name encodes a binary claim: (1) that sinning is a *wilful* act — not accidental, not compelled, but chosen by the inner person with awareness of what is being done; and (2) that this is *sinning* — a relational act that violates a standard. The name signals that the defining feature is not the category of wrong committed but the quality of the inner act: the will's knowing engagement with the wrong. This is confirmed by the definitional separation from CHAR-2 (Unintentional sinning) — that characteristic occupies its own sub-group precisely because the corpus distinguishes deliberate from inadvertent wrongdoing. The name "Wilful sinning" thus foregrounds volition as the constitutive element: what makes this characteristic analytically distinct is not the content of the sin but the inner quality of the will that commits it.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Specialised sinful mechanisms." The name signals three things. (1) *Specialised*: the mechanisms are not the general categories of sinning (wilful, unintentional, habitual) but specific named inner processes — enticement through desire, identity-falsification through collective hypocrisy, covenantal-identity abandonment through apostasy. Each mechanism names a distinct pathway through which sin captures the person. (2) *Sinful*: despite the diversity of mechanisms, all three result in moral failure — they are all pathways to sin, not merely morally neutral processes. (3) *Mechanisms*: the term signals that the characteristic is about the *how* of sinning — the inner operational process — rather than the *what* (the specific sinful act) or the *who* (the sinning person's character). CHAR-10 is the characteristic of sinning's methods.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Sin as universal condition." Three signals: (1) *Sin*: the moral-spiritual reality that separates the creature from God — not a single act but the comprehensive inner state. (2) *Universal*: the scope is every human being without exception — Rom 3:9 — "all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin" — and Rom 3:23 — "all have sinned" — and Heb 5:3 — even the high priest must sacrifice for his own sins. The universality distinguishes this characteristic from sin-as-specific-act (CHAR-1) or sin-as-habitual-pattern (CHAR-6): CHAR-11 is the bedrock condition underlying all other sinning characteristics. (3) *Condition*: the characteristic is a structural state rather than a discrete event — "under sin" (Rom 3:9), "dead in trespasses and sins" (Eph 2:1), "sold under sin" (Rom 7:14), "die in your sin" (Joh 8:21). The name signals: every person stands in this state regardless of whether they have committed a specific sinful act, because the condition is ontological — part of their fallen human constitution.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Sin as enslaving power." Three signals. (1) *Sin*: the moral-spiritual reality at stake is sin in its power-register — not a specific act but sin operating as a force. (2) *Enslaving*: the characteristic's defining mark is that sin is not merely present but actively captures and holds the will; Joh 8:34 — "everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin" — slavery names the constitutive inner relationship. The enslaving signal distinguishes CHAR-12 from CHAR-11 (universal condition — under sin) by naming sin's *active governing function over the will* specifically. (3) *Power*: the term signals that sin operates as an active agent, not merely a state; Gal 3:22 — "the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin" — sin is the imprisoning force; it has the power to confine. The name thus encodes: sin operating as an active governing master that holds the will captive.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Sin as divine record." Three signals. (1) *Sin*: the moral reality being tracked is sin — not a neutral human limitation but moral offense against God. (2) *Divine record*: the characteristic is not the subjective experience of guilt (which would be CHAR-17) but the objective moral weight existing before God — whether the person feels it or not. The record exists independently of the person's awareness. (3) *Record*: the metaphor signals documentary retention — Hos 13:12 — "his sin is kept in store"; Exo 32:33 — "I will blot out of my book"; Jer 17:1 — "written with a pen of iron... engraved on the tablet of their heart." The name thus signals: an objective, retained, divine-witnessed moral account that is not destroyed by the person's ignorance, self-deception, or concealment from others.

**[CHAR-14]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Forgiveness sought and received." Three signals. (1) *Forgiveness*: the moral-relational transaction at stake — not merely guilt-relief but the objective removal of the sin-record that separates the person from God; (2) *Sought*: the inner movement originates in the person — a volitional turning toward God to appeal for what only God can grant; Act 2:38 — "repent and be baptized... for the forgiveness of your sins" — the seeking is a commanded human movement; (3) *Received*: the characteristic names completion — not merely seeking but the divine response of granting; Luk 7:48 — "your sins are forgiven" — the declaration closes the transaction. The name's compound form ("sought and received") signals the characteristic's bi-directional structure: the human movement of seeking and the divine act of granting are both necessary constituents.

**[CHAR-15]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Generational sin." Two signals. (1) *Generational*: the defining mark is the transmission-across-generations dimension — the sin-condition is not merely the individual's own accumulated acts but enters through lineage, family, or national belonging; Isa 43:27 — "your first father sinned" — the present generation is addressed through the ancestral chain. (2) *Sin*: the transmitted condition is specifically a moral condition — guilt or moral liability, not merely a cultural or behavioural tendency. The name signals: a sin-condition whose origin and weight extends beyond the individual to encompass ancestors and the communities that shaped them.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The programme names this characteristic "The sinner as moral character." Three signals. (1) *The sinner*: the noun-form — not "sinning" (the act) or "sinfulness" (the condition) but "the sinner" as a person-type; the definite article signals a recognisable category. (2) *As moral character*: the characteristic is a constituted inner moral identity — who the person *is* at their moral core, not what they have done or stand in. (3) *Moral*: the characterisation is specifically moral, not social or cultural — though the social dimension (VCG-01's exclusion and stigma) is a consequence. The name signals: sin has become a defining feature of the person's moral identity, not merely their behaviour or legal standing.

**[CHAR-17]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Guilt as inner-being state." Three signals. (1) *Guilt*: the moral condition of having violated a standard and bearing its weight — not merely the legal verdict but the lived inner experience of that verdict; (2) *As inner-being state*: the characteristic is specifically the subjective inner experience, not the objective record (CHAR-13 — sin as divine record) or the act (CHAR-1). The "state" naming signals duration: guilt is not a momentary sensation but a condition the person inhabits; (3) *Inner-being*: the guilt operates within — it is the conscience's recognition of moral liability before God. The name signals: a sustained inner-experiential condition of moral-liability awareness, distinguishable from the act that produced it and the divine record that holds it.

**[CHAR-18]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Iniquity as accumulated moral crime." Three signals. (1) *Iniquity*: the English rendering of a.von (H5771G) — the OT's comprehensive term for moral wrongdoing at its deepest register; not merely a sinning act but the moral weight of that act accumulated before God; (2) *As accumulated*: the defining modifier — iniquity here is not the single act but the store of wrongdoing built up over time and generations; Gen 15:16 — "not yet complete" — the accumulation is quantifiable and progressive; (3) *Moral crime*: the "crime" dimension signals the forensic register — iniquity-as-crime stands before a judge (God) as an offence requiring adjudication. The name signals: the person's moral account of wrongdoing before God, built up over time, constituting a standing moral-legal liability.

**[CHAR-19]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Transgression as deliberate boundary-crossing." Three signals. (1) *Transgression*: the English rendering of the primary vocabulary family (pe.sha/pa.sha; parabasis); the word carries both the legal sense of crossing a line and the relational sense of betrayal; (2) *As deliberate*: the defining modifier — not inadvertent error (CHAR-2) but knowing, wilful choice; Rom 4:15 — "where there is no law there is no transgression" — a known boundary is required; (3) *Boundary-crossing*: the spatial-moral image that names the core act — the will steps over a line it knows to exist. The name signals: the most distinctively volitional category in M10 — the will that knows and chooses to defy.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The programme name "Unintentional sinning" contains a qualifier ("unintentional") that is definitionally load-bearing: the name signals that the sinning act occurred without the inner person's deliberate defiance of a known command. The qualifier distinguishes this from CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning) not by minimising the moral weight of the act but by specifying the inner quality of the will at the moment of commission. Lev 4:2 uses the adverb *bishgagah* ("unintentionally / in error / by mistake") — embedded in the name is the Hebrew concept of *shegagah* (inadvertence, mistake, error), which carries the sense of wandering from the path without intending to. The name thus signals: this is real sinning (the same cha.ta term applies), but the inner-being state at the moment of the act lacked the knowing quality that characterises CHAR-1.

**[CHAR-20]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Faithlessness as covenant-breaking sin." Three signals. (1) *Faithlessness*: not the discrete act of sin but the dispositional inner quality of the person who breaks covenant — the opposite of the faithfulness (*ʾĕmûnāh*) that the image-bearer was designed to sustain; (2) *As covenant-breaking*: the defining context — faithlessness is not generic disloyalty but specifically the breaking of a known covenantal bond; Mal 2:14 — "your wife by covenant" — the covenant is what makes the faithlessness betrayal rather than mere preference-change; (3) *Sin*: the moral-theological classification — faithlessness is not merely relational failure but sin against God and the covenant-order. The name signals: the most relational sin-category in M10 — the will that dissolves what God constituted to be binding.

**[CHAR-21]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Perversion as inner inversion." Three signals. (1) *Perversion*: the English rendering covers moral distortion, twisting, and corruption — the turning of what was designed to be straight into something bent; (2) *As inner inversion*: the defining modifier — the perversity operates from within, not merely as external misbehaviour; the inversion is of the moral order from inside the person; (3) *Inner*: the characteristic is at the level of the person's moral faculties — mind, heart, will, speech — not merely behavioural. The name signals: the most comprehensive inner distortion-category in M10 — the person whose moral-inner constitution has been twisted against its grain.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Injustice as moral failure of right conduct." Three signals. (1) *Injustice*: the antonym of justice (*mishpat*/dikaiosynē) — what violates the right standard in dealings with persons; (2) *As moral failure*: not merely legal breach but the inner-moral dimension — the heart's orientation toward wrong conduct against others; (3) *Of right conduct*: the failure is specifically of right-conduct (*tsedaqah*/*dikaiosynē*) — the M26 cross-register cluster. The name signals: M10's most explicitly other-directed characteristic — injustice is done *toward* persons and *against* right order; it cannot exist without a victim and a violated standard.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Confession." The name signals three things. (1) *Speech-act*: confession is inherently verbal — it is a naming, a speaking, an act that moves from inner to outer through language. (2) *Past-reference*: confession names what has *already been done* — it is retrospective, not prospective. Every instance in the corpus names a committed sin: "this time I have sinned" (Exo 9:27), "I have sinned greatly in what I have done" (2Sa 24:10), "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood" (Mat 27:4). (3) *Relational direction*: confession is always addressed to someone — God (Luk 15:18 — "against heaven and before you"), persons (Exo 10:16 — "against the Lord your God, and against you"), or a public audience (Job 33:27 — "he sings before men"). The name "Confession" thus encodes: a speech-act directed at a relational recipient, naming a past wrong as wrong.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Conscience suppression." The name encodes a specific inner-being claim: (1) *Conscience* — the moral-witness faculty that registers sin, guilt, and moral reality — is the faculty at stake; (2) *Suppression* — this faculty is not absent by original design but is being held down, refused, or prevented from operating. The name implies an active dimension: something that could function is being prevented from functioning. This is evidenced in the spectrum of the corpus: Jer 2:35 (active verbal denial — "I have not sinned" — is active suppression), Jer 16:10 (failure to recognise — passive suppression), Ecc 8:12 (ongoing sinning without the fear of God — conscience-absent by habituation), 1Cor 15:34 (ongoing sinning linked to ignorance of God — stupor rather than alert), Tit 3:11 (self-condemned but not self-aware — implicit conscience operating under explicit suppression).

**[CHAR-5]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Refusal to repent." The name encodes three claims: (1) *Refusal* — this is an active act of the will, not a passive failure. The verb "refuse" implies that turning was available and the will said no. This is confirmed throughout the corpus: "he did not depart from" (2Ki 3:3; 13:2/11; 14:24; 15:9/28), "he did not turn aside from" (2Ki 10:29), "they would not obey" (Neh 9:29), "sinning deliberately" (Heb 10:26). (2) *To repent* — the thing refused is a moral turning, a departure from the sinful course. Repentance is the available alternative that the will refuses. (3) The name implies a *known alternative*: one can only refuse what one is called to do. The definition confirms this: "turning actively withheld." The name signals: the will possesses the capacity to turn, is called to turn, and chooses not to.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Habitual defection." The name encodes two claims. (1) *Habitual*: the characteristic is not a single act but a pattern settled over time — the will's default direction has been established toward sin. This contrasts with CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning — single act) and CHAR-5 (Refusal to repent — the decision-point of non-departure). The habit dimension signals that the sinning has moved beyond the episodic into the dispositional: it is the will's natural default rather than a departure from it. (2) *Defection*: the sinning is a going-away-from, an abandonment of loyalty — the image of someone who was in or should be in a covenant relationship but has repeatedly moved away from it. 2Ki 17:7 — "sinned against the Lord their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt" — the redemptive background makes the sinning a defection: they were brought out, they have defected back. The name signals: a formed inner orientation of departure from God, not merely occasional sin but the will's settled direction.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Contagious sin." The name signals three things. (1) *Contagious*: the characteristic is not self-contained in the leader but spreads outward — as a disease passes from one person to another, the leader's sinful inner commitment is transmitted to the community. The contagion metaphor names the mechanism: proximity to the source (the leader) and the medium (authority relationship) combine to transmit the moral direction. (2) *Sin*: the transmitted content is specifically the leader's sinful direction, not merely their moral influence. What spreads is the wrong thing — the defection from God. (3) The name implies a *source and a recipient*: unlike other sinning characteristics that name the internal state of a single person, contagious sin requires a transmission structure — a leader (source) and a community (recipient). The name thus encodes the relational-authority framework within which the characteristic uniquely operates.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Political revolt." The name encodes three things. (1) *Political*: the characteristic operates in the political-social domain — the relationships of governing authority between peoples, nations, and kingdoms. This distinguishes it from other pa.sha registers that address theological-covenantal revolt (CHAR-19). The corpus is uniformly political: Moab against Israel (2Ki 1:1; 3:5/7), Edom and Libnah against Judah (2Ki 8:20/22; 2Ch 21:8/10), Israel against the house of David (1Ki 12:19; 2Ch 10:19). (2) *Revolt*: the characteristic is an active breaking-away — not passive non-compliance but a decisive act of defection from the governing relationship. 2Ki 8:20 — "Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and *set up a king of their own*" — the positive act of establishing independent authority is part of the revolt. (3) The name implies both a *prior relationship* (submission to authority) and a *decisive rupture* — revolt can only occur where prior submission existed.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The programme names this characteristic "Sinful speech." The name encodes three things. (1) *Sinful*: the speech originates in and expresses inner moral corruption — it is not merely offensive or socially inappropriate but morally sinful, carrying the weight of transgression. (2) *Speech*: the characteristic is constitutively the speech-act — the externalisation of the inner corruption through the mouth. Mat 15:19 — "out of the heart come evil thoughts... slander" — the inner (heart) and the outer (speech) are related as source and expression. (3) The name signals that the characteristic is defined by both its inner origin (sinful) and its outer form (speech) — distinguishing it from inner sinful states that remain unexpressed. The characteristic is the completion of the inner-to-outer movement: the corrupted heart speaks.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic is named "Wickedness as settled person-identity." The name has three components, each analytically significant. "Wickedness" signals a moral-character category — not a discrete act but a quality of the inner person. "Settled" signals a stable, consolidated state rather than a transient condition or a series of episodes — it has become definitional for the person who possesses it. "Person-identity" signals that the characteristic names a type of inner-being person rather than an experience that passes through the person. The name as a whole communicates that the evidence concerns the human being whose moral character has been organised around wickedness as its centre of gravity — it is who the person is, not merely what they have done. This contrasts with M10 (sin-act, the doing) and M10c (defilement, the contagion effect) to which M10b-A is a sibling.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The characteristic is named "Evil as constitutional inner nature." Three components matter analytically. "Evil" (ponēros / kakia / adikia / ponēria) names a moral-quality designation — not a specific act but a characterisation of what the person is at their inner core. "Constitutional" signals that this is not a transient state or episodic failure but a structural condition of the inner person — what they are constituted as. "Inner nature" signals that the characteristic concerns the generative architecture of the person's moral being, not its surface expressions. The name as a whole communicates that the evidence addresses the person whose inner generative nature is structurally oriented toward evil — not merely who has done evil things but from whom evil things necessarily flow. This differs from CHAR-1 (wickedness as settled person-identity) by emphasising structural-generative condition over settled directional orientation.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic is named "Abomination — divine revulsion on moral character." Three components carry analytical weight. "Abomination" signals a category of extreme moral repugnance that violates a sacred boundary — not merely wrongdoing but a quality of inner being or conduct that produces active revulsion. "Divine revulsion" specifies the agent of the response: the revulsion is God's, not merely human social disapproval, establishing the characteristic as a relational category defined at the God-human interface. "On moral character" limits the scope: this is the moral-character sub-register of abomination, distinct from M10b-D (idolatrous abomination). The name signals that the characteristic operates at the intersection of divine holiness (God's capacity for revulsion) and human moral character (the inner conditions that trigger it): Pro 11:20 (vc=1677 — VCG-01 — "those of crooked heart are an abomination"), Pro 16:5 (vc=1689 — VCG-02 — "everyone who is arrogant in heart is an abomination").

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic is named "Idolatrous abomination." Two components carry analytical weight. "Idolatrous" specifies the register: this is abomination rooted in false devotion — the attachment of the heart/soul/will to idol-objects rather than to God. This distinguishes CHAR-4 from CHAR-3 (moral-character abomination), where the abominable quality resides in inner moral conditions (pride, dishonesty). "Abomination" signals the divine-relational verdict: the characteristic provokes God's active revulsion. The name as a whole signals that idolatrous abomination is the specific form of abomination arising from the devotion-capacity's misdirection: Eze 11:21 (vc=1631 — VCG-05): "those whose heart goes after their detestable things and their abominations" — the heart's directional faculty is what goes after idols; Isa 66:3 (vc=1633 — VCG-04): "their soul delights in their abominations" — the soul's delight-faculty is what is engaged. The name names the specific inner-being dynamics of false devotion.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic is named "Iniquity as active inner scheming and evil generation." Three components carry analytical weight. "Iniquity" names the moral category — wrongdoing conceived and produced from within. "Active inner scheming" specifies the generative mode: this is not passive moral failure but deliberate, premeditated inner activity. "Evil generation" names the output: the inner scheming produces evil as its child. The name signals that the characteristic is constitutively generative: Psa 7:14 (vc=38245 — VCG-02): "conceives evil… pregnant with mischief… gives birth to lies" — the birth metaphor is embedded in the characteristic's definitional core. Mic 2:1 (vc=38217 — VCG-02): "those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it" — the devising (inner) and performing (outer) sequence names both dimensions the name covers. The name orients toward the inner generative process, not merely the outer wicked act.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic is named "Evil expressed through speech." Three components signal its essential nature. "Evil" names the inner moral source — wickedness that originates from within the person. "Expressed through" signals the medium: speech is the instrument, not the source; the evil precedes its expression and uses speech as its vehicle. "Speech" specifies the mode of operation — the characteristic is constitutively verbal. The name signals that the characteristic is an expression-phenomenon: it requires the inner evil to exist before speech can express it, and requires speech as the specific channel through which inner wickedness becomes socially operative. This distinguishes CHAR-6 from characteristics where speech is incidental; here speech is constitutive. Rev 13:6 (vc=14356 — VCG-01): the beast "opened its mouth to utter blasphemies" — the opening of the mouth is the act through which inner defiant orientation becomes operational blasphemy.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Across the six characteristics, the cluster's naming reveals a systematic analytical vocabulary covering inner evil across its five primary modes: identity (Char 1 — "settled person-identity"), constitution (Char 2 — "constitutional inner nature"), verdict/response (Chars 3 and 4 — "abomination"), process (Char 5 — "active inner scheming and evil generation"), and expression (Char 6 — "expressed through speech"). The names collectively reveal the cluster's analytical scope: M10b addresses inner evil not as a single phenomenon but as a family of related but distinct inner-being forms. The "settled" marker in Char 1 and "constitutional" marker in Char 2 distinguish identity-state from nature-structure. Chars 3 and 4 share the "abomination" category but distinguish moral-character (Char 3) from idolatrous devotion (Char 4) as its two sub-registers. Char 5 introduces the process-generative dimension absent from Chars 1-4. Char 6 introduces the expressive-instrumental dimension — evil as expressed through the speech-faculty. The cluster's six names together map six analytically distinct angles on inner evil: who the evil person is (Char 1), what they are constituted by (Char 2), how God responds to their moral corruption (Char 3) and false devotion (Char 4), what their inner faculties are doing (Char 5), and what their inner wickedness produces through speech (Char 6).

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic is named "Ritual defilement-state." The name signals three things. First, *ritual*: this is the register governed by cultic law and sacral practice, distinguishing this characteristic from the moral-inner defilement register (Characteristic 2) and the corporate-covenantal register (Characteristic 3). Second, *defilement*: the term names an active contamination — something has been transmitted, incurred, or declared; the person has not merely failed but has acquired a condition. Third, *state*: this is a condition of the person, not an act — the characteristic names what the person is in (a status), not what they do. The name therefore signals: a legally and ritually defined condition of contamination that attaches to the inner-being person through bodily mechanism or authoritative verdict.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The characteristic is named "Moral-inner defilement-state." Three elements of the name are analytically significant. *Moral*: the defilement is located in the moral domain — it concerns the inner person's orientation toward good, evil, right, and wrong, not merely a ritual or bodily condition. *Inner*: the locus is the interior of the person — conscience, will, heart — not external contact or authoritative verdict (that is Characteristic 1). *Defilement-state*: it is a condition, not an act — the person is in a state of corruption, not merely performing corrupt acts. The name signals that this characteristic is the inner-being condition of a morally compromised interior, which the evidence confirms: Mat 23:27 (VCG-04) — "within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness"; Eph 4:19 (VCG-02) — "greedy to practice every kind of impurity" arising from a silenced conscience.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic is named "Corporate/covenantal defilement." Three elements of the name are analytically significant. *Corporate*: the defilement extends beyond the individual to the community as a body — shared land, shared sanctuary, shared name, shared moral failure. *Covenantal*: the defilement operates within and against the covenantal relationship; it is betrayal of a specific relational bond between God and his people, not merely moral failure in general. *Defilement*: the state of contamination that results from the betrayal, spreading to the physical and sacral environment the community inhabits. The name thus signals: a condition of contamination that arises from corporate covenantal unfaithfulness and extends from the inner will of the community outward to land, sanctuary, and divine name.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic is named "Defilement by external spiritual agency." Four elements are analytically significant. *Defilement*: the characteristic produces the same inner-being condition as Characteristics 1-3 — the person is in a defiled state. *External*: the source of the defilement is outside the person, not from bodily contact (Characteristic 1), moral self-corruption (Characteristic 2), or corporate moral defection (Characteristic 3). *Spiritual*: the defiling agent is a spiritual being. *Agency*: the defiling force is an agent — purposeful, self-aware, volitional. The name signals: a condition of defilement imposed by a purposeful, external spiritual agent onto the inner and bodily life of the human person.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The four names collectively reveal the M10c cluster's governing architecture. Each name encodes a different locus of the defilement-condition: *Ritual defilement-state* — locus is the person's sacral-cultic status, defined by bodily mechanism and authoritative verdict. *Moral-inner defilement-state* — locus is the interior of the person, conscience, will, and heart corrupted from within. *Corporate/covenantal defilement* — locus is the sacred relational order the community inhabits, extending from inner will outward to land, sanctuary, and divine name. *Defilement by external spiritual agency* — locus is the person's inner constitution as invaded and dominated by an external purposeful force. The four names together map the defilement concept across its full creaturely domain: from bodily-sacral status (Char 1) through individual moral-interior (Char 2) through corporate-relational environment (Char 3) through external-spiritual invasion (Char 4). All four share the term "defilement" — naming a condition, not an act. All four name a state the person or community is in, not something they do. This stative core is the cluster's definitional constant.

questions.question_text: What do the primary Hebrew and Greek terms show at the definitional level?

findings.session_b_note:
At the definitional level, three primary terms establish the immediate semantic profile:

**Hebrew:**
- **H5545 (sa.lach)** — "to forgive": a verb naming the act itself, with divine-exclusive subject in all OT occurrences. At the definitional level this signals: forgiveness in its deepest register is something God does, not something that originates with the human person.
- **H5547 (se.li.chah)** — "forgiveness" (abstract noun): names forgiveness as a possession or quality, something that "belongs" to God (Psa 130:4 — "with you there is forgiveness"). At the definitional level: forgiveness can be named as a thing that exists, located with a person, not merely a passing act.

**Greek:**
- **G0859 (afesis)** — "forgiveness, release": a noun naming the state of release — the condition of having been let go. At the definitional level: forgiveness produces a state in the recipient, not only an event at the moment of granting.
- **G0863H (afiēmi)** — "to release, forgive": the primary NT verb, with the widest usage (64 occurrences in the forgive-sense). At the definitional level: the root meaning is *sending away* or *releasing* — the act removes something (the debt, the claim) from the relational field.

First-level observation: the vocabulary encodes both the *act* (verb forms) and the *resultant condition* (noun forms) of forgiveness. This duality is present from the opening of the vocabulary.

findings.session_b_note:
H2580 chen (favour) signals relational standing — being seen with favour by one who has power to grant or withhold. H8469 tachanum (supplication) signals the receiving side — the posture of the creature appealing for what it cannot command. G5485 charis signals the full semantic arc. Together the primary terms reveal a two-faced definitional structure: the disposition of the giver (chen, charis) and the posture of the receiver (tachanum). The vocabulary embeds the relational architecture before analysis begins: grace requires both a giver and a receiver oriented toward each other.

*Adds structure: the two-faced definitional structure (giver/receiver) as a T1-level observation — the vocabulary encodes the relational architecture at first encounter.*

findings.session_b_note:
The primary terms immediately signal the following at the definitional level:

**Hebrew:** The dominant primary terms are H7356B ra.cha.mim (compassion, 39 XREF occurrences, plural noun), H7355 ra.cham (to have compassion, 43 XREF), and H7349 ra.chum (compassionate, 13 XREF). All three are from the RACHAM root, which is the same root as H7358 re.chem (womb). Before any deeper analysis, this root tells us: compassion is named after the most intimate space of the human body. Its definitional ground is somatic, maternal, and generative. The plural form ra.cha.mim (mercies/compassions) signals that compassion is not a single act but a settled, multiple, ongoing disposition — grammatically plural in its most common form.

**Greek:** The primary term is G4697 splanchnizō (to pity, 12 active occurrences). Its root is splanchnon (G4698, entrails/affections) — the abdominal organs. Before any deeper analysis, this tells us: the Greek vocabulary also grounds compassion in the body's interior. The compound G4184 polusplanchnos (very compassionate) intensifies this: literally "of many/great entrails." At definitional entry, the Greek term already announces that compassion is a gut-movement, a bodily stirring, not a cognitive determination.

The convergence of the Hebrew and Greek primary terms at the definitional level is itself analytically significant: two distinct root families, drawn from two linguistic traditions, both independently ground compassion in the body's interior cavity (womb; entrails). This is not coincidence — it is a shared anthropological perception across linguistic traditions that compassion is felt from the inside, in the deepest bodily space.

findings.session_b_note:
The vocabulary is exclusively Hebrew — there are no Greek terms in this registry (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag applies; the entire corpus is Old Testament). At the definitional level, the primary Hebrew terms reveal the following:

- **H1792 da.kha** ("to crush") and its cognates H1793A dak.ka ("contrite"), H1793B dak.ka ("dust"), H1794 da.khah ("to crush"), H1795 dak.kah ("crushing"): these terms cluster around the physical image of being crushed, pressed down, pulverised. The inner-being meaning arises from the passive forms — the one who has been crushed becomes contrite. The definitional signal is that contrition is received, not constructed — it is what happens to the inner being under certain conditions.

- **H3807 ka.tat** ("to crush, beat"): a parallel crushing verb with predominantly physical or military uses. Its single inner-being group (7556-001) occupies the terror/panic register — the furthest from the penitential meaning. Definitionally, this term marks the outer edge of the vocabulary: the crushing that produces inner dismay under external defeat.

- **H5223 na.kheh** ("crippled/smitten"): from the nkh root (to smite, strike). Definitionally, this term carries the image of the person who has been struck or crippled — applied metaphorically to the spirit as the one who has been struck in their inner person. It is the most explicitly metaphorical of the terms at the definitional level.

findings.session_b_note:
**Greek — koinōnia (G2842):** The root *koinos* means "common, shared." At the definitional level, koinōnia signals that what is held is common — belonging to both parties. This is not merely relational proximity but genuine sharing of a common possession. The registry description confirms: "having in common, sharing in, participating in." The term carries implications of joint ownership or joint access.

**Greek — koinōnos (G2844):** A person-type term — the one who shares or participates. At the definitional level, it names the fellowship-person, not the fellowship-quality. This adds an agentive dimension: fellowship can be a constituting identity, not only a state experienced.

**Hebrew — chavar root family (H2266 cha.var, H2270 cha.ver, H2267 che.ver, H2271–H2279, H4225–H4226):** The root sense of *chavar* is joining or binding together. At the definitional level, the Hebrew vocabulary foregrounds the *act of joining* — fellowship is fundamentally about things or persons being bound together. This is more structural and even physical in its primary resonance than the Greek, which foregrounds the shared content. The Hebrew says: things are joined; the Greek says: things are held in common.

findings.session_b_note: H2896A (tov): the primary Hebrew term is an adjective of extremely wide semantic range. At the definitional level, it names what is genuinely and concretely beneficial, pleasing, and right — a quality observable in persons, things, actions, words, and states. It does not begin with an abstract ethical definition; it begins with the quality of things that genuinely satisfy and benefit. G0019 (agathōsunē): a NT-era abstract noun derived from agathos (good). At the definitional level, it names goodness as a stable inner virtue — a characterological quality that the NT isolates from the broader agathos adjective to name as a specific inner-being phenomenon. G5544 (chrēstotēs): derived from chrēstos (useful, serviceable, good). At the definitional level it names a relational quality — the disposition of generous goodwill and kindness — that is the outward-facing expression of inner goodness. The three terms thus reveal, even before lexical analysis, that goodness operates at multiple registers: experiential-phenomenological (tov), characterological-virtuous (agathōsunē), and relational-dispositional (chrēstotēs). (OBS-067-OBS-007, OBS-067-OBS-008, OBS-067-OBS-009, OBS-067-OBS-088)

findings.session_b_note: At the definitional level, the primary terms reveal a structured vocabulary rather than a single concept. Hebrew: chesed (covenant-faithfulness, binding loyalty), ahavah (intense personal love including eros), racham/rachamim (compassion — love responding to suffering), dod (beloved, erotic love of the Song). Greek: agapē (willed self-giving love, LXX/NT coinage), phileō (natural affection), philia compounds (love directed toward a specified object). The terms do not all name the same inner state at different intensities — they name structurally distinct modes of love's operation. Chesed is obligatory-covenantal; agapē is volitional-unconditional; phileō is naturally affective; racham is compassion-responsive. At the definitional level, 'love' in this registry is not one thing but a family of related inner orientations sharing the common structure of directed-attachment-to-an-other (OBS-103-033).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-103-001: Love's definition resolves to a structured family of inner-being orientations sharing one mechanism — directed attachment toward an object — whose moral character is entirely determined by the object …
findings.finding_value: Love's definition resolves to a structured family of inner-being orientations sharing one mechanism — directed attachment toward an object — whose moral character is entirely determined by the object chosen. Within this shared mechanism, the vocabulary distinguishes three structural registers: love as disposition (the stable inner orientation — chesed, agapē as character), love as act (the commanded and exercised expression — agapaō, enemy-love), and love as condition (the identity-constituting state of being-loved — agapētos). These are not three separate loves but three aspects of love's single operation: the person has a deep stable orientation (disposition), exercises it in specific acts (act), and exists within the love-relationship as constituted by it (condition). The vocabulary arc runs from the ontologically highest (God is love — 1Jo 4:8) through the morally normative (chesed, commanded agapē) to the affective-natural (phileō, dod) to the morally inverted (love of darkness, love of self). No other characteristic in the programme commands a comparable vocabulary range. The definition's boundary with adjacent characteristics (compassion, mercy, kindness) is partially drawn: love is the broader orientation; compassion is love's suffering-triggered mode; mercy and kindness are love's formal relational expressions. The boundaries require Session D precision.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-003: Love's definition as directed attachment reaches its relational specification in T4's three-axis architecture. The object-determination principle (Q&A-144) — that love's moral quality depends entirely…
findings.finding_value: Love's definition as directed attachment reaches its relational specification in T4's three-axis architecture. The object-determination principle (Q&A-144) — that love's moral quality depends entirely on its object — is enacted relationally when the proper objects are named: God (vertical-ascending), neighbour and enemy (horizontal), and the beloved community (horizontal-mutual). The definition's three registers map onto the relational axes: the dispositional register (stable inner orientation) grounds the covenantal-faithful love in the GOD→HUMAN axis (God's chesed never ceasing — Lam 3:22); the active register (commanded, exercised) grounds the love of neighbour and enemy (Lev 19:18, Mat 5:44); the condition register (being-loved as identity) is the GOD→HUMAN axis's effect in the person (agapētos — constituted as beloved). The relational interfaces reveal what the definition describes abstractly: love's mechanism in concrete directional operation. The most significant inter-tier finding: the definition's requirement that love be directed toward an object is fulfilled eschatologically when the object is perfectly and permanently God — Jer 31:34, 1Jo 4:18 (perfect love).

findings.session_b_note: Three primary term families: (1) *eleos/eleeō* (Greek) — compassionate concern expressed in action; from *hilaos* (propitious, gracious). findings.session_b_note: Three root families: (1) dkh (H1792–H1794) — to crush/be crushed; generates both the verbal process (H1792) and the adjectival settled state (H1793A dak.ka — contrite; H1793B dak.ka — dust/pulverised). The homograph dak.ka carries simultaneous meanings of "contrite" and "reduced to dust." (2) ktt (H3795/H3807) — to beat/crush fine; the physical image of pounding grain or crushing metal. At the definitional level these terms reveal that contrition is: a passive condition (received, not self-generated), physically grounded (crushing, pulverising, striking), and expressed in settled adjectival states (the contrite person is the one who has been and remains crushed). findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-013: The definition tier (T1) establishes the three-mode structure (penitential, anguish, substitutionary); the evidential tier (T7) reveals that this three-mode structure is encoded in the grammar of the …
findings.finding_value: The definition tier (T1) establishes the three-mode structure (penitential, anguish, substitutionary); the evidential tier (T7) reveals that this three-mode structure is encoded in the grammar of the primary vocabulary. The Pual passive at Isa 53:5 (most intensive form of received crushing) corresponds to the substitutionary mode; the Niphal (received crushing) corresponds to the anguish mode; the adjectival settled states (dak.ka, na.kheh) correspond to the penitential condition. The vocabulary's grammatical range (T7) is not incidental — it encodes the definitional complexity (T1) at the lexical level. The two tiers are mutually explanatory: T7 explains why T1's definitional complexity is textually grounded; T1 explains why T7's grammatical range is analytically significant.

findings.session_b_note: The chavar family (H2266–H2279): root meaning of physical joining/binding — a wound joins force to body; a seam joins curtain to curtain; a companion joins life to life. The underlying logic is being-bound-to-something such that the bond is real and consequential. The koinōn family: from koinos (common) — koinōnia is the state of having-in-common; what is shared defines the fellowship. Together: Hebrew emphasises the binding/joining act; Greek emphasises the common object shared. Both point to genuine participation as the definitional core. OBS-062-005, OBS-062-007, OBS-062-017.

findings.session_b_note: H5545 (sa.lach — verb): to forgive; exclusively divine subject in OT. H5546 (sal.lach — adjective): forgiving as dispositional character attribute of God (Psa 86:5 alone).
