T1's three Hebrew form-types (act, disposition, possession) correspond precisely to the three Hebrew terms (H5545 verb, H5546 adjective, H5547 noun). T1's four modes map onto the vocabulary's grammatical range (Niphal passive = covenantal-objective received status; Qal active = divine forgiving act; human commanded = G0863H in imperative/hortatory forms; seeking = H5545 imperative in intercessory prayer). T7's cross-testament development finding (NT applies divine-forgiveness vocabulary to commanded human forgiveness) is the lexical expression of T1's structural claim about the human horizontal mode being shaped by the divine model. T1 and T7 are mutually encoded — the vocabulary is structured to carry the definition.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-001: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanch…
findings.finding_value: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanchnizō — the moment of being-moved), condition of its object (eleeinos — the pitiable state that calls compassion forth), and externalised act (almsgiving, mercy-act). No other characteristic in the programme review set operates across all four kinds simultaneously. The four root families (RACHAM, CHASAD, SPLANCHN, OIKTIROM) identify four constituent dimensions of the single characteristic, each naming a distinct register — somatic-maternal, covenantal-relational, visceral-immediate, and deliberative-pitying respectively. The structural opposites are two distinct kinds: willed judicial hardness (the hardened heart that refuses compassion) and unwilled prosperity-blindness (Eze 16:49 — the one who does not see the need because they are satiated). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed by the consistent outward-facing structure: compassion cannot exist without a suffering other. The definitional tier's most critical gap — the receiver's inner-being experience — is entirely absent from the data, affecting T1.5, T1.6, and T1.7 throughout. This gap is the single most significant analytical absence in the registry.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the v…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the verbal forms (G4697, H7355); the externalised-act kind by the noun forms and compound forms (G1656, H2617B). T7's vocabulary arc (womb to almsgiving) is the lexical expression of T1's range from the most interior character quality to the most exterior externalised act — the same spectrum named by the definition is traversed by the vocabulary. The dual primary anchor (T7) maps onto T1's dimensional analysis: Hos 11:8 provides the evidence for the divine relational disposition; Luke 10:33 provides the evidence for the human relational disposition as moral norm.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-001: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition of being in favour — charis as inhabited state), enabling capacity (the specific power given for specific tasks — 2Cor 12:9), and character quality (gracious speech, gracious conduct — chen in 889-003). No single English equivalent captures all four. The four modes of operation (sovereign bestowal, covenantal-relational sustaining, capacity-conferring, character-forming) correspond to the four kinds without collapsing them. Two structural opposites are identified: pride (the self-elevation that refuses the favour of the greater, active and willed) and ingratitude/gracelessness (acharistos — the failure to register and respond to grace received, which T3 confirms as image-impairment). The immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle) is a T1.5 finding confirming that grace does not bypass creaturely recognition but requires and produces it as a transitional state. The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed throughout: grace is constitutively directional — it flows from the greater to the lesser and requires the receptor's inner-being engagement to complete its operation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verba…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verbal forms. The completed-state kind (charitoō — NT coinage, G5487) required a new word because existing vocabulary could not carry the concept of standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state. The character-quality kind (chen in conduct and speech — 889-003) is carried by chen's adjectival and behavioural register. The vocabulary is structurally complete for the four kinds — each kind has a corresponding lexical form. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō) is the lexical evidence that T1's four-kind analysis is correct: the fourth kind (standing as completed state) required new vocabulary because it was conceptually unique.

findings.session_b_note: Three definitional-level revelations: (1) Hebrew berit (H1285 — OBS-034-009, OBS-034-010): the core term spans man-to-man and God-to-man bonds — covenant is not exclusively divine-human but covers the full range of solemn human relational commitments including marriage, treaty, and friendship. The BARA root connection (tentative — OBS-034-010) suggests covenant meals as a sealing mechanism. (2) Hebrew karat (H3772G/H — OBS-034-013, OBS-034-014): the idiom 'karat berit' (cut a covenant) reveals that covenant-making in Hebrew thought involves a physical, enactive dimension — the cutting ritual as bodily enactment of the commitment. Covenant is not only inner intention but somatic performance. (3) Greek diathēkē (G1242 — OBS-034-019, OBS-034-069): carries the semantic dual of covenant and testamentary will. In the NT, this dual meaning is theologically exploited: the new covenant takes effect through the testator's death (Christ's). The Greek term imports the death-and-inheritance structure into covenant theology — the new covenant is an inheritance received because the testator has died.

findings.finding_value: T1 reveals that kindness is a structurally composite, other-oriented disposition — not a simple quality. Its essential character is loyal goodwill (chesed = faithfulness + kindness in a single concept), constituted internally by faithfulness, justice, compassion, and forgiveness. It operates in three distinct modes — dispositional orientation, deliberate volitional act, and Spirit-produced formation — and these are not alternatives but layers of a single integrated phenomenon. The immediate and sustained effects are distinct in kind: the immediate response to received kindness is receptive and affective (praise, relief, petition); the sustained effect is formative and dispositional (the person becomes the chasid — one whose character is shaped by chesed over time). The structural opposite is the self-enclosed inward orientation; the counterfeit (chrēstologia) is not merely an absence but an active imposture. T1's most significant intra-tier finding: kindness is primarily dispositional, but the disposition is itself composite — removing any one of its constituent elements (faithfulness, compassion, justice) changes what remains into something that is no longer fully kindness.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-013: T1's working definition of kindness and T7's lexical foundation finding are in direct productive tension. T7 reveals that the Hebrew chesed cannot be translated as "kindness" without loss of its faith…
findings.finding_value: T1's working definition of kindness and T7's lexical foundation finding are in direct productive tension. T7 reveals that the Hebrew chesed cannot be translated as "kindness" without loss of its faithfulness/loyalty dimension — every English rendering is reductive. T1's working definition ("stable inner disposition of loyal goodwill") attempts to bridge this gap by combining both dimensions, but T7's finding that chesed's semantic range spans goodness/kindness/faithfulness as a single unified concept means that the programme's registry name ("kindness") is itself a definitional understatement. This tension is analytically productive: it means that Session C's prose on "what kindness is" must grapple with a characteristic whose Hebrew name is richer than its English label, and that every claim made about kindness in the programme should be held against the chesed evidence where the fuller concept is preserved. T7's finding about chrēstologia as a possible NT coinage also illuminates T1: if chrēstologia was coined precisely to name the pathology of pleasant speech without inner disposition, then the Greek-speaking community around Paul had a clear concept of kindness-as-disposition whose counterfeit needed a specific name — confirming T1's finding that the distinction between genuine and counterfeit kindness was analytically important to the early church.

findings.session_b_note: Strong continuity. The LXX translates shalom with eirēnē throughout the Hebrew Bible, establishing the semantic correspondence as the foundational datum of the NT peace vocabulary. The NT eirēnē carries the full shalom range: (1) Inner felt state (Phili 4:7 — "the peace of God... will guard your hearts and your minds," corresponding to shalom 2508-001); (2) Covenantal gift (Rom 5:1 — "peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ," corresponding to 2508-002); (3) Moral orientation (Eirēneuō, G1514 — "live peaceably with all," corresponding to 2508-003); (4) Messianic embodiment (Eph 2:14 — "he himself is our peace," corresponding to 2508-004). The correspondence is not merely semantic but structural — the NT's peace vocabulary is the OT's shalom vocabulary transposed into the key of Christ. No significant discontinuity; the NT deepens rather than revises.

findings.session_b_note: The OWNER term H5414G na.tan ("to give, put, set") reveals at the definitional level that faithfulness in this registry is accessed through action — specifically through the act of transferring something to another. The semantic range (OBS-060-011) encompasses giving as gift, appointment, consecration, covenantal pledge, and judicial verdict. At the definitional level, the verb signals: (a) a relational act — there is always a giver and a receiver; (b) a directional act — something moves from one party to another; (c) a volitional act — giving requires an inner decision, not a mechanical process. These three definitional signals (relational, directional, volitional) are present in every classified use of na.tan regardless of context. The XREF vocabulary (emunah, emet, aman, hesed, pistis, pistos — OBS-060-006) would reveal the character-quality dimension of faithfulness, but these are not OWNER terms in this registry. The definitional portrait from na.tan alone is of faithfulness as enacted rather than as constituted.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-001: T1 as a whole reveals that faithfulness in this registry is structurally composite and directional. The name ("faithfulness") promises a character quality; the OWNER term (na.tan) delivers an action. …
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that faithfulness in this registry is structurally composite and directional. The name ("faithfulness") promises a character quality; the OWNER term (na.tan) delivers an action. These are not contradictory — they are complementary aspects of the same inner-being reality: the dispositional quality only becomes faithfulness when it enacts itself (Q&A-016, Q&A-018). The triadic architecture (inner-being source → act → object given) is the definitional shape of this characteristic: it cannot be reduced to disposition alone or act alone (Q&A-017). The five operational modes (Q&A-022) show that this single definitional structure produces radically different expressions depending on what is given and from what inner state — the characteristic is definitionally unified but expressionally plural. The primary dimension (Moral Character) grounds this — it is the character quality that makes the giving faithful rather than merely generous. The definition's most distinctive feature is its disposition-in-action structure: faithfulness is a verb that must be enacted to be real, not a noun that can be possessed without expression.

Five terms:
- **H8130 sa.ne** — the primary verb "to hate," carrying the sense of sustained hostility. The grammatical range (active, passive, agent-noun, infinitive construct) encodes hatred as a condition, a defining characteristic of a person-type, and a legally operative prior state. The most attested term (139 active verses).
- **H8135 sin.ah** — the noun form "hating/hatred as a condition" — hatred as a thing that subsists in a person or relationship, with causal force (Pro 10:12: "hatred stirs up strife").
- **H7852 sa.tam** — persistent grudge-bearing hatred that waits, smoulders, and drives toward action. Distinct from sa.ne: it is not momentary but persistently hostile.
- **H4895 mas.te.mah** — hatred as a communal inner climate or accumulated hostile atmosphere pervading a community (Hos 9:7-8).
- **H8131 se.na** — Aramaic cognate of sa.ne; used only as a person-type designation in Dan 4:19.

Six terms across distinct registers:
- **H5006 na.ats** — the dominant term (25 verses); spurning, rejecting as insignificant. Almost exclusively vertical: human person treating God, his word, or his servants as beneath regard.
- **H0959 ba.zah** — to despise; broader object range (birthright, Servant, God's name). Names the inner act of treating as valueless.
- **H0937 buz** — contempt as experienced; most present in contexts where contempt is received. The most socially-relational of the terms.
- **H0963 biz.za.von** — contempt as social contagion; one act spreading the disposition through a community (Est 1:18).
- **H5007B ne.a.tsah** — blasphemous contempt expressed in speech; the speech-act of reviling that reveals the heart's rejection.
- **H7590 shut** — contempt from surrounding nations toward Israel; always from the receiving side and always met by divine judgment.

Five terms:
- **H8581 ta.av** — the dominant term; loathing/nauseating resonance. Crucially directionally neutral: the same root covers righteous abhorrence of evil (252-001), inverted abhorrence of justice (252-002), and divine sustained abhorrence (252-003). The direction is entirely contextual.
- **H8374 ta.av** — a cognate root (distinct Strong's number); only in Amo 6:8 for divine loathing of pride.
- **H8263 she.qets** — detestation; names primarily what is worthy of abhorrence (idolatrous objects) rather than the disposition itself.
- **H1860 de.ra.on** — a terminal term; appears only in Isa 66:24 and Dan 12:2, naming abhorrence as a permanent eschatological condition.
- **G0948 bdelussomai** — the Greek stench-root; moral revulsion expressed through the body-metaphor of offensive smell. Two NT uses: genuine vs hypocritical abhorrence (Rom 2:22) and the abhorrent person at the eschatological horizon (Rev 21:8).

Four terms in a coherent family:
- **H6184 a.rits** — the dominant term (20 verses); "ruthless, violent, terrifying." The root carries the sense of terrifying power exercised without restraint. Psa 54:3 names its inner-being ground: those who "do not set God before themselves."
- **H0394 akh.za.ri** — "cruel" as an inner quality characterising persons and nations. Pro 12:10: "the mercy of the wicked is cruel" — the quality pervades all the person's acts.
- **H0393 akh.zar** — "cruel" as a disposition named in specific acts (Job 30:21, Lam 4:3).
- **H0395 akh.ze.riy.yut** — "cruelty" as abstract noun; Pro 27:4: "wrath is cruel (akh.ze.riy.yut)" — names cruelty as the quality wrath possesses when mercy is absent.

Five terms covering different registers:
- **H2781 cher.pah** — the dominant term (72 verses); reproach, disgrace, taunt, insult. Operates across individual and corporate levels with the same word — from "reproaches have broken my heart" (Psa 69:20) to "I will make you a desolation and an object of reproach among the nations" (Eze 5:14).
- **H5007A ne.a.tsah** — disgrace as an inner condition in extremity (2Ki 19:3); the acute overwhelming shame-experience when crisis produces incapacity.
- **H8146 sa.ni** — the disfavoured/unloved; chronic relational condition of being the less-loved spouse with legal consequences (Deu 21:15).
- **H8103 shim.tsah** — derision; the mocking contempt of enemies (Exo 32:25).
- **G5195 hubrizō** — to mistreat shamefully; insolent treatment that violates the person's dignity. More agentive than cher.pah: it names the act of the one who mistreats.

Four terms naming relational positions:
- **H3401 ya.riv** — adversary/one who contends; legal contention register. Always in the appeal context (Psa 35:1, Isa 49:25, Jer 18:19).
- **G0476 antidikos** — adversary/opponent/accuser; the Greek legal term for the opposing party. Spans legal (Mat 5:25, Luk 12:58), human-appeal (Luk 18:3), and cosmic (1Pe 5:8 — the devil) registers.
- **H0340 a.yav** — enemy, to be hostile; one verse (Exo 23:22) where God adopts this posture.
- **H7009 qim** — adversary as the object of divine judgment; one verse (Job 22:20); the inner response is relief.

One term:
- **H7589 she.at** — malice, spite, wickedness. Appears only in three Ezekiel verses. The root carries the sense of active malice rather than mere hostility. Its rarity is consistent with its specificity: malice as a compound is a recognisable inner-being reality requiring its own term because it is not reducible to its constituent parts.

Hebrew chesed (covenantal loyalty/kindness), ahavah (intense personal love), rachamim (womb-derived compassion); Greek agapē (willed self-giving), phileō (natural affection), philia compounds (love directed by specified object). Together: love is a family with a clear centre (directed attachment) and multiple modes.

Hebrew ra.cham/ra.cha.mim (womb-root — maternal inner movement), ra.chum (compassionate as divine attribute); Greek splanchnizō (bowel-located visceral stirring), oiktirmos/oiktirmōn (compassion as inner character quality), sumpathēs/sumpatheō (fellow-feeling). Together: compassion is constitutively somatic at its root.

All Greek — eleos (mercy as covenantal-judicial favour), eleeō (to have mercy), eleēmōn (mercifulness as character). The exclusively Greek vocabulary (no Hebrew terms in M05-C groups) is structurally significant — mercy in this sub-group is framed by the NT judicial-covenantal vocabulary without the Hebrew root-family.

Greek chrēstotēs/chrēstos/chrēsteuomai (kindness — what is useful/serviceable/fitting); agathos and compound family (goodness — what is morally excellent). Together: kindness as gracious goodwill; goodness as moral excellence — two poles of the same outward-oriented inner disposition.

Greek praus/praotēs/prautēs (tamed strength); epieikeia/epieikēs (gracious reasonableness willing to yield); anexikakos (patient endurance without resentment); Hebrew a.na.vah/an.vah (humility/meekness before God). Together: the vocabulary names restrained power across multiple registers.

Hebrew na.cham (breathing deeply in relief/regret — the emotional sigh of comfort); tan.chum (consolation as received gift); la.vav (captivating/stirring the heart); Greek parakaleō/paraklēsis (calling alongside). Together: comfort is constitutively directional toward the distressed person.

Greek koinōnia (shared-life bond), koinōnos (participant/sharer), katallagē (restoration of broken bond), homofrōn (same-minded), isopsuchos (same-souled), epoikodomeō (building upon a foundation). Together: fellowship is the irreducibly communal characteristic — every term requires at least two parties.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** The primary OT terms — tsad.diq (H6662), tse.da.qah (H6666), tse.deq (H6664G/H) — share the root ts.d.q, whose core meaning is conformity to a norm or standard. Applied to God in A1, the terms reveal that God is the one who conforms perfectly to the norm — indeed, he IS the norm. The Greek term dikaiosunē (G1343) carries the same semantic weight: rightness, conformity to the standard of what is just and true. Both root families point to a relational-judicial concept: being right in relation to the standard.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** The same Hebrew root (ts.d.q) and Greek root (dik-) govern A2, applied to the human person. The human is tsad.diq — one who conforms to the norm, who is right in relation to the standard. The definitional revelation: righteousness in the human is relational, not self-referential. To be righteous is to be right in relation to God's standard.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** The B terms — yo.sher (H3476), me.shar (H4339), ne.kho.chah (H5229), ye.sha.rah (H3483) — come from a different root family (y.sh.r: to be straight, level, right). The euthutēs (G2118) is the Greek equivalent. These terms reveal a spatial-moral concept: the inner being oriented in a straight line, not deviously or crookedly. The B vocabulary is distinct from the A vocabulary — different root, different primary metaphor, overlapping semantic territory.

**[C — Justification]** The primary terms — tsa.deq (H6663, verb: to be or declare righteous), dikaioō (G1344, verb: to justify/declare righteous), dikaiōsis (G1347, noun: justification) — reveal a process character. These are action terms: the focus is on the act of declaring or making righteous. The Greek dikaioō in particular carries a judicial sense: to pronounce a verdict of righteousness, to acquit.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** The D terms — ekdikeō (G1556), ekdikēsis (G1557), ekdikos (G1558), antapodidōmi (G0467), dikaiokrisia (G1341) — all carry the ek- prefix meaning "out from" or the anti- prefix meaning "in return." The definitional revelation: D-terms are response terms. They name actions that arise from a prior wrong — they require a prior violation as their trigger.

**[E — Condemnation]** The E terms — katakrinō (G2632), katadikazō (G2613), katakrisis (G2633), dikē (G1349), autokatakritos (G0843) — all carry the kata- prefix meaning "down against" or "in accord with." The definitional revelation: E-terms name downward judicial acts — verdicts directed against a person on the basis of assessed guilt. The reflexive form (autokatakritos) reveals that the inner person can turn the judicial faculty against itself.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The F terms — logizomai (G3049), axioō (G0515), a.rakh (H6186B), hupodikos (G5267), adiakritos (G0087) — reveal a cognitive-judicial faculty. The logizomai root (related to logos: word, reason) reveals that moral reckoning is a rational act — it involves inner deliberation, assessment, and conclusion. The faculty is cognitive in mode but moral in content.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** The G terms — ra.sha (H7561: to be wicked; H7563: the wicked one), a.val (H5765: to act unjustly; H5766A: injustice) — name states and acts that are directionally opposed to the ts.d.q root. Ra.sha is consistently paired with tsad.diq throughout the OT as its exact opposite. A.val names a deviation from the straight — a perversion of what should be upright.

**[CLUSTER]** Two distinct root families govern the cluster: ts.d.q / dik- (rightness, conformity to standard) and y.sh.r (straightness, uprightness). These carry different primary metaphors and occupy different semantic territory. F has its own distinct vocabulary (logizomai, axioō, a.rakh). G draws on a third root (ra.sha, a.val). The three root families together reveal that "righteousness and justice" is a composite cluster holding together conformity-to-standard, straightness-of-orientation, and cognitive-reckoning as related but distinct aspects of one moral reality.

Cha.kham (adjective → adjectival noun) reveals wisdom as character-state. Chokh.mah (noun) reveals it as a substantive inner reality. Sofizo (causative verb) reveals it as something another can produce in a person. The terms collectively show: wisdom is a constituted quality held in the heart that governs the whole person's operation. Pro 16:23 (VCG03 anchor).

findings.finding_value: Three root families converge in M39-A: (1) BARAK (H1288 ba.rakh) — the root is shared with "knee" (H1290 be.rekh), suggesting the bowing/kneeling associated with blessing; the act of blessing involves an orientation of deference or reverence even when God is the agent blessing the creature. (2) CHANAN/CHEN (H2603A/H2580) — root meaning: "to bend toward, to show partiality; the inclination of the greater toward the lesser." Grace as an inclination — a turning toward. (3) CHAR- (G5485 charis; G5483 charizō; G5487 charitoō) — root shared with chairo (to rejoice); grace and joy share a root, naming grace as joyful giving. The science extract (Section 1) confirms: the psychological intensity of gratitude is amplified when the benefactor acted at personal cost — the root meanings encode this structure.

findings.finding_value: Two terms: (1) TOV (H2895) — one of the most semantically broad terms in Biblical Hebrew; spans aesthetic goodness (pleasant, beautiful), moral goodness (right, excellent), relational goodness (well-off, content), and divine goodness (what God evaluates as good). The breadth is the theological point: goodness in the biblical frame is unified, not compartmentalised. (2) YA.TAV (H3190) — the verbal form of goodness — doing good, being made good, going well. The verb form makes explicit what tov implies: goodness is both a quality possessed and an action enacted.

findings.finding_value: The primary Hebrew terms operate in four registers at first encounter. Material-state terms (o.sher, hon, cho.sen — riches, substance, wealth) name the condition of having material goods, with no intrinsic moral valence. Process terms (a.shar — to become rich; da.shen — to prosper/grow fat; sha.men verb — to grow fat) name the dynamic of material acquisition or increase, again without intrinsic moral valence but loaded with contextual moral weight. Inner-state terms (sha.a.nan — at ease/complacent; autarkēs — self-sufficient/content; cha.san — to hoard) name specific inner orientations in relation to material circumstance. Person-type terms (a.shir, plousios — the rich person; ptōchos — the poor person) name the social-moral category of persons defined by their material condition. The Greek terms (plousios, ploutos, plouteō, ploutizō, ptōchos, ptōcheuō) follow the same fourfold pattern but with the additional NT theological loading: plousios in Rev 3:17 and ptōchos in Mat 5:3 both carry inner-being extensions that exceed their Greek economic senses.

findings.finding_value: The primary M01-A terms reveal at definitional level: (1) *ya.re* (H3372H, H3372G, H3373 — the core fear root, verb) — fear as a relational inner state that governs conduct; (2) *yir.ah* (H3374 — nominal form) — fear as a possession, a stable inner disposition; (3) *pa.chad* (H6343 — dread/awe) — fear with intensity and weight; (4) *mo.rah/mo.ra* (H4172A, H4172B — fear-inspiring object) — the quality of inspiring awe; (5) *fobeō* (G5399) / *fobos* (G5401) — the Greek equivalents carrying the same relational-fear range; (6) *deos* (G6015, Heb 12:28) — reverence as worshipful respect. The root *ya.re* is a stative verb, which signals that the characteristic is a stable inner state, not merely a momentary reaction.

M01-B introduces: *de.chal* (H1763 Aramaic — fear/dread), *za.chal* (H2119B — to shrink in fear), *ya.gor* (H3016 — to dread, fear specific objects), *ekthambeo* (G1568 — to be amazed/alarmed), *ekthambos* (G1569), *ekfobos* (G1630 — terrified), *emfobos* (G1719 — afraid, alarmed), *ptoeō* (G4422 — to terrify/frighten), *ptoēsis* (G4423), *pturomai* (G4426 — to be startled/alarmed). These Greek terms are compounds (ek-, em- prefixes) that intensify the fear — they signal terror or alarm at an extreme level rather than measured reverential posture.

M01-C's primary terms are all nouns — *e.mah* (H0367 — terror, dread), *bal.la.hah* (H1091 — sudden terror, consternation), *chit.tah* (H2847 — terror that paralyzes), *chit.tit* (H2851 — the terror projected by military power), *ma.gor* (H4032 — encircling terror), *me.chit.tah* (H4288 — crushing terror/ruin). The noun-dominance signals that M01-C's characteristic is less about the inner state and more about the terror as an entity with its own character and agency.

M01-D's primary terms: *ba.hal* (H0926 — to dismay, alarm, agitate, rush), *be.hal* (H0927 Aramaic — to alarm, frighten), *cha.tat* (H2865 — to be dismayed, shattered, broken), *ze.va.ah* (H2113 — trembling horror), *re.tet* (H7374 — trembling panic), *tim.ma.hon* (H8541 — bewilderment, confusion). *ba.hal* uniquely captures both the shock-state and the rash-urgency that follows (evidenced in the dual character of M01-D-VCG-01 and VCG-05).

M01-E's primary terms are all motion/state terms: *cha.rad* (H2729 — to tremble, quake), *cha.red* (H2730 — trembling as posture), *cha.ra.dah* (H2731 — trembling noun), *a.rats* (H6206 — to be in dread, tremble), *pal.la.tsut* (H6427 — shuddering, horror), *ra.gaz* (H7264 — to tremble, quake), *ra.ad* (H7460/H7461A — to tremble), *re.a.dah* (H7461B), *sa.ar* (H8175A, H8178A — to shudder, bristle), *entromos* (G1790 — trembling), *tromos* (G5156 — trembling). The term proliferation signals that M01-E's territory is highly differentiated — Hebrew and Greek both attend to specific kinds and registers of somatic trembling.

M01-F's primary terms: *de.a.gah* (H1674 — anxiety, worry), *ya.gor* (H3025 — to fear, dread anticipatorily), *me.go.rah* (H4034 — fear, terror of what may come), *me.gu.rah* (H4035 — fear harbored, anticipated), *pa.chad* (H6342 — dread, with a pa.chad noun form), *foberos* (G5398 — fearful, dreadful). The *de.a.gah* root signals the cognitive-worrying dimension (cf. Borkovec's verbal-linguistic anxiety); the *ya.gor* root signals the dread of what has not yet occurred.

M01-G's primary terms: *deilia* (G1167 — timidity, cowardice), *deiliaō* (G1168 — to be timid), *deilos* (G1169 — cowardly). These are evaluative terms — they carry moral weight, not merely descriptive content. The Greek *deilos* was a technical term in Greek ethics for the coward, the person who fails under pressure.

The Hebrew vocabulary is anchored in the *ya.re* root (the broadest fear term, spanning M01-A through B and beyond) and the *pa.chad* family (dread with intensity). The Greek vocabulary is anchored in *fobeō/fobos* (the primary NT fear terms, spanning M01-A through G) with specialized intensifiers for extreme and somatic registers. The term range confirms that "fear" in Scripture is a multi-register characteristic, not a single experience.

The primary Hebrew terms: *cha.rah* (to kindle/be incensed) — a verb root meaning to burn or kindle, foregrounding the heat metaphor as definitional; *che.mah* (rage/wrath) — related to heat, the noun of the burning interior state; *cha.ron* (burning anger) — an intensifying noun specifically for the burning quality of anger at its most intense; *orgē* (Greek, wrath) — at the definitional level, a settled, purposeful inner disposition; *orgizō* (Greek, to anger) — the verb of the anger-event, the eruption. These terms reveal that the characteristic is definitionally thermal and reactive at root — it is the inner being heating up in response to moral violation. The Greek *orgē* adds the judicial-structural dimension absent from the pure-heat Hebrew vocabulary.

The Hebrew vocabulary reveals two primary registers. The weeping and tears register (ba.khah, be.khi, dim.ah — M03-A) names the somatic-vocal expression of grief: the act of weeping, its sound, its physical substance. The mourning register (sa.phad, mis.ped, a.val, e.vel, a.vel — M03-B) names the structured, socially recognised act of lamentation, often with embodied forms (tearing garments, sackcloth, fasting). The sorrow register (ya.gon, tu.gah, makh.ov — M03-C, F) names the inner phenomenology — grief as a weight carried in the heart, the soul's experienced suffering. The anguish/distress register (tsar, tsa.rah, me.tsu.qah — M03-D) names grief at its most acute and pressing, the crushing experience of overwhelming adversity. The groaning register (a.nach, a.na.chah, ne.a.qah — M03-E) names grief's involuntary vocal-somatic expression. The Greek vocabulary maps broadly: lupeō (to grieve), perilupos (deeply sorrowful), penthos/pen.the.o (mourning), klauthmos/klaiō (weeping/to weep), odunaō/odunē (anguish), sunochē (anguish seated in the heart), stenagmos/sustenazō (groaning). The Greek vocabulary is less formally structured around mourning rites and more focused on the inner state and its expression — consistent with NT's inward focus.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The primary OT terms are: **gil_verb** (H1523 — to rejoice, exult; verbal form of the root that names spinning or leaping movement, capturing the kinetic energy of the inner state); **su.s** (H7797 — to rejoice, exult, take delight in; used both for human and divine exultation, with a strong affective-volitional force); **re.na.nah** (H7445 — triumphing joy, joyful crying, exultant sound; the sonic-expressive form of exultation); **cha.dah** (H2302 — to rejoice, be glad, more infrequent; used notably for Jethro's rejoicing at hearing of God's works, Exo 18:9); **te.ev** (H2868, Aramaic — to be glad, used in Dan 6:23 of the king's exceedingly glad response at Daniel's safety). No primary Greek term appears in this characteristic's corpus — M04-A is entirely OT. The root meanings consistently emphasise movement (spinning, leaping — gil), affective intensity and relational direction (su.s), and sonic expression (re.na.nah) — suggesting exultation is constitutively outward-moving, not merely interior.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Primary terms across the four sub-groups:

**OT (M04-B, M04-E):** **sa.mach** (H8055 — to rejoice, be glad; verb; the dominant term with 147 instances in M04-B, appearing across every literary register); **sim.chah** (H8057 — joy, gladness; noun; 89 instances in M04-B; names the state that sa.mach produces); **sa.me.ach** (H8056 — joyful, glad; adjective; 21 instances in M04-B; describes the person in the state of joy); **ma.s.vo.s** (H4885 — joy, exultation, rejoicing; noun; 16 instances in M04-B; often associated with festive and communal contexts); **sa.s.von** (H8342 — gladness, joy, exultation; noun; 22 instances in M04-E; strongly restoration-oriented); **gi.lah** (H1525 — rejoicing, exultation; noun; 2 instances in M04-E); **ched.vah** (H2304 — joy, gladness; Aramaic/Hebrew; 2 instances in M04-C-VCG-01 and M04-D-VCG-01).

**NT (M04-C, M04-D, M04-E):** **chairo** (G5463 — to rejoice, be glad; verb; 58 instances in M04-C; the primary NT rejoicing verb); **chara** (G5479 — joy; noun; 57 instances in M04-C; names the state); **agalliao** (G0021 — to exult, rejoice greatly; verb; 11 instances in M04-E-VCG-02; a more intense exultant-joy term); **agalliasis** (G0020 — exultation, joy; noun; 4 instances in M04-C); **eufrosune** (G2167 — gladness, good cheer; 2 instances in M04-C); **sunchairo** (G4796 — to rejoice with, co-rejoice; verb; 8 instances in M04-D); **eucharistia/eucharistos** (G2169/2170 — thanksgiving/thankful; M04-C-VCG-06); **euthumeō/eupsucheō** (G2114/2174 — to be cheerful, encouraged; M04-C-VCG-04).

At the definitional level, the primary roots consistently name an inner state of positive, engaged, participatory gladness (sa.mach/chairo — active rejoicing; sim.chah/chara — the resulting inner state of joy). The Aramaic ched.vah and Greek eufrosune confirm the characteristic's cross-linguistic stability.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Primary terms: (1) **agalliao** (G0021) — to exult, leap for joy, rejoice greatly; 11 instances in M04-E-VCG-02. Root meaning: to exult, from agan (very much) + hallesthai (to leap) — the intensified-leaping form of joy. At definitional level: agalliao names an intense, outward-reaching, Spirit-enabled rejoicing that is characteristically present when circumstances offer no natural ground for joy. Its appearance in suffering contexts (1Pe 1:6; 4:13; Mat 5:12; Act 16:34) is not despite its intensity but because of it — the intensity is required to leap over the suffering context; (2) **ba.lag** (H1082) — to smile, to be cheerful; 3 instances in M04-F-VCG-01 (Job 9:27; 10:20; Psa 39:13). Root meaning: to gleam, smile; connotes a fragile, brief brightening — the opposite of agalliao's intensity; (3) **mav.li.git** (H4010) — consolation, comfort (1 instance: Jer 8:18). Root meaning related to comfort and solace. At definitional level: the three terms together span the full range from fragile attempted cheerfulness (ba.lag) through grief-without-comfort (mav.li.git) to Spirit-enabled exultation (agalliao) — the characteristic has a wide phenomenological range within its suffering-context definition.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary terms: (1) **tov** (H2896A) — the dominant term across both sub-groups (83 M04-L instances + 50 M04-O instances = 133 total). Tov as noun/adjective/verbal-function names the quality of genuine goodness — pleasant, beneficial, agreeable, right, fitting. At the definitional level it reveals Gladness as rooted in objective goodness rather than subjective preference; (2) **makarismos** (G3108) — blessedness; 3 NT instances in M04-O-VCG-04 (Rom 4:6, 9; Gal 4:15). Makarismos names the inner state of one who has received divine favour; (3) **sa.s.von** (H8342) — appears in the M04-E-VCG-01 corpus which overlaps with Characteristic 3 at the VCG-01 level (sa.s.von as gladness-of-restoration). At definitional level: tov's breadth (moral, relational, circumstantial, divine-character goodness) establishes Gladness as the widest-scope positive inner-being characteristic in M04 — broader than Joy (which has its own primary vocabulary), though the two share the experience.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Primary terms span a wide vocabulary: (1) **sha.a.shu.im** (H8191) — delights, cherished things (noun, plural of intensity): used of God's darling child Ephraim (Jer 31:20), Wisdom as God's daily delight (Pro 8:30–31), the psalmist's delight in God's testimonies (Psa 119:24, 77, 92, 143, 174), Isa 5:7 (Israel as God's pleasant planting), Jer 31:20. The plural-of-intensity form signals the full, rich, multiple-faceted quality of treasured pleasure; (2) **sha.a** (H8173B) — to delight, play, carefree enjoyment: Psa 94:19 (God's consolations cheer the soul); Psa 119:16, 47, 70 (delight in statutes); Isa 11:8 (nursing child playing over cobra); Isa 66:12 (bounced on knees in peace); the root carries a carefree, playful quality of delight; (3) **a.nog** (H6026) — to be delicate, to delight oneself: Psa 37:4, 11; Job 22:26; 27:10; Isa 55:2; 58:14; 66:11; Deu 28:56 — the term implies a luxuriating, resting, pampered quality of inner satisfaction; (4) **o.neg** (H6027) — delight as noun (Isa 58:13); (5) **cha.phets** (H2654A) — verbal: to take delight in, to be pleased, to desire — the dominant M04-H verbal form covering both divine volitional pleasure and human desire/delight; (6) **che.phets** (H2656) — noun: delight, desire, matter — the dominant M04-H nominal form; (7) **cha.phets** adj (H2655) — delighting in; (8) **eudokeo** (G2106) — to be well pleased, think it good, take delight: 17 NT instances across M04-H-VCG-01 (divine pleasure in the Son) and VCG-02 (human willing-pleasure); (9) **arestos** (G0701) — pleasing, acceptable: M04-M-VCG-02 (Joh 8:29; Act 6:2; 1Jo 3:22); (10) **sunēdomai** (G4913) — to delight together with: Rom 7:22 (delight in God's law in the inner being); (11) **ta.a.nug** (H8588) — daintiness, delight: Mic 1:16 (parental delight); (12) **che.med** (H2531) — desire, delight, covetousness: Eze 23:6, 12, 23 (lustful captivation); (13) **a.li.tsut** (H5951) — exultation, predatory joy: Hab 3:14; (14) **ni.cho.ach** (H5207) — soothing aroma: M04-M-VCG-01 (correct worship) and M04-P-VCG-01 (misdirected worship); (15) **thaumazō** (G2296) — to marvel, wonder: Rev 13:3; 17:8 (beast-captivation). At definitional level: the vocabulary spans from playful carefree pleasure (sha.a) through luxuriating satisfaction (a.nog) through cherished treasuring (sha.a.shu.im) through directed volitional willing (cha.phets/eudokeo) through obedient-pleasing orientation (arestos) through corrupt-lustful desire (che.med) to predatory elation (a.li.tsut).

**[CHAR-5]** E — Primary terms: (1) **na.im** (H5273A) — pleasant, agreeable, lovely; 8 instances in M04-J; root na.em — to be pleasant, agreeable; the quality of what is fitting and agreeable to the inner sense; Psa 133:1; 135:3; 147:1; Psa 16:6; Job 36:11; Song 1:16; 2Sa 1:23; Pro 22:18; (2) **na.em** (H5276) — to be/feel pleasant; 7 instances in M04-J; the verbal experience of pleasantness; 2Sa 1:26 — "very pleasant have you been to me"; Pro 2:10 — "knowledge will be pleasant to your soul"; Pro 9:17; 24:25; Song 7:6; Psa 141:6; Isa 32:12; (3) **no.am** (H5278) — pleasantness, beauty, favour; 5 instances in M04-J; the noun naming the quality: Psa 27:4 (Lord's beauty); Psa 90:17 (Lord's favour); Pro 3:17 (wisdom's ways); Pro 15:26; 16:24; Zec 11:7, 10; (4) **na.a.man** (H5282) — pleasant plants: Isa 17:10; (5) **ni.cho.ach** (H5207) — soothing, pleasing (aroma); 38 instances in M04-K-VCG-01 — the dominant term for the sacrificial-worship Pleasure register; root: to rest, settle, give rest; the quality of the worship-aroma that calms and settles God's regard; (6) **a.nog** (H6026) — to be tender/delicate/luxuriant: Deu 28:54, 56 (the pampered person); Isa 47:1 (Babylon's delicateness); (7) **a.las** (H5965) — to exult, delight (in pleasure): Job 20:18 (the wicked gets no a.las from profits); Pro 7:18 (seductress's carnal a.las); (8) **ta.a.nug** (H8588) — daintiness, luxury: Pro 19:10 (luxury unfit for fools); Ecc 2:8 (concubines as "delight of the sons of man"); Mic 2:9 (delightful houses); Song 7:6; (9) **ed.nah** (H5730B) — pleasure, luxury: 2Sa 1:24 (luxurious scarlet); Psa 36:8 (river of delights); Jer 51:34 (Jerusalem's delicacies consumed); (10) **tov** (H2896A) in the M04-K-VCG-03 better-than-comparatives; (11) **thambeō** (G2284) — to be amazed: Mar 10:24 (disciples amazed at Jesus' teaching). At definitional level: the vocabulary cluster reveals Pleasure as covering a spectrum from the lightest agreeableness (na.im — pleasant, fitting) through the sensory-luxury of delicate living (a.nog, ta.a.nug, ed.nah) through the worship-pleasantness of correctly-offered sacrifice (ni.cho.ach) through the moral-comparative Pleasure of preferring integrity (tov better-than).

**[CHAR-6]** E — Primary terms: (1) **pa.la** (H6381) — to be extraordinary, surpassing, beyond ordinary; 47 instances in M04-I; the dominant term; root meaning: to be distinct, separated out from the ordinary; at definitional level: Wonder is the response to what is 'separated out' from ordinary reality — what cannot be accounted for by normal categories; (2) **pe.le** (H6382) — wonder, marvel; the nominal form: Exo 15:11 ("doing wonders"); Isa 9:6 ("Wonderful Counselor"); Psa 77:11 ("wonders of old"); Isa 25:1; 28:29; Lam 1:9; Dan 12:6; 7 instances; (3) **miph.la.ah** (H4652) — wondrous work: Job 37:16 ("the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge"); (4) **thambeō** (G2284) — to be amazed/seized with astonishment: Mar 1:27; 10:24; 10:32; the NT wonder term involving being seized with astonishment at Jesus' teaching and advance; (5) **thauma** (G2295) — wonder, marvel: 2Cor 11:14; Rev 17:6; (6) **thaumazō** (G2296) — to marvel, be astonished: Gal 1:6; Rev 17:6, 7, 8 (M04-N-VCG-02 cross-assigned). At definitional level: pa.la/pe.le names Wonder as the response to what is categorically extraordinary; thambeō names Wonder as the inner state of being seized/arrested by what is confronted; thauma names the wondering itself as an experience.

**[CLUSTER]** E — At the definitional level, the vocabulary across the seven characteristics reveals three structural features of the cluster: (1) **Breadth of the primary vocabulary** — the cluster spans from the single dominant term (Wonder's pa.la/pe.le — 47+ instances of one root) through the dual-characteristic (Joy's sa.mach/sim.chah — 147/89 OT instances) to the five-register vocabulary (Delight's sha.a.shu.im, a.nog, cha.phets, eudokeo, sunēdomai). Delight has the widest vocabulary breadth; Wonder has the most root-concentrated vocabulary; Joy has the largest single-term corpus; (2) **OT-NT continuity patterns** — the terms with the clearest OT-NT continuity are: Joy (sa.mach → chairo, both active rejoicing); Delight (cha.phets → eudokeo, both volitional pleasure); Suffering-Joy (OT ba.lag → NT agalliao — here is also the most significant OT-to-NT escalation: the fragile ba.lag is replaced/surpassed by the more intense agalliao). The terms with least NT development of their OT range: Gladness (tov has no single NT equivalent for its full evaluative range); Pleasure (na.im/no.am have no direct NT equivalents); (3) **Root meanings** — the root etymologies cluster around three movement types: leaping/surging (gil — spinning/leaping; agalliao — intensified leaping), settling/resting (no.am/nuach — pleasantness/rest; sha.a.shu.im — cherishing-resting), and being separated out/arrested (pa.la — set apart from the ordinary; thambeō — seized/arrested). These three movement types confirm the phenomenological differentiation of the cluster: surge, rest, arrest.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The primary Hebrew root *bosh* (H0954, 108 verses in cluster, majority in CHAR-1) means to be ashamed, to feel shame — a stative verb whose basic sense is the felt inner state of shame. The root produces the nominal forms *bo.shet* (H1322 — shame as noun, the condition itself) and *bu.shah* (H0955 — the covering/enveloping shame). *Ke.lim.mah* (H3639 — dishonour, ignominy) names the experience of being publicly exposed and reduced — the social-facing dimension of shame. *Cha.pher* (H2659) adds the element of embarrassment and being disgraced, often with the connotation of being found out or let down. The Greek *aischunē* (G0152) and *aischunō* (G0153) are closely parallel to *bosh* — the noun and verb of the felt shame experience. *Kataischunō* (G2617) adds the prefix kata- (down, thoroughly) giving "to thoroughly shame" or "to put to shame completely." Together the terms confirm at the definitional level: CHAR-1 is about what happens *inside the person* — the felt state of inner collapse in the face of exposure, inadequacy, or moral failure.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Ka.lam (H3637): root sense of wounding or cutting — humiliation is something done to the person that wounds their social existence. The shaved-beard episodes (2Sa 10:5; 1Ch 19:5) show ka.lam in its most concrete bodily register. Sha.phel (H8213): root means to be low, to be brought down; Hiphil (causing to be low) expresses God's active execution of the downward movement against the proud. Together: CHAR-2 is both physically embodied (ka.lam) and spiritually judicial (sha.phel).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Atimazō (G0818) — to dishonour, treat as worthless; root: atimos — without honour, without worth. Atimia (G0819) — dishonour as a state of assigned worth-denial. Entrepō (G1788) — "to have regard for" in its absence: the judge who "does not respect man" lacks the inner movement of regard that would recognise worth. Paradeigmatizō (G3856) — to expose publicly, to hold up to contempt. Together these terms reveal CHAR-3 as constituted by the failure or refusal of the worth-recognition act: one sees another person and assigns them less worth than they have.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Aischros (G0150) — shameful, base, disgraceful — an adjective naming the moral quality of conduct or objects. Aischunē (G0152) in its evaluative register (2Cor 4:2; Phili 3:19) — the shame-quality of conduct recognised by conscience. Aschēmosunē (G0808) — indecency, improper form — the quality of what violates proper form or order. Atimia (G0819) in VCG-02 — dishonorable passions — names the moral-evaluative quality of certain appetites. Together: CHAR-4 is the adjectival-quality register of shame — shameful is a quality of things and conduct, not only an experience of persons.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Exoutheneō (G1848): the primary term — to treat as of no account, to utterly despise, to regard as nothing. Root: ex (out of) + ouden (nothing) = to make out of nothing. This is the strongest contempt-vocabulary in the NT: the person being treated as if they were literally nothing. Atimazō (G0818) in VCG-02: to dishonour through violent contemptuous action. Loidoria (G3059): verbal reviling as reputation-attack. The root meanings together reveal CHAR-5's source-mechanism: the contempt-er assigns zero worth to the contempt-ed, producing shame in the recipient by the force of that worth-cancellation.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Niq.qa.von (H5356A): innocence, cleanness — from naqah (to be clean, to be free from guilt). The root sense is freedom from moral blemish or guilt-stain — the state of being morally uncontaminated by deliberate wrongdoing. Qe.ha.von (H5356B): in this context functions as a near-synonym or parallel term to niq.qa.von — the bluntness/cleanness of hands, pointing to the same moral-freedom condition. Both terms together locate CHAR-6 in the hands-and-heart moral-integrity domain: the inner will (heart) and the outward action (hands) both free from guilt-stain.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's vocabulary divides into three lexical families across the six characteristics. Family 1 — the experiential register: bosh (H0954), bo.shet (H1322), ke.lim.mah (H3639), aischunē (G0152), kataischunō (G2617) — terms naming the felt experience or condition of shame. Primarily Char 1, with secondary presence in Chars 2 and 3. Family 2 — the mechanism/act register: ka.lam (H3637), sha.phel (H8213), atimazō (G0818), exoutheneō (G1848), qa.lon (H7036) — terms naming the enacted downward movement or contemptuous dismissal that produces shame. Primarily Chars 2, 3, and 5. Family 3 — the qualitative register: aischros (G0150), aschēmosunē (G0808) — terms naming the property of shamefulness as a quality of conduct or objects. Primarily Char 4. Char 6's vocabulary (niq.qa.von H5356A, qe.ha.von H5356B) stands alone as the only positively-framed vocabulary in the entire cluster. Cluster-level finding: M07 has the most lexically rich shame-vocabulary in the programme, distributed across experiential, mechanistic, and qualitative registers, with a single protective counter at Char 6.

**[CHAR-1]** E — At the definitional level, the primary terms converge on a single spatial-metaphorical core: upward movement of the self beyond proper station. Hebrew rum (H7311A) — to be high, to rise, to lift up — is the most voluminous term; its active form evidences the will's upward drive (Num 15:30, vc=65731, M08-A4-VCG-05: acting "with a high hand" as deliberate self-exaltation against God; Isa 14:13, vc=34233, M08-A4-VCG-05: "I will ascend to heaven"). Hebrew ga.vah (H1361) — to exalt, to rise proudly — is most closely associated with the heart-seat idiom (Eze 28:2, vc=34040, M08-A1-VCG-02: "your heart is proud"; 2Ch 26:16, vc=34044, M08-A1-VCG-01: "he grew proud"). This is the same root as CHAR-1 and CHAR-2, but in CHAR-3 the characteristic is not the sinning itself but the *naming of the sinning* — the confessional form. The definitive grammatical marker is the first-person perfect (or its corporate equivalent "sinned we/our fathers"): the act is complete, and the confession names it as such. The NT primary term is **hamartanō (G0264)** in the aorist/perfect confession form: Mat 27:4 ("I have sinned"), Luk 15:18/21 ("I have sinned against heaven and before you"). At the definitional level, both terms reveal that confession deploys the sinning-vocabulary in the self-application mode — not describing someone else's sin but naming one's own.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The primary term is **cha.ta (H2398)** and its participial/person-type forms, used here not in the confessional mode (CHAR-3) but in the *unacknowledged* mode — sinning that is not named as such by the sinner. Jer 2:35 — "I have not sinned" (*lo chatati*) — the negative first-person perfect is the definitive evidence: the sinning vocabulary is explicitly denied. Jer 16:10 — "what is the sin that we have committed?" — the question-form of *chatanu* (we sinned) applied without self-recognition. The NT terms are **hamartanō (G0264)** (1Cor 15:34 — "do not go on sinning") applied to those in a stupor, and the adjectival *hamartōlos* equivalent in Tit 3:11 ("sinful"). At the definitional level: the sinning vocabulary is present throughout, but conscience's normal response (recognition, confession) is absent. The characteristic is defined by the gap between the objective sinning fact and the person's absent or refused inner recognition.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The primary Hebrew term is **cha.ta (H2398)** in the phrase construction "did not depart from the sins of..." — the characteristic is not expressed by a single dedicated term but by the combination of cha.ta (sins) with verbs of non-departure: *lo sar min* (did not turn aside from — 2Ki 10:29), *lo sar min* (did not depart from — 2Ki 13:2/11), *lo sur* (did not turn away — 2Ki 15:24), "clung to" (*davaq* — 2Ki 3:3). The secondary OT term is in Neh 9:29 where sinning (*chatanu*) is accompanied by the physical metaphor "stubborn shoulder" (*natan kateph sorerah* — gave a stubborn shoulder) and "stiffened their neck" (*qashu et-orpam*). The primary NT term is **hamartanō (G0264)** in its persistent/deliberate mode: 1Ti 5:20 — "persist in sin" (*hamartanontōn*); Heb 10:26 — "go on sinning deliberately" (*hekousiōs hamartanontōn*). The definitional revelation: the characteristic has no single dedicated term but is expressed through the combination of sinning-vocabulary with non-departure language.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The primary Hebrew term is **cha.ta (H2398)** in its person-type participial/nominal forms: *hachotet* ("the sinner" — Ecc 7:26; 9:2/18; Pro 11:31; 13:22) and as a verb in pattern-contexts (Exo 9:34 — "sinned yet again"; Hos 8:11/10:9 — recurring sinning; Heb 3:17). The participial/nominal form *hachotet* is the distinctive marker of this characteristic: it names the settled person-type ("the sinner") rather than a specific act of sinning. The NT primary term is **hamartanō (G0264)** in the *present continuous* form: 1Jo 3:6 — *hamartanōn* (present participle: "the one keeping on sinning") — the continuous present aspect names the ongoing pattern rather than the completed act. The definitional revelation: habitual defection is expressed primarily through *person-type* terms (the sinner) and *continuous-action* forms (keeps on sinning), both of which distinguish settled pattern from single act.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The defining Hebrew term is the **Hiphil stem of cha.ta (H2398)**: *heheti* — "caused to sin," "made to sin." This is the causative form of the standard sinning verb: where the Qal (basic) stem names the person who sins themselves (CHAR-1/2/4/5/6), the Hiphil names the person who causes or enables another's sinning. The Hiphil construction appears across the corpus in the formula *heheti et-Israel* ("he made Israel to sin") and its Judah equivalent. This grammatical distinction — Qal personal sinning vs Hiphil caused-sinning — is the vocabulary-level marker that separates CHAR-7 from all adjacent characteristics. The NT does not contribute distinct terms in the 19-verse corpus; the characteristic is an OT-Hebrew phenomenon expressed through the Hiphil causative. The definitional revelation: CHAR-7 is the characteristic that the Hiphil of cha.ta uniquely names — sinning that operates through causing another to sin.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The primary term is **pa.sha (H6586)** in its political-revolt register. The root meaning of pa.sha is *to break away from, to revolt, to transgress* — it names the action of decisive separation from an established binding relationship. In CHAR-8's political register, pa.sha is used exclusively of the breaking of governing authority relationships: "Moab rebelled against Israel" (2Ki 1:1), "Edom revolted from the rule of Judah" (2Ki 8:20), "Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David" (1Ki 12:19). At the definitional level, pa.sha reveals that political revolt is not merely passive non-compliance but an active transgressive breaking-away — the same root that names sin-as-transgression in CHAR-19 is here applied to the political-authority domain, confirming that political revolt carries the full moral weight of wilful transgression. No NT Greek vocabulary appears in the 9-verse corpus — the characteristic is exclusively OT Hebrew.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The primary term is **blasfēmia (G0988)** — noun — and **blasfēmos (G0989)** — adjective. The Greek root combines *blapto* (to harm, injure) and *phēmi* (to speak) — literally "harmful speech," "injurious speech." At the definitional level, the root reveals: sinful speech is speech that harms — directed at God (blasphemy in the theological sense) or at persons (slander). The 22-verse corpus is exclusively NT Greek; no OT Hebrew vocabulary appears in CHAR-9 (the OT pa.sha/cha.ta registers for verbal sin are covered in other characteristics). The Greek blasfēmia thus encompasses both the God-directed (blasphemy-proper) and person-directed (slander) registers — its semantic range is wider than the English "blasphemy" suggests.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The primary Hebrew term ra.sha (H7563, 179 of 190 verses) is an adjective/noun designating the wicked person as a type — one constitutionally oriented toward evil. Its root covers both the moral-character meaning (the wicked person) and the forensic-legal meaning (the guilty, legally condemnable party — M10b-A-VCG-01's 5V carry this polysemy with M10 cross-register flag). re.sha (H7562, 9V) is the abstract noun counterpart: wickedness as a condition, state, and coercive force. mir.sha.at (H4849, 1V) names the collective — the wicked woman as type. The definitional revelation at this level is that Hebrew constructs an entire person-type vocabulary: the wicked person (ra.sha), wickedness as their condition (re.sha), and the wicked collective (mir.sha.at). This vocabulary suite is unusually complete, signalling that Scripture treats wickedness-as-person-identity as a coherent, classifiable inner-being category requiring multiple lexical tools to name adequately.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Four primary Greek terms carry this characteristic. ponēros (G4190, 63V): the most comprehensive term — spanning evil as a quality of persons, deeds, thoughts, and cosmic powers; at root it names what is characteristically bad or corrupt in a moral sense. kakia (G2549, 11V): specifically names settled inner badness — malice, ill-will, wickedness as an entrenched inner residue; the term's usage in Eph 4:31 (VCG-05), Col 3:8 (VCG-05), 1Pe 2:1 (VCG-05) consistently addresses it as something deeply seated requiring deliberate stripping off. adikia (G0093, 8V): unrighteousness — the condition of being structurally not-right, especially in relation to moral and legal norms; Rom 1:18 (VCG-05) names it as actively suppressing truth. ponēria (G4189, 7V): wickedness, villainy — typically naming active malicious intent; Mar 7:22 (VCG-05) lists it as an inner vice emerging from the heart. faulos (G5337, 1V): a term for what is cheap, bad, or worthless — applied to deeds in 2Cor 5:10 (VCG-06). Collectively the terms map evil across quality (ponēros), residual badness (kakia), structural wrongness (adikia), active malice (ponēria), and evaluative worthlessness (faulos).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary Hebrew: to.e.vah (H8441, ~35V in this characteristic) — the term names that which is ritually or morally abhorrent; its root may connect to a verb of loathing or turning away in disgust. At the definitional level, to.e.vah designates a category of violation so severe that it provokes active revulsion rather than mere disapproval. The term is consistently relational — "an abomination to the Lord" or "to the righteous" — signalling that abomination is defined in relationship (the revulsion of the other), not self-referentially. Primary Greek: bdelugma (G0946, 4V — Luk 16:15; Rev 17:4; 17:5; 21:27) — from bdeo, to stink; the root names what is repugnant through its putrid, offensive quality. bdeluktos (G0947, 1V — Tit 1:16) — the adjectival form: the detestable or loathsome person. The Greek root's derivation from the concept of stench adds a sensory-disgust dimension: abomination is that which morally stinks in the divine nostrils.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Two primary Hebrew terms and one Greek. to.e.vah (H8441, ~72V idolatry sub-corpus) — the general abomination term: see CHAR-3 for root analysis. Applied to the idolatrous register it names: idol-practices as abominable to God (Deu 7:25 — VCG-02: idols "an abomination to the Lord"), the person who practises divination as abominable (Deu 18:12 — VCG-02), and accumulated idolatrous acts as abominations (Eze 5:9 — VCG-05). shiq.quts (H8251, 25V) — from a root of loathing/abhorrence; specifically names detestable idolatrous objects — the idol-things themselves as objects of abhorrence. 1Ki 11:5 (vc=65898 — VCG-03): "Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites" — the foreign deity is named a shiq.quts. Eze 20:7 (vc=1634 — VCG-05): "the detestable things your eyes feast on" — the idol-objects as shiq.quts. bdelugma (G0946, 2V — Mat 24:15; Mar 13:14 — VCG-06): the sacrilegious desecration-event in the holy place. Definitionally: to.e.vah names the quality of divine revulsion toward idolatrous practice; shiq.quts names the specific idol-objects that are abhorrent; bdelugma names the event of sacrilegious desolation.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Two primary Hebrew terms carry this characteristic. a.ven (H0205G, 66V) — its root denotes emptiness, nothingness, and trouble; at the definitional level it names iniquity as a morally empty-but-troublesome quality — wrongdoing that is both hollow (without genuine moral substance) and actively harmful. The term covers the scheming agent's inner state and the trouble their scheming generates. ro.a (H7455, 13V evil-deeds sub-corpus) — from the root r-'-' (to be bad, evil, harmful); names the badness-quality of deeds. At the definitional level, ro.a names evil as a quality of deeds that flows from inner moral corruption. Deu 28:20 (vc=38439 — VCG-05): "the evil of your deeds" — ro.a names the moral quality attached to the acts. No NT Greek terms appear in this characteristic's corpus — it is exclusively OT Hebrew, which T7.1.8 will address. Definitionally: a.ven names the emptiness-that-troubles; ro.a names the badness-quality of the resulting deeds.

**[CHAR-6]** E — No primary Hebrew terms appear in the 17-verse corpus (exclusively NT Greek). Three Greek terms carry the characteristic. blasfēmeō (G0987, 11V) — the primary term: from blapto (to harm, injure) + phēmē (speech, reputation). At the definitional level, blasfēmeō names harmful speech — speech that injures a person's or God's reputation by misrepresentation. The harm is carried in the speech act itself. Rev 13:6 (VCG-01): blasphemies against God's name — the injury is to the divine name's honour. kakopoios (G2555, 5V) — from kakos (evil, bad) + poieo (to do, make): "evil-doer" or "one who does evil." As used in VCG-03, it names the identity attributed through hostile accusation — the charge that someone is an evil-doer. atopos (G0824, 1V — Act 25:5 — VCG-03) — from a (not) + topos (place): literally "out of place," hence irregular, improper, wrong. In legal context it names verifiable wrongdoing. These three terms span: harmful speech directed at God/persons (blasfēmeō), the evil-doer as charged identity (kakopoios), and legally defined wrongdoing (atopos).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's vocabulary reveals a striking OT-NT structural divide. Chars 1 and 5 are exclusively OT Hebrew (ra.sha/re.sha — Char 1; a.ven/ro.a — Char 5). Char 6 is exclusively NT Greek (blasfēmeō/kakopoios/atopos). Chars 3 and 4 span both testaments via the shared to.e.vah (H8441) vocabulary and its NT bdelugma (G0946) equivalent. Char 2 is primarily NT Greek (ponēros/kakia/adikia/ponēria/faulos). This distributional pattern is analytically significant: the cluster's inner-evil vocabulary is not a single unified lexical field but a cross-testament network of related terms. The OT Hebrew terms (ra.sha, a.ven, to.e.vah, shiq.quts) tend toward person-type and condition vocabulary (the wicked person, the iniquitous condition, the detestable thing). The NT Greek terms (ponēros, blasfēmeō, kakopoios) tend toward moral-quality and speech-act vocabulary. The to.e.vah/bdelugma bridge (Chars 3 and 4) shows the most direct OT-NT continuity within the cluster — the same relational-verdict concept (what provokes divine revulsion) carried by equivalent vocabulary across both testaments.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Three terms carry this characteristic. H2930A (ta.me, verb): "to be/become unclean" — the dynamic acquisition of the defilement-state; the action of contracting or entering it. H2931 (ta.me, adjective): "unclean" — the condition itself, the static description of one who has the state. H5079 (nid.dah): "menstrual impurity / impurity of separation" — the paradigm case of a time-bound, physiologically-sourced defilement state that governs not only menstruation (Lev 15:19-33, M10c-A-VCG-05) but bodily discharge impurity more broadly, and becomes the term for the water of impurity used in corpse-defilement cleansing (Num 19:9, M10c-A-VCG-07). G0169 (akathartos): "unclean" — the NT categorical term, carrying the same clean/unclean distinction into conscience-level conviction (Act 10:14, M10c-B-VCG-05) and covenantal-status application (1Cor 7:14). At the definitional level, the Hebrew verb/adjective pair shows defilement as both a dynamic event (acquiring the state) and a static condition (being in it); nid.dah shows it as a paradigm case governing a whole category; akathartos shows the categorical conviction operative in the inner conscience.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Five terms carry this characteristic. H2931 (ta.me adj): "unclean" — appearing in its Hebrew metaphorical-inner register here (Job 14:4, Isa 6:5, Isa 35:8, Isa 52:11, Isa 64:6, Hag 2:14, VCG-01 and -03/05), pointing to the inner condition of moral uncleanness before God. G0167 (akatharsia): "impurity" — the primary NT noun, appearing 10 times (VCG-02 and -04), consistently naming the inner condition of moral corruption in the flesh-desire register. G3435 (molunō): "to defile, soil" — a verb for the act of defiling the inner person (1Cor 8:7, Rev 3:4, Rev 14:4, VCG-03 and -05). G3436 (molusmos): "defilement" — the noun from the molunō root (2Cor 7:1, VCG-03). G3394 (miasmos): "defilement" — from miainō, to stain or pollute (2Pe 2:10, VCG-03). Definitionally, these terms together reveal the characteristic as: an inner condition of contamination (akatharsia, molusmos, miasmos — state nouns), producible through actions of the will (molunō — verb), and affecting the whole constitution of the person.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Three terms carry this characteristic, all Hebrew (the characteristic has no NT Greek evidence in its corpus): H2930A (ta.me verb, 63V): "to be/become unclean, to defile" — the dominant term, capturing both the act of defiling and the resulting condition. Its verb form is critical for Characteristic 3: the characteristic is frequently expressed as an active defiling of the land (Eze 36:17/18, VCG-04), sanctuary (Eze 5:11, VCG-03), and name (Eze 43:7/8, VCG-03) by the community's acts — the verb captures the dynamic of defilement as an act with consequences for sacred objects and spaces. H2931 (ta.me adj, 11V): "unclean" — the stative form naming the condition of persons, spaces, or objects once defiled (Eze 22:5 — "your name is defiled"; Lam 4:15 — "Unclean!"; Jos 22:19). H5079 (nid.dah, 9V): "impurity, menstrual impurity" — in the corporate-prophetic register, nid.dah is used metaphorically for moral uncleanness: Eze 36:17 ("their ways before me were like the uncleanness of a woman in her menstrual impurity"), Lam 1:17 ("Jerusalem has become a filthy thing among them").

**[CHAR-4]** E — One Greek term carries this characteristic exclusively: G0169 akathartos (alpha-privative + katharos — "not clean/pure"), always appearing as the modifier of pneuma ("unclean spirit" — pneuma akatharton). At the definitional level the term names the spirit's character — it is the un-clean spiritual force whose nature is the absence of holiness and the presence of defilement. Unique to Characteristic 4: the term names the character of the agent producing the condition, not the condition of the person. In Characteristics 1-3, the ta.me/akatharsia vocabulary names the condition of the person; here akathartos names the character of the agent.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's vocabulary reveals a unified root with differentiated deployment. The ta.me root (H2930A verb + H2931 adj) is shared across Characteristics 1, 2, and 3 — the same Hebrew root carrying bodily-ritual defilement (Char 1), inner moral defilement (Char 2), and corporate-covenantal defilement (Char 3). The Greek akathartos (G0169) is shared across Characteristics 1, 2, and 4: in Char 1's NT register (Act 10:14 — categorical conscience), in Char 2's moral-inner register (2Cor 6:17 — "touch no unclean thing"), and in Char 4 exclusively as the modifier of pneuma ("unclean spirit"). This produces the cluster's most analytically significant vocabulary finding: G0169 akathartos operates in three registers simultaneously — as a conscience-held categorical conviction (Char 1), as a moral-inner condition descriptor (Char 2), and as a spiritual agent character-descriptor (Char 4) — showing that the same Greek term addresses the sacral, moral, and spiritual dimensions of defilement without differentiation. The ta.me root carries the OT's integrative weight across all three OT-dominant characteristics. Characteristic 4 alone is exclusively Greek, confirming its register as the NT's distinctive contribution to the defilement domain.

questions.question_text: What directional, relational, or constitutional implication does the name carry?

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — all three types of implication are present:

**Directional:** The registry description names the core direction: from the offended party toward the offender, releasing the claim. The vocabulary confirms this — aphiēmi (send away, release) moves the debt away from the relational field. The direction is consistently *from* one who holds a claim *toward* one who owes it.

**Relational:** Forgiveness is constitutively relational — it cannot exist without a two-party structure. The name and vocabulary together imply: a wrong done, a claim registered, a relationship under strain, and the act that addresses the strain. The programme's dimension assignment (Relational/Social) is directly implied by the name itself.

**Constitutional:** The sb_classification (Spirit-soul interface) is also implied at the definitional level. The vocabulary names both the divine disposition (spirit-level: sal.lach as divine attribute) and the human commanded act (soul-level: forgive from the heart, Mat 18:35). The name "forgiveness" spans both levels — it names what God does and what the human person is called to do, suggesting from the outset that the characteristic operates at the interface of the two.

findings.session_b_note:
All three implications are present and carry significant analytical weight:

**Directional:** The name encodes a specific direction — outward, toward the suffering other. Compassion does not turn inward (unlike grief or shame); it faces the other. The registry description confirms: "Compassion always faces outward toward the one suffering." The vocabulary confirms it: splanchnizō is always triggered by the sight of the other's condition; ra.cham always has an object. The enquiry is oriented from the outset toward the relational interface — T4 will be particularly rich.

**Relational:** The name presupposes a two-party structure — the one moved and the one suffered-with. Unlike forgiveness (which also presupposes two parties but in a judicial/moral frame), compassion's relational structure is one of vulnerability and need on one side, and responsive movement on the other. The name does not encode a moral claim (debt, guilt, obligation) — it encodes a condition (suffering, need) that calls forth a response. This orients the enquiry away from judicial frameworks and toward constitutional and affective ones.

**Constitutional:** The womb-root and entrails-root both point toward the deep inner body as the constitutional seat of compassion. This orients the enquiry toward T2 (constitutional location) with a strong prior signal: compassion will be located in the body's interior in a way that few characteristics in the programme are. The constitutional question is not merely whether compassion has a body-level expression — the root vocabulary indicates that the body is its originating ground.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — all three.

**Directional**: The name and its vocabulary imply a downward direction — the inner being is brought low, crushed toward the ground. This directional signal immediately orients the enquiry toward the question of what produces the downward movement and what follows from it. The data answers both: moral self-awareness or suffering produces the downward movement; divine revival lifts the contrite.

**Relational**: The name implies a two-party structure — the one who is contrite and the one before whom they are contrite. In the verse evidence, the relational frame is almost exclusively vertical: the human before God. This orients the enquiry toward divine-human relationship as the primary context, and toward the question of how contrition functions in the horizontal (human-to-human) direction — a question the data largely leaves unanswered.

**Constitutional**: The name points to an inner-being condition rather than an external act. Contrition is located in "spirit" and "heart" (Psa 34:18; Isa 57:15; Psa 51:17) — the constitutional core of the person. This orients the enquiry toward the constitutional location question (T2) and toward the distinction between genuine contrition (an inner-being state) and ritual or performative penitence (an external act that may or may not reflect the inner state).

findings.session_b_note:
**Relational implication:** The name fellowship is inherently relational — it cannot be possessed or exercised in isolation. Unlike joy (which can be solitary) or strength (which is an individual quality), fellowship by definition requires an other. This orients the enquiry toward relational interface (T4) as a primary site of analysis.

**Directional implication:** The registry evidence shows fellowship operating in two distinct directions — vertical (human to God, God to human) and horizontal (human to human). These are not the same phenomenon: 2Pe 1:4 (participation in divine nature) and 1Jo 1:3 (fellowship with Father and Son) represent the vertical axis; Ecc 4:10 (lifting up the fallen companion) and Psa 119:63 (companionship with those who fear God) represent the horizontal. The name itself does not specify the direction, but the term inventory encodes both axes.

**Constitutional implication:** The joining vocabulary of the Hebrew root family (chavar) suggests that fellowship is not merely a relational event but potentially a constitutional reality — persons or things that are joined are bound together at a structural level. This anticipates T2 (Constitutional Location) as a productive tier.

findings.session_b_note: "Goodness" carries all three implications. Directional: the name points upward (to God as the origin and standard of goodness) and outward (to others as the recipients of goodness extended). Goodness is not self-enclosed — its very definition as beneficial implies a direction of benefit-toward. Relational: goodness is named as a characteristic that operates in relationship — to God (divine-human goodness), to others (moral-social goodness), and to the good itself as the standard (evaluative goodness). Reading T1 as a whole reveals a four-element structure (Q&A-017: felt disposition, institutional mechanism, petition-response, spatial locus) operating across four distinct modes (Q&A-022: dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, institutional) with a two-pole boundary structure (mercy as character quality / mercilessness as constitutional collapse). findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-001: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanch…
findings.finding_value: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanchnizō — the moment of being-moved), condition of its object (eleeinos — the pitiable state that calls compassion forth), and externalised act (almsgiving, mercy-act). No other characteristic in the programme review set operates across all four kinds simultaneously. The four root families (RACHAM, CHASAD, SPLANCHN, OIKTIROM) identify four constituent dimensions of the single characteristic, each naming a distinct register — somatic-maternal, covenantal-relational, visceral-immediate, and deliberative-pitying respectively. The structural opposites are two distinct kinds: willed judicial hardness (the hardened heart that refuses compassion) and unwilled prosperity-blindness (Eze 16:49 — the one who does not see the need because they are satiated). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed by the consistent outward-facing structure: compassion cannot exist without a suffering other. The definitional tier's most critical gap — the receiver's inner-being experience — is entirely absent from the data, affecting T1.5, T1.6, and T1.7 throughout. This gap is the single most significant analytical absence in the registry.
