findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the verbal forms (G4697, H7355); the externalised-act kind by the noun forms and compound forms (G1656, H2617B). T7's vocabulary arc (womb to almsgiving) is the lexical expression of T1's range from the most interior character quality to the most exterior externalised act — the same spectrum named by the definition is traversed by the vocabulary. The dual primary anchor (T7) maps onto T1's dimensional analysis: Hos 11:8 provides the evidence for the divine relational disposition; Luke 10:33 provides the evidence for the human relational disposition as moral norm.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-001: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition of being in favour — charis as inhabited state), enabling capacity (the specific power given for specific tasks — 2Cor 12:9), and character quality (gracious speech, gracious conduct — chen in 889-003). No single English equivalent captures all four. The four modes of operation (sovereign bestowal, covenantal-relational sustaining, capacity-conferring, character-forming) correspond to the four kinds without collapsing them. Two structural opposites are identified: pride (the self-elevation that refuses the favour of the greater, active and willed) and ingratitude/gracelessness (acharistos — the failure to register and respond to grace received, which T3 confirms as image-impairment). The immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle) is a T1.5 finding confirming that grace does not bypass creaturely recognition but requires and produces it as a transitional state. The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed throughout: grace is constitutively directional — it flows from the greater to the lesser and requires the receptor's inner-being engagement to complete its operation.

findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verbal forms. The completed-state kind (charitoō — NT coinage, G5487) required a new word because existing vocabulary could not carry the concept of standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state. The character-quality kind (chen in conduct and speech — 889-003) is carried by chen's adjectival and behavioural register. The vocabulary is structurally complete for the four kinds — each kind has a corresponding lexical form. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō) is the lexical evidence that T1's four-kind analysis is correct: the fourth kind (standing as completed state) required new vocabulary because it was conceptually unique.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Relational and constitutional both present. Relational: God's righteousness is expressed toward his people (covenant faithfulness, A1-003), toward the world (judgment, A1-002), toward the Messiah (A1-007). Constitutional: righteousness is the foundation of the throne (Psa 89:14; 97:2) — structural to God's nature, not circumstantial.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Strongly relational: righteousness in the human is always defined in relation to God's standard, to covenant, and to other persons. The directional implication runs consistently: oriented toward God (A2-014), toward others (A2-012), toward God's standard (A2-006). Constitutional also: righteousness becomes a governing state, not merely a quality applied situationally.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Constitutional and directional: the y.sh.r vocabulary names an inner orientation — a direction of the inner being toward what is straight. The person walks in uprightness (a path metaphor), and the inner being is either straight or devious (Pro 2:13–14).

**[C — Justification]** Directional and relational: justification is always directed from the judging party toward the judged person — a one-directional act with a specific relational structure. The relational implication: justification changes the standing of the person before God.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Directional: avenging justice flows from the wronged party (or their advocate) toward the wrongdoer. Always responsive — triggered by prior injustice. Relational: involves at minimum three parties — the wronged, the wrongdoer, and the avenger.

**[E — Condemnation]** Directional: the kata- prefix in all E-terms names a downward direction — sentence passed down on the condemned person. The directional implication of autokatakritos (self-condemned) is reflexive: judgment turns back on the self. Relational: condemnation always involves judge and condemned.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Object-directed: one always reckons something. The directional implication: reckoning moves from the inner faculty outward toward the object being assessed, then back inward as a basis for action (Rom 6:11). Constitutional: the faculty itself is a structural feature of the inner person.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Constitutional and directional: wickedness and injustice name constitutional orientations of the inner person that set the person against the moral order. The directional implication: the ra.sha person moves away from God and toward harm of others.

**[CLUSTER]** The dominant implication across the cluster is relational: righteousness in all its sub-group forms is defined in relation to God's standard, to covenant, to other persons, and to the moral order. The secondary implication is directional: each sub-group names a specific direction. The constitutional implication appears specifically in A1, A2, and G — the governing-state character of righteousness at its fullest.
Constitutional (the wise person IS); directional (toward God, VCG09; toward worldly ends, VCG07); relational (wisdom given by God to the asker, Jam 1:5 VCG02 anchor).

findings.finding_value: The name "Blessing and Grace" does not fully capture three things the verse evidence reveals: (1) The supplication dimension — the human cry for grace (cha.nan 984-001, 72 verses) is not captured by "grace" as a static noun; grace generates the inner posture of dependent petition. (2) The propagating dimension — received grace becomes extended grace; the charizō forgiveness corpus (5470-002) shows grace in motion from God through person to person. (3) The acceptance dimension — ra.tsah names the pleasure/delight face of grace, which is distinct from the giving face; the inner divine pleasure is not captured by "blessing" or "grace" without qualification.

"Goodness" does not fully capture the volitional-preference register of ya.tav (632-003): the inner faculty of moral judgment by which what seems good determines action. This is not merely "goodness" but moral discernment in action. Nor does it capture the somatic dimension: Pro 17:22's "a joyful heart is good medicine" shows goodness as physically generative — the inner state has bodily consequences.

findings.finding_value:
The cluster name "Abundance, Prosperity and Wealth" does not itself carry directional or relational implications — but the verse evidence immediately imposes them. The moment wealth appears in Scripture it has a direction: toward God or toward self (Luk 12:21); toward others or away from them (Luk 16:19-21; Jam 2:2-6); toward trust in God or trust in riches (Psa 52:7; Pro 11:28). The constitutional implication is that wealth is never a neutral inner state — it is always an inner-being testing domain in which the direction of the person's fundamental orientation is revealed and shaped.

[Cluster-level addition — Phase 9 cross-sub-group review] The directional character of the wealth domain is the governing structural principle across all four sub-groups. Every term in M46 operates directionally in its verse evidence — wealth is never a neutral inner state. The inner-being content is always: wealth oriented toward self or toward God and others; trust placed in riches or in God; becoming rich in the self-directed form (M46-A) or in the toward-God form (M46-D). This directionality is not incidental but constitutive of the domain: the question the wealth domain always poses is not "how much?" but "toward whom and for what?"

findings.finding_value: The name "Reverential Fear / Fear of God as Governing Orientation" carries all three implications: (1) directional — the fear is directed toward God, not diffuse or undirected; (2) relational — it is the inner posture within a specific God-human relationship; (3) constitutional — "governing orientation" signals that this is a stable constitutional disposition, not a passing event. The name orients the enquiry toward the person's relational standing before God as the primary question.

"Acute Fear and Alarm" implies a directional dimension (fear of a specific triggering object or event) and a constitutional implication (the inner constitution is responsive to genuine threat). The relational dimension is present but secondary: the fear is relational in that it responds to a person, encounter, or display of power.

"Terror as Overwhelming Force" carries a directional implication: the force comes from outside and acts upon the inner person. This orients the enquiry toward the source and agency of the terror rather than the inner state per se.

"Dismay and Inner Collapse" carries constitutional implications: the inner person is not holding together but dissolving. The name orients the enquiry toward the structural integrity of the inner person under stress.

"Trembling / Fear Made Somatic" carries a directional implication (from inner to body) and a constitutional implication (the somatic register of the inner life). The name orients the enquiry toward the body-soul interface.

"Anticipatory Dread and Anxiety" carries a strong directional implication (forward-looking in time) and a relational implication (the dread has an object — something feared). The name orients the enquiry toward the temporal structure of fear, not just its intensity.

"Timidity and Cowardly Shrinking" carries a moral-evaluative implication from the outset: this is fear being named as a failure. The constitutional implication (the inner constitution should not be like this) orients the enquiry toward the norm from which timidity departs.

Across M01, the sub-group names collectively orient the enquiry from the outset toward: object-direction (what the fear is of), temporal structure (present-responsive vs. future-oriented), constitutional depth (orientation vs. event vs. collapse), and moral evaluation (appropriate vs. failed). These four orienting dimensions are the cluster's analytical framework.

The name carries relational implications from the outset: anger, wrath, and indignation are inherently directed — they require an object (the wrongdoing, the person who committed it, the situation that is wrong). The cluster is not about a free-floating inner temperature but about a reactive state with a specific directional structure: something is perceived as wrong and the inner being fires against it. The directionality is intrinsic to the characteristic's definition.

Yes on all three counts. Directional: the mourning vocabulary consistently shows grief oriented upward toward God (distress driving prayer — M03-D-VCG-01) or toward another person in empathic solidarity (Job's soul weeping for the needy — M03-A-VCG-04; Rom 12:15 — M03-A-VCG-05). Relational: grief is almost always relational in the corpus — it arises from the loss of or damage to a relational bond (bereavement weeping, M03-A-VCG-01; anguish at relational loss, Act 20:38 — M03-D-VCG-05). Constitutional: grief consistently involves the soul and heart as its location (Jesus's soul sorrowful to death, Mat 26:38; sorrow lodged in the heart, Psa 13:2; anguish of my spirit, Job 7:11), signalling that it is a deep inner-being state rather than a surface emotional response.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, all three. Directional: the evidence shows exultation consistently moving toward an object — "exult in your name" (Psa 89:16), "rejoice in the Lord" (Psa 32:11), "exult in his salvation" (Psa 35:9), "rejoice over you" (Zep 3:17). The characteristic is inherently directional. Relational: the dominant register is the divine-human relation — exultation is the inner state produced by and directed toward the covenant relationship. Constitutional: the evidence explicitly names the soul (Psa 35:9; 63:5; Isa 61:10), the heart (Psa 13:5; 32:11; 66:14; Zec 10:7), and the whole being (Psa 16:9) as constitutional loci, and extends to the bones (Psa 51:8) as the body's participation in the state.

**[CHAR-2]** E — All three. **Directional**: joy consistently requires an object — "rejoice in the Lord" (Deu 12:7; Psa 32:11; Phili 4:4); "rejoice at his birth" (Luk 1:14); "rejoice in hope" (Rom 12:12). The name implies directionality. **Relational**: the sunchairo corpus (M04-D) and the Pauline joy (1Th 2:19–20; Phili 4:1; 3Jo 3–4) show joy as constitutively relational — persons are described as the content of joy. The name carries the implication of joy-between-persons. **Constitutional**: the heart is the most frequently named constitutional locus across both OT and NT (Exo 4:14 — "glad in his heart"; Psa 4:7 — "more joy in my heart"; Psa 33:21 — "heart is glad in him"; Pro 15:13 — "glad heart makes a cheerful face"; Jer 15:16 — "joy and the delight of my heart"; Joh 16:22 — "your hearts will rejoice"; Song 3:11 — "gladness of his heart"). Joy is constitutionally located in the heart.

**[CHAR-7]** E — (1) **Directional** — agalliao is consistently directed toward a specific ground: God my Savior (Luk 1:47), the Father's gracious revelation (Luk 10:21), the unseen Christ believed in (1Pe 1:8), the future glory (1Pe 4:13), Christ's day (Joh 8:56). The name implies a Godward or eschatological direction for the joy component; (2) **Relational** — Act 16:34 (the jailer and his entire household) and Mat 5:12 (the persecuted community) show the characteristic operating in relational and communal contexts; (3) **Constitutional** — Luk 1:47 ("my spirit rejoices") explicitly names the spirit level; Luk 10:21 ("rejoiced in the Holy Spirit") confirms Spirit-level constitutional location as primary for agalliao.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Moderate directional, strong cognitive, moderate relational implications: (1) **Cognitive-directional**: tov consistently points toward an object that is good — the glad person is glad about or in something; M04-L's evaluative appraisals ("better than," "not good," "good to those who wait") always name an object or situation; M04-O's circumstantial responses always have an occasion; (2) **Relational**: the "good man" (Pro 12:2; 13:22; 14:14) and the relational comparatives (Rut 4:15; 2Sa 18:3) show Gladness as relationally-embedded — it arises in and from relationships; (3) **Constitutional**: unlike Exultation and Joy, Gladness's primary constitutional language is not "heart" first — the tov corpus is more frequently directed at objects, circumstances, and character than at the heart's location. The heart is named in specific instances (Ecc 5:20; Jer 15:16 — but these are M04-E sa.s.von rather than M04-L/O tov), revealing Gladness as somewhat more cognitively-distributed than heart-centred.

**[CHAR-4]** E — (1) **Directional**: Delight always has an object it is directed toward — the directional implication is the most distinctive feature; Psa 73:25 ("there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you") shows Delight at its most purely directional — entirely toward God; (2) **Relational**: the relational implications are pervasive — Delight in persons (parental: Jer 31:20; Mic 1:16; interpersonal: 1Sa 19:1; Psa 16:3; 1Th 2:8; divine-human: Psa 18:19; Isa 62:4) shows that Delight is fundamentally relational in most of its registers; (3) **Constitutional**: Rom 7:22 ("in my inner being") is the most explicit constitutional location statement in the corpus — the deepest layer of the self; Mat 12:18's "my soul is well pleased" locates divine Delight in the soul (psychē); (4) **Volitional**: the cha.phets/che.phets vocabulary implies an act or orientation of the will — Delight is not merely felt but chosen and directed.

**[CHAR-5]** E — (1) **Receptive rather than directed** — the na.im/na.em vocabulary consistently describes a quality the inner person receives or recognises rather than generates or directs; (2) **Relational** — most M04-J instances are relational: Psa 133:1 (brotherly pleasantness), 2Sa 1:26 (Jonathan's pleasantness to David), Song 1:16; 7:6 (beloved's pleasantness), Pro 2:10 (wisdom pleasant to the soul), Pro 16:24 (gracious words nourishing soul and body); (3) **Constitutional** — Pro 2:10 names the soul explicitly ("pleasant to your soul"), Pro 16:24 names both soul and body ("sweetness to the soul and health to the body"); Pleasure is constitutionally distributed across soul and body in a way that no other M04 characteristic is as explicitly.

**[CHAR-6]** E — (1) **Directional** — Wonder is consistently directed toward God's acts and character (VCG-01 and VCG-02) or toward extraordinary events (VCG-03); it always has an object that exceeds ordinary categories; (2) **Cognitive** — Wonder specifically engages the cognitive-perceptive faculty; Job 37:5 ("great things that we cannot comprehend") names the cognitive limit as the trigger for Wonder; Wonder is constitutionally located at the boundary of comprehension; (3) **Relational-asymmetrical** — Wonder is not a symmetric characteristic; it is experienced by the lesser before the greater; the creature wonders at the Creator; Mar 10:32 (thambeō at Jesus' advance toward Jerusalem) shows Wonder as a response to one who is greater than oneself and who one cannot fully understand.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The names carry consistent implications across the cluster that differentiate the characteristics: (1) **Directional implications** — Exultation: always toward God or a specific ground (never self-directed in its legitimate form); Delight: always toward a specific object; Wonder: always toward what exceeds categories; Joy: toward God, persons, and what is celebratable; Gladness: toward what is genuinely good (though more diffusely than Delight); Pleasure: receptive from what surrounds the person; Suffering-Joy: toward eschatological and divine reality as a ground for present paradox; (2) **Relational implications** — Delight is the most explicitly relational in its name (it always names a relational direction); Pleasure has a strong relational register in M04-J (the pleasantness of persons); Joy is inherently communal (feast-joy, sunchairo); Suffering-Joy is communally shared (Act 16:34's whole household); Wonder is communally proclaimed (Tell-Remember-Meditate); Exultation moves outward from the inner person to communal expression; Gladness is distributed across relational appraisal; (3) **Constitutional implications** — Suffering-Joy's unique constitutional location (spirit-level, Char 7) is signalled by the paradox in the name; Delight's depth in the "inner being" (Rom 7:22) is suggested by its object-resting quality; Wonder's cognitive-perceptive primary is suggested by its arrested quality; Pleasure's embodied quality is consistent with its receptive-ambient name; Gladness's cognitive quality is consistent with its settled-brightness name.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Directional: shame moves the person *downward* — toward collapse, withdrawal, covering, face-hiding. The evidence consistently shows the shamed person unable to lift their head (Job 10:15, vc=37502), covering their face (Jer 14:3, vc=38535; Eze 7:18, vc=34978), unable to lift their face toward God (Ezr 9:6, vc=65495). Relational: shame is inherently relational — it arises in the face of someone (God, enemies, community). The three sub-group registers (unjust wound, moral consequence, divine encounter) all locate shame in a relational field. Constitutional: the name's "inner state" tag signals that the primary register is psychological/volitional — the collapse happens to the faculty of dignity, confidence, and self-perception. These implications together orient the enquiry: CHAR-1 is a downward, relational, inner event.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Strongly directional (downward); relational (inflicted by an agent on a recipient); constitutional (operates at the social-bodily interface — the body bears the sign of disgrace and community recognises it).

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 is relational by definition — it always operates in the space between persons. Directionally, it moves from the dishonour-er toward the dishonoured. The constitutional implication is that CHAR-3 engages the moral-evaluative and relational faculties: it is produced by a failure of moral perception and has its primary effect in the relational standing of the dishonoured.

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 is constitutive rather than directional: it names a quality (what is shameful) rather than a direction. The relational implication is toward God's sight and the community's moral standard — the shameful is what cannot bear scrutiny before God (2Cor 4:2) or community (Eph 5:12). The constitutional implication is that CHAR-4 is located in the conscience — the faculty that registers moral quality.

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 is relational by definition — it always arises from the interaction between a contempt-er and a contempt-ed. Directionally: contempt moves from the dismisser toward the dismissed, producing shame in the recipient. Constitutional implication: CHAR-5 engages the person's sense of worth (the inner faculty that registers their standing before others), which is affected by the contempt-verdict even when that verdict is false.

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 is constitutive: it names an inner state rather than a direction. However, it carries a directional implication as a counter: it moves against guilt-shame, protecting the person from the inner collapse that guilt-shame would produce. Constitutional implication: CHAR-6 is located primarily in the conscience (the moral-recognitive faculty that registers guilt or its absence) and in the will (the faculty whose freedom from deliberate wrongdoing constitutes the innocence).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The six names collectively establish three consistent directional implications. (1) Downward movement: all five negative characteristics involve a person's standing being moved downward (Chars 1, 2, 3, 5) or conduct being assessed as below the proper moral level (Char 4). (2) Relational constitution: all six are inherently relational — they arise in, or are expressed through, relations between person and God (Char 1 across all three registers), person and persons (Chars 2, 3, 5), person and moral community (Char 4), and person and God in the cultic context (Char 6). (3) Constitutional location at soul level: all six operate primarily at the level of the person's inner moral life (conscience, will, relational standing, felt experience) rather than at the level of body alone or spirit alone.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The name carries all three. Directional: the characteristic moves upward — Deu 17:20 (vc=34231, M08-A1-VCG-01): "his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers"; Dan 11:36 (vc=34235, M08-A1-VCG-02): the king "exalts himself and magnifies himself above every god." The direction is constitutively comparative — elevation is always elevation over someone or something. Relational: the upward movement is measured against God and other human beings simultaneously; Psa 138:6 (vc=12086, vc=34300, M08-A4-VCG-02) evidences the relational consequence: "the haughty he knows from afar" — divine relational distance as the structural outcome. Constitutional: the evidence immediately locates CHAR-1 in the heart (Pro 16:5, vc=12083, M08-A1-VCG-03: "arrogant in heart"), the spirit (Pro 16:18, vc=34073, M08-A1-VCG-03: "haughty spirit"), and the eyes/posture (Pro 6:17, vc=34247, M08-A2-VCG-01: "haughty eyes") — pointing to a characteristic that penetrates to the deepest constitutional levels of the person.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The name carries all three. Directional: CHAR-2 moves against — against the authority that established the limit, against the command that defined it. Deu 1:43 (vc=34123, M08-B-VCG-01): "you acted presumptuously and went up" — the movement is upward and against despite divine prohibition. Relational: CHAR-2 requires a relational other (God, appointed authority, revealed law) against whom to assert; it is inherently comparative and oppositional. Psa 86:14 (vc=34097, M08-B-VCG-02): "the insolent have risen up against me, a band of ruthless men seek my life; they do not set God before them." Constitutional: the zid/zed/za.don vocabulary roots CHAR-2 in the will — the volitional faculty, not the affective or cognitive. It is an act of the will's self-assertion more than a felt impulse or a cognitive error.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The name carries directional and relational implications. Directional: "boasting" is always about something — the direction of the boast determines its legitimacy. Jer 9:23 (vc=33342, M08-C-VCG-01) identifies three wrong directions (wisdom, might, wealth) that imply one right direction (knowing God). The kauchaomai family inherits this directional structure — the same verb boasting toward self (VCG-01), toward God (VCG-03), or toward legitimate examined grounds (VCG-02). Relational: boasting/self-display requires an audience — CHAR-3 is constitutively social; it is performed for others' reception. Pro 25:14 (vc=33358, M08-C-VCG-01): boasting of a gift never given — the gift-claim is for social consumption and produces nothing. Constitutional: alazoneia (Jam 4:16, vc=33866; 1Jo 2:16, vc=33865) names the inner disposition that generates the boasting act.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The name carries constitutional implications primarily. "Conceit" locates the characteristic in the cognitive faculty — the mind's self-assessment function. Rom 12:3 (vc=60866, M08-D-VCG-02): "think of yourself" — the froneō root directly addresses the thinking/mind faculty. The constitutional implication is that CHAR-4 operates at the mind/cognitive level rather than the heart/volitional level (CHAR-1/2) or the speech/social level (CHAR-3). Relational implications: 1Cor 13:4 (vc=33936, M08-D-VCG-01): "love is not arrogant [fusioō]" — CHAR-4 is relationally incompatible with love; the inflated cognitive self-picture displaces the other-oriented cognition that love requires.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The name carries relational and constitutional implications. Relational: "power and position" are inherently relational — they are defined relative to others (power over others; position above others). Eze 16:49 (vc=33979, M08-E-VCG-01): Sodom's CHAR-5 is evidenced by failure to aid the poor — the structural superiority expressed in contempt and neglect of the vulnerable. Constitutional: the ga.on proud-might vocabulary names both the structural external power and the inner confidence that rests on it — CHAR-5 is constitutionally anchored in the heart (Eze 28:5 — heart proud; Eze 16:30 — impetuousness in the heart) even though its medium is external structural goods.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All five names carry directional implications, but in different axes. CHAR-1 names an upward direction (self-elevation — against God's position). CHAR-2 names an outward-against direction (defiance — against an authority). CHAR-3 names an outward-social direction (display — toward an audience). CHAR-4 names an inward-upward direction (conceit — the mind thinking above its warranted measure). CHAR-5 names a structural-elevation direction (power and position — above others via received structural goods). The cluster-synthesis: the directional taxonomy across the five shows that M08 comprehensively maps the directions in which the self moves illicitly — against God (CHAR-1, CHAR-2), toward social validation (CHAR-3), within the mind's self-assessment (CHAR-4), and through structural goods (CHAR-5).

**[CHAR-2]** E — All three. *Directional:* submission runs downward in the authority-structure sense — toward God (Rom1:5; Heb5:9), toward parents (Eph6:1; Col3:20), toward legitimate apostolic instruction (Phili2:12; 2Th3:14). *Relational:* the terms are constitutively relational — one submits to someone; the characteristic is always triangulated between the submitting person, the authority, and the ground of the submission (theological — "in the Lord," Eph6:1; "as to Christ," Eph6:5). *Constitutional:* Rom6:17 ("obedient from the heart") and Phili2:12 (sustained without external accountability — in "my absence") locate the characteristic constitutionally in the heart and conscience rather than in external compliance — it must originate in the inner person to be genuine.

**[CHAR-3]** E — All three. *Constitutional:* Psa34:18 locates the characteristic in spirit ("crushed in spirit") and heart ("brokenhearted") — two explicit constitutional locations. *Relational:* both verses are constitutively Godward — contrition is the inner state before God specifically; Isa57:15 names God's dwelling with the contrite as the relational orientation. The characteristic does not exist in isolation but always in relation to the divine holy presence that occasions or responds to it. *Directional:* the crushing is downward — from self-sufficiency and pride toward genuine interior brokenness. The direction is the opposite of self-assertion; the crushed spirit is the one that no longer stands in self-sufficiency before God.

**[CHAR-4]** E — All three. *Relational:* both terms are constitutively relational — metriopatheō names the quality of the high priest's engagement *with* the erring (Heb5:2 — "deal gently with the ignorant and wayward"); okneō names the responsiveness *to* others' call for help (Act9:38 — "come to us without delay"). The characteristic is always directed toward another. *Constitutional:* metriopatheō grounds the capacity in "shared weakness" (Heb5:2) — an inner awareness of one's own creaturely limitation that mediates the character of engagement. *Directional:* the characteristic's movement is outward toward others in need — the meek/gentle person moves toward the erring and the calling without self-protective hesitation.

**[CHAR-5]** E — All three. *Relational:* semnotēs is always visible in relation — 1Ti2:2 in public life, 1Ti3:4 in household governance, Tit2:7 in teaching. The characteristic shapes how the person inhabits their social relationships and roles. *Constitutional:* the characteristic is named as an inner quality (Pass A meanings: "inner gravity," "sober weighty seriousness of character," "inner quality") that expresses itself outwardly. *Directional:* the characteristic's direction is inward-first (settled inner moral gravity) expressing outward (in public life, household, teaching) — from the grounded inner person outward into social existence, not from social expectation inward.

**[CHAR-6]** E — All three. *Directional:* the freely-moved heart/spirit moves *toward* God and toward his service — Exo35:5 (toward the Lord's contribution), 2Ch29:31 (toward burnt offerings), Psa51:12 (toward joyful devotion). The direction is outward-Godward from the inner person. *Relational:* the characteristic is constitutively relational toward God — the free offering is always directed toward the one who calls for it (Exo35:5 — "a contribution to the Lord"). *Constitutional:* the characteristic is located in the heart (Exo35:5 — "of a generous/willing heart"; Exo35:22; 2Ch29:31 — "willing heart") and in the spirit (Psa51:12 — "a willing spirit"). Both the heart and spirit are named as constitutional locations.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, all three. *Directional:* humility is consistently downward — toward God (Jam4:10; 1Pe5:6; 2Ch7:14), toward others (Phili2:3; Eph4:2; 1Pe5:5), and away from self-elevation (Mat23:12; Luk14:11). The direction is built into the name. *Relational:* ka.na and the Greek tapein- terms are almost never reflexive-only; they name a posture before another (before God, before elders, before one another). The relational target is structural to the characteristic, not incidental. *Constitutional:* Mat11:29 locates lowliness explicitly "in the heart" — the innermost personal centre. Lev26:41 names the "uncircumcised heart" that must be broken for humility to emerge. The characteristic is constitutionally interior: the relational posture originates from the heart's orientation, not from external behaviour alone.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics carry all three implications, but with different weightings that reveal their distinctive identities. *Directionality* is most constitutively present in CHAR-2 Submission (the hupo- prefix encodes the downward-under direction into the root) and CHAR-6 Willing-heartedness (the na.div root encodes the freely-springing forward movement). *Relational constitution* is most prominent in CHAR-4 Meekness — both terms are constitutively relational (metriopatheō names the quality of dealing-with; okneō names responsiveness-to). *Constitutional depth* is most explicitly encoded in CHAR-3 Contrition (dak.ka — the spirit and heart as named sites) and CHAR-6 Willing-heartedness (heart and spirit both named). CHAR-5 Dignity is distinctive in being constitutional (inner quality) without being directional in the same strong sense as the others — it has no built-in directional movement, which is precisely what makes it a resting-place rather than a movement-characteristic. The cluster-level finding: M09 is a cluster in which most characteristics are constitutively in-motion (humbling, submitting, contriting, willing) with only CHAR-5 naming a settled state rather than a movement.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The name "Wilful sinning" carries strong relational and directional implications. The corpus structures sinning along three directional axes: (1) vertical — sinning against God (VCG-01: "sin against God" Gen 39:9; "against you, you only" Psa 51:4; "sinned against me" Eze 14:13); (2) horizontal — sinning against persons (VCG-02: "sin against his neighbor" 1Ki 8:31; "sins against you" Mat 18:15); and (3) reflexive — sinning against oneself (1Cor 6:18: "the sexually immoral person sins against his own body"; Pro 8:36: sinning injures oneself). These three directions are constitutive: the name implies that wilful sinning is always sinning *against* someone — it is irreducibly relational. The constitutional implication is that sinning engages the will in a movement *away from* a relational bond that was owed, making the will the primary constitutional faculty at stake.

**[CHAR-10]** E — All three mechanisms carry distinct directional and relational implications. *Enticement (deleazō)*: directional — the lure draws the person from their current position toward sin (Jam 1:14 — "lured and enticed"); relational — the enticement operates through the person's own desire, making the relationship between the self's desire-faculty and the temptation the operative relational field. *Hypocrisy (sunupokrinomai)*: directional — the person moves from authentic identity toward performed identity; relational — the collective dimension (*sun-*) makes it constitutively social, requiring others to hypo-krinomai alongside. *Apostasy (apostasia)*: directional — a standing-away-from, a departure; relational — the departure is from a covenantal relational standing (the Mosaic covenant — Act 21:21).

**[CHAR-11]** E — All three implications are present at characteristic scope. *Directional*: Rom 3:23 — "fall short of the glory of God" — the direction is downward (falling short, not reaching the standard) and inward (the condition is in the person, not merely their acts). *Relational*: the condition is always measured against God — "under sin" (Rom 3:9) is a relational position relative to a power; Joh 8:21 — "die in your sin" where Jesus is the one departing — the relational consequence of dying in sin is separation from where Jesus goes. Heb 5:1 — sin creates the need for priestly mediation between human and divine — the relational distance is the characteristic's relational implication. *Constitutional*: the condition is a structural feature of every human person — Joh 9:34 — "born in utter sin" — the birth-origin framing; Eph 2:1 — "dead in trespasses and sins" — a constituted inner state, not an external label.

**[CHAR-12]** E — All three implications are present. *Directional*: the enslaving power moves inward — from sin's external pull to the internal capture of the will; Joh 8:34's practice (outward acts) → slavery (inner constitutional captivity) reveals the direction. *Relational*: the characteristic is constitutively relational — a master-slave relationship between sin (master) and the person (slave — Joh 8:34). *Constitutional*: 1Jo 3:9 — "God's seed abides in him... he cannot keep on sinning" — the cannot-keep-sinning is a constitutional impossibility grounded in the new birth; the liberation from the enslaving power is equally constitutional. The name thus implies: the will's constitutional direction, the relational master-slave structure, and the inner-directional movement of capture.

**[CHAR-13]** E — All three. *Directional*: the record accumulates in one direction — from the person upward toward God; Isa 59:12 — "our sins testify against us" — the testimony runs from the person toward divine judgment. *Relational*: the record is constitutively relational — it exists before God (Lev 4:26 — "the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and he shall be forgiven" — the atonement addresses a relational deficit). *Constitutional*: Jer 17:1 — "engraved on the tablet of their heart" — the record is also internally inscribed; Psa 51:5 — "in sin did my mother conceive me" — the record begins constitutionally, at birth. The directional, relational, and constitutional dimensions are all evidenced in the 205-verse corpus.

**[CHAR-14]** E — All three. *Directional*: "sought" names a movement from the person toward God; "received" names the return movement from God to the person. The directional structure is toward-God then from-God — a bilateral movement that constitutes the full forgiveness-event. *Relational*: the characteristic is constitutively relational — it requires the person-God relationship as its operative field; forgiveness cannot be sought from or granted by anyone else (Mar 2:7 context — "who can forgive sins but God alone?" — referenced in CHAR-11 but structurally operative here). *Constitutional*: Act 2:38 — repentance + baptism → forgiveness → Spirit-reception — the constitutional change (receiving the Spirit) is the consequence of the characteristic's completion.

**[CHAR-15]** E — All three. *Directional*: the condition moves backward (from ancestors to present) and forward (from present to descendants); Isa 43:27's "first father sinned" is the backward direction; the ongoing pattern (Psa 78:17/32 — still sinning) is the forward continuation. *Relational*: the condition is constitutively relational — it operates within lineages, families, and covenant communities; it cannot be inherited without the relational bond of ancestry. *Constitutional*: Isa 64:5 — "in our sins we have been a long time" — the prolonged duration suggests the condition has become constitutional, not merely episodic.

**[CHAR-16]** E — All three. *Directional*: Jam 5:20 — "whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering" — the sinner is characterized by directional drift away from God; the direction of the sinner's moral character is away-from-God. *Relational*: Psa 1:1 — "the way of sinners" as a social-moral class whose company shapes inner orientation; Luk 15:2 — Pharisees' complaint that Jesus "receives sinners and eats with them" — the relational dimension is constitutive. *Constitutional*: Rom 5:19 — "the many were made sinners" — the constitutional imputation of the sinner-identity through Adam's disobedience names this as a constituted inner status, not merely a behavioural descriptor.

**[CHAR-17]** E — All three. *Directional*: guilt is directed toward God — Ezr 9:15 — "we are before you in our guilt" — the guilt-state faces toward the divine judge; guilt is always guilt-before-someone. *Relational*: guilt is constitutively relational — it requires both the guilty person and the one wronged; Num 5:6 — "any of the sins that people commit by breaking faith with the Lord" — guilt arises from a broken relationship; Gen 42:21 — "we are guilty concerning our brother" — guilt arises from wrong against another person. *Constitutional*: Ezr 9:6 — guilt as a condition that has mounted up over time; Hos 10:2 — "their heart is false; now they must bear their guilt" — the guilt is a constitutional weight the false-hearted person must carry.

**[CHAR-18]** E — All three. *Directional*: iniquity has a trajectory of accumulation — Gen 15:16 — "not yet complete" — moving toward fullness; Hos 14:1 — "you have stumbled because of your iniquity" — the iniquity operates as a directional force pulling the person away from God. *Relational*: iniquity is always iniquity-before-God — Psa 90:8 — "you have set our iniquities before you" — the relational frame is the moral account in God's presence; Isa 43:24 — "you have wearied me with your iniquities" — iniquity is a relational burden between the person and God. *Constitutional*: Psa 51:5 — "I was brought forth in iniquity" — the iniquity-condition is constitutional, prior to individual acts; Eze 18:20 — "the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself" — it attaches constitutionally to the person who commits it.

**[CHAR-19]** E — All three. *Directional*: transgression is movement across a boundary — the will moves from the permitted side to the forbidden side; Isa 59:20 — "those who turn from transgression" — the turn-from presupposes a direction-toward; Isa 31:6 — "turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted" — the revolt is a directional departure. *Relational*: transgression is always against someone — Jer 2:29 — "you have all transgressed against me"; Eze 2:3 — "rebelled against me"; Gen 31:36 — "what is my offense against you?" — the relational frame is constitutive. *Constitutional*: Isa 48:8 — "from before birth you were called a rebel" — transgression as a pre-personal constitutional label; Isa 57:4 — "children of transgression" — a hereditary identity.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The name carries primarily *constitutional* implications: unintentional sinning locates the characteristic within the inner person's epistemic constitution — the capacity to act without full knowledge. The relational implication is present but muted compared to CHAR-1: Lev 4:2 ("in any of the Lord's commandments about things not to be done") locates the standard relationally (God's commands), but the violation occurs without the relational *defiance* that characterises wilful sinning. The directional implication is toward God: even uninstructed violation is "unintentional in any of the Lord's commandments" — God remains the reference point. But the direction lacks the volitional turning-against that VCG-01 of CHAR-1 carries. Constitutional epistemic limitation is the defining implication.

**[CHAR-20]** E — All three. *Directional*: faithlessness is directed against someone — Lev 26:40 — "treachery that they committed against me"; Jer 3:20 — "treacherous to me, O house of Israel" — the direction is always against a covenant-partner; *Relational*: the characteristic is constitutively relational — Mal 2:14 — "though she is your companion and your wife by covenant" — the prior covenant-bond is what makes the faithlessness treachery rather than mere departure; *Constitutional*: Isa 48:8 — "from before birth you were called a rebel... I knew you would surely deal treacherously" — faithlessness is a constitutional inner bent that God foreknew; 2Ch 28:22 — "in time of his distress he became yet more faithless" — deepening under pressure confirms constitutional character.

**[CHAR-21]** E — All three. *Directional*: perversion always inverts something — a direction of moral movement that turns back on itself; Jer 3:21 — "perverted their way" — the directional turning of the life-path away from God; *Relational*: perversion damages the God-relationship and human relationships — Isa 29:16 — the creature denying the creator (relational inversion); Pro 6:14 — "continually sowing discord" — perversity fractures relational bonds; *Constitutional*: Eph 4:22 — "old self corrupt through deceitful desires" — the corruption is constitutional to the fallen "old self"; 1Ti 6:5 — "depraved in mind" — the depravity is at the constitutional level of the mind's functioning.

**[CHAR-22]** E — All three. *Directional*: injustice is always directed toward someone — Psa 58:2 — "your hands deal out violence on earth" — the violence is toward others; Eze 3:20 — "commits injustice" as an act against the righteousness-standard; *Relational*: injustice damages persons — Psa 43:1 — "from the deceitful and unjust man deliver me"; Job 6:29 — "let no injustice be done" to Job; *Constitutional*: Luk 16:10 — "one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much" — injustice is a settled character trait scaling across all contexts; Zep 3:5 — "the unjust knows no shame" — the constitutional insensibility to their own wrongdoing.

**[CHAR-3]** E — All three implications are present. *Directional*: confession moves from inner (the conscientious recognition) to outer (the spoken word) — 2Sa 24:10 shows the sequence: "David's heart struck him" (inner) → "David said to the Lord" (outer direction, God-ward). *Relational*: every confession is addressed to a party: God (VCG-01 predominant), persons (Exo 10:16 — "against you"), or a public community (VCG-02 corporate confessions). The relational direction is constitutive — confession is not self-addressed monologue but a speech-act directed at a relational other. *Constitutional*: confession engages the conscience (the inner witness), the will (which must agree to name the act as wrong), and the mouth (through which the naming is enacted). The constitutional depth runs from conscience to will to speech.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The name carries primarily *constitutional* implications: the faculty of conscience is a constituted inner capacity, and suppression names what is done to that capacity. The constitutional implication is a malfunction at the conscience-level of the inner person. *Relational* implications are secondary but present: Jer 2:35 — the denial of sin is directed at God ("I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me") — the suppression operates in the vertical relational context, claiming a standing before God that does not exist. The directional implication runs *inward*: conscience suppression prevents the inward moral recognition that should move toward confession and repentance. It is a blockage of the inward-to-outward moral movement that CHAR-3 (Confession) represents.

**[CHAR-5]** E — All three implications are present. *Directional*: the refusal to repent is a refusal to turn — the will is held in a direction away from God and away from righteousness; the turning that is refused would be a directional change. "He did not turn aside from... he did not depart from" (2Ki 10:29; 13:2) — the language is directional. *Relational*: the refusal is against God's law (2Ki 10:31 — "not careful to walk in the law of the Lord") and against his warnings (Neh 9:29 — "you warned them... yet they would not obey"). The refusal is exercised in the context of a relational claim. *Constitutional*: Neh 9:29 — "stubborn shoulder and stiffened their neck" — these bodily-metaphor terms describe a constitutional posture of resistance, not a single act. 2Ki 10:31 — "not with all his heart" — the constitutional incompleteness of the inner commitment.

**[CHAR-6]** E — All three implications are present. *Directional*: "defection" names a movement away-from — the habitual sinner is oriented away from God and toward sin as the default direction. 2Ki 17:7 — "sinned against the Lord... and had feared other gods" — the directional movement is from God-fearing to other-gods-fearing, a reorientation of the will's basic directional commitment. *Relational*: habitual defection occurs within and against a relational context — the Lord who "brought them up out of the land of Egypt" (2Ki 17:7) is the relational foundation against which the defection is measured. *Constitutional*: "habitual" signals a constitutional formation — the will has been shaped into its sinning direction by repeated acts. 1Jo 3:6's "no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him" names a constitutional-relational condition: the habitual sinner lacks the fundamental inner-being relationship with Christ.

**[CHAR-7]** E — All three implications are present. *Directional*: contagious sin moves from inner (the leader's sinful commitment) to outer (the community's sinning) — the direction is source-to-recipient, inner-to-community. 2Ki 17:21 — "Jeroboam drove Israel from following the Lord" — the directional movement is explicitly outward from the leader's act to the community's redirection. *Relational*: the transmission requires the authority relationship — 1Ki 16:2 — "I made you leader over my people Israel" — the leader-people relationship is the medium through which sin travels. Without the authority relationship, there is no contagious sin, only personal sinning. *Constitutional*: the community's inner moral orientation is reshaped by the leader's transmitted sinning — what was oriented toward God is driven away (2Ki 17:21) and turned toward idols (2Ki 21:11). The recipients' constitutional inner direction is altered.

**[CHAR-8]** E — All three implications are present. *Directional*: revolt is a movement away from — breaking out of the governing relationship, moving from submission to independence. 2Ki 8:20 — "revolted *from* the rule of Judah" — the directional preposition (*min* — from) names the movement away from authority. *Relational*: revolt requires a pre-existing governing relationship; the revolt breaks that relationship. 2Ki 3:7 — "the king of Moab has rebelled against me" — the revolt is understood within a prior suzerain-vassal relationship. *Constitutional*: 2Ch 21:10's causal link — "because he had forsaken the Lord" — implies that the inner constitutional condition of forsaking God is what produces the outward political revolt. The political revolt is the constitutional expression of the inner spiritual abandonment.

**[CHAR-9]** E — All three implications are present. *Directional*: sinful speech moves from inner (the corrupted heart — Mat 15:19) to outer (the spoken word). The direction is inner-to-outer, with the speech being the externalisation of the inner condition. *Relational*: sinful speech is always directed at a relational target — God (VCG-02: Mar 2:7; Joh 10:33; VCG-03: Rev 13:6) or persons (VCG-01: Eph 4:31; Col 3:8). The characteristic has no non-relational form — it is always aimed. *Constitutional*: Mat 15:19 — the heart is the constitutional origin; the speech is its symptom. The constitutional implication is: sinful speech reveals the heart's condition. 1Ti 6:4 — conceit and diseased will as the constitutional ground.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The name carries all three implications. Directional: the Ezekiel corpus (M10b-A-VCG-07, 22V) uses ra.sha consistently with "way" (Eze 3:18; 33:8; 33:11) — wickedness is a direction the will has taken, a trajectory the inner person is on. Isa 55:7 reinforces: "let the wicked forsake his way." Relational: the evidence locates wickedness relationally against the righteous (Gen 18:23; Psa 1:1; Mal 3:18), against God (Psa 10:4; 9:17 — forgetting God), and against the vulnerable (Psa 10:2; 37:14). Constitutional: Pro 21:10 ("the soul of the wicked desires evil") and the VCG-02 practical-atheism cluster show the characteristic lodged at the constitutional level of the inner person — soul, heart, and the deepest thought-life (Psa 10:4: "all his thoughts are 'There is no God'"). The name therefore is accurate to the evidence in all three registers.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The name "constitutional inner nature" carries constitutional implications most prominently. Mat 7:11 (vc=14438 — VCG-02): "you who are evil" — the "are" is constitutive, not episodic. Mat 7:17-18 (vc=14439-14440 — VCG-02): "a diseased tree cannot bear good fruit" — the constitutional metaphor directly names the inner generative architecture. Mar 7:23 (vc=14422 — VCG-03): "all these evil things come from within" — the inside is the constitutional source. The name also carries relational implications: the constitutional evil produces relational harm (3Jo 10 — VCG-04 — domineering malice against community; 2Jo 11 — VCG-04 — communicated through association; 2Th 3:2 — VCG-06 — faithlessness grounding moral depravity). The directional implication is that the characteristic generates evil outward (from the treasury — Mat 12:35, Luk 6:45 — VCG-03) rather than being received from outside.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The name carries all three, with the relational dimension most prominent. Relational: to.e.vah is structurally relational — it names the inner condition from the perspective of the one who is revolted (God or the righteous). Every instance is "an abomination to the Lord" or "an abomination to the righteous" — the characteristic is defined by the divine-relational response, not by an internal self-assessment. Pro 29:27 (vc=65959 — VCG-01): the mutual repulsion of wicked and righteous confirms the relational definition. Constitutional: Pro 11:20 (vc=1677 — VCG-01) and Pro 16:5 (vc=1689 — VCG-02) locate abomination in the heart (crooked heart, arrogant heart) — constitutional inner conditions, not merely surface acts. Directional: Eze 14:6 (vc=65984 — VCG-04): "turn away your faces from all your abominations" — the characteristic names the direction the will is currently facing, and repentance requires a directional reversal.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The name carries all three implications. Directional: Eze 11:21 (vc=1631 — VCG-05): "whose heart goes after their detestable things" — the characteristic is directional; the heart is moving toward idol-objects. Eze 20:7 (vc=1634 — VCG-05): "the detestable things your eyes feast on" — the eyes are oriented toward the idolatrous objects. Jer 4:1 (vc=65903 — VCG-04): "remove your detestable things from my presence" — the call to repentance is directional (remove from before the divine presence). Relational: Deu 32:16 (vc=65938 — VCG-02): "they stirred him to jealousy" — idolatrous abomination is a relational betrayal that provokes divine jealousy. Eze 5:11 (vc=65969 — VCG-05): the divine presence withdraws — the characteristic produces relational breakdown. Constitutional: Hos 9:10 (vc=1632 — VCG-04): "they became detestable like the thing they loved" — sustained idolatrous devotion transforms the person's inner character at the constitutional level.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The name carries all three implications. Directional: "active inner scheming" implies a direction — from within outward. Mic 2:1 (vc=38217 — VCG-02): iniquity devised inward at night → performed outward at dawn. The characteristic moves in a consistent inside-to-outside direction. Constitutional: "evil generation" places the characteristic at the generative heart of the person — in the heart (Isa 32:6 — vc=38181 — VCG-02: "heart is busy with iniquity") and in the thought-life (Isa 59:7 — vc=38203 — VCG-02: "their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity"). Relational: VCG-03 (24V — evildoer class) shows the characteristic as relational in its harm — Psa 14:4 (vc=38229 — VCG-03): "evildoers who eat up my people" — the scheming targets other persons; Psa 28:3 (vc=38232 — VCG-03): "speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts" — the relational dimension of deception is constitutive of the characteristic's expression.

**[CHAR-6]** E — All three implications are present. Directional: "expressed through speech" names an outward direction — from inner evil through the speech-faculty into the social-relational world. Rev 16:9 (vc=14352 — VCG-01): people "cursed the name of God" — the inner hardened-will state moves outward through cursing speech. Relational: the characteristic is constitutively targeted at another — blasphemy is directed at God (VCG-01) or at persons through false accusation (VCG-03). Rom 2:24 (vc=14357 — VCG-02): God's name blasphemed "among the Gentiles" — the relational audience (Gentiles) is part of the characteristic's definition. Constitutional: Jude 8 (vc=14354 — VCG-01): the dreamers "reject authority and blaspheme the glorious ones" — the blasphemy arises from a constitutional inner posture of authority-rejection; the inner constitutional orientation (rejection of authority, sensory self-indulgence) produces the speech expression.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics carry all three implications, confirming that M10b names inner evil across every register of the inner-being framework. Directional: Char 1 (the wicked "way" — Isa 55:7; Eze 3:18/33:8/33:11), Char 4 (heart "goes after" idol-objects — Eze 11:21), Char 5 (iniquity chosen "rather than affliction" — Job 36:21), Char 6 (will refusing repentance — Rev 16:9). Relational: Char 1 (against God and righteous), Char 3 (divine revulsion as the constitutive relational response), Char 4 (covenant-betrayal through false devotion — Deu 32:16), Char 6 (blasphemy directed at God and persons). Constitutional: Char 2 ("constitutional inner nature" as the defining term), Char 3 (the inner moral character that triggers divine revulsion), Char 5 (heart and thought-life as the generative constitutional locus). The cluster reveals that inner evil simultaneously has directional (where the will is oriented), relational (toward whom/what the evil is directed and who responds), and constitutional (what the inner person's faculties are doing) dimensions — all six characteristics collectively cover this three-dimensional space.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, all three. Directional: the defilement-state is always moving toward something — toward restriction (from sacred participation), toward remedy (washing, waiting, examination), or toward communal re-entry. The corpus is structured around this directionality. Relational: the characteristic is inherently relational — it affects one's standing before God (access to the tabernacle, Lev 15:31 VCG-08), within community (social exclusion, Lev 13:46 VCG-03), and toward others (the duty not to transmit, Lev 15:11 VCG-06). Constitutional: the name "state" signals a condition of the whole person — not a faculty, not an act, but a status that bears on the person's constitutional integrity as a participant in the sacral community.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, all three. Directional: "moral-inner" immediately orients the enquiry toward the interior of the person — the question is not what the person has touched or done outwardly but what has happened to the interior. The direction is inward, from the surface to the core. Relational: the defilement-state positions the person in a specific relational posture — away from divine holiness (1Th 4:7 — what God has not called the person for), away from Christ (Rev 3:4 — those not defiled walk with him), and in a corrupted relational posture toward God (Eph 5:5 — the impure person as idolater displacing God with corrupt desire). Constitutional: "state" signals that the enquiry is into the person's condition, not merely their behaviour — the characteristic is something the person is in, which has implications for the whole person's constitution (2Cor 7:1: "defilement of body and spirit").

**[CHAR-3]** E — All three. Directional: the defilement moves outward from the inner will of the community to the land, sanctuary, and divine name — a centrifugal movement from the community's inner disposition outward to the sacred environment it inhabits. Relational: the characteristic is constitutively relational — it requires the prior covenantal relationship (God-Israel) as the context within which the defilement of name, sanctuary, and land makes sense; outside that relationship there would be no "name" to defile, no "holy place" to desecrate. Constitutional: the characteristic spans individual and community — VCG-01 shows individual acts (adultery, Nazirite defilement) that have corporate consequences; VCG-02 and VCG-03 show the community as a whole (the city, the land, the house of Israel) as the subject of defilement.

**[CHAR-4]** E — All three. Directional: *external* signals an inward invasion — the defilement moves from outside the person into the person's inner being, the opposite of Characteristic 2 (originating within the person's own desires). Constitutional: the defilement penetrates the whole person — will (Luk 8:29 — overriding all restraint), faculties (Mar 9:25 — speech and hearing suppressed), and bodily agency (Luk 8:29 — driven into the desert). Relational: the characteristic positions the person dominated by the unclean spirit, severed from communal life (Mar 5:2), accessible to divine authority (Mar 3:11), and in need of external intervention (Mat 10:1).

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics carry all three types of implication, but the specific content of each differs in ways that reveal the cluster's internal structure. Directionally: Characteristics 1 and 2 move toward the interior (Char 1 — toward restriction and remedy; Char 2 — inward from surface to conscience/will/heart core). Characteristics 3 and 4 move in opposite directions: Char 3 moves centrifugally outward (from inner corporate will to land, sanctuary, name); Char 4 moves from outside inward (external spiritual invasion entering the person). The cluster thus contains both an inward movement (Chars 1, 2) and outward-centrifugal (Char 3) and inward-invasion (Char 4) directions — revealing defilement as capable of moving in multiple constitutional directions simultaneously. Relationally: all four are constitutively relational but at different relational levels (bodily-sacral community for Char 1, individual-to-divine for Char 2, corporate-covenantal for Char 3, adversarial-spiritual for Char 4). Constitutionally: Chars 1, 2, and 4 each affect the whole person (body, soul, spirit) in different proportions; Char 3 affects both individual and community and extends to the environment (land, sanctuary, name).

questions.question_text: What kind of inner-being phenomenon is the characteristic — an act, a disposition, a condition/status, a quality, or something else?

findings.session_b_note:
The data establishes that forgiveness is **all four simultaneously**, with lexical differentiation across forms. Q039 answer states this directly:

1. **Act** — the discrete event of pronouncing or releasing forgiveness ("your sins are forgiven" — Luk 7:47-48; Lev 4:20 atonement outcome). Verb forms: sa.lach, afiēmi.
2. **State** — the condition of being forgiven (afesis — the state of release from guilt; group 879-001). The recipient enters a new condition as a result of the act.
3. **Disposition** — readiness-to-forgive as divine character (sal.lach — Psa 86:5: God is "forgiving" as a character description). The adjective form names an ongoing orientation.
4. **Quality** — the abstract possession of forgiveness as a divine attribute (se.li.chah — Psa 130:4; Dan 9:9). The abstract noun names forgiveness as something God possesses.

The four forms are linguistically distinct and analytically distinct. The kind of phenomenon is therefore **multiple and layered**, not simple. The vocabulary itself requires this conclusion.

findings.session_b_note:
All four kinds — and this is analytically significant. SD021's four semantic faces of charis establish that grace is: a divine **disposition** (face 1: 888-001); a **condition** created in the recipient (face 2: 888-002 — "this grace in which we stand"); a **capacity** gifted into the person (face 3: 888-004); a **quality** expressed outward in character and speech (face 4: 889-003). Grace is not reducible to any single kind. It is a disposition that creates a condition that produces a capacity that expresses itself as a quality — the four faces are sequential and constitutive, not parallel.

findings.session_b_note:
The data reveals that compassion is not a single kind of inner-being phenomenon — it operates across multiple kinds simultaneously, and the vocabulary differentiates them precisely.

**Compassion as constitutive character quality (disposition):** H7349 ra.chum (compassionate) and G4835 sumpathēs (sympathetic) are adjectival forms naming the settled character quality — what kind of person one is. Lam 4:10 uses ra.cha.ma.ni (compassionate women) to name a character type. The person who is ra.chum or sumpathēs is constitutively compassionate — it describes their inner being, not a single act.

**Compassion as inner movement (event/act):** G4697 splanchnizō and H5150 ni.chum both name the moment of compassion as a movement — a stirring, a kindling, a being-moved. Hos 11:8 ("my compassion grows warm and tender") captures the event quality: something happens inside at a specific moment. Splanchnizō in the Gospels consistently names a discrete event that precedes action.

**Compassion as condition of the one who needs it:** G1652 eleeinos (pitiful) names the condition that calls forth compassion — the pitiable state. This is not compassion itself but its proper object, and its presence in the vocabulary reveals that compassion's operation is constitutionally linked to a condition of need.

**Compassion as externalised act:** G1654 eleēmosunē (almsgiving) names the normalised outer form of compassion — the concrete act into which the inner movement arrives. The semantic development from inner pity to outer giving is encoded in this term's history (Pass 1).

**Summary:** Compassion in this registry is a layered inner-being phenomenon: a character disposition that generates event-movements when triggered by need, which produce outward acts. The vocabulary differentiates all three layers, and the distinction between them is analytically essential.

findings.session_b_note:
Contrition is primarily a **condition** — a settled inner-being state that a person inhabits, not a single act they perform. The grammatical forms of the vocabulary support this: H1793A dak.ka is an adjective ("contrite"), H5223 na.kheh is an adjective ("crippled/contrite in spirit"), and participial uses of H1792/H1794 describe the person characterised by the state. Isa 66:2 identifies "the one who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word" — an ongoing orientation, not a discrete act.

However, the condition has a history: it is produced by a process (crushing, breaking). This suggests contrition has both a **formative moment** (the crushing encounter that produces the condition) and a **sustained state** (the condition of lowliness that results). The data does not describe contrition as a capacity (something the person has in reserve to deploy) but as something that happens to the inner being and from which a posture results.

A secondary classification: in its penitential-relational mode, contrition functions as an **inner-being posture before God** — the orientation of lowliness from which the person stands before the holy God. This is condition-sustained-as-posture: a stable orientation rather than a momentary state.

findings.session_b_note:
The registry data establishes that fellowship is not one kind of phenomenon but several operating simultaneously under the same vocabulary.

**As act:** H2266 cha.var is used as a verb — active joining. Group 7565-001 (Hos 4:17: *Ephraim is joined to idols*) and group 7566-004 (Eze 37:19: God joining the sticks) both represent fellowship as an action event — a specific moment of joining.

**As disposition:** Groups 5367-001 and 5367-002 (koinōnos) describe inner orientation — the person as a sharer-by-disposition in divine nature or in moral complicity. Group 7566-001 (Psa 119:63: *I am a companion of all who fear you*) names a sustained inner orientation, not a single act.

**As condition:** Group 873-001 (koinōnia — vertical fellowship with God) names an ongoing relational condition — the believer's communion with Father and Son. This is not initiated at each prayer but is a constituted state.

**As quality:** Group 7573-001 (Jer 13:23: leopard's spots as fixed inner moral character) names fellowship vocabulary in the service of describing indelible character — the joining is internal, constitutive of who the person is.

**New finding:** Fellowship is structurally plural — it operates as act, disposition, condition, and quality depending on which group and which term is in view. This plurality is not a weakness of definition but a structural feature: the joining-participation vocabulary covers the full range from moment of joining to constituted state of being joined. The classification as "disposition" in the dimension label does not capture this plurality adequately.

findings.session_b_note: Goodness is primarily a quality — a settled characterological property of the inner being. H2896A functions predominantly as an adjective, naming what someone or something is. Agathōsunē as an abstract noun confirms this: it names the virtue, not the act. However, the registry's 12 distinct modes (OBS-067-OBS-048) reveal that goodness also operates as: a disposition (chrēstotēs — the inner orientation of generous goodwill, 886-001 and 886-002); a condition (884-009 — the inner well-being state, shalom-condition); and an evaluative act (884-007 — the divine pronouncement-of-good as a creative-constitutive act; 884-004 — the cognitive comparative assessment). The primary kind is quality, but goodness is one of the more multi-modal characteristics in the programme — it operates across quality, disposition, condition, and evaluative act depending on context and term. (OBS-067-OBS-048, OBS-067-OBS-016, OBS-067-OBS-017)

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-001: T1 as a whole reveals that goodness is constitutively multi-modal but unified in origin. The characteristic's 12 distinct operational modes (Q&A-022) span quality, disposition, condition, and evaluati…
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that goodness is constitutively multi-modal but unified in origin. The characteristic's 12 distinct operational modes (Q&A-022) span quality, disposition, condition, and evaluative act — and yet all share a single definitional structure: goodness is what proceeds from and returns to God. The immediate response varies by encounter type (Q&A-025-026), the sustained effect is constitutive rather than reactive (Q&A-030), and the dimension structure is bipartite — Moral Character for human-subject goodness, Divine-Human Correspondence for divine-subject (Q&A-034). What the tier as a whole reveals is that the apparent definitional complexity of goodness (12 modes, multiple dimensions, varied immediate responses) resolves into a coherent characterological portrait: goodness is the quality of alignment with the character of the one who is Good — variable in its expression but unified in its source and standard.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-008: What T1 named (goodness as primarily a quality — a settled characterological property) is confirmed and located by T2. The constitutional movement identified in T2 (six-step: Spirit → soul → heart → v…
findings.finding_value: What T1 named (goodness as primarily a quality — a settled characterological property) is confirmed and located by T2. The constitutional movement identified in T2 (six-step: Spirit → soul → heart → volition → agency → expression) explains how a characterological quality (T1's finding) is not a static property but a dynamic disposition that moves through the person from its deepest level outward. T1's four constituent poles (ontological, moral-character, experiential, volitional) map directly onto T2's constitutional levels: the ontological pole operates at Spirit-level origin; the moral-character pole at soul and heart; the experiential pole at soul-seeking; the volitional pole at the volitional step. The two tiers read together reveal that goodness is a quality that is simultaneously constitutionally located and constitutionally mobile — it has its deepest root at the Spirit level and its expression at the social-ethical level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-013: T1 identified that goodness is complex in structure — the name "goodness" does not capture the semantic breadth of the vocabulary (Q&A-013). T7 confirms and explains this complexity through the vocabu…
findings.finding_value: T1 identified that goodness is complex in structure — the name "goodness" does not capture the semantic breadth of the vocabulary (Q&A-013). T7 confirms and explains this complexity through the vocabulary arc (Q&A-177): the three-stage development (H2896A's phenomenological breadth → agathōsunē's virtuous precision → chrēstotēs's relational precision) corresponds precisely to T1's finding that goodness operates across quality, disposition, condition, and evaluative act (Q&A-016). Each stage of the vocabulary arc covers a different aspect of T1's definitional complexity: H2896A covers quality, condition, and evaluative act; agathōsunē covers the character-quality and virtuous-resolve aspect; chrēstotēs covers the dispositional-relational aspect. T7 thus provides the lexical grounding for T1's multi-modal portrait — the vocabulary complexity matches the definitional complexity.

findings.session_b_note: Love in the data is simultaneously a disposition (stable inner orientation toward), an act (commanded, exercised, expressed — agapaō is consistently verbal), and a condition (one who is loved — agapētos — is in a constitutive relational state). It is not primarily an emotion, though it produces emotional states (joy, grief, rest). The commanded form (Mat 22:37 — 'you shall love') establishes love as an act of the will, not purely a felt state. The dispositional form (chesed as God's defining attribute, OBS-103-025) establishes love as a stable character quality. The received form (agapētos as identity, OBS-103-040) establishes love as a constitutive condition the person exists within. Love is therefore tripartite: disposition + act + condition — inner orientation that produces acts and exists within a condition of being-loved. This is the most structurally complex inner-being phenomenon in the programme.
