findings.finding_value:
M01-A is a disposition — a stable, sustained inner orientation that governs conduct, cognition, and relationship without being triggered afresh by specific events. Pro 1:7 ("foundational inner disposition from which all knowledge begins"), Deu 14:23 ("cultivate an enduring inner reverence"), Jer 32:40 (God implants it as a "permanent inner disposition preventing them from turning away") all confirm the dispositional character. The nominal Hebrew forms (*yir.ah*, *pa.chad* as "Fear of Isaac") confirm this — fear-of-God functions as a noun, a possession, a stable feature of the person.

**[Folded from wa_session_b_findings.id=67; finding_id=DIM-61-001; registry=fear]**
fobeō (G5399) shows a tripartite inner-being structure: (1) theophanic/miraculous fear leading to worship (Spiritual/God-ward), (2) reverential life-shaping fear of God (Spiritual/God-ward), (3) practical self-interested fear before humans or consequences (Affective/Emotional). This tripartite structure is the most analytically important pattern in Registry 61 and should be the organising frame for Session B analysis.

M01-B is a condition — an inner state that arises in response to a specific stimulus and passes when the stimulus is resolved or addressed. Gen 32:7 (fear arising acutely, driving strategic action) and the "do not fear" corpus (fear being commanded away after it arises) both confirm that B is an episodic condition, not a stable disposition. It is more like an acute emotional event than a character trait.

**[Folded from wa_session_b_findings.id=67; finding_id=DIM-61-001; registry=fear]**
fobeō (G5399) shows a tripartite inner-being structure: (1) theophanic/miraculous fear leading to worship (Spiritual/God-ward), (2) reverential life-shaping fear of God (Spiritual/God-ward), (3) practical self-interested fear before humans or consequences (Affective/Emotional). This tripartite structure is the most analytically important pattern in Registry 61 and should be the organising frame for Session B analysis.

M01-C is a quality attributed to entities (terror is a quality of God's acts, of Leviathan, of the war horse, of the Babylonians) and a condition imposed on recipients (enemies are struck by terror, it falls upon them). It has dual nature: a quality in the source, a condition in the recipient.

M01-D is a condition — the state of inner collapse that follows overwhelming shock, news, or judgment. It is not a disposition (not stable) and not primarily an act (not chosen). It is something that happens to the inner person.

M01-E is primarily a condition (the body's involuntary trembling in response to fear or reverence) with one sub-group (E-VCG-02, "trembling at God's word") that approaches a disposition — the cha.red terms (Isa 66:2; Ezr 9:4; 10:3) describe a habitual, qualitative inner posture of reverence.

M01-F is a condition with dispositional features. The chronic pervasive anxiety (Eze 12:18-19, anchor F-VCG-01) and the covenantal-curse dread (Deu 28:66-67, anchor F-VCG-03) are conditions — states the person is in. The pastoral anxiety (2Cor 12:20 anchor, F-VCG-05) and the fear-of-judgment anticipation (Heb 10:27, anchor F-VCG-04) approach a disposition — a settled forward-looking inner state.

M01-G is a disposition that constitutes a failure — timidity (deilia, 2Ti 1:7 anchor) is named as a spirit-level disposition, a settled inner quality of the person rather than a momentary event. The evaluative character of G confirms this: it is a character trait (or its failure), not an episode.

The cluster spans the full phenomenological range: stable disposition (M01-A, G), acute condition (M01-B, D), attributed quality (M01-C), somatic condition with dispositional subset (M01-E), and condition with dispositional features (M01-F). The cluster's complexity is intrinsic to its scope.

Wrath and burning rage in the primary corpora appear to be primarily a condition — a state of the inner being that arises, intensifies, persists, and resolves. Joh 3:36 (M02-A-VCG-05) presents wrath as a settled abiding condition; Gen 27:44 (M02-B-VCG-03) presents rage as a state requiring time and distance to resolve; Psa 7:11 (M02-C-VCG-01) presents indignation as a persistent disposition. But the condition has a strong dispositional element — orgilos (Tit 1:7, M02-C-VCG-02) names it as a character trait — and an act element in the eruption moments (orgizō in Mat 5:22; Exo 32:19, M02-B-VCG-02). The phenomenon is a condition that generates both dispositions and acts.

But the condition has a strong dispositional element — orgilos (Tit 1:7, M02-C-VCG-02) names it as a character trait — and an act element in the eruption moments (orgizō in Mat 5:22; Exo 32:19, M02-B-VCG-02). The phenomenon is a condition that generates both dispositions and acts.
Indignation (M02-C) is primarily a disposition — a principled inner stance maintained toward wrongdoing. Psa 7:11 makes this explicit: not an occasional emotion but a daily disposition.
Provocation (M02-D) is primarily relational dynamic and act — the action of one party that kindles anger in another. Ka.as is consistently the act of provoking rather than the state of anger itself.
Jealousy (M02-E) is a condition (Num 5:14 describes it as a spirit that comes over a person) and a disposition (divine jealousy as constitutional identity, Exo 34:14).

The cluster evidences a complex phenomenon that is simultaneously: a condition (a state of the inner being that persists through an episode), a disposition (a constitutional orientation that makes one prone to anger responses), and an act (the specific eruption moment). Different VCGs capture different faces of the same fundamental phenomenon.

M03's characteristic is primarily a condition — a state that the inner person is in rather than an act it performs. Grief settles into the heart (Psa 13:2 — M03-C-VCG-01), makes the soul melt (Psa 119:28 — M03-C-VCG-01), presses in as anguish (tsa.rah corpus — M03-D-VCG-01), and drains life (Psa 31:10 — M03-C-VCG-01). However, several sub-groups name grief as also an act: the act of weeping (ba.khah — M03-A), the act of mourning (sa.phad, a.val — M03-B), the act of groaning (a.nach — M03-E). The cluster therefore spans three kinds: condition (settled inner state of grief), quality (the phenomenological texture of sorrow — bitter, heavy, melting), and act (weeping, mourning, groaning as outward expressions of the inner condition). The condition is primary; the acts are the condition overflowing outward.
M03-A (weeping/tears) is primarily an act — the act of weeping — that arises from and expresses the inner condition of grief.
M03-B (mourning/lamentation) is primarily a socially structured act of mourning that externalizes the inner condition.
M03-C (sorrow/inner grief), M03-D (anguish/distress), and M03-G (bitterness) are primarily conditions — the characteristic as a settled inner state or quality of the person.

**[Folded from wa_session_b_findings.id=73; finding_id=DIM-13-001; registry=bitterness]**
Bitterness in Reg 13 operates in two structural registers: (a) affective quality — bitter grief, anguish, affliction (something that happens to the inner person), and (b) dispositional-character state — root of bitterness, bitter jealousy as heart-state, bitter rebellion (something the inner person becomes). Session B should examine whether biblical bitterness is primarily an experience or a condition, and whether the two registers are sequential or independent.

M03-E (groaning/sighing) is primarily an act (groaning, sighing) arising from the inner condition. M03-F (pain/inner ache) is primarily a condition — the phenomenological quality of grief as pain experienced in the body and inner being.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence shows exultation operating as both an **act** and a **disposition**. As an act: Psa 35:9 ("my soul will rejoice") and Hab 3:18 ("yet I will rejoice") are volitional, deliberate acts of exultation chosen despite circumstances. Psa 118:24 ("let us rejoice and be glad in it") is a commanded act. As a disposition: Psa 89:16 describes exulting "all the day" — a sustained inner orientation, not a momentary act. The commands throughout (Psa 2:11; 32:11; Isa 65:18; 66:10; Zec 9:9) presuppose that exultation can be a cultivated orientation, not only a spontaneous response. The characteristic is primarily **an act that can become a sustained disposition** — the volitional-affective surge that, when habituated, orients the whole inner life Godward.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence shows Joy operating as all four, but primarily as a **disposition that generates acts**: (1) **Disposition** — "Rejoice in the Lord always" (Phili 4:4; 1Th 5:16) names joy as a standing inner orientation, not a momentary act; (2) **Act** — the commanded feast-rejoicings (Deu 16:11, 14; Lev 23:40) and the responsive rejoicings (Exo 4:14; 1Sa 6:13; Dan 6:23; Mat 28:8) are discrete inner-being acts; (3) **Condition** — "fullness of joy" (Psa 16:11; Joh 15:11; 16:24) names Joy as a state of being the person can inhabit fully or partially; (4) **Quality** — "joyful heart is good medicine" (Pro 17:22); "receiving food with glad and generous hearts" (Act 2:46) — joy as an inner quality that colours the whole of a person's engagement with life. The dominant register across the corpus is joy as a disposition that expresses itself through acts of rejoicing in specific circumstances while remaining the standing inner orientation of the covenant person.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Suffering-Joy is primarily an **act with dispositional grounding**: (1) **Act** — Mat 5:12 ("rejoice and be glad"); 1Pe 4:13 ("rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings") — commanded active responses requiring volitional engagement; Jas 1:2 ("count it all joy") — a deliberate cognitive-volitional act of reframing; (2) **State** — 1Pe 1:8's "joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory" names an ongoing inner state, not a momentary act; the jailer's rejoicing (Act 16:34) is a state that encompasses his entire household in a moment of post-crisis stability; (3) **Fragile attempted condition** — M04-F (ba.lag in Job 9:27; 10:20; Psa 39:13) shows Suffering-Joy attempted as a desired condition that the sufferer cannot fully reach. The characteristic therefore spans from the attempted (M04-F) through the commanded-volitional (Mat 5:12; Jas 1:2) to the Spirit-produced state (1Pe 1:8; Luk 10:21).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Gladness operates as a **condition and a quality** more than as an act: (1) **Condition** — "it is well with the man who deals generously" (Psa 112:5); "it shall be well with you" (Deu 19:13); Saul "was refreshed and was well" (1Sa 16:23) — these name an inner state of being-well, not an act of doing; (2) **Quality** — "a good man" (Pro 12:2; 13:22) names goodness as a stable character quality; "the Lord is good" (Psa 100:5) names divine goodness as an intrinsic attribute; (3) **Evaluative act** — M04-L-VCG-02's "better than" comparatives (Rut 4:15; 2Sa 18:3; Pro 8:11; 16:16) show Gladness as an act of judgment; but even here the act is a cognitive recognition rather than an affective surge. Gladness is primarily a condition/quality that the evaluative faculty perceives and the inner person inhabits.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Delight is a complex phenomenon spanning four kinds: (1) **Disposition** — the most common form: a stable inner orientation toward a specific object (sha.a.shu.im in Psa 119 series — the law as the psalmist's settled delight; Psa 1:2 — the blessed man's delight in the law as a defining character disposition; Psa 73:25 — God as the exclusive object of directed desire); (2) **Act** — cha.phets frequently marks a specific act of will: Gen 34:19 (Shechem's delight driving immediate action); Psa 40:8 (delighting to do God's will); the diplomatic "as it pleases you" idiom throughout M04-H-VCG-03; (3) **State** — a.nog (Psa 37:4, 11) and sha.a (Isa 66:12) name a resting, luxuriating condition of the inner being; (4) **Quality** — arestos (pleasing, acceptable) and ni.cho.ach (soothing aroma) name a quality of what the inner being produces or embodies before God. Delight is therefore an inner-being phenomenon that is simultaneously a disposition directing the will, an act of the will choosing its object, a state of resting satisfaction in the found object, and a quality of the person before God.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Pleasure is primarily a **quality** and **condition** rather than an act or disposition: (1) **Quality** — na.im/na.em/no.am name a quality of what is pleasant (Psa 133:1 — unity is pleasant; Pro 3:17 — wisdom's ways are pleasantness); (2) **Condition** — the state of pleasantness enjoyed or inhabited: Psa 16:6 (lines fallen in pleasant places — an inherited condition); Job 36:11 (years in pleasantness — a condition of life); Psa 16:11 (pleasures at God's right hand — a permanent condition); (3) **Receptive experience** — Pro 2:10 (knowledge "will be pleasant to your soul" — a felt inner experience received when wisdom enters); Pro 16:24 (gracious words as received nourishment); (4) **Divine inner state** — Gen 8:21 (God's inner calmed response to ni.cho.ach — a state of settled reception). Pleasure is primarily the quality-condition of what is agreeable, received and inhabited by the inner person, rather than an act directed outward.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Wonder is primarily a **state** (a perceptual-cognitive inner condition) that is **momentarily arrested**: (1) **State** — "they were all amazed" (Mar 1:27 — thambeō); "I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14 — an ongoing recognition, not a momentary act); "things too wonderful for me" (Job 42:3 — an inner state of humility before the incomprehensible); (2) **Response-event** — thambeō in Mark is consistently a sudden inner seizure: Mar 1:27 ("they were all amazed"); Mar 10:32 ("they were amazed"); (3) **Sustained contemplative orientation** — VCG-01's "tell of / proclaim / remember / meditate on" verbs (Psa 26:7; 71:17; 119:27; 145:5) show Wonder as sustained contemplative engagement, not merely a momentary flash; (4) **Cognitive-humility condition** — Psa 131:1 ("I do not occupy myself with things too marvellous for me") — Wonder as a sustained epistemological posture of not overreaching one's cognitive capacity.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The seven characteristics distribute across four inner-being phenomenon types: (1) **Primarily acts that become dispositions**: Exultation (Char 1) and Suffering-Joy (Char 7) — both are volitional-affective acts that, when habituated, become sustained inner orientations; Exultation begins as a surge and becomes a standing orientation (Psa 89:16 — "all the day"); Suffering-Joy begins as a commanded act (Jas 1:2 — "count it all joy") and, when Spirit-enabled, becomes a sustaining orientation; (2) **Primarily dispositions generating acts**: Joy (Char 2) — the standing inner gladness ("Rejoice always" — Phili 4:4) that is expressed through specific acts of rejoicing; (3) **Primarily quality-conditions**: Gladness (Char 3) and Pleasure (Char 5) — both are conditions the person inhabits rather than acts they perform; the glad person is in a state of recognized-goodness; the person in Pleasure receives what is pleasant; (4) **Spanning multiple types**: Delight (Char 4) is the most complex, operating simultaneously as an act (Gen 34:19's immediate action), a disposition (Psa 1:2's delight-in-law as the blessed man's defining character), a state (a.nog's resting), and a quality (arestos and ni.cho.ach); Wonder (Char 6) is primarily a state (arrested astonishment) that generates acts (proclamation) and becomes a disposition (Psa 71:17's lifelong proclamatory vocation). The cluster therefore does not reduce to a single phenomenological type but is a genuine ensemble of different inner-being phenomena.

**[CHAR-1]** E — CHAR-1 appears primarily as a *condition* — a state that falls upon the person or arises within them — rather than a discrete act or a stable disposition. The bosh corpus evidences this: "they are ashamed" (stative), "shame has covered my face" (condition received), "my days are spent in shame" (ongoing condition). However, CHAR-1 also has a volitional dimension: the corrective-shame register (M07-C-VCG-03, M07-B-VCG-05) shows shame being invoked or directed — used as a moral tool. And the borne-for-God's-sake register (M07-A-VCG-03) shows shame voluntarily accepted, which requires an act of the will. CHAR-1 is therefore primarily a *condition* with volitional dimensions — the condition can be received passively, resisted by trust, accepted willingly, or deployed correctively.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 is a condition imposed from outside — it arrives through external agents (armies, God, social community) and produces an inner-standing collapse in the recipient. It is neither a discrete act by the recipient nor a stable inner disposition they possess, but a condition that falls upon them as the result of what others do.

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 is primarily an act in VCG-01 — the willful act of dishonoring another: boasting in the law while breaking it (Rom 2:23, vc=35002); showing favoritism to the rich while dishonoring the poor (Jam 2:6); holding Christ up to contempt (Heb 6:6). In VCG-02, CHAR-3 is a condition — assigned or received standing (the potter's assignment, Rom 9:21; nature's teaching about disgrace, 1Cor 11:14). The characteristic spans act, presumption, and constituted character.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence establishes wickedness-as-settled-person-identity as primarily a disposition — a stable, habitual inner orientation of the whole person toward evil, away from God, and toward harm to others. It is not primarily an act (that register belongs to M10 sin-act); it is not primarily a condition imposed from outside; it is the inner person's characteristic directional bent. Evidence: Psa 36:1 (transgression speaking as an inner voice, displacing God-fear — the disposition as an interior governance structure), Pro 4:19 (the way of the wicked characterised by moral blindness — a perceptual consequence of the disposition), 1Sa 24:13 ("out of the wicked comes wickedness" — the disposition as generative source). The characteristic also has qualities of a condition (it is stable and self-perpetuating) and a quality (it marks the person morally). But "disposition" is the primary classification: it is something the person habitually is in their inner orientation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Evil as constitutional inner nature is primarily a condition — a structural state of the inner person — rather than primarily an act, a disposition, or a quality. The constitutional-condition classification is supported by the tree-nature metaphor (Mat 7:17-18 — VCG-02): a tree's nature determines its fruit; the condition precedes and generates the output. It also has quality aspects (ponēros as a moral-quality term — Mat 5:45 — VCG-04) and disposition aspects (kakia as settled inner badness — Eph 4:31 — VCG-05; Col 3:8 — VCG-05). But the defining evidence for "condition" is the constitutional-baseline framing: Mat 7:11 (VCG-02) — "you who are evil" as a fact about human nature, not a description of a specific volitional alignment. The condition is what makes the dispositions and acts possible; it is the underlying structural reality from which they emerge.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic is analytically a compound phenomenon: it is simultaneously a quality of the inner person (what makes them abominable), a condition of the inner person (the state of their heart/conscience), and a relational judgment (the divine verdict of revulsion). The Proverbs evidence (VCG-01, VCG-02) treats abomination primarily as a quality — the quality of dishonest practice (Pro 11:1 — vc=65954), of the crooked heart (Pro 11:20 — vc=1677), of the arrogant heart (Pro 16:5 — vc=1689). The VCG-04 conscience evidence treats it as a condition — a state the inner person is in relative to their conscience's engagement with abominable acts (Jer 6:15 — vc=1680: conscience wholly silenced). The relational verdict (divine revulsion as response) is the frame within which both quality and condition are assessed. The most analytically precise classification is: a quality of the inner moral character that provokes divine relational revulsion, constituting a sacred-boundary violation.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic is primarily a dispositional-attachment phenomenon — the sustained inner orientation of the devotion-faculty (heart, soul, will) toward idol-objects. It is not primarily an act (individual acts of idolatrous worship belong to M10c cultic defilement) but a dispositional condition: the habitual going-after of the heart (Eze 11:21 — VCG-05 — "heart goes after their detestable things") and the active delight of the soul (Isa 66:3 — VCG-04 — "soul delights in their abominations"). The Ezekiel VCG-05 corpus (43V) documents this characteristic as an accumulated communal disposition — "all your abominations" — not individual episodic acts. The characteristic also has a constitutional quality dimension: Hos 9:10 (VCG-04) — "became detestable like the thing they loved" — the sustained attachment transforms character quality. The best single classification is: a dispositional inner attachment of the devotion-capacity to idolatrous objects, producing accumulated abomination as its characteristic output.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic is primarily a generative-dispositional phenomenon — an active, ongoing inner process of producing evil from within. It is not merely a static condition or quality but a process: Psa 36:4 (vc=38235 — VCG-02): "He plots trouble while on his bed" — plotting is an active inner cognitive-volitional act. Isa 32:6 (vc=38181 — VCG-02): "his heart is busy with iniquity" — "busy" confirms ongoing inner activity. Job 15:35 (vc=38208 — VCG-02): "they conceive trouble and give birth to evil" — the conception-to-birth arc is processual. Alongside this generative dimension, the characteristic also presents as a stored condition in VCG-04 (23V): Psa 66:18 (vc=38182 — VCG-04): "cherished iniquity in my heart" — iniquity is harboured as an inner holding. The characteristic therefore has two aspects: generative process (VCG-02) and stored condition (VCG-04), unified by the same a.ven vocabulary.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic is primarily an expressive-dispositional phenomenon: an expressive act (speech) that flows from and reveals an inner moral disposition (wickedness, hardened will, malicious false judgment). It is not merely an act (individual utterances) but the expression of a constitutive inner posture. Rev 13:6 (vc=14356 — VCG-01): "a total inner orientation of defiant contempt toward the divine" expressed through the opened mouth. Jude 8 (vc=14354 — VCG-01): the dreamers' blasphemy flows from their wilful inner rejection of authority and sensory self-indulgence — the speech is expressive of a settled inner disposition. The characteristic also has a social-perlocutionary dimension: the speech acts cause harm to others — defamation reduces the slandered to refuse (1Cor 4:13 — VCG-02) and causes God's name to be dishonoured (Rom 2:24 — VCG-02). It is an inner-moral-disposition expressed through speech with harmful social consequences.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The six characteristics collectively map the complete taxonomy of inner evil's phenomenological forms: identity (Char 1 — a settled person-type), constitution (Char 2 — a structural condition of the generative nature), verdict-category (Char 3 — a divine-relational response to specific inner conditions; note: CHAR-3 is a verdict-layer, not a primary inner-being condition), devotional-misdirection (Char 4 — an attachment of the devotion-faculty to idol-objects), generative process (Char 5 — an active ongoing inner cognitive-volitional process of producing evil), and expressive act (Char 6 — an enacted speech-event). The cluster reveals that inner evil is not phenomenologically simple: it can be a settled identity, a constitutional condition, a divine-verdict category, a misdirected devotional attachment, an active generative process, or a speech-expression. These six phenomenological forms are not reducible to each other. The most analytically distinctive is Char 3 (abomination as divine-verdict category applied to other inner-being conditions) — it functions as a meta-characteristic that applies over the top of Chars 1, 2, 4, and 5's inner-being conditions rather than being a primary inner-being condition itself.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic is a condition — a state the person is in, not an act they perform or a disposition they hold. The verse evidence consistently uses stative language: "he shall be unclean," "she is unclean," "his uncleanness is still on him" (Num 19:13, M10c-A-VCG-07). The condition has two acquisition mechanisms, both carrying their own structure: (1) the bodily-contact mechanism (M10c-A): the condition is incurred through specific physical interactions with defiling agents — touch, carry, proximity, ingestion; (2) the verdict mechanism (M10c-B): the condition is established through authoritative pronouncement — "the priest shall pronounce him unclean" (Lev 13:3 et al.). In both cases, the person is in the defilement-state; they did not choose it as a disposition and they do not enact it as an act — they are subject to it. However, within the condition, the will is engaged: one may seek remedy or refuse it (Num 19:20, M10c-A-VCG-07); one may volitionally avoid what causes it (Lev 11:43-44, M10c-A-VCG-04) or be warned to guard against it. The characteristic is a condition with strong volitional engagement at its perimeter.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Primarily a condition, but with a strong dispositional dimension. The noun forms (G0167 akatharsia, G3436 molusmos, G3394 miasmos) all name states the person is in. Rom 6:19 (VCG-02) — "slaves to impurity" — frames it as a condition of slavery: the will is not free but bound. Eph 4:19 (VCG-02) — "given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity" — shows a dispositional dimension: the person has developed a habitual appetite for impurity once conscience has been silenced. 2Cor 12:21 (VCG-02) — "impurity... that they have practiced" — shows the condition as persistently practiced, revealing a dispositional pattern. The characteristic is thus a condition (present state of the inner person) with an entrenched dispositional character (habitual orientation of will and desire toward corruption) — not a single act, but a sustained state generated by repeated acts of will.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic is a condition with a strong dispositional-volitional generating force. As a condition: the land, sanctuary, and divine name are named as "defiled" — a stative condition of contamination that has been produced by the community's acts (H2931 ta.me adj — Eze 22:5: "your name is defiled"). As a dispositional-volitional generator: the evidence shows the acts of defiling arising from sustained corporate inner dispositions — habitual unfaithfulness (2Ch 36:14 VCG-03: "exceedingly unfaithful, following all the abominations of the nations"); persistent idolatrous lust (Eze 23:7 VCG-02: "she defiled herself with all the idols of everyone after whom she lusted"); deliberate will-acts (Jer 7:30 VCG-03: the sons of Judah "set their detestable things in the house that is called by my name, to defile it"). The characteristic is thus a condition (of land, sanctuary, name) produced by a dispositional-volitional inner reality (habitual unfaithfulness, desire-driven idolatry, deliberate desecration).

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic is a condition — a state of being invaded and dominated by an external spiritual agent, not an act the person performs or a disposition they hold. Mar 1:23 (VCG-01): "a man with an unclean spirit" — the having is a condition. Luk 8:29 (VCG-01): the spirit "had repeatedly seized him" — the seizure is an event producing a persisting condition of domination. The condition arises through spiritual invasion that bypasses the person's will entirely — distinct from all three other M10c characteristics in this regard.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics converge on condition as their primary classification — a state the person or community is in, not an act performed or a disposition held. The stative vocabulary is consistent: H2931 ta.me adj (unclean as a predicate), G0167 akatharsia (impurity as noun/state), echōn pneuma akatharton (having an unclean spirit — stative participial). However, the relationship between the condition and the person's own volitional engagement differs markedly across the four. Characteristic 1: condition at the perimeter of the will (the will engages with the condition through response — seeking remedy or refusing it — but does not generate the condition). Characteristic 2: condition generated by the will's own desire and habituation, then entrenching itself as a prior master over the will (Rom 6:19 — "slaves to impurity"). Characteristic 3: condition generated by the corporate will's defection and extending outward, with the will as the primary generating agent (Eze 23:7 — "she defiled herself with all the idols of everyone after whom she lusted"). Characteristic 4: condition imposed entirely without volitional cooperation, the will overridden rather than engaged or corrupted. The cluster reveals condition as the shared primary category and volitional engagement as the differentiating variable: from will-engaged-at-perimeter (Char 1), to will-self-generating (Char 2), to will-corporately-generating-externally-extending (Char 3), to will-completely-bypassed (Char 4).

questions.question_text: Is the characteristic simple in structure, or does it combine constituent elements; if compound, which?

findings.session_b_note:
Forgiveness is **not simple in structure**. Even at first encounter, the vocabulary and registry structure reveal constituent elements:

- A **subject** (the one who forgives — exclusively divine in OT salach-root; divine and human in NT aphiēmi)
- An **object** (the one forgiven, and the debt/sin being released)
- A **mechanism** (atonement/sacrifice in OT; repentance, faith, confession in NT; Christ's blood as the cosmic mechanism)
- A **resultant state** (afesis — the condition of release in the recipient)
- A **downstream effect** (love-orientation produced in the recipient, Luk 7:47; fear/reverence, Psa 130:4)

These constituent elements are present across the term inventory and group descriptions from the outset. The programme's 14 distinct verse-context groups reflect the complexity — no single group captures the whole.

findings.session_b_note:
Compassion has a clearly complex structure at first encounter. The vocabulary itself reveals four distinct root families, each naming a different constituent dimension:

1. **RACHAM/SPLANCHN** — visceral, somatic, movement-compassion (womb/bowels origin): the inner-body stirring
2. **CHESED/CHANNUM** — covenantal, characterological, steadfast compassion (loyalty/faithfulness): the constitutive character quality of loyal, enduring care
3. **SYM-PATH** — participatory, solidarity compassion (shared-suffering/fellow-feeling): genuine entry into another's experience
4. **ELEEIN/CHUS** — relational, responsive compassion (pity/mercy/almsgiving): the response to perceived need, including its externalised form

These are not synonyms. They name genuinely different aspects of what the programme registers under "compassion." Pass 1 identifies these four families explicitly. SD-016 proposes a three-stage movement model (visceral stirring → mercy orientation → concrete act of giving) that assembles elements from RACHAM/SPLANCHN, ELEEIN, and the almsgiving vocabulary into a developmental sequence.

The structural complexity of compassion is therefore already visible at definitional entry. This has significant implications for T2 (where to locate each element constitutionally) and T3 (which faculties each element engages).

findings.session_b_note:
Contrition is not simple in structure. Three distinct modes of operation have been identified (Q003 answer; OBS-030-023):

1. **Penitential-relational mode** — the spirit/heart crushed by moral self-awareness before God (5 of 9 groups; dominant axis). This is the conventionally named "contrition."
2. **Experiential-anguish mode** — the inner being crushed by suffering, enmity, or divine chastisement without explicitly penitential content (3 of 9 groups; Emotion — Negative dimension).
3. **Substitutionary mode** — the Servant's crushing on behalf of others, producing peace and healing for the community (1 group; Divine-Human Correspondence dimension).

Within the penitential-relational mode, there are further structural elements: the three-fold posture of Isa 66:2 (humble + contrite + trembling at word) suggests contrition is part of a constellation of inner-being states that together constitute the posture before God. It is not a single note but part of a chord.

findings.session_b_note:
Fellowship is structurally complex at first encounter. Finding 062-OPER-001 identifies six distinct modes of operation: ontological participation, moral complicity, volitional alignment, transformational mechanism, spiritual bondage, and cognitive construction. These are not variants of a simple core — they represent genuinely distinct structural operations of the same vocabulary.

**Constituent elements visible at first encounter:**
1. **The joining-agent:** who or what performs the act of joining (divine or human)
2. **The joining-object:** what is being joined (persons, communities, sticks — physical or spiritual)
3. **The joining-content:** what is held in common or shared through the joining
4. **The joining-orientation:** toward what or whom the joining is directed (God, others, idols, evil)
5. **The joining-effect:** what the joining produces (participation in divine nature, moral culpability, hope, purification, bondage)

Each group in the registry specifies these five elements differently. The characteristic is not simple — it is a relational-structural complex with five variable constituent elements.

findings.session_b_note: Goodness is structurally complex — it has constituent elements at first encounter. DIM-67-001 (resolved via OBS-022, OBS-023, OBS-048) confirmed that the 12 modes of operation are genuinely distinct inner-being phenomena. The constituent elements at definitional level are: (1) the ontological pole — what God is in his being (divine goodness as character attribute); (2) the moral-character pole — what the human person is in their inner life (human goodness as quality); (3) the experiential pole — what is genuinely good for the person (goodness as the content of genuine satisfaction and benefit); (4) the volitional pole — what the person chooses and prefers (goodness as the criterion of the will). These four poles are constitutive of goodness as a category. They are unified theologically (all derive from and respond to God's goodness) but they are analytically distinct phenomena. (OBS-067-OBS-022, OBS-067-OBS-023, OBS-067-OBS-048)

findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that goodness is constitutively multi-modal but unified in origin. The characteristic's 12 distinct operational modes (Q&A-022) span quality, disposition, condition, and evaluative act — and yet all share a single definitional structure: goodness is what proceeds from and returns to God. The immediate response varies by encounter type (Q&A-025-026), the sustained effect is constitutive rather than reactive (Q&A-030), and the dimension structure is bipartite — Moral Character for human-subject goodness, Divine-Human Correspondence for divine-subject (Q&A-034). What the tier as a whole reveals is that the apparent definitional complexity of goodness (12 modes, multiple dimensions, varied immediate responses) resolves into a coherent characterological portrait: goodness is the quality of alignment with the character of the one who is Good — variable in its expression but unified in its source and standard.

findings.finding_value: What T1 named (goodness as primarily a quality — a settled characterological property) is confirmed and located by T2. The constitutional movement identified in T2 (six-step: Spirit → soul → heart → volition → agency → expression) explains how a characterological quality (T1's finding) is not a static property but a dynamic disposition that moves through the person from its deepest level outward. T1's four constituent poles (ontological, moral-character, experiential, volitional) map directly onto T2's constitutional levels: the ontological pole operates at Spirit-level origin; the moral-character pole at soul and heart; the experiential pole at soul-seeking; the volitional pole at the volitional step. The two tiers read together reveal that goodness is a quality that is simultaneously constitutionally located and constitutionally mobile — it has its deepest root at the Spirit level and its expression at the social-ethical level.

findings.session_b_note: Structurally complex from the first encounter. The four-mode taxonomy (OBS-103-033) — willed covenantal, compassionate responsive, relational-social, intense erotic — is the first-level complexity. Beneath that, the common structure: directed attachment toward an object, whose moral quality is entirely determined by the object (OBS-103-009, OBS-103-017). The disordered forms (OBS-103-036) share the same structure as the righteous forms. The three-axis directional structure (OBS-103-035) adds spatial complexity: love operates in three directions simultaneously. The tripartite kind (Q&A-016) adds ontological complexity: disposition, act, and condition. Love appears to be the programme's most structurally composite inner-being characteristic — not simple but architecturally layered.

findings.session_b_note: Mercy is complex in structure. The registry contains at least four analytically distinct elements: (1) inner compassionate disposition (*oiktirmos*, *racham* — the feeling toward the suffering); (2) atoning mechanism (*kipper/kaphar* — the act that removes guilt); (3) supplication vocabulary (*techinah*, *chanan* — the seeking of mercy); and (4) the mercy-seat locus (*kapporet/hilastērios* — the spatial-institutional embodiment). *New finding: mercy has a four-element structure: felt disposition, institutional mechanism, petition-response, and spatial locus. These are not synonyms but structurally distinct elements of the same reality.* OBS-111-008, OBS-111-009, OBS-111-010, OBS-111-015.

findings.finding_value: Mercy's definition is irreducibly complex — it cannot be reduced to a single act, disposition, or condition. Reading T1 as a whole reveals a four-element structure (Q&A-017: felt disposition, institutional mechanism, petition-response, spatial locus) operating across four distinct modes (Q&A-022: dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, institutional) with a two-pole boundary structure (mercy as character quality / mercilessness as constitutional collapse). The definitional synthesis is: mercy is the compassionate inner orientation of the greater toward the lesser in need or guilt, expressed through a structured range of mechanisms (atoning, supplicatory, dialogic, institutional), received through specific enabling inner postures (guilt-awareness, humility, persistence), and producing specific inner-state sequences (joy, shame, identity, belonging). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition primary, Transformation/GOD secondary) holds the two poles of the definition together: mercy is a disposition that is also a transforming mechanism.

findings.finding_value: T1 defines mercy as a four-element structure (disposition, mechanism, petition-response, spatial locus) and T2 maps mercy's constitutional architecture across all levels. Reading T1 and T2 together: the constitutional location of mercy precisely maps the four definitional elements. The felt disposition (T1) corresponds to the spirit-soul interface location (T2). The institutional mechanism (T1) corresponds to the soul-level atoning operation (T2). The petition-response (T1) corresponds to the embodied seeking and heart-level engagement (T2). The spatial locus (T1) corresponds to the mercy seat as constitutional-institutional anchor (T2). T1's definitional complexity is explained by T2's constitutional complexity — mercy's definition is complex because its constitutional location is complex.

findings.finding_value: T1's four-element structure (disposition, mechanism, petition-response, spatial locus) maps to T6's finding that mercy is a structural hub. Each of mercy's four elements connects to a different cluster of adjacent characteristics: the disposition element connects to compassion/love/anger adjacencies; the mechanism element connects to forgiveness/guilt/atonement adjacencies; the petition-response element connects to prayer/calling/despair adjacencies; the spatial locus connects to holiness/mind/soul adjacencies. Mercy's definitional complexity (T1) is what enables its structural hub position (T6).

findings.session_b_note: Contrition has a three-mode internal structure: (1) Penitential-relational — the spirit/heart crushed by moral self-knowledge before God (5 groups; primary register); (2) Experiential-anguish — the inner being crushed by external adversity, suffering, or divine chastisement (3 groups; secondary register); (3) Substitutionary — the Servant's crushing by divine will on behalf of others (1 group; unique register). The three modes share the crushing metaphor but differ in agent, relational context, and inner-being outcome. *New finding: contrition is structurally complex — its three modes are not synonyms but applications of the same physical metaphor along different relational axes.* OBS-030-022, OBS-030-023, OBS-030-025, OBS-030-026.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-030-001: T1 as a whole reveals that contrition is a definitionally complex inner-being condition whose structure is determined by its origin (passive, produced by encounter), its constitutional location (spiri…
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that contrition is a definitionally complex inner-being condition whose structure is determined by its origin (passive, produced by encounter), its constitutional location (spirit and heart), and its directional logic (downward into brokenness, then threshold toward divine response). The three-mode structure (penitential, anguish, substitutionary) is unified by the crushing metaphor but differentiated by the agent and relational context of the crushing. The definition tier establishes contrition's primary asymmetry: the person is not the author of their own contrition — they receive it from encounter with reality they cannot deflect — and this passivity is precisely what positions them for divine nearness. The structural opposite (inner self-enclosure) and the blocking condition (merit-claiming) together define contrition negatively as the absence of self-sufficiency before God.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-008: The definition tier (T1) establishes contrition as a settled inner condition produced by encounter; the constitutional tier (T2) maps where that condition lives and how it moves. Together they reveal …
findings.finding_value: The definition tier (T1) establishes contrition as a settled inner condition produced by encounter; the constitutional tier (T2) maps where that condition lives and how it moves. Together they reveal that contrition's definition is constitutionally grounded: the characteristic cannot be understood apart from its constitutional loci (spirit and heart as primary sites) and its constitutional movement (downward crushing, upward reviving). The three-mode structure (T1) maps precisely onto the constitutional evidence (T2): the penitential mode is primarily spirit-level; the anguish mode is primarily soul-level (nephesh crushed to the ground); the substitutionary mode is primarily somatic (bodily wounds). Definition and constitutional location are structurally co-determining for this characteristic.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-010: The definition tier (T1) establishes that contrition operates in three modes along different relational axes; the relational interface tier (T4) maps those axes to specific directional relationships. …
findings.finding_value: The definition tier (T1) establishes that contrition operates in three modes along different relational axes; the relational interface tier (T4) maps those axes to specific directional relationships. The mapping is precise: the penitential mode (T1) corresponds to the human-to-God direction (T4.2) and generates the divine-to-human response (T4.1). The substitutionary mode (T1) corresponds to the only evidence of contrition operating horizontally (T4.3 — Isa 53:5). T1's three-mode structure and T4's directional structure are the same phenomenon described from two perspectives: modes describe what kind of crushing; directions describe who is involved in the relational event. The convergence confirms that contrition is inherently a relational event — its definition cannot be separated from its directional structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-013: The definition tier (T1) establishes the three-mode structure (penitential, anguish, substitutionary); the evidential tier (T7) reveals that this three-mode structure is encoded in the grammar of the …
findings.finding_value: The definition tier (T1) establishes the three-mode structure (penitential, anguish, substitutionary); the evidential tier (T7) reveals that this three-mode structure is encoded in the grammar of the primary vocabulary. The Pual passive at Isa 53:5 (most intensive form of received crushing) corresponds to the substitutionary mode; the Niphal (received crushing) corresponds to the anguish mode; the adjectival settled states (dak.ka, na.kheh) correspond to the penitential condition. The vocabulary's grammatical range (T7) is not incidental — it encodes the definitional complexity (T1) at the lexical level. The two tiers are mutually explanatory: T7 explains why T1's definitional complexity is textually grounded; T1 explains why T7's grammatical range is analytically significant.

findings.session_b_note: Fellowship has constituent elements: (1) an object (what or who is fellowshipped with — God, persons, wickedness, idols); (2) a mode of joining (volitional alignment, existential given, divine initiative); (3) a quality-transfer mechanism (the person participates in what the object is and is formed by it); (4) a duration dimension (momentary companionship → habitual alignment → constitutional formation). OBS-062-019, OBS-062-048, OBS-062-058.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-062-001: T1 establishes fellowship as a structurally complex characteristic whose definitional core (genuine participation-in, determined by its object) is expressed through five distinct modes and whose susta…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes fellowship as a structurally complex characteristic whose definitional core (genuine participation-in, determined by its object) is expressed through five distinct modes and whose sustained operation produces constitutional character formation. The definition tier's key insight: fellowship is formally unified by the object-determines-character logic but materially diverse across five modes (existential, companionship, moral complicity, transformative suffering, ontological). The structural negative (misdirected fellowship) is more dangerous than absence of fellowship — Hos 4:17 and Mat 23:30 present the active wrong-direction as the primary threat, not non-participation. The definitional complexity of fellowship explains why the single English word is analytically inadequate: it covers a range from minimal existential participation (Ecc 9:4) to maximal ontological transformation (2Pe 1:4) under the same label.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-013: T1's five-mode structure is encoded in the vocabulary's semantic arc (T7): existential → companionship → moral complicity → suffering → ontological maps precisely onto the semantic range (Ecc 9:4 → Ps…
findings.finding_value: T1's five-mode structure is encoded in the vocabulary's semantic arc (T7): existential → companionship → moral complicity → suffering → ontological maps precisely onto the semantic range (Ecc 9:4 → Psa 119:63 → Mat 23:30 → Phili 3:10 → 2Pe 1:4). The vocabulary is not a loose collection but a precisely structured arc corresponding to the definitional five modes. T7's grammatical analysis confirms T1's dispositional/act/constitutional distinction: the Hithpael (self-joining act) corresponds to T1's active dimension; the Pual (being-joined condition — Hos 4:17) corresponds to T1's constitutional dimension; the adjectival terms (H2270 companion, H2278 consort) correspond to T1's dispositional dimension.

findings.session_b_note: Four constituent modes (from v1 Q&A-017): (1) Covenantal-objective — external ritual mechanism producing declared forgiveness; (2) Divine relational-personal — personal declaratory act with inner access-postures (faith, repentance, confession); (3) Human horizontal — commanded release of inner claim against offender, from the heart; (4) Intercessory — seeking forgiveness on behalf of another, grounded in God's character not the community's merit. These four modes are layered — each assumes the prior modes are operative. OBS-064-014, OBS-064-015, OBS-064-016, OBS-064-031.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-064-001: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act (not primarily a feeling or condition) whose definitional core is the release of a legitimate claim — the cancellation of a debt that was real, by a creditor who c…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act (not primarily a feeling or condition) whose definitional core is the release of a legitimate claim — the cancellation of a debt that was real, by a creditor who could have retained it. The four-mode structure (covenantal-objective, divine relational-personal, human horizontal, intercessory) is layered: each mode assumes the prior modes are operative. The structural negative (retained claim producing inner torment) is as analytically significant as the positive: forgiveness withheld damages the withholder. The two downstream inner states (love — Luk 7:47; reverence — Psa 130:4) are named with precision: they arise in different contexts (love from having personally received; reverence from encountering the quality as divine attribute) and constitute the immediate inner-being consequences of the act. The definition tier's single most important structural claim: forgiveness is not a terminal state but a transitional act producing further inner states.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-008: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act; T2 maps where the act is constitutionally located. The four modes (T1) each engage different constitutional levels (T2): covenantal-objective mode engages no name…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act; T2 maps where the act is constitutionally located. The four modes (T1) each engage different constitutional levels (T2): covenantal-objective mode engages no named inner-being locus (external mechanism); divine relational-personal mode engages the full constitutional range (spirit, heart, cognition — via the access-postures of faith, repentance, confession); human horizontal mode explicitly requires the heart (Mat 18:35); intercessory mode requires the dependence-posture at the constitutional level of the plea. The somatic compassion origin-point (T2.5 — splagchnizomai) is the constitutional expression of the volitional-release act (T1.4.1 — the act must be chosen). Definition and constitutional location are co-determining: the mode of forgiveness determines which constitutional level is engaged.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-010: T1's four modes map directly onto T4's relational directions. Covenantal-objective mode = God-to-human (cultic ritual mediated); divine relational-personal = God-to-human (personal declaratory); inter…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes map directly onto T4's relational directions. Covenantal-objective mode = God-to-human (cultic ritual mediated); divine relational-personal = God-to-human (personal declaratory); intercessory = human-to-God on behalf of others; human horizontal = human-giving and human-receiving. The vertical-horizontal interdependence (T4 — the structural claim that receiving divine forgiveness enables extending human forgiveness) is the relational expression of T1's layered modes (the horizontal mode assumes the divine relational-personal mode has operated). T1's structural negative (retained claim = inner torment) is T4's receiving-blocked condition (Hos 4:17 parallel — wrong prior alignment blocks reception of right offering; Mat 18:35 — unforgiveness calling into question whether divine forgiveness was genuinely received).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-011: T1 establishes forgiveness as transitional (not terminal); T5 confirms this and maps the formation arc. T1's downstream states (love, reverence) are T5's immediate formation products. T1's sustained c…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes forgiveness as transitional (not terminal); T5 confirms this and maps the formation arc. T1's downstream states (love, reverence) are T5's immediate formation products. T1's sustained conditions (freed access to God, enabled worship, capacity to extend) are T5's longer-arc formation outcomes. T1's eschatological orientation (Jer 31:34 as the forward-pointing fullness) is T5's eschatological telos. The two mechanisms in T5 (declaratory and atoning) correspond to T1's two primary mode-types: the divine relational-personal mode operates through the declaratory-atoning mechanism; the human horizontal mode operates through the heart-level-release mechanism. T1 and T5 together reveal the complete arc from definition to formation endpoint.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-013: T1's definitional structure is encoded in the vocabulary's lexical and grammatical architecture (T7). T1's three Hebrew form-types (act, disposition, possession) correspond precisely to the three Hebr…
findings.finding_value: T1's definitional structure is encoded in the vocabulary's lexical and grammatical architecture (T7). T1's three Hebrew form-types (act, disposition, possession) correspond precisely to the three Hebrew terms (H5545 verb, H5546 adjective, H5547 noun). T1's four modes map onto the vocabulary's grammatical range (Niphal passive = covenantal-objective received status; Qal active = divine forgiving act; human commanded = G0863H in imperative/hortatory forms; seeking = H5545 imperative in intercessory prayer). T7's cross-testament development finding (NT applies divine-forgiveness vocabulary to commanded human forgiveness) is the lexical expression of T1's structural claim about the human horizontal mode being shaped by the divine model. T1 and T7 are mutually encoded — the vocabulary is structured to carry the definition.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-001: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanch…
findings.finding_value: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanchnizō — the moment of being-moved), condition of its object (eleeinos — the pitiable state that calls compassion forth), and externalised act (almsgiving, mercy-act). No other characteristic in the programme review set operates across all four kinds simultaneously. The four root families (RACHAM, CHASAD, SPLANCHN, OIKTIROM) identify four constituent dimensions of the single characteristic, each naming a distinct register — somatic-maternal, covenantal-relational, visceral-immediate, and deliberative-pitying respectively. The structural opposites are two distinct kinds: willed judicial hardness (the hardened heart that refuses compassion) and unwilled prosperity-blindness (Eze 16:49 — the one who does not see the need because they are satiated). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed by the consistent outward-facing structure: compassion cannot exist without a suffering other. The definitional tier's most critical gap — the receiver's inner-being experience — is entirely absent from the data, affecting T1.5, T1.6, and T1.7 throughout. This gap is the single most significant analytical absence in the registry.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-008: T1's four-kind structure (character quality, inner event, condition of object, externalised act) maps precisely onto T2's constitutional levels. The character-quality kind (ra.chum — dispositional com…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure (character quality, inner event, condition of object, externalised act) maps precisely onto T2's constitutional levels. The character-quality kind (ra.chum — dispositional compassionate character) operates at the soul level (T2.2 — chesed as soul-character). The inner-event kind (splanchnizō — the moment of being-moved) operates at the somatic level (T2.6 — the gut as the site of the stirring). The condition-of-object kind (eleeinos — the pitiable state) is the constitutional trigger that activates the somatic-constitutional movement. The externalised-act kind is the constitutional endpoint of T2.10's four-stage movement sequence. T1's definition and T2's constitutional account are co-determining: the characteristic cannot be adequately defined without specifying the constitutional levels at which its four kinds operate.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the v…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the verbal forms (G4697, H7355); the externalised-act kind by the noun forms and compound forms (G1656, H2617B). T7's vocabulary arc (womb to almsgiving) is the lexical expression of T1's range from the most interior character quality to the most exterior externalised act — the same spectrum named by the definition is traversed by the vocabulary. The dual primary anchor (T7) maps onto T1's dimensional analysis: Hos 11:8 provides the evidence for the divine relational disposition; Luke 10:33 provides the evidence for the human relational disposition as moral norm.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-001: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition of being in favour — charis as inhabited state), enabling capacity (the specific power given for specific tasks — 2Cor 12:9), and character quality (gracious speech, gracious conduct — chen in 889-003). No single English equivalent captures all four. The four modes of operation (sovereign bestowal, covenantal-relational sustaining, capacity-conferring, character-forming) correspond to the four kinds without collapsing them. Two structural opposites are identified: pride (the self-elevation that refuses the favour of the greater, active and willed) and ingratitude/gracelessness (acharistos — the failure to register and respond to grace received, which T3 confirms as image-impairment). The immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle) is a T1.5 finding confirming that grace does not bypass creaturely recognition but requires and produces it as a transitional state. The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed throughout: grace is constitutively directional — it flows from the greater to the lesser and requires the receptor's inner-being engagement to complete its operation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-008: T1's four-kind structure (disposition, standing, capacity, character quality) maps onto T2's constitutional levels. The divine-disposition kind operates at the level of grace's origin (T2.9 — God's ow…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure (disposition, standing, capacity, character quality) maps onto T2's constitutional levels. The divine-disposition kind operates at the level of grace's origin (T2.9 — God's own disposition; not a human constitutional level). The standing kind operates at the soul level (T2.2 — Rom 5:2 "this grace in which we stand"). The capacity kind operates at the spirit-soul interface — the specific enabling for specific tasks (2Cor 12:9) is received at the deepest level and expressed through specific faculties. The character-quality kind operates at the soul-to-body level (T2.7 — gracious conduct and speech expressing the received inner character outward). T1's constitutional movement finding (SD021 four-faces sequence) is the longitudinal form of T2's spatial map: T2 identifies the constitutional levels; T1 identifies the movement between them.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-009: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3…
findings.finding_value: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3.4 (affect is the first named faculty engaged by grace) and T3.6 (the agency-constituting paradox of 1Cor 15:10) together explain why T1.5 finds the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle: grace first produces the affective recognition (fear, mourning) before constituting the agency through which the person responds (prostration as the body enacting the inner posture that grace has produced). T1's finding that grace requires creaturely recognition to complete its operation (T1.7) is T3.1's finding at the faculty level: grace requires and enables perception simultaneously.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verba…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verbal forms. The completed-state kind (charitoō — NT coinage, G5487) required a new word because existing vocabulary could not carry the concept of standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state. The character-quality kind (chen in conduct and speech — 889-003) is carried by chen's adjectival and behavioural register. The vocabulary is structurally complete for the four kinds — each kind has a corresponding lexical form. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō) is the lexical evidence that T1's four-kind analysis is correct: the fourth kind (standing as completed state) required new vocabulary because it was conceptually unique.

findings.session_b_note: Covenant is structurally complex — it has identifiable constituent elements that recur across the verse evidence. The elements visible in the data are: (1) Parties — covenant always involves at least two parties in relationship (God-human, human-human); (2) Commitment mechanism — oath, self-curse, cutting ritual, or blood (H0423 alah, karat, dam — OBS-034-007, OBS-034-013, Q&A-014); (3) Covenantal content — specific obligations, promises, or terms (law at Sinai; promise of land and descendants to Abraham; promise of dynasty to David; law on the heart in the new covenant); (4) Sign or seal — a confirmatory act or object (rainbow, circumcision, Sabbath, ark, blood of the covenant, Eucharistic cup); (5) Sanctions — blessings for keeping, curses for breach (H0423 — OBS-034-007, OBS-034-036). This five-element structure (parties, mechanism, content, sign, sanctions) is not explicitly systematised in the verse evidence as a formula, but the elements recur across the different covenant traditions in the data.

findings.session_b_note: Composite — four consistent internal constituents: (a) faithfulness/truth (emet) — chesed is persistently paired with emet [XREG: H2617A, OBS-099-089]; (b) justice (mishpat) — Mic 6:8 pairs kindness with justice and humility as a single moral-relational complex [OBS-099-052]; (c) tenderheartedness (compassion) — Eph 4:32 [OBS-099-077]; (d) forgiveness — same verse [OBS-099-077, SP-099-009]. Internal structure: loyalty element + justice element + compassion element + forgiveness element. Structurally composite.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-099-001: T1 reveals that kindness is a structurally composite, other-oriented disposition — not a simple quality. Its essential character is loyal goodwill (chesed = faithfulness + kindness in a single concept…
findings.finding_value: T1 reveals that kindness is a structurally composite, other-oriented disposition — not a simple quality. Its essential character is loyal goodwill (chesed = faithfulness + kindness in a single concept), constituted internally by faithfulness, justice, compassion, and forgiveness. It operates in three distinct modes — dispositional orientation, deliberate volitional act, and Spirit-produced formation — and these are not alternatives but layers of a single integrated phenomenon. The immediate and sustained effects are distinct in kind: the immediate response to received kindness is receptive and affective (praise, relief, petition); the sustained effect is formative and dispositional (the person becomes the chasid — one whose character is shaped by chesed over time). The structural opposite is the self-enclosed inward orientation; the counterfeit (chrēstologia) is not merely an absence but an active imposture. T1's most significant intra-tier finding: kindness is primarily dispositional, but the disposition is itself composite — removing any one of its constituent elements (faithfulness, compassion, justice) changes what remains into something that is no longer fully kindness.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-012: T1's finding that kindness is composite — constituted by faithfulness, justice, compassion, forgiveness — is confirmed and extended by T6's co-occurrence data. The T6 finding that kindness consistentl…
findings.finding_value: T1's finding that kindness is composite — constituted by faithfulness, justice, compassion, forgiveness — is confirmed and extended by T6's co-occurrence data. The T6 finding that kindness consistently co-occurs with faithfulness (Reg 60), justice (Reg 98), love (Reg 103), and compassion (Reg 23) is not merely a co-occurrence pattern but reflects the T1 structural composition: these co-occurring characteristics are partially internal to kindness itself, not merely adjacent to it. This has a significant implication: kindness cannot be fully studied within a single registry — it requires the cluster analysis that Session D will provide. The T6 causal network (divine kindness → praise + repentance → reproduced human kindness) is the T1 relational mechanism made explicit at the T6 structural level. The T1 boundary finding (kindness is not love, not compassion, not grace — Q&A-021) is where T6's distinction analysis (Q&A-082) begins and cannot resolve without Session D cross-registry work. The two tiers together reveal the tension: kindness is internally composite in ways that make its boundary with adjacent characteristics difficult to draw precisely.

findings.session_b_note: All four, in structured combination: (1) State: shalom as the inner condition of the person (2508-001 — inner peace as felt experience; 2509-001 — welfare as existential condition); (2) Act: shalom as active orientation and pursuit (2508-003 — "I am for peace"; Psa 34:14 — "seek peace and pursue it"; G1514 eirēneuō — actively being at peace with others); (3) Quality: shalom as the stable character quality of the peaceable person (Mal 2:6 — walked in peace and uprightness; G1516 eirēnikos — peaceableness as quality of heavenly wisdom; G2272 — gentle and quiet spirit as character); (4) Relationship: shalom as the condition of the God-human relationship (2508-002 — covenant peace; G1517 — making peace through the blood of Christ; Rom 5:1 — peace with God). The evidence does not privilege any one of these over the others — they are structurally interdependent. The relational dimension (covenant) is the ground; the state dimension (felt condition) is the fruit; the quality dimension (character) is the formed expression; the act dimension (pursuit, peacemaking) is the volitional engagement.

findings.finding_value: The T1 analysis establishes that shalom/eirēnē names a structured four-dimensional reality — not alternative descriptions of one thing but a connected sequence: (1) Covenantal ground (God's covenant of peace, Isa 54:10); (2) Divine gift received (Num 6:26, Joh 14:27); (3) Inner condition experienced (Isa 26:3, Psa 4:8, Lam 3:17); (4) Eschatological embodiment in a Person (Isa 9:6, Mic 5:5, Eph 2:14). These four dimensions are not parallel alternatives but a causal sequence — each presupposes the preceding: covenant is the ground of the gift; the gift is what produces the inner condition; the inner condition points toward its eschatological fullness. This resolves DIM-117-002.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-003: T1 names peace as integrative wholeness; T4 shows its relational structure is not incidental but constitutive. The peace-wholeness of T1 is not achievable in isolation — it is given by God (T4.1), ori…
findings.finding_value: T1 names peace as integrative wholeness; T4 shows its relational structure is not incidental but constitutive. The peace-wholeness of T1 is not achievable in isolation — it is given by God (T4.1), oriented toward God (T4.2), extended toward others (T4.3), and contested cosmically (T4.6). The interiority (T1) and the relationality (T4) are co-constitutive (confirmed from T3.11.3): the person at peace is the person in right relation — with God, with others, and with themselves. T4's expanding scope (covenant → universal) maps onto T1's eschatological dimension (the peace that has no end, Isa 9:7): the scope expands toward the same fullness that the essence reaches toward.

findings.session_b_note: The characteristic is structurally complex — it has at minimum three constituent elements visible in the data. (1) An inner-being source: the orientation, commitment, or emotional state from which the giving proceeds (covenant faithfulness, compassion, anger, trust, obedience). (2) The act of giving itself: na.tan in its specific contextual configuration (bestowing, endowing, giving-over, self-offering, glory-ascribing). This triadic structure (source → act → object) is the constituent architecture of faithfulness-as-giving in the data.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-001: T1 as a whole reveals that faithfulness in this registry is structurally composite and directional. The name ("faithfulness") promises a character quality; the OWNER term (na.tan) delivers an action. …
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that faithfulness in this registry is structurally composite and directional. The name ("faithfulness") promises a character quality; the OWNER term (na.tan) delivers an action. These are not contradictory — they are complementary aspects of the same inner-being reality: the dispositional quality only becomes faithfulness when it enacts itself (Q&A-016, Q&A-018). The triadic architecture (inner-being source → act → object given) is the definitional shape of this characteristic: it cannot be reduced to disposition alone or act alone (Q&A-017). The five operational modes (Q&A-022) show that this single definitional structure produces radically different expressions depending on what is given and from what inner state — the characteristic is definitionally unified but expressionally plural. The primary dimension (Moral Character) grounds this — it is the character quality that makes the giving faithful rather than merely generous. The definition's most distinctive feature is its disposition-in-action structure: faithfulness is a verb that must be enacted to be real, not a noun that can be possessed without expression.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-001: The definition of faithfulness-as-giving (T1 — disposition-in-action, triadic architecture) aligns precisely with the constitutional movement patterns (T2 — constitutive, expressive, transformative). …
findings.finding_value: The definition of faithfulness-as-giving (T1 — disposition-in-action, triadic architecture) aligns precisely with the constitutional movement patterns (T2 — constitutive, expressive, transformative). The disposition-in-action structure is not abstractly defined: it is enacted through specific constitutional pathways. The constitutive mode (Spirit→mind) corresponds to the endowing operational mode (T1.4). The expressive mode (inner→body) corresponds to the self-giving mode (T1.4). The transformative mode (outside-in→inside renewed→inside-out) corresponds to the eschatological operational mode (T1.4). What neither T1 nor T2 states alone: the definition of this characteristic is constitutionally embedded — each definitional mode maps onto a distinct constitutional movement pattern. The characteristic is not defined independently of its constitutional location; it is what it is through how it moves across the spirit-soul-body structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-003: The five operational modes of giving (T1.4) map onto the four relational interfaces (T4) in a specific structural way. Performative and covenantal giving (modes 1) operate through the God-to-human int…
findings.finding_value: The five operational modes of giving (T1.4) map onto the four relational interfaces (T4) in a specific structural way. Performative and covenantal giving (modes 1) operate through the God-to-human interface (T4.1) with a covenantal basis. Responsive giving (mode 2) operates through the God-to-human interface with a responsive basis. Endowing giving (mode 3) operates through God-to-human with a formative basis. Judicial giving (mode 4) operates through God-to-human with a moral-consequential basis. Relinquishing self-giving (human mode) operates through the human-to-God interface. Glory-giving operates through the human-to-God interface. The relational interface is not external to the definition — it is a structural element of each operational mode. What this pair reveals: the characteristic cannot be defined without specifying its relational direction. The same act-concept (giving) becomes a different operational mode depending on which interface it operates through.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-006: The disposition-in-action definition (T1) is confirmed and grounded by the vocabulary arc (T7). The grammatical structure of na.tan (exclusively verbal) is precisely the lexical form of the dispositio…
findings.finding_value: The disposition-in-action definition (T1) is confirmed and grounded by the vocabulary arc (T7). The grammatical structure of na.tan (exclusively verbal) is precisely the lexical form of the disposition-in-action structure: a verb cannot be possessed without being enacted. The full vocabulary arc (T7.1.10) — enacted pole (na.tan) + constituted pole (emunah/hesed/pistis) — maps directly onto the T1 finding that the registry captures the enacted dimension while the XREF vocabulary carries the dispositional. Hos 11:8 as primary anchor (T7.2.5) confirms the T1 finding that the characteristic's most analytically revealing expression is the one that shows the inner-being decision mechanism — precisely because that is where disposition and act are most visibly integrated. What this pair reveals: the lexical evidence independently confirms the definitional analysis. The characteristic is verbally grounded because faithfulness as enacted commitment is inherently event-shaped — it happens at a moment, from an inner state, toward a recipient. It cannot be abstracted from this event structure.
