findings.finding_value: T1's primary dimension (Relational Disposition) and T6's co-occurrence landscape are mutually confirming. The love co-occurrence dominance (196 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T1's relational-disposition classification: love and compassion co-occur at this extraordinary rate because they share the relational-disposition register. T1's finding that compassion is constitutively outward-facing explains why the co-occurrence landscape shows the C17 cluster (love, mercy, kindness) as the primary co-occurrence family. T6's unresolved compassion/mercy distinction (SD-009) is the most critical consequence of T1's definitional incompleteness — the boundary between compassion and mercy as adjacent Relational Disposition characteristics is the definitional question T1 cannot answer without T6 data.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-001: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition of being in favour — charis as inhabited state), enabling capacity (the specific power given for specific tasks — 2Cor 12:9), and character quality (gracious speech, gracious conduct — chen in 889-003). No single English equivalent captures all four. The four modes of operation (sovereign bestowal, covenantal-relational sustaining, capacity-conferring, character-forming) correspond to the four kinds without collapsing them. Two structural opposites are identified: pride (the self-elevation that refuses the favour of the greater, active and willed) and ingratitude/gracelessness (acharistos — the failure to register and respond to grace received, which T3 confirms as image-impairment). The immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle) is a T1.5 finding confirming that grace does not bypass creaturely recognition but requires and produces it as a transitional state. The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed throughout: grace is constitutively directional — it flows from the greater to the lesser and requires the receptor's inner-being engagement to complete its operation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-010: T1's four modes of operation map onto T4's four relational directions. The sovereign-bestowal mode corresponds to the God-to-human direction (T4.1 — primary and dominant). The covenantal-relational-su…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes of operation map onto T4's four relational directions. The sovereign-bestowal mode corresponds to the God-to-human direction (T4.1 — primary and dominant). The covenantal-relational-sustaining mode corresponds to the relational scope (T4.5 — grace operating within and across covenantal boundaries). The capacity-conferring mode corresponds to the human-to-God direction in its supplication register (T4.2 — SD026: grace giving even the capacity to appeal). The character-forming mode corresponds to the human-giving direction (T4.3 — gracious conduct and speech as the horizontal expression of received grace-character). The vocabulary's structural insight (T4 synthesis: giving-side and receiving-side built from the same root, chen/tachanum) explains T1's finding that grace requires the receptor's inner engagement to complete its operation — the vocabulary encodes the two-sidedness because grace is constitutively a two-sided circuit.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-012: T1's dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) and T6's co-occurrence pattern are mutually confirming. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is the co-occurrence ex…
findings.finding_value: T1's dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) and T6's co-occurrence pattern are mutually confirming. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is the co-occurrence expression of T1's finding that grace requires the receptor's inner posture of appeal: seeking is the relational posture before grace arrives, and the vocabulary encodes this (tachanum — built into the same root as chen). T6's structural uniqueness finding (grace is not produced by any other characteristic) is T1's definitional consequence: because grace is constitutively the uncaused inclination of the greater toward the lesser, it cannot be produced by anything in the lesser's constitutional system. T1's definition predicts T6's structural uniqueness.

findings.session_b_note: From the data, several partial boundaries can be named. (1) Covenant is not the same as the love (hesed) that sustains it — covenant is the structural bond; hesed is the relational quality holding it (Deu 7:9 — OBS-034-039, SP-034-003). Covenant is the form; love is the substance. (2) Covenant is not law — though the Mosaic covenant contains law, the covenant itself is the relational bond within which law operates. The new covenant reframes this explicitly (2 Cor 3:6 — OBS-034-061): not of the letter but of the Spirit. (3) Covenant is not promise, though it includes promises — promise (epangelia) and covenant (diathēkē) are distinguished in Gal 3:17 (covenant previously ratified; law 430 years later does not annul it). (4) Covenant is not the same as the signs that seal it (circumcision, Sabbath, ark, blood) — the signs point to and confirm the covenant without being the covenant itself. What is not adequately answered from the current data: the precise boundary between covenant and oath — the XREF of H7621 (shevuah — oath) to R019 (calling) means the covenant-oath boundary is unresolved in the programme's structural arrangement. This is a genuine analytical gap for Session D.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — the data shows at least four levels: (1) Shalom shalom (Isa 26:3 — perfect/complete peace, OBS-117-144) — the doubled word signals the superlative form, the fullest inner peace available to the trust-directed mind; (2) Great peace (Psa 119:165 — "great peace have those who love your law," OBS-117-144) — abundant but not doubled; (3) Present peace — the ordinary condition of shalom available to the covenant person (Psa 4:8, Num 6:26); (4) Absent peace — the condition of the bereft soul (Lam 3:17, Jer 30:5, Eze 7:25). The doubled shalom (Isa 26:3) and the "no end" formulation (Isa 9:7) mark the extreme ends of the spectrum.

Anger is not hatred. Hatred is settled; anger can be momentary. Gen 27:41 shows sa.tam (settled hatred) persisting after the heat of anger has passed — the grudge remains when the emotion dissipates. Deu 19:6 distinguishes judicial killing from hateful murder by the absence of prior hatred: "he had not hated his neighbour in the past." Contempt (M06-B) is adjacent: contempt is a worth-evaluation (treating as beneath regard), hatred is relational hostility (being against). One can despise without hating; one can hate without despising.

Not hatred: hatred is sustained relational enmity; contempt is a worth-evaluation that can be directed at things and words as much as persons. Not abhorrence (M06-C): abhorrence is visceral moral recoil; contempt is cool evaluative dismissal. Not anger: contempt can be cool and comfortable (Job 12:5 — "in the thought of one who is at ease"). Contempt is the cool verdict; abhorrence is the visceral recoil; hatred is the sustained enmity.

Not hatred: hatred is sustained relational opposition; abhorrence is visceral moral recoil that may be momentary. Not contempt: contempt is the cool dismissal of worth; abhorrence is the intense visceral recoil from what is morally repugnant. One can be contemptuous without being repulsed; one can be repulsed without being contemptuous.

Not hatred: hatred is a relational hostile disposition toward a specific person or thing; cruelty is a character quality that operates independently of any specific relational object. A cruel person is cruel even to those they do not hate. Not anger: Pro 27:4 distinguishes cruelty from wrath and anger — wrath and anger are emotional states; cruelty is the quality wrath has when mercy is absent from it.

Not guilt: guilt is an inner conviction of wrongdoing; reproach is the social-inner condition that may or may not correspond to actual wrongdoing. Many verses document unjust reproach (Psa 69:4: "those who hate me without cause"). Not shame: shame can be an inner state independent of social designation; reproach is specifically the social-outer designation felt inwardly. They often co-occur (Psa 69:19: "my reproach, and my shame and my dishonor") but are distinguishable.

Not hatred (M06-A): hatred is an inner disposition of the agent; the adversary relationship is a relational structure. Not cruelty (M06-D): the ruthless person is characterised by an inner character void; the adversary person occupies a relational position that may or may not involve the inner character qualities of the other sub-groups. An adversary can be just (God in Exo 23:22) or unjust (the devil in 1Pe 5:8).

Not hatred alone: hatred does not necessarily take pleasure in harm; malice specifically does. Not contempt alone: contempt dismisses; malice celebrates destruction. Not cruelty: cruelty is the character void (absence of mercy); malice is the positive presence of pleasure in harm. All three can co-occur but they are distinct inner-being realities.

Not merely sentiment (it is commanded — Mat 22:37); not natural affection only (agapē exceeds phileō in reach); not the same as compassion, mercy, or goodness though it overlaps with all.

Not a static disposition (it is an inner movement — triggered, not permanent); not the same as love (love is the prior orientation; compassion is its activation under suffering); not the same as mercy (compassion is affective-somatic; mercy is judicial-relational).

Not the same as compassion (compassion is triggered by suffering; mercy operates in the frame of guilt/authority); not an emotion (it is a disposition exercised in a judicial frame); not unconditional in its human economy (Mat 18:33 — Group 1630 — the mercy-received generates mercy-obligation).

Not merely performance (goodness is a heart-treasury that produces; not external conduct without inner ground); not the same as love (love is the relational orientation; goodness is the moral quality of the inner person).

Not weakness or passivity (the meek king has royal authority — Mat 21:5 — Group 1261); not indifference (Gal 6:1 — Group 1104 requires active engagement); not the same as patience/makrothumia (which appears alongside praotēs as a distinct quality in Eph 4:2 — Group 1104).

Not the same as compassion (compassion is the inner stirring; comfort is the specific directed response to grief); not all parakaleō is comfort (Group 604-b — social requests — is parakaleō in a non-comfort register); not passive presence (the comforter actively moves toward the distressed person).

Not mere proximity or social co-presence (1Jo 1:6 — Group 1055 names false fellowship where presence exists without inner reality); not the same as love (love is the relational orientation; fellowship is the shared-participation bond); not friendship (friendship is love-oriented attachment; fellowship is holding-in-common).

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Not identical with mercy, though they coexist. "Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other" (Psa 85:10, VSG M26-A1-003). The meeting implies distinction. Not identical with God's power or holiness — though paired with them. Righteousness specifically names conformity to the moral standard of right.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Not moral performance — not identical with the accumulation of righteous acts (Eze 33:12–13: "the righteous shall not be able to live by his righteousness when he sins"). Not self-righteousness (Rom 10:3). Not sinlessness — the righteous person in the OT can sin and repent. Not transferable (Eze 18:20). It ends where unbelief and deliberate turning to wickedness begins.

Most precisely, human righteousness is not a self-generated state. The verse evidence establishes a hard distinction between two versions of what presents as righteousness. Phili 3:9 is the sharpest statement: Paul explicitly contrasts "a righteousness of my own that comes from the law" — which he names and counts as rubbish (Phili 3:8) — with "that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God." These are not two points on a spectrum; they are structurally different things. The self-generated version has enough surface reality to be named and contrasted; it is not merely nothing. But it is not the same state. Paul exercised the self-generated version to apparent perfection ("blameless" under the law, Phili 3:6) and judged it as a loss compared to the genuine state. This two-righteousness distinction is not peripheral — it is where the NT's account of righteousness becomes most precise about what human righteousness actually is: received from God through faith, not generated from within through moral effort, however sustained or impressive that effort appears.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Not identical with righteousness (tse.deq) even though they consistently co-occur (Pro 2:9; Isa 33:15). Uprightness names the inner disposition of straightness; righteousness names the condition of being right. One can have the disposition without having the full condition.

**[C — Justification]** Not sanctification — it does not make the person morally better in the moment of declaration. It changes standing, not necessarily immediate conduct. It ends where practical moral formation begins — C establishes the ground; A2 (practiced righteousness, 950-002) is what follows.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Not personal revenge (Rom 12:19). Not identical with mercy — they serve different functions in the moral economy. Avenging justice ends where personal emotion-driven retribution begins.

**[E — Condemnation]** Not the same as discipline (1Cor 11:32: "judged by the Lord... disciplined so that we may not be condemned with the world"). Discipline is formative; condemnation is judicial verdict. Condemnation ends where forgiveness and freedom from verdict begin.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Not the same as intuition, emotion, or impulse — it is an inner act of deliberation and conclusion. It ends where unreflective response begins. Not the same as the moral conscience (though related) — the conscience registers right and wrong; the reckoning faculty weighs and assigns standing.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Wickedness is not merely weakness or failure — it is a governing orientation, not an isolated lapse. The ra.sha is not the same as the person who sins and returns (who is covered by the A2-002 Ezekiel material). Wickedness names a settled condition of opposition to the moral order, not temporary deviation.

**[CLUSTER]** Adjacent characteristics not covered by M26: mercy and love (M05, C17), holiness (a separate cluster), faithfulness (C17). The cluster explicitly excludes these adjacent characteristics even while frequently co-occurring with them in the verses.

findings.finding_value: M01-A reverential fear is not: (1) mere external compliance (Isa 29:13: "lips perform reverence but hearts far from him" — this is not genuine fear); (2) servile dread of punishment (Rom 8:15: "the Spirit of adoption displaces the spirit of slavery and its associated fear" — the fear that remains is not servile but filial); (3) ordinary acute emotional alarm (Exo 20:20: Moses distinguishes "panic-fear — do not fear" from the God-given reverential fear that remains as moral restraint). The boundary between M01-A and M01-B is directness and disposition vs. episode.

M01-B acute fear is not: (1) the reverential orientation of M01-A (it is episodic, not dispositional); (2) the shattering collapse of M01-D (it is alarmed but still responsive; dismay is the state after fear has overwhelmed); (3) the chronic burden of M01-F (it is triggered by present threat, not future anticipation).

M01-D dismay is not M01-B fear: the sub-group description explicitly notes "dismay is the state after fear has overwhelmed — the shattering, not just the shock." Dismay involves the dissolution of capacity to function; acute fear may preserve the person's responsive capacity.

M01-E trembling is not identical to M01-D collapse. Trembling is the somatic expression of an inner state; dismay is the dissolution of inner coherence. The body trembles while the person may still function (Ezr 10:9 anchor: trembling from two sources simultaneously but still making a covenant decision). Collapse in D involves functional dissolution; trembling in E may coexist with continued action.
M01-F anxiety is not M01-D dismay. Anxiety is forward-looking and sustained; dismay is immediate and reactive. Anxiety anticipates; dismay registers what has arrived.

M01-G timidity is not M01-B acute fear. Acute fear is an involuntary episodic condition; timidity is a dispositional failure. The evidence distinguishes them at Mat 8:26 / Mar 4:40 where the disciples' storm fear is called *deilos* (timidity, evaluative) rather than merely *fobeō* (acute alarm): Jesus evaluates the inner disposition, not just the momentary state.

The cluster ends where: (1) other characteristics begin — grief (M03), guilt/shame (M10), anger (M02) all share adjacency with fear but are analytically distinct; (2) the characteristic becomes purely external — the cluster's set-aside pattern consistently removed uses where the term named physical terrain or cosmic events rather than inner states. The inner-being scope is the cluster's boundary.

[E] **Contrast: A vs B:** Wrath-as-judicial-verdict (M02-A) is not the same as burning-heat-rage (M02-B). Wrath is settled, purposeful, and structurally operative; burning rage is thermally intense, eruptive, and consuming. The distinction is within the cluster — the same base reality operating at different registers and with different structural emphases.

---

[E] **Contrast: B vs C:** Burning rage (M02-B) is not indignation (M02-C). Burning rage is thermally intense and erupts; indignation is a principled moral posture that may be maintained without eruption. The difference is intensity and form of expression.

---

[E] **Contrast: M02 vs M06:** Anger is not hate (M06). Hate is an inner disposition of directed aversion toward a person or thing; anger is a reactive response to perceived violation. A person can hate without anger (sustained cold contempt); a person can be angry without hate (the anger can coexist with genuine care for the person whose action caused the anger). Cross-routing flag from Phase 7: Neh 4:7's "collective hostility reaction" toward Israel's restoration sits at the M02/M06 boundary — the inner content there is closer to hostile enmity than to burning anger.

---

[E] **Contrast: M02-E vs M28:** Jealousy-as-possessive-protective-passion (M02-E-VCG-01/02/03) is not envy-as-covetous-desire (M28). Jealousy protects what is already claimed; envy desires what belongs to another. The phase 3 debate retained the jealousy vocabulary in M02 because the dominant register is protective-possession, but M02-E-VCG-04 (possessive covetous envy) sits closest to the M28 register.

Several distinctions emerge from the corpus and from the programme's earlier decisions. Grief is not fear (M01 — terror/dread), though distress and anguish can co-occur with fear; the grief register is characteristically oriented toward loss and relationship, while fear is characteristically oriented toward threat and danger. Grief is not anger (M02) — the bitterness vocabulary was split at Phase 3, with anger-bitterness (pikria, pikros) transferring to M02; M03's bitterness is grief-bitterness arising from suffering and loss, not anger-bitterness arising from hostile disposition. Grief is not guilt (M10) — though godly grief produces repentance and conscience-driven grief is evidenced (Eze 9:4; Joh 21:17 — M03-C-VCG-02), the cluster's characteristic is the felt weight of loss and suffering, not the moral assessment of fault. Grief is not despair (M20-Doubt) — though some grief verses touch despair (Psa 88:3 — BOUNDARY), the distinctive of M03 is movement and expression, while despair is characterised by paralysis and closure. Grief is not weakness (M24) — though the two overlap in the BOUNDARY terms, M03 grief is constitutively relational (it is grief over something or someone), while M24 weakness names the constitutional vulnerability and depletion of the person.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Exultation is not Gladness (M04-O, M04-L), which is the settled warm inner brightness without the surge and directional intensity. Exultation is not Pleasure (M04-J, M04-K), which is the receptive agreeableness without the upward movement. Exultation is not Wonder (M04-I), which arrests and stills the inner being rather than surging it. The evidence clarifies the boundary with Joy (M04-B, M04-C): Psa 14:7 uses both gil_verb and sa.me.ach — "let Jacob rejoice (gil), let Israel be glad (sa.me.ach)" — in synonymous parallel, suggesting the boundary is porous in some usages; but the overall evidence pattern shows exultation (gil, su.s) as more intense, more directional, and more expressive than the broader gladness vocabulary.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Joy is not: (1) **Gladness** (Characteristic 3) — Gladness is the warm, settled, positive inner brightness; Joy is more active, directed, participatory, and commands engagement. The two co-occur frequently (Psa 51:8 — "joy and gladness"; Isa 35:10 — "gladness and joy") but are not identical. Gladness is the inner state of one who is well; Joy is the inner state of one actively rejoicing. (2) **Exultation** (Characteristic 1) — Exultation is more intense and surging, specifically Godward. Joy is broader in its occasions and less exclusively upward-directed. (3) **Delight** (Characteristic 4) — Delight is the receptive inner state of treasuring a specific object; Joy is the active state of rejoicing in what is celebratable. Delight rests in its object; Joy engages with it. (4) **Pleasure** (Characteristic 5) — Pleasure is the inner-being's receptive agreeableness; Joy is engaged and participatory. (5) **Thanksgiving** — the eucharistia sub-corpus (M04-C-VCG-06) within this characteristic is adjacent to Joy but specifically concerns Godward gratitude; thanksgiving is an act of the will directed Godward; Joy is the inner state that thanksgiving often accompanies and expresses.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Suffering-Joy is not: (1) **Joy** (Characteristic 2) — Joy rejoices in what is genuinely good and celebratable; Suffering-Joy specifically arises through suffering rather than from the presence of the good; the overlap is in the agalliao term (shared across both characteristics' evidence), but the determining context is different; (2) **Gladness** (Characteristic 3) — Gladness is the warm inner state of one whose circumstances are assessed as genuinely good; Suffering-Joy arises precisely when circumstances are not good; (3) **Resignation or stoicism** — the ba.lag fragile cheerfulness of M04-F is not stoic acceptance; it is a desired but barely-attainable inner brightness, not a philosophical detachment from feeling; (4) **Masochism** — the suffering-context is not sought for its own sake; 1Pe 4:13's "insofar as you share Christ's sufferings" frames the suffering as the context of kingdom participation, not as desired in itself.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Gladness is not: (1) **Joy** (Characteristic 2) — Joy is active, participatory, engaged; Gladness is settled, warm, and diffuse. The "joy and gladness" formulaic pairing (confirmed in Char 2 Phase 9) places them adjacent but distinct. (2) *Not CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning)*: CHAR-1 is the discrete sinning act; CHAR-18 is the accumulated store of moral crime that sinning acts have produced; (3) *Not CHAR-15 (Generational sin)*: CHAR-15 is the transmission mechanism through generations; CHAR-18 includes the generational dimension (VCG-02) but is not limited to it — it also encompasses individual personal crime (VCG-04 — Eze 18:20).

**[CHAR-19]** E — Three boundaries. (1) *Not CHAR-2 (Unintentional sinning)*: CHAR-2 lacks the knowing-deliberate dimension; Rom 4:15 — "where there is no law there is no transgression" — requires knowledge of the boundary; 1Ti 2:14 — "the woman was deceived and became a transgressor" — deception diminishes the deliberate dimension; (2) *Not CHAR-18 (Iniquity as accumulated moral crime)*: CHAR-18 is the accumulated crime-weight before God; CHAR-19 is the specific act of boundary-crossing that generates that accumulation; the two overlap (Exo 34:7 names both) but CHAR-19 is the act while CHAR-18 is the account; (3) *Not mere social offence*: Gen 50:17 — the brothers' transgression required forgiveness; but CHAR-19 is specifically the *knowing* crossing of a moral line, not merely offensive behaviour without moral definition.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Three clear boundaries. (1) *Not CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning)*: the boundary is at the point of inner knowledge — CHAR-1 requires the person to know the act is wrong and proceed; CHAR-2 occurs when that knowledge is absent. (2) *Not CHAR-3 (Confession)* as such: Lev 5:5 ("when he realizes his guilt... and confesses") shows confession as the *response* to unintentional sinning once awareness arrives — confession is the adjacent characteristic that follows, not the characteristic itself. (3) *Not the cultic-purification process per se*: VCG-02 uses cha.ta in its ritual-cleansing sense for sacred objects — this is not a person sinning unintentionally but a ritual process. The cultic register is included in the sub-group because it shares the same vocabulary and some of the same theological logic (objective defilement requiring remedy), but its inner-being content for persons is minimal.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Three boundaries. (1) *Not CHAR-19 (Transgression as deliberate boundary-crossing)*: CHAR-19 is the knowing-crossing of a known boundary (law-violation requiring a law — Rom 4:15); CHAR-20 is the betrayal of a relational covenant bond (requiring a prior trust relationship); CHAR-20 adds the intimate-bond dimension — the betrayal of someone who counted on you; (2) *Not CHAR-5 (Refusal to repent)*: CHAR-5 is the ongoing hard heart that refuses to turn; CHAR-20 is the active act of betrayal within an existing covenant; the unfaithful person may not yet have refused repentance — their unfaithfulness may trigger remorse (Ezr 10:6 — Ezra mourned the faithlessness); (3) *Not mere social unreliability*: CHAR-20 requires a covenant context — the prior bond that is broken; Pro 25:19 — the treacherous man in time of trouble — this enters CHAR-20 territory when the trust was covenantal rather than mere social expectation.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Three boundaries. (1) *Not CHAR-19 (Transgression as boundary-crossing)*: CHAR-19 is the knowing step-over of a known line; CHAR-21 is the structural inner distortion that bends the moral faculty itself — a twisted mind (Pro 12:8) is not primarily transgressing a law but operating from a corrupted cognitive apparatus; (2) *Not CHAR-18 (Iniquity as accumulated crime)*: CHAR-18 is the accumulated moral-crime account before God; CHAR-21 is the inner structural corruption that generates those crimes — the twisted heart (Pro 6:14) that produces continuous evil; (3) *Not purely physical decay*: Several VCG-05 NT verses (1Cor 15:42/50; 2Cor 4:16; Col 2:22; Rom 8:21) address bodily perishability in a cosmological-anthropological sense more than moral inner-being content. These carry cross-register flags (M23/M35) — noted.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Three boundaries. (1) *Not CHAR-21 (Perversion as inner inversion)*: CHAR-21 is the inner structural distortion of the moral faculty; CHAR-22 is that distortion specifically expressed as wrong-conduct toward others; CHAR-21 is constitutive, CHAR-22 is other-directed and conduct-specific; (2) *Not CHAR-19 (Transgression)*: CHAR-19 is the knowing boundary-crossing; CHAR-22 adds the specific other-victim dimension — injustice is done *toward* persons, not merely *past* a known boundary; (3) *Not mere carelessness*: Psa 58:2 — "in your hearts you devise wrongs" — injustice is a deliberate devising; Psa 64:6 — "they search out injustice, saying, 'We have accomplished a diligent search'" — the active, purposeful character distinguishes CHAR-22 from inadvertent wrong.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Three clear boundaries. (1) *Not repentance itself*: confession is the naming of sin; repentance (CHAR-5's opposite) is the turning of the will away from it. They are contiguous: Num 21:7 shows confession followed by intercession request (the turning); Deu 1:41 (VCG-03) shows confession without the turning — the hollow form. Confession can occur without repentance, which is what makes VCG-03's hollow acknowledgment analytically possible. (2) *Not forgiveness*: Eze 33:16 — the cancellation of sin — is the adjacent characteristic (CHAR-14) that follows confession; the verse evidences what God does in response to confession, not confession itself. (3) *Not mere recognition of guilt*: CHAR-17 (Guilt as inner-being state) is the inner condition that precedes or accompanies confession; confession is the externalisation of that recognition in speech. Guilt is the inner state; confession is its voiced expression.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Three clear boundaries. (1) *Not CHAR-2 (Unintentional sinning)*: unintentional sinning involves genuine ignorance of the prohibition at the moment of the act; conscience suppression involves ongoing non-recognition of sin despite available moral knowledge (Jer 16:10 — the people have been told God's words; their ignorance is not innocent). (2) *Not CHAR-5 (Refusal to repent)*: CHAR-5 is where the person recognises sin but refuses to turn from it; CHAR-4 is where the recognition itself is absent or denied. The boundary is at the conscience's registration: CHAR-4 ends and CHAR-5 begins when the person knows what they did and is refusing to turn — not when they are denying they did it. (3) *Not simple ignorance*: Jer 16:10's people are not without moral instruction; Jer 2:35's person is actively claiming innocence. Both cases involve a failure of conscience that goes beyond mere lack of information.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Three clear boundaries. (1) *Not CHAR-4 (Conscience suppression)*: conscience suppression is where the person does not recognise they have sinned or need to turn; refusal to repent is where the person knows (Heb 10:26 — "after receiving the knowledge of the truth") and refuses. The boundary is at conscience-registration: CHAR-4 = conscience not registering; CHAR-5 = conscience registers (or knowledge is present) but the will refuses to act on it. (2) *Not CHAR-6 (Habitual defection)*: habitual defection is the sustained pattern of sinning without the specific will-act of refusing; refusal to repent implies a decision-point where turning was available and withheld. (3) *Not CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning)*: wilful sinning is the single act of committing the known wrong; refusal to repent is the ongoing decision not to stop and reverse.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Three clear boundaries. (1) *Not CHAR-1 (Wilful sinning)*: CHAR-1 is the discrete act of committing a known wrong; CHAR-6 is the settled pattern that those acts have established over time. The single act of CHAR-1 may not constitute CHAR-6; CHAR-6 requires the pattern. (2) *Not CHAR-5 (Refusal to repent)*: CHAR-5 is the specific volitional moment of withholding the turn; CHAR-6 is the dispositional state that makes that refusal natural rather than contested — the habitual sinner may not need to actively refuse to repent because turning has become so alien to the formed will's direction. (3) *Not CHAR-4 (Conscience suppression)*: conscience suppression is the failure of the conscience to register sin; habitual defection is the settled pattern of sinning regardless of whether the conscience registers it. The two can co-exist but are analytically distinct.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Three boundaries. (1) *Not CHAR-5 (Refusal to repent)*: contagious sin is the Hiphil-caused transmission of sin through authority; CHAR-5 is the individual will refusing to turn. The community members who receive the contagious sin may themselves exhibit CHAR-5, but the contagious sin itself is the transmission event, not the recipient's volitional response. (2) *Not CHAR-6 (Habitual defection)*: habitual defection is the formed dispositional pattern in an individual over time; contagious sin is the causal mechanism through which a leader transmits their sinful direction. The community's habitual defection may result from sustained contagious sin, but the contagious sin is the transmission, not the resulting disposition. (3) *Not mere bad example*: contagious sin involves the authority relationship as the transmission channel — the leader's sin reaches the community specifically because the leader has authority over them. Peer influence without authority is not contagious sin in the CHAR-7 sense; the characteristic requires the Hiphil causative authority structure.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Three boundaries. (1) *Not CHAR-19 (Transgression as deliberate boundary-crossing)*: the same root pa.sha operates in both, but CHAR-8 uses it in the political-military submission-breaking register (peoples and kingdoms), while CHAR-19 uses it in the personal-covenantal moral register (individuals crossing God's moral boundaries). (2) *Not CHAR-5 (Refusal to repent)*: political revolt is a decisive break-away action, not the sustained volitional refusal to turn from sinning; CHAR-5 requires a recognised sinning course that the will refuses to exit. (3) *Not mere political non-compliance*: political revolt involves a positive assertion of independence (2Ki 8:20 — "set up a king of their own") and a decisive relational rupture, not merely passive non-performance of obligations.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Three boundaries. (1) *Not merely offensive speech without inner moral origin*: sinful speech in this corpus is specifically speech that originates in inner moral corruption (Mat 15:19 — from the heart) or constitutive identity (VCG-03). Culturally offensive speech without this inner-corruption origin falls outside the characteristic. (2) *Not every sin that involves speech*: the definition specifies "blasphemy and slander" — the blasfēmia/blasfēmos vocabulary specifically. Other speech-sins (lying, deceptive speech, idle words) fall in other M10 characteristics. (3) *Not the accusation of blasphemy itself*: the false charge of blasphemy against Jesus (VCG-02) is not itself CHAR-9 in its primary form — rather, the accusation reveals what blasphemy is by its false application to the one who cannot blaspheme because he is God.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The forensic-verdict VCG (M10b-A-VCG-01, 5V — Exo 23:7, Deu 25:1, 25:2, 1Ki 8:32, 2Ch 6:23) marks the boundary between wickedness-as-settled-person-identity and the legal-status use of ra.sha. In these verses, "wicked" is a judicial label applied to the guilty party in a legal dispute — it describes a socially adjudicated status rather than an inner moral orientation. This is a cross-register boundary with M10 (sin-act / forensic). Beyond this, the characteristic ends where the falling-away of a righteous person begins (Eze 18:24: "when a righteous person turns to wicked ways" — this is the moment of transition, not yet the settled condition). The characteristic is also distinct from isolated sinful acts (M10): the corpus's primary terms (ra.sha as person-type) consistently describe the person-type rather than the act-instance.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The VCG-01 cosmic-evil sub-corpus (13V — Mat 6:13, 13:19, 13:38, Joh 17:15, Eph 6:16, 2Th 3:3, 1Jo 2:13, 2:14, 5:18, 5:19, Gal 1:4, Eph 5:16, 6:13) marks the most important boundary: these verses name the evil one / evil age as supra-personal powers, which is the M27 cross-register. The evil one is external to the person's constitutional condition; the constitutional condition is internal. The INTEGRATION_NOTE carry-forward applies here: VCG-01 is structurally separated from the personal-constitutional VCGs. The characteristic also ends where the legal-forensic register begins (Act 18:14 — vc=14462; Act 25:18 — vc=14463; Act 28:21 — vc=14464 — VCG-06 minimal inner-being content — these are barely within the characteristic and mark its outer edge at the legal-category boundary, where ponēros names a crime-category rather than an inner condition). Mat 6:34 (vc=14371 — VCG-02 — kakia as "trouble" — M03 cross-register flag-only) marks the edge where kakia's semantic range intersects circumstantial distress rather than moral evil.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic ends at the boundary with M10b-D (idolatrous abomination). The §2 VCG descriptions explicitly separate moral-character abomination (M10b-C = CHAR-3) from idolatry-based abomination (M10b-D = CHAR-4). Within the present corpus, Deu 27:15 (vc=65937 — VCG-04 here) and Isa 41:24 (vc=65960 — VCG-05) and Isa 44:19 (vc=65961 — VCG-05) touch the idolatrous boundary — they are assigned to M10b-C because their primary inner-being content concerns the conscience (Deu 27:15 — secret idol with knowing heart) or the inner faculty of reflection/discernment (Isa 44:19 — absence of discernment). The characteristic also ends where mere sin-act begins (M10): an act of dishonesty is a sin-act (M10); the dishonest practice becoming an abomination specifically requires the divine-revulsion verdict and the inner-character dimension (the habitual dishonest dealer — Deu 25:16: "all who act dishonestly, are an abomination"). Abomination names the registration of the sin-act as provoking divine revulsion at the inner-character level.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic ends at the boundary with CHAR-3 (moral-character abomination) — CHAR-4 specifically roots abomination in idolatrous devotion, not in moral-character failures like dishonesty or pride. Within CHAR-4's own corpus, VCG-01 (Levitical — 6V) marks the inner boundary with M10c (cultic/ritual defilement): Lev 18:22-30 (VCG-01) addresses specific acts whose primary content is category-boundary violation rather than inner idolatrous attachment — these verses are at the edge of the characteristic. VCG-06 (5V — Dan 9:27; 11:31; 12:11; Mat 24:15; Mar 13:14) marks the inner boundary with M27 (concrete abomination/idol-object): these verses have minimal inner-being content (the abomination-of-desolation is an objective sacrilegious event rather than an inner devotion pattern). The characteristic's core (VCGs 02-05) is most clearly CHAR-4; the margins (VCGs 01 and 06) share vocabulary and category with adjacent clusters.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic ends at the boundary with: (1) CHAR-1 (wickedness as settled person-identity): CHAR-1 addresses the settled ra.sha inner orientation using H7563/H7562 vocabulary; CHAR-5 addresses the active generative scheming process using a.ven vocabulary. Both involve the evildoer-type but CHAR-5 emphasises the active inner process of devising and generating evil, while CHAR-1 emphasises the settled dispositional identity. (2) CHAR-3/4 (abomination): CHAR-3 is a divine-verdict category; CHAR-5 is an inner-process category — the scheming produces what may then be named abominable, but the scheming itself is CHAR-5. (3) VCG-01's trouble-suffered register (7V — Psa 55:3; 55:10; 94:16; Hab 1:3; Zec 10:2; Neh 2:2; Ecc 7:3): these verses carry a.ven in the victim/affliction-received sense — the harm that falls on a person from outside — which borders on M03 (grief/sorrow) and M27 (calamity). The characteristic's core is the agent's inner scheming; VCG-01 marks the boundary where a.ven names the trouble received rather than perpetrated.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic ends at the boundary with M06 (contempt/hostile speech/defiant rejection of authority) — the §2 VCG description notes the M06 cross-register flag on blasfēmeō. CHAR-6 names the evil expressed through speech as an inner-being characteristic; M06 names the contempt and hostile speech as the relational and communicative act. The overlap is real but the primary focus differs: CHAR-6 analyses the inner wickedness finding expression through speech; M06 analyses the contemptuous relational act itself. Within CHAR-6, the characteristic ends where speech is not primarily evil-expressive: Rom 14:16 (vc=14359 — VCG-02) and 1Cor 10:30 (vc=14360 — VCG-02) involve speech that calls good things evil — the evil here is in the misrepresentation, not in a directly wicked inner state of the speaker. The characteristic also does not include all harmful speech — only speech that is the instrument of inner wickedness (blasphemy, slander, false accusation).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's boundaries with adjacent clusters are mapped by two primary boundary-lines: the M10 boundary (sin-acts) and the M27 boundary (cosmic evil / concrete evil objects / calamity). The M10 boundary: all six M10b characteristics concern the inner person's moral character and orientation rather than specific acts of moral transgression — M10 (guilt / sin-act) is the act-side of the same moral domain. Char 1's forensic-verdict VCG-01 (M10b-A-VCG-01, 5V — Observation #80) sits precisely on the M10 boundary: ra.sha as legal-guilty-status vs. ra.sha as inner-moral-character. The M27 boundary: Chars 3 and 4 share vocabulary with M27 (concrete evil objects / cosmic evil agents): Char 4's shiq.quts (idol-objects as detestable — M27 cross-register, Observation #81 direction). Char 2's ponēros cosmic-evil-agent sub-corpus (VCG-01, 13V — Observation #81) sits on the M10b-M27 boundary. Char 5's a.ven trouble-suffered sub-corpus (VCG-01, 7V — Observation #82) sits on the M10b-M03/M27 boundary. Within the cluster, the boundaries between characteristics are: Char 3 vs. Char 4 (moral-character abomination vs. idolatrous abomination — same to.e.vah vocabulary, different inner-being content), and Char 1 vs. Char 5 (settled identity vs. active generative process — overlapping evildoer-type, different primary dimensions).

**[CHAR-1]** E — Characteristic 1 (Ritual defilement-state) is not: (1) moral guilt arising from sin-acts (that is M10 territory — the cross-register flags on H2930A point to M10 where the sin-act producing defilement is the focus); (2) moral-inner defilement of the conscience, will, and heart by desire or habitual corruption (that is Characteristic 2, M10c-C sub-group); (3) corporate-covenantal defilement of land, sanctuary, and divine name through apostasy (that is Characteristic 3, M10c-D sub-group); (4) defilement by external spiritual agency (Characteristic 4, M10c-E sub-group). Within Characteristic 1's domain, the defilement-state is not identical to shame (M07 cross-register): the men at Num 9:7 grieve but are not shamed — their state is involuntary and accommodated. The defilement-state ends where the verdict of clearance is pronounced (Lev 13 — priestly re-examination clears the disease), where the waiting period expires and washing completes (Lev 11:24: "shall be unclean until the evening"), or where the water of impurity is applied (Num 19:19-20).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Characteristic 2 (Moral-inner defilement-state) is not: (1) Characteristic 1 (Ritual defilement-state) — the moral-inner register operates through the inner person's own volitional and dispositional corruption, not through bodily contact with defiling agents or authoritative verdict; (2) the sin-act itself (M10) — the moral-inner defilement-state is the condition produced by or accompanying the sin-act, not the act itself; at Rom 1:24 (VCG-02), God's giving over to impurity follows the sin-act of rejecting God (Rom 1:21-23), not simultaneous with it; (3) shame (M07) — the defilement-state is an interior moral condition, not the social-relational experience of disgrace; (4) Characteristic 3 (Corporate-covenantal defilement) — Characteristic 2 operates in the individual inner person's conscience, will, and heart, not in the corporate-sacral space; (5) Characteristic 4 (External spiritual agency defilement) — Characteristic 2 originates from within the person's own desires and choices, not from an inhabiting spiritual force. The boundary with Characteristic 1 is the most important: same vocabulary (ta.me, akathartos) but different locus (inner-volitional vs bodily-mechanical).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Characteristic 3 (Corporate/covenantal defilement) is not: (1) Characteristic 1 (Ritual defilement-state) — Characteristic 3 operates through moral defection and covenantal betrayal, not through bodily contact with defiling agents; Eze 44:25 (VCG-03) — priestly corpse-contact defilement — sits at the boundary; it is in Characteristic 3's corpus because of its priestly-vocational context (guarding the sanctuary), not because it is a ritual contact defilement; (2) Characteristic 2 (Moral-inner defilement-state) — Characteristic 3 extends to land, sanctuary, and name; Characteristic 2 remains within the individual inner person; the prophetic Ezekiel material in Characteristic 3 shows the community's inner disposition producing contamination of the external sacred environment, which is the distinctive Characteristic 3 feature; (3) M10 (Sin-act) — the sin-acts that produce Characteristic 3 belong to M10; Characteristic 3 is the defilement-state that results from those acts, not the acts themselves; (4) M10b (Wickedness/abomination) — the Ezekiel idolatry corpus carries both M10b and M10c flags; Characteristic 3 owns the defilement-state produced by the idolatrous acts; M10b owns the abomination character of those same acts.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Characteristic 4 is not: (1) Characteristic 1 (Ritual defilement-state) — Characteristic 4's defilement is produced by a spiritual agent, not bodily contact with a material defiling object; (2) Characteristic 2 (Moral-inner defilement-state) — Characteristic 4's condition arrives from outside the person without volitional cooperation; the person is not morally guilty for the condition; (3) Characteristic 3 (Corporate/covenantal defilement) — Characteristic 4 operates at the individual level through direct spiritual invasion; (4) M27 (Cosmic-evil agents) — Characteristic 4 is the defilement-state produced in the human person; M27 analyses the character and nature of the unclean spirits themselves. The two are complementary analytical lenses, not the same characteristic.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's four boundary-setting findings collectively map the internal distinctions within the M10c domain itself and the cross-cluster boundaries. Within the cluster: Characteristic 1 is not Characteristic 2 (the distinction is locus — bodily-mechanism vs inner-volitional, same vocabulary but different site of operation). Characteristic 2 is not Characteristic 3 (scale — individual inner person vs corporate-sacral environment extending outward). Characteristic 3 is not Characteristic 4 (origin — corporate interior generating outward extension vs external invasion entering the individual). Characteristic 4 is not M27 (analytical level — defilement-state produced in the person vs agent's nature). Cross-cluster boundaries: all four characteristics distinguish themselves from M10 (sin-act producing the defilement-state vs the state itself), M07 (shame as social-relational disgrace vs defilement as a condition affecting sacred access), and M10b (abomination as moral-character assessment vs defilement as the condition produced by or expressed in abominable acts). The cluster's boundary work confirms its coherence: M10c owns the condition of defilement/uncleanness as a state; adjacent clusters own the acts that produce it (M10, M10b), the social consequences of it (M07), and the agents that produce it (M27).

questions.question_text: In what distinct mode(s) does the characteristic operate within the inner person in this verse — including its grammatical/stem form and the manner of functioning?

findings.session_b_note:
Q003 answer and OBS-064-003 together establish four distinct modes, each with supporting evidence:

1. **As divine vertical act:** God releases the person from guilt and penalty — the inner person receives a new standing before God (groups 5377-001, 5379-001, 5379-002, 5379-003, 879-001). This mode operates from outside the person inward.

2. **As human horizontal act:** The person releases another from the inner claim of injury (group 5377-002). This mode is commanded, volitional, and operates from within the person outward toward another.

3. **As disposition (readiness-to-pardon):** Sal.lach (Psa 86:5) names forgiveness as a settled character orientation — not a discrete act but an abiding posture of the inner being. This mode is constitutional rather than episodic.

4. **As received condition:** Afesis (G0859, groups 879-001, 879-002) names the state of being forgiven — the condition the inner person occupies as a result of the divine act. This mode is passive — it is what the inner person *is* rather than what they *do*.

F-003 adds a fifth mode: **as structural enabler** — forgiveness received creates the inner conditions from which horizontal forgiveness flows. This is the indirect mode: divine forgiveness → inner transformation → human forgiveness.

findings.session_b_note:
At least six distinct modes: (1) Sovereign bestowal — grace given from above, constituting the recipient's standing (888-001, 889-001); (2) Relational standing — the condition of being-in-grace (888-002: "this grace in which we stand"); (3) Enabling power — animating force of ministry and identity (888-004; 1Cor 15:10); (4) Forgiving act — release of debt patterned on divine forgiveness (5470-002); (5) Character quality — gracious disposition expressed in speech and conduct (889-003); (6) Supplication posture — the appeal of the creature to the greater for what it cannot supply (890-001).

*Consistent with prior analysis (SD021, 11 verse context groups). Adds structure: six named modes — more complete than SD021's four-face model. Modes 4 (forgiving), 5 (character quality), and 6 (supplication) were not explicitly included in SD021's sequential model.*

findings.session_b_note:
The data reveals four distinct modes of operation, mapped to the four root families identified in Pass 1:

**Mode 1 — Visceral stirring (RACHAM/SPLANCHN):** Compassion operates as a somatic event — an involuntary inner movement triggered by the perception of suffering. Splanchnizō and ni.chum both name this mode. It is pre-volitional in character: the movement happens before the person chooses to act. Hos 11:8 captures this vividly: the divine inner life is moved before judgment can proceed.

**Mode 2 — Constitutive character quality (CHESED/CHANNUM):** Compassion operates as a settled inner disposition that defines what kind of person one is. Ra.chum (compassionate), sumpathēs (sympathetic), and channum (gracious) all name this mode. The characteristic is not merely something that happens — it is something one is. This mode operates continuously rather than in response to specific triggers.

**Mode 3 — Participatory solidarity (SYM-PATH):** Compassion operates as genuine entry into another's experience. Sumpatheō and sumpaschō name this mode — not feeling-for but feeling-with, suffering-with. This mode involves a constitutional movement toward the other's inner space, not merely an emotional response to their condition from one's own.

**Mode 4 — Responsive pity and mercy (ELEEIN/CHUS):** Compassion operates as a relational response to perceived need — the inner impulse to spare, to help, to give. This mode is the most explicitly action-generating: eleēmosunē (almsgiving) is its normalised social form. Chus names the pity that naturally arises toward the needy; eleeinos names the pitiable condition that calls it forth.

Three modes, as established in Q003 and OBS-030-023, OBS-030-025, OBS-030-026:

1. **Penitential-relational mode**: The spirit and heart are crushed by moral self-awareness before God; the inner being is brought low; this posture draws divine nearness, revival, and acceptance. Dominant mode (5 of 9 groups, Dependence/Creatureliness dimension).

2. **Experiential-anguish mode**: The inner being is crushed by suffering, enmity, or divine chastisement. No explicitly penitential element; the inner state is grief/dismay/pain. Three groups: enemy-produced anguish (Psa 143:3), corporate desolation under divine crushing (Psa 44:19), inner terror under military defeat (Jer 46:5).

3. **Substitutionary mode**: The Servant's inner person is crushed on behalf of others' iniquity, producing peace and healing for the community (Isa 53:5). Unique — operates through vicarious bearing rather than personal moral self-awareness. One group, Divine-Human Correspondence dimension.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-001: T1 as a whole reveals that goodness is constitutively multi-modal but unified in origin. The characteristic's 12 distinct operational modes (Q&A-022) span quality, disposition, condition, and evaluati…
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that goodness is constitutively multi-modal but unified in origin. The characteristic's 12 distinct operational modes (Q&A-022) span quality, disposition, condition, and evaluative act — and yet all share a single definitional structure: goodness is what proceeds from and returns to God. The immediate response varies by encounter type (Q&A-025-026), the sustained effect is constitutive rather than reactive (Q&A-030), and the dimension structure is bipartite — Moral Character for human-subject goodness, Divine-Human Correspondence for divine-subject (Q&A-034). What the tier as a whole reveals is that the apparent definitional complexity of goodness (12 modes, multiple dimensions, varied immediate responses) resolves into a coherent characterological portrait: goodness is the quality of alignment with the character of the one who is Good — variable in its expression but unified in its source and standard.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-009: T1 identified goodness as an integrating characteristic with 12 modes of operation. T3 confirms the mechanism of integration: goodness is integrating because it engages and aligns every inner faculty …
findings.finding_value: T1 identified goodness as an integrating characteristic with 12 modes of operation. T3 confirms the mechanism of integration: goodness is integrating because it engages and aligns every inner faculty simultaneously. The T1 finding that goodness has a communicative mode (doxological declaration and divine revelatory speech — Q&A-024) connects to T3's perceptual (Q&A-066) and relational (Q&A-096) faculty findings: the communicative mode of goodness engages perception (tasting and seeing), activates conscience (the divine word naming what is good calibrates the conscience's standard), and builds relational capacity (community-forming declaration). The T3 finding that goodness is fundamentally integrating (Q&A-095) is what makes its T1 multi-modality coherent: the 12 modes are not fragmented operations but facets of a single faculty-integrating reality.

findings.session_b_note:
Four primary modes of operation, each evidenced across the anchor verse corpus:
(1) **Covenantal-dispositional mode** (chesed, agapē): Love as stable inner orientation of faithful loyalty — not feeling-contingent, not revocable by the beloved's failure. God's chesed 'never ceases' (Lam 3:22, OBS-103-088); human chesed is written on the heart as character (Pro 3:3, OBS-103-090). This mode operates at the level of character — the deep stable orientation.
(2) **Compassionate-responsive mode** (racham, splanchnizō): Love that is activated by the beloved's suffering — the inner-organ movement (OBS-103-105, OBS-103-116). This mode responds to need; it is not passive but activated.
(3) **Volitional-costly mode** (agapē — enemy-love, self-giving): Love that operates against the inner grain of natural preference. Mat 5:44 (OBS-103-143), Joh 15:13 (OBS-103-125). This mode requires the will's deliberate engagement to exceed what natural affection would produce.
(4) **Affective-relational mode** (phileō, ahavah-intense, dod): Love as naturally felt warm attachment — the affection for friends, the longing for the beloved. This mode is experienced; it is love in its felt dimension.
The four modes are not always distinguishable in a single verse but are analytically distinct operations of the same inner orientation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-103-001: Love's definition resolves to a structured family of inner-being orientations sharing one mechanism — directed attachment toward an object — whose moral character is entirely determined by the object …
findings.finding_value: Love's definition resolves to a structured family of inner-being orientations sharing one mechanism — directed attachment toward an object — whose moral character is entirely determined by the object chosen. Within this shared mechanism, the vocabulary distinguishes three structural registers: love as disposition (the stable inner orientation — chesed, agapē as character), love as act (the commanded and exercised expression — agapaō, enemy-love), and love as condition (the identity-constituting state of being-loved — agapētos). These are not three separate loves but three aspects of love's single operation: the person has a deep stable orientation (disposition), exercises it in specific acts (act), and exists within the love-relationship as constituted by it (condition). The vocabulary arc runs from the ontologically highest (God is love — 1Jo 4:8) through the morally normative (chesed, commanded agapē) to the affective-natural (phileō, dod) to the morally inverted (love of darkness, love of self). No other characteristic in the programme commands a comparable vocabulary range. The definition's boundary with adjacent characteristics (compassion, mercy, kindness) is partially drawn: love is the broader orientation; compassion is love's suffering-triggered mode; mercy and kindness are love's formal relational expressions. The boundaries require Session D precision.

findings.session_b_note: Four distinct modes of operation emerge from the data: (1) Disposition mode — mercy as stable inner orientation (Col 3:12 — "compassionate hearts"; Mat 5:7 — "the merciful"); (2) Atoning mechanism mode — mercy as atoning act covering guilt (Lev 4:20, Psa 78:38); (3) Petition-response mode — mercy as the dynamic of supplication answered (Luk 18:13; Gen 25:21; Dan 2:18); (4) Naming/institutional mode — mercy given spatial and calendar form (mercy seat, Day of Atonement). *New finding: mercy operates in four structurally distinct modes — dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, and institutional — that together constitute its full operational range.* OBS-111-015, OBS-111-016, OBS-111-047, OBS-111-056.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-111-001: Mercy's definition is irreducibly complex — it cannot be reduced to a single act, disposition, or condition. Reading T1 as a whole reveals a four-element structure (Q&A-017: felt disposition, institut…
findings.finding_value: Mercy's definition is irreducibly complex — it cannot be reduced to a single act, disposition, or condition. Reading T1 as a whole reveals a four-element structure (Q&A-017: felt disposition, institutional mechanism, petition-response, spatial locus) operating across four distinct modes (Q&A-022: dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, institutional) with a two-pole boundary structure (mercy as character quality / mercilessness as constitutional collapse). The definitional synthesis is: mercy is the compassionate inner orientation of the greater toward the lesser in need or guilt, expressed through a structured range of mechanisms (atoning, supplicatory, dialogic, institutional), received through specific enabling inner postures (guilt-awareness, humility, persistence), and producing specific inner-state sequences (joy, shame, identity, belonging). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition primary, Transformation/GOD secondary) holds the two poles of the definition together: mercy is a disposition that is also a transforming mechanism.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-009: T1 identifies the enabling conditions for mercy-reception (guilt-awareness, humility, persistence, soul-affliction) and T3 maps mercy's faculty engagements. Reading T1 and T3 together: the enabling co…
findings.finding_value: T1 identifies the enabling conditions for mercy-reception (guilt-awareness, humility, persistence, soul-affliction) and T3 maps mercy's faculty engagements. Reading T1 and T3 together: the enabling conditions for mercy-reception (T1) are precisely the conditions that require the full faculty activation identified in T3. Guilt-awareness requires conscience (T3.9) and moral evaluation (T3.8); humility requires affect (T3.4) and embodied posture; persistence requires volition (T3.6) and agency (T3.7); soul-affliction requires affect (T3.4) and relational capacity (T3.11). T1's enabling conditions are T3's faculty activation in a single moment — mercy-reception requires the whole inner faculty system to be engaged.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-010: T1's four modes of mercy's operation (dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, institutional) map directly onto T4's four relational directions. The dispositional mode corresponds to God→human mercy (sove…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes of mercy's operation (dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, institutional) map directly onto T4's four relational directions. The dispositional mode corresponds to God→human mercy (sovereign disposition). The mechanical mode corresponds to the atoning mechanism of the God→human direction. The dialogic (petition-response) mode corresponds to the human→God direction. The institutional mode (mercy seat, Day of Atonement) structures all three directions simultaneously. T1 and T4 together: mercy's operational modes are relationally differentiated — each mode is specific to a relational direction, and together they constitute the full relational architecture of mercy.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-012: T1's four-element structure (disposition, mechanism, petition-response, spatial locus) maps to T6's finding that mercy is a structural hub. Each of mercy's four elements connects to a different cluste…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-element structure (disposition, mechanism, petition-response, spatial locus) maps to T6's finding that mercy is a structural hub. Each of mercy's four elements connects to a different cluster of adjacent characteristics: the disposition element connects to compassion/love/anger adjacencies; the mechanism element connects to forgiveness/guilt/atonement adjacencies; the petition-response element connects to prayer/calling/despair adjacencies; the spatial locus connects to holiness/mind/soul adjacencies. Mercy's definitional complexity (T1) is what enables its structural hub position (T6).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-030-001: T1 as a whole reveals that contrition is a definitionally complex inner-being condition whose structure is determined by its origin (passive, produced by encounter), its constitutional location (spiri…
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that contrition is a definitionally complex inner-being condition whose structure is determined by its origin (passive, produced by encounter), its constitutional location (spirit and heart), and its directional logic (downward into brokenness, then threshold toward divine response). The three-mode structure (penitential, anguish, substitutionary) is unified by the crushing metaphor but differentiated by the agent and relational context of the crushing. The definition tier establishes contrition's primary asymmetry: the person is not the author of their own contrition — they receive it from encounter with reality they cannot deflect — and this passivity is precisely what positions them for divine nearness. The structural opposite (inner self-enclosure) and the blocking condition (merit-claiming) together define contrition negatively as the absence of self-sufficiency before God.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-010: The definition tier (T1) establishes that contrition operates in three modes along different relational axes; the relational interface tier (T4) maps those axes to specific directional relationships. …
findings.finding_value: The definition tier (T1) establishes that contrition operates in three modes along different relational axes; the relational interface tier (T4) maps those axes to specific directional relationships. The mapping is precise: the penitential mode (T1) corresponds to the human-to-God direction (T4.2) and generates the divine-to-human response (T4.1). The substitutionary mode (T1) corresponds to the only evidence of contrition operating horizontally (T4.3 — Isa 53:5). T1's three-mode structure and T4's directional structure are the same phenomenon described from two perspectives: modes describe what kind of crushing; directions describe who is involved in the relational event. The convergence confirms that contrition is inherently a relational event — its definition cannot be separated from its directional structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-011: The definition tier (T1) positions contrition as a threshold event (not an end-state but a passage toward divine response); the formative tier (T5) confirms and extends this by showing that contrition…
findings.finding_value: The definition tier (T1) positions contrition as a threshold event (not an end-state but a passage toward divine response); the formative tier (T5) confirms and extends this by showing that contrition's productive function is precisely its threshold character — it is the recurring event through which the person is returned to receptivity. T1's sequence (crushing → contrite posture → divine response) maps directly onto T5's formative arc (dissolution-through-encounter → contrite state → character of lowliness formed through repeated cycles). The definitional claim that contrition is a passage rather than a terminal state (T1) is confirmed by T5's formation account: the sustainable inner posture produced is not permanent brokenness but the characterological lowliness that emerges from repeated breaking-and-reviving.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-062-001: T1 establishes fellowship as a structurally complex characteristic whose definitional core (genuine participation-in, determined by its object) is expressed through five distinct modes and whose susta…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes fellowship as a structurally complex characteristic whose definitional core (genuine participation-in, determined by its object) is expressed through five distinct modes and whose sustained operation produces constitutional character formation. The definition tier's key insight: fellowship is formally unified by the object-determines-character logic but materially diverse across five modes (existential, companionship, moral complicity, transformative suffering, ontological). The structural negative (misdirected fellowship) is more dangerous than absence of fellowship — Hos 4:17 and Mat 23:30 present the active wrong-direction as the primary threat, not non-participation. The definitional complexity of fellowship explains why the single English word is analytically inadequate: it covers a range from minimal existential participation (Ecc 9:4) to maximal ontological transformation (2Pe 1:4) under the same label.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-008: T1's five-mode structure maps precisely onto T2's constitutional levels: existential mode (soul/nephesh), companionship mode (heart), desire-driven mode (desire-faculty), suffering mode (somatic), ont…
findings.finding_value: T1's five-mode structure maps precisely onto T2's constitutional levels: existential mode (soul/nephesh), companionship mode (heart), desire-driven mode (desire-faculty), suffering mode (somatic), ontological mode (spirit — inferential). Definition and constitutional location are co-determining: the mode of fellowship determines the constitutional level at which it operates. The T1 definition (object determines character) is confirmed by T2's constitutional evidence — the desire-faculty as the constitutional engine of fellowship direction means desire determines the object, and the object determines which constitutional level is most engaged.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-009: T1 establishes that fellowship is object-determined and progressively constitutional; T3 shows that fellowship shapes every inner faculty in conformity with its object. These are two descriptions of t…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes that fellowship is object-determined and progressively constitutional; T3 shows that fellowship shapes every inner faculty in conformity with its object. These are two descriptions of the same reality: "object determines character" (T1) is the principle; "every faculty shaped by fellowship direction" (T3) is the mechanism. The five-mode structure (T1) explains why T3 finds diverse faculty effects: existential mode primarily engages affect and relational capacity; companionship mode primarily engages volition, moral evaluation, and conscientiousness; suffering mode primarily engages affect and agency; ontological mode primarily engages relational capacity at its deepest level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-010: T1's five modes correspond directly to T4's relational directions: existential mode = all-the-living (widest scope); companionship mode = human-to-human (giving and receiving); covenantal mode = coven…
findings.finding_value: T1's five modes correspond directly to T4's relational directions: existential mode = all-the-living (widest scope); companionship mode = human-to-human (giving and receiving); covenantal mode = covenant partner; ontological mode = human-to-God (deepest). The scope-narrows-as-depth-increases finding (T4, Q&A-119) is the relational expression of T1's definition: as the fellowship object becomes more specific (from all-the-living to divine nature), the depth increases while the scope narrows. T1's structural negative (misdirected fellowship) maps onto T4's receiving-direction analysis (Hos 4:17 — prior wrong fellowship blocks reception of right fellowship).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-011: T1 establishes that habitual fellowship produces constitutional character formation; T5 maps this as the primary formation mechanism and identifies the sequence (volitional alignment → habituation → c…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes that habitual fellowship produces constitutional character formation; T5 maps this as the primary formation mechanism and identifies the sequence (volitional alignment → habituation → constitutional fixing). Together T1 and T5 reveal the full arc: the definitional claim that fellowship's object determines character (T1) is the endpoint of a formation process that moves through distinct phases (T5). The five-mode structure (T1) generates two distinct formation mechanisms in T5: participatory-transfer (companionship → habituation → character) and wound-as-cleansing (suffering → inner purification). T1's most radical mode (ontological, 2Pe 1:4) is T5's eschatological telos (divine nature participation as the formation endpoint).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-012: T1's five-mode structure explains T6's co-occurrence pattern. The desire-R43 co-occurrence (6 shared verses — strongest signal) reflects T1's finding that desire is the internal motivating state direc…
findings.finding_value: T1's five-mode structure explains T6's co-occurrence pattern. The desire-R43 co-occurrence (6 shared verses — strongest signal) reflects T1's finding that desire is the internal motivating state directing fellowship — they co-occur because desire directs fellowship. The unity-R167 co-occurrence reflects T1's finding that fellowship is the participatory inner reality of which unity is the corporate outcome — they co-occur because fellowship produces unity. The structural connections in T6 are the cross-registry expression of T1's definitional relationships.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-013: T1's five-mode structure is encoded in the vocabulary's semantic arc (T7): existential → companionship → moral complicity → suffering → ontological maps precisely onto the semantic range (Ecc 9:4 → Ps…
findings.finding_value: T1's five-mode structure is encoded in the vocabulary's semantic arc (T7): existential → companionship → moral complicity → suffering → ontological maps precisely onto the semantic range (Ecc 9:4 → Psa 119:63 → Mat 23:30 → Phili 3:10 → 2Pe 1:4). The vocabulary is not a loose collection but a precisely structured arc corresponding to the definitional five modes. T7's grammatical analysis confirms T1's dispositional/act/constitutional distinction: the Hithpael (self-joining act) corresponds to T1's active dimension; the Pual (being-joined condition — Hos 4:17) corresponds to T1's constitutional dimension; the adjectival terms (H2270 companion, H2278 consort) correspond to T1's dispositional dimension.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-064-001: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act (not primarily a feeling or condition) whose definitional core is the release of a legitimate claim — the cancellation of a debt that was real, by a creditor who c…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act (not primarily a feeling or condition) whose definitional core is the release of a legitimate claim — the cancellation of a debt that was real, by a creditor who could have retained it. The four-mode structure (covenantal-objective, divine relational-personal, human horizontal, intercessory) is layered: each mode assumes the prior modes are operative. The structural negative (retained claim producing inner torment) is as analytically significant as the positive: forgiveness withheld damages the withholder. The two downstream inner states (love — Luk 7:47; reverence — Psa 130:4) are named with precision: they arise in different contexts (love from having personally received; reverence from encountering the quality as divine attribute) and constitute the immediate inner-being consequences of the act. The definition tier's single most important structural claim: forgiveness is not a terminal state but a transitional act producing further inner states.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-008: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act; T2 maps where the act is constitutionally located. The four modes (T1) each engage different constitutional levels (T2): covenantal-objective mode engages no name…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act; T2 maps where the act is constitutionally located. The four modes (T1) each engage different constitutional levels (T2): covenantal-objective mode engages no named inner-being locus (external mechanism); divine relational-personal mode engages the full constitutional range (spirit, heart, cognition — via the access-postures of faith, repentance, confession); human horizontal mode explicitly requires the heart (Mat 18:35); intercessory mode requires the dependence-posture at the constitutional level of the plea. The somatic compassion origin-point (T2.5 — splagchnizomai) is the constitutional expression of the volitional-release act (T1.4.1 — the act must be chosen). Definition and constitutional location are co-determining: the mode of forgiveness determines which constitutional level is engaged.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-009: T1's four modes explain T3's faculty engagement pattern. The covenantal-objective mode (no inner-being prerequisite) corresponds to T3's absence of any faculty requirement for that mode. The divine re…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes explain T3's faculty engagement pattern. The covenantal-objective mode (no inner-being prerequisite) corresponds to T3's absence of any faculty requirement for that mode. The divine relational-personal mode (faith, repentance, confession as access-postures) engages volition, conscience, and cognition. The human horizontal mode ("from your heart") requires volition, conscience, and moral evaluation. The intercessory mode requires the dependence-posture that engages cognition (accurate assessment of the grounds of the plea — God's character, not human merit) and volition. T1's definition of forgiveness as transitional (not terminal) is confirmed by T3's finding that every faculty engaged by forgiveness is deepened toward further engagement — not closed by the act but opened by it.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-010: T1's four modes map directly onto T4's relational directions. Covenantal-objective mode = God-to-human (cultic ritual mediated); divine relational-personal = God-to-human (personal declaratory); inter…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes map directly onto T4's relational directions. Covenantal-objective mode = God-to-human (cultic ritual mediated); divine relational-personal = God-to-human (personal declaratory); intercessory = human-to-God on behalf of others; human horizontal = human-giving and human-receiving. The vertical-horizontal interdependence (T4 — the structural claim that receiving divine forgiveness enables extending human forgiveness) is the relational expression of T1's layered modes (the horizontal mode assumes the divine relational-personal mode has operated). T1's structural negative (retained claim = inner torment) is T4's receiving-blocked condition (Hos 4:17 parallel — wrong prior alignment blocks reception of right offering; Mat 18:35 — unforgiveness calling into question whether divine forgiveness was genuinely received).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-011: T1 establishes forgiveness as transitional (not terminal); T5 confirms this and maps the formation arc. T1's downstream states (love, reverence) are T5's immediate formation products. T1's sustained c…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes forgiveness as transitional (not terminal); T5 confirms this and maps the formation arc. T1's downstream states (love, reverence) are T5's immediate formation products. T1's sustained conditions (freed access to God, enabled worship, capacity to extend) are T5's longer-arc formation outcomes. T1's eschatological orientation (Jer 31:34 as the forward-pointing fullness) is T5's eschatological telos. The two mechanisms in T5 (declaratory and atoning) correspond to T1's two primary mode-types: the divine relational-personal mode operates through the declaratory-atoning mechanism; the human horizontal mode operates through the heart-level-release mechanism. T1 and T5 together reveal the complete arc from definition to formation endpoint.
