(2) *Leadership/priestly context* (Lev 4:3; Lev 8:15/9:15): the anointed priest's sinning "brings guilt on the people" — the same unintentional act carries communal consequence when the actor holds representative authority, requiring a bull (costlier offering) and broader atonement. (3) *Communal context* (Lev 9:15 — "the people's offering"): the community's collective sin addressed through Aaron's prescribed communal sin offering. (4) *Cultic-spatial context* (VCG-02 — altar, sanctuary): the cha.ta verb applied to sacred spaces rather than persons. The direction also differs: individual sin operates vertically (person → God's standard violated); priestly sin radiates outward to the community.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Yes across the three VCG registers. (1) *Vertical toward God* (VCG-01): faithlessness operates as direct covenant-betrayal against the God who constituted the bond; Eze 20:27 — treachery equated with blasphemy; the relational damage is at the deepest level; (2) *Horizontal toward persons* (VCG-02): faithlessness operates as betrayal of human trust within a known relational bond — marital (Num 5:12; Mal 2:14), fraternal (Job 6:15), civic (Judg 9:23); (3) *Constitutional character* (VCG-03): faithlessness operates as an identity-level character trait — Isa 24:16 (compounded betrayal), Isa 33:1 (the one who will be betrayed in turn), Isa 48:8 (foreknown from birth). VCG-01 is the primary theological register; VCG-02 the relational-human register; VCG-03 the character-level register.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Yes across the five VCG registers. (1) *Speech context* (VCG-01): perversity operates through the tongue — Pro 6:14 — twisted heart devising evil sown through speech; (2) *Judicial context* (VCG-02): perversity operates through bribery corrupting the discernment faculty (Exo 23:8); (3) *Personal moral context* (VCG-03): perversity operates as the twisted inner life direction — Jer 3:21 — "perverted their way and forgotten the Lord"; (4) *Sexual-created-order context* (VCG-04): perversity operates as violation of the categories God established in creation (Lev 18:23 — te.vel); (5) *Cosmic-spiritual context* (VCG-05): perversity operates as a universal corruption from which all of creation needs liberation (Rom 8:21).

**[CHAR-22]** E — Yes across the three VCG registers. (1) *Judicial context* (VCG-01): injustice operates as partiality and bribery — Psa 82:2 — "judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked" — the relational-authority context shapes the judicial mode; Lev 19:15 — "you shall do no injustice in court" — the court context defines this mode; (2) *Oppression context* (VCG-02): injustice operates as violent harm against persons — Psa 58:2 — "your hands deal out violence on earth"; Job 15:16 — thoroughly internalised appetite for wrong; (3) *Character context* (VCG-03): injustice operates as a stable identity-level disposition — Luk 16:10 — fixed across small and large; shameless insensibility (Zep 3:5).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. *By context*: individual confession (VCG-01) operates at the personal conscience level and produces personal plea (2Sa 24:10 — "please take away the iniquity of your servant"); corporate confession (VCG-02) operates at community level and produces collective appeal (1Sa 7:6 — corporate fasting + confession precedes Samuel's mediation). *By direction*: God-directed confession (predominant in VCG-01: "I have sinned against the Lord," Dan 9:11) and person-directed acknowledgment (2Sa 19:20 — Shimei confessing before the returning king; Mat 27:4 — Judas confessing to the priests). *By depth*: Daniel's extended multi-dimensional confession (Dan 9:5 — "sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled") represents constitutional-depth engagement; Pharaoh's single-sentence formula (Exo 9:27) represents surface engagement. The constitutional depth of the confession correlates with the genuineness of the inner-being transformation it produces.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. By *context*: the Jeremiah passages (Jer 2:35; 16:10) show conscience suppression operating within the covenantal relationship — Israel claiming innocence before the Lord who has declared judgment. The Ecclesiastes passages (Ecc 2:26; 8:12) show it within the wisdom register — the sinner as a general human type defined by absence of God-orientation. The NT passages (1Cor 15:34; Tit 3:11) show it within the community-of-faith context — believers warned against or described as exhibiting conscience suppression. By *constitutional level*: the active-denial mode (Jer 2:35) operates at the speech/will level; the perceptual blindness mode (Jer 16:10) operates at the cognitive-perceptive level; the habituated absence (Ecc 8:12; 1Cor 15:34) operates at the dispositional/formational level.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. (1) *Leadership context*: the Kings pattern (1Ki 16:31; 2Ki 3:3; 10:29–31; 13:2/6/11; 14:24; 15:9/18/24/28) shows refusal to repent operating at a leadership level where the leader's refusal transmits the sinful course to the people ("which he made Israel to sin"). The leader's inner refusal has communal scope. (2) *Communal context*: 2Ki 13:6; Neh 9:29 — the whole community "did not depart from" or "would not obey" — collective refusal operating through communal formation. (3) *Individual post-truth context*: Heb 10:26 — a single person who has received knowledge of truth and deliberately continues sinning — individual refusal in a context of maximum available information. (4) *Formerly-righteous context*: Eze 18:24 / 33:12 — the person who has been righteous and then turns away, sinning against their prior standing.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. (1) *Individual psychological context*: Exo 9:34 — Pharaoh's individual will-hardening cycle (plague ceases → sin again → harden heart → next plague) — the pattern operates through individual psychological cycles of relief-from-pressure enabling sinning. (2) *National/communal context*: 2Ki 17:7; Hos 10:9 — habitual defection as a communal pattern of a whole people — national defection from covenant allegiance operating through shared practices (idolatry, false worship). (3) *Institutional context*: Hos 8:11 — the characteristic operating through religious institutions (altars) that have been misdirected and now reproduce the sinning orientation. (4) *Ontological/theological context*: 1Jo 3:6 — habitual sinning as the defining marker of not knowing Christ — the characteristic operates as an indicator of fundamental spiritual condition.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes. (1) *Pre-emptive/warning context*: Exo 23:33; Deu 20:18 — contagious sin is anticipated before it occurs; the warning names the mechanism in advance (foreign nations will cause Israel to sin through proximity and teaching). (2) *Monarchic leadership context*: the Kings corpus (1Ki 14:16 through 2Ki 23:15) — contagious sin operates through the formal authority of kingship; the king's inner commitment is transmitted to Israel through royal authority. (3) *Prophetic accusation context*: Jer 32:35 — specific leaders building specific sinning structures (high places) that cause specific abominations (child sacrifice). (4) *Historical retrospect/judgment context*: 2Ki 17:21 — the narrator explaining Israel's exile as the consequence of Jeroboam's contagious sin across generations.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Yes, across two clear contexts. (1) *Vassal-state political context*: 2Ki 1:1; 3:5/7 (Moab), 2Ki 8:20/22; 2Ch 21:8/10 (Edom) — smaller nations breaking from the control of Israel or Judah; the revolt is a bid for national independence. (2) *Intra-covenantal political context*: 1Ki 12:19; 2Ch 10:19 — the northern tribes of Israel breaking from the house of David; the revolt is within the covenant community, breaking the Davidic governing structure. The intra-covenantal revolt is theologically weightier because it breaks not merely a political authority but a covenantally grounded one.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Yes, across the three VCG contexts. (1) *Communal-relational context (VCG-01)*: slander operates between persons within community relationships — Eph 4:31; Col 3:8 address this within the church community; the characteristic damages interpersonal relationships. (2) *Judicial-christological context (VCG-02)*: blasphemy operates as a formal legal charge in the trial of Jesus (Mat 26:65; Mar 14:64) — the judicial context makes the speech-act a capital offense with death-sentence consequence. (3) *Eschatological-cosmic context (VCG-03)*: blasphemy operates as the defining characteristic of the eschatological anti-God power (Rev 13:1/5/6) — the cosmic context makes it the constitutive orientation of the creature entirely given over to God-defiance.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence shows variation by context and level. At the individual constitutional level, wickedness operates as the internal voice displacing God (Psa 36:1 — VCG-02) and the soul's desire-orientation (Pro 21:10 — VCG-09). At the social/relational level, it operates as directed hostility (VCG-03), predatory exploitation (Jer 5:26; Job 24:6), and the perversion of speech (VCG-08). At the institutional level, it operates as structural corruption of justice (Isa 5:23; Hab 1:4; Pro 17:23 — VCG-09). Eze 13:22 (VCG-07) shows it operating through prophetic enablement — false prophets encourage the wicked not to turn. The characteristic also operates differently in the phase of judgment versus the phase of apparent prosperity (Job 21:7 — VCG-10 — "why do the wicked live and grow mighty?" poses the paradox that under apparent prosperity the characteristic continues but its consequences are deferred).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. The evidence shows variation across contexts. At the individual constitutional level: the heart-as-treasury mode (VCG-03) and the constitutional-baseline mode (VCG-02) — the characteristic is the structural condition from which all else flows. At the social/communal level: the spreading-leaven mode (1Cor 5:8 — VCG-05 — spreading through the community), the relational-complicity mode (2Jo 11 — VCG-04 — whoever greets the wicked person shares in their works), and the community-destruction mode (3Jo 10 — VCG-04 — domineering malice against the church). At the legal-forensic level: ponēros operates in a reduced sense as a crime-category (Act 18:14; 25:18; 28:21 — VCG-06 — minimal inner-being content). At the cosmic level: VCG-01's evil-one/evil-age register addresses the characteristic's supra-personal dimension. The characteristic therefore operates more intensely in the personal constitutional register and diminishes toward the legal-categorical register.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. The evidence shows variation by register. At the inner-character level (VCG-02), the characteristic operates as a quality of the heart/thoughts: Pro 16:5 (arrogant heart), Pro 15:26 (wicked thoughts) — the abomination resides in what the person is and thinks. At the commercial/social level (VCG-01), it operates as a quality of practice revealing inner character: Pro 11:1 (false balance), Deu 25:16 (dishonest practice) — the outward act reveals and expresses the inner moral deficiency. At the worship level (VCG-03), it operates as the contamination of religious approach by inner corruption: Pro 15:8 (wicked person's sacrifice), Isa 1:13 (incense alongside iniquity) — the inner condition renders outward worship repugnant. At the conscience level (VCG-04), it operates through the silence or awakening of the moral faculty. At the identity-eschatological level (VCG-05), it operates as total self-constitution by abomination (Rev 17:5) or fundamental incompatibility with the divine (Rev 21:27).

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. The evidence shows variation by context. At the individual constitutional level: the heart going after idols (Eze 11:21 — VCG-05), the soul delighting in abominations (Isa 66:3 — VCG-04). At the communal-institutional level: VCG-03 (17V — kings institutionalizing or purging abominations — 1Ki 14:24; 2Ki 21:2; 2Ch 36:14 etc.): the characteristic is embedded in political structures and national practice. At the sanctuary/ritual level (VCG-05 — Ezekiel's vision of progressively greater abominations in the sanctuary — Eze 8:6-17): the characteristic operates in the sacred-space dimension, driving the divine presence away through its presence in the sanctuary. At the eschatological-sacrilegious level (VCG-06 — Dan 9:27; Mat 24:15): the characteristic reaches its most extreme outer-event form. The intensity and inner-being content vary: VCGs 04 and 05 have the richest inner-being content; VCG-06 has the least.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. By context: the active-scheming mode (VCG-02) is most concentrated in prophetic and Psalm contexts that address specific acts of devising (Isa 10:1 — VCG-02: institutionalised iniquitous decrees; Eze 11:2 — VCG-02: counsel-giving). The habitual-character mode (VCG-03) operates across the Psalter's evildoer corpus as a generalised person-type. The stored-condition mode (VCG-04) is concentrated in wisdom and prayer contexts (Job 4:8; 11:14; 36:21; Psa 66:18). By constitutional level: the scheming-mode operates at the cognitive level (thoughts, devising — Isa 59:7; Jer 4:14 — VCG-02); the conceiving-mode at the heart level (Isa 32:6 — VCG-02); the stored-mode at the heart-and-hand level (Job 11:14 — VCG-04: "iniquity is in your hand"); the evil-deeds mode (VCG-05) at the deed-level expressing the inner orientation. The constitutional level of operation varies by VCG.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. By direction: VCG-01 operates from the human will outward toward God (blasphemy against God's name/dwelling) — vertical-ascending direction of defiance. VCG-03 operates from one human agent outward toward another (false accusation against the innocent) — horizontal direction of hostile speech. VCG-02 operates in both directions — toward God (Rom 2:24: name dishonoured) and toward persons (Rom 3:8: false attribution of teaching; 1Cor 4:13: slandered to refuse). By constitutional level: VCG-01 evidences the deepest constitutional operation — the hardened will as the source of sustained blasphemy. VCG-03 evidences a more surface-cognitive operation — the malicious false judgment about another. VCG-02 spans from deep (moral failure producing God-dishonour — Rom 2:24) to reactive (denouncing thankful freedom — 1Cor 10:30).

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics show context-dependence, but the pattern of variation differs by characteristic. Chars 1 and 5 vary primarily by context: the evildoer and iniquity-schemer operate in wisdom contexts (Proverbs), Psalmic contexts (lament and complaint), and prophetic contexts (oracular judgment) with different emphases in each. Chars 3 and 4 vary by constitutional level within their VCG structures: Char 3 spans inner-character (VCG-02), corrupt worship (VCG-03), conscience-state (VCG-04), and identity-constitution (VCG-05); Char 4 spans category-violation (VCG-01), volitional resistance (VCG-02), historical institutionalisation (VCG-03), prophetic-stubbornness (VCG-04), and divine-presence-driving (VCG-05). Char 2 varies by direction (VCG-01 cosmic-evil direction vs. VCG-02-06 personal constitutional direction). Char 6 varies most acutely by direction — VCG-01 (vertical toward God), VCG-02 (social defamation), VCG-03 (horizontal false accusation). The cluster's variation confirms that inner evil is context-sensitive while maintaining its core identity across contexts.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, the characteristic operates with different severity, duration, and moral weight depending on the defiling agent and mechanism. In the bodily-contact register (M10c-A): carcass-contact and discharge-contact are typically one-day (until-evening) defilements; corpse-contact is seven-day with the prescribed remedy of water of impurity (Num 19:11, M10c-A-VCG-07) — the most severe and elaborate. Object contamination (M10c-A-VCG-03) is irreversible for earthenware (Lev 11:33 — must be broken). In the verdict/categorical register (M10c-B): disease in persons may be permanent for the duration (Lev 13:46 — "as long as he has the disease"); disease in objects and structures may culminate in demolition (Lev 14:44-45). At the constitutional level, the characteristic operates across the body (as the locus of acquisition), the conscience (as the site of awakening and guilt), and the will (as the site of volitional response). The NT register (M10c-B-VCG-05) shows the characteristic operating at the conscience-level conviction formed by the categorical system — Peter's resistance (Act 10:14) is a deeply formed inner conviction, not mere ritual compliance.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, across three evident distinctions. By depth: the constitutional-existential register (VCG-01 — Job 14:4, Isa 64:6) describes the condition at the deepest constitutional level — the human person as inherently morally compromised before God; this is prior to specific acts. The habitual-dispositional register (VCG-02 — Rom 6:19, Eph 4:19, Col 3:5) describes the condition as it operates through sustained patterns of will and desire. The conscience-faculty register (VCG-03 — 1Cor 8:7) describes it operating in a specific faculty (conscience) through a specific act (eating food against conviction). By direction: the passive direction — defilement as a state the person is already in (Rom 6:19: "once presented as slaves"); and the active direction — the greedy pursuit of more defilement once the constraint of conscience is removed (Eph 4:19). By scope: individual conscience (1Cor 8:7) vs corporate moral state (Isa 64:6: "we have all become...") — the condition operates at both individual and corporate dimensions.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, across three axes. By object of defilement: the characteristic operates differently when it defiles a person (sexual betrayal — VCG-01), a place (land — VCG-04, sanctuary — VCG-03), or a name (divine name — Eze 43:7/8, VCG-03). The inner-being content shifts: personal defilement engages the will's volitional choice (Lev 18:20: "make yourself unclean"); sanctuary defilement engages the corporate leadership's habitual defection (2Ch 36:14: "exceedingly unfaithful"); land defilement engages the community's moral conduct over time (Eze 36:17: "habitual conduct defiled the land"). By direction: active self-defilement (Eze 22:3 — "a city that makes idols to defile herself") vs passive-receptive defilement (Eze 23:17 — "the Babylonians... defiled her with their whoring lust" — external agents defiling through corrupting relations). By outcome: some defiling acts produce judicial consequences in the body (Num 5:27 — ordeal-water producing physical judgment); others produce social expulsion (Lam 4:15 — "Unclean! Away!"); others produce divine withdrawal (Eze 5:11).

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. By severity: Mar 5:2/8 (VCG-01) — the Gerasene demoniac is the most severe case; Luk 8:29 — "repeatedly seized him, overpowering all human restraint." Mar 7:25 (VCG-01) — a child with an unclean spirit is a less severe case. By faculty affected: Mar 9:25 — specifically mute and deaf; Luk 8:29 — bodily agency overridden; Mar 1:26 — convulsing. By social setting: Mar 1:23 (VCG-01) — the synagogue; Mar 5:2 — social exclusion among tombs. Expulsion dynamics also vary: some depart with loud cries (Mar 1:26, Act 8:7); Mat 12:43/Luk 11:24 show the spirit's post-expulsion restlessness.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics operate with significant contextual and directional variation, but the axis of variation differs by characteristic. Characteristic 1 varies by severity (one-day defilement vs seven-day corpse-defilement vs potentially-permanent disease defilement) and by mechanism (bodily-contact vs verdict). Characteristic 2 varies by constitutional depth (constitutional-existential at Job 14:4 vs habitual-dispositional at Eph 4:19 vs specific-conscience at 1Cor 8:7) and direction (passive condition already-in vs active greedy pursuit). Characteristic 3 varies by object of defilement (person/land/sanctuary/name engage different inner registers) and by direction (active self-defilement vs passive reception through corrupting alliance — Eze 23:17). Characteristic 4 varies by severity (Gerasene demoniac's total domination vs child's affliction) and by faculty affected (mute-and-deaf, bodily-agency-overridden, convulsing). Cluster-level pattern: the axis of variation in Characteristic 1 is severity/mechanism (governed by the cultic system); in Characteristic 2 it is constitutional depth and direction; in Characteristic 3 it is the object of extension (what is defiled); in Characteristic 4 it is the faculty dominated. The variation reveals defilement as a highly contextually sensitive condition that cannot be described by a single mode — each characteristic has its own internal differentiation.

findings.session_b_note:
The data addresses this partially and the finding has not been named as a communicative mode explicitly.

**Evidence that it does:**
- Forgiveness is declared verbally in the NT: "Your sins are forgiven" (Luk 7:47-48 — Jesus's declaration to the woman; Mar 2:5 — "Son, your sins are forgiven"). The verbal declaration is the act — it is not merely the announcement of an inner event but the performative speech act itself.
- Joh 20:23 — "if you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them" — the disciples' verbal declaration is given forgiveness-authority. The speech act carries the authority.
- The intercessory corpus (group 5379-002) operates through speech directed toward God — "O Lord, forgive" (Dan 9:19). The inner act of dependence is voiced as petition.
- Mar 11:25 — "whenever you stand praying, forgive" — the horizontal forgiveness act is commanded in the context of prayer, suggesting the inner act is embedded in or expressed through speech.

**How it functions:** The speech-based mode is performative — it enacts the release, not merely describes it. The declaration "your sins are forgiven" does not report an already-completed inner event; it constitutes the forgiveness in the relational field. This is structurally distinct from other modes where the inner act precedes any outer expression.

*New finding:* The communicative/speech mode of forgiveness (performative declaration) has not been identified as a distinct mode in the existing observations. It is implied by the data but not assembled. This is an analytically significant mode: forgiveness can operate as a speech act that constitutes the relational reality it names.

findings.session_b_note:
The data provides partial evidence.

**Speech as the expression of compassion:** Zec 1:13 (group 733-001) — "gracious and comforting words" (ni.chum words). Compassionate inner movement produces comforting speech. Luke 7:13 — Jesus, "moved with compassion" (splanchnizō), says to the widow of Nain: "Do not weep." The compassion-movement produces a direct speech-act of comfort.

**The supplication vocabulary as compassion-seeking speech:** H8467 techinah (supplication) and H8469 tahanun (entreaty) are XREF terms in the compassion vocabulary. They name the speech-acts by which the person appeals to God's compassion — pleading as the verbal form of vulnerability and need (SD-021). This is the communicative mode of compassion's reception: the person who needs compassion verbalises that need in the form of earnest appeal.

**What is missing (P):** The data does not contain a developed analysis of the speech-based mode of compassion. Whether compassion has a normative verbal form — a word, a tone, a genre of speech — is not examined. The comforting-words evidence is suggestive but not fully developed. This is a gap; no existing SD pointer addresses it specifically.

findings.session_b_note:
The data evidences a partial communicative dimension. Psa 38:8 — "I groan because of the tumult of my heart" — presents the contrite/crushed state expressing itself through vocal groaning. This is a speech-adjacent form: not articulate communication but the inarticulate voiced expression of inner anguish. Psa 51:8 — "let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones that you have broken rejoice" — is petition: the contrite person addressing God in speech from their broken position. Psa 143:3 is a lament — structured speech from the crushed condition.

The communicative mode of contrition appears to be **lament and petition**: the contrite inner being speaks to God from its broken position, not from articulateness or confidence but from need. The groan, the lament, the petition are the characteristic speech-forms. However, the data does not develop this dimension comprehensively.

*Partial: lament/petition as the speech-mode of contrition is evidenced but not fully analysed.*

findings.session_b_note:
Yes. Two distinct speech-based modes are evidenced.

**Proclamatory mode:** 1Jo 1:3 — *that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us*. Here proclamation is the instrument by which fellowship is extended: the speaking of what has been witnessed creates the relational bond of shared participation. Speech produces fellowship.

**Rhetorical construction mode:** Job 16:4 — *I could join words together against you*. Here the joining vocabulary (chavar) is applied to the act of verbal argument — words are *joined* as a constructive inner act. This is fellowship vocabulary applied at the cognitive-verbal level: the joining of words as an act of inner rhetorical assembly.

These are distinct: in 1Jo 1:3, speech creates relational fellowship externally; in Job 16:4, the joining capacity operates internally as cognitive-verbal construction. Finding 062-OPER-001 identifies both within the six modes.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-103-001: Love's definition resolves to a structured family of inner-being orientations sharing one mechanism — directed attachment toward an object — whose moral character is entirely determined by the object …
findings.finding_value: Love's definition resolves to a structured family of inner-being orientations sharing one mechanism — directed attachment toward an object — whose moral character is entirely determined by the object chosen. Within this shared mechanism, the vocabulary distinguishes three structural registers: love as disposition (the stable inner orientation — chesed, agapē as character), love as act (the commanded and exercised expression — agapaō, enemy-love), and love as condition (the identity-constituting state of being-loved — agapētos). These are not three separate loves but three aspects of love's single operation: the person has a deep stable orientation (disposition), exercises it in specific acts (act), and exists within the love-relationship as constituted by it (condition). The vocabulary arc runs from the ontologically highest (God is love — 1Jo 4:8) through the morally normative (chesed, commanded agapē) to the affective-natural (phileō, dod) to the morally inverted (love of darkness, love of self). No other characteristic in the programme commands a comparable vocabulary range. The definition's boundary with adjacent characteristics (compassion, mercy, kindness) is partially drawn: love is the broader orientation; compassion is love's suffering-triggered mode; mercy and kindness are love's formal relational expressions. The boundaries require Session D precision.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-001: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanch…
findings.finding_value: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanchnizō — the moment of being-moved), condition of its object (eleeinos — the pitiable state that calls compassion forth), and externalised act (almsgiving, mercy-act). No other characteristic in the programme review set operates across all four kinds simultaneously. The four root families (RACHAM, CHASAD, SPLANCHN, OIKTIROM) identify four constituent dimensions of the single characteristic, each naming a distinct register — somatic-maternal, covenantal-relational, visceral-immediate, and deliberative-pitying respectively. The structural opposites are two distinct kinds: willed judicial hardness (the hardened heart that refuses compassion) and unwilled prosperity-blindness (Eze 16:49 — the one who does not see the need because they are satiated). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed by the consistent outward-facing structure: compassion cannot exist without a suffering other. The definitional tier's most critical gap — the receiver's inner-being experience — is entirely absent from the data, affecting T1.5, T1.6, and T1.7 throughout. This gap is the single most significant analytical absence in the registry.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-008: T1's four-kind structure (character quality, inner event, condition of object, externalised act) maps precisely onto T2's constitutional levels. The character-quality kind (ra.chum — dispositional com…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure (character quality, inner event, condition of object, externalised act) maps precisely onto T2's constitutional levels. The character-quality kind (ra.chum — dispositional compassionate character) operates at the soul level (T2.2 — chesed as soul-character). The inner-event kind (splanchnizō — the moment of being-moved) operates at the somatic level (T2.6 — the gut as the site of the stirring). The condition-of-object kind (eleeinos — the pitiable state) is the constitutional trigger that activates the somatic-constitutional movement. The externalised-act kind is the constitutional endpoint of T2.10's four-stage movement sequence. T1's definition and T2's constitutional account are co-determining: the characteristic cannot be adequately defined without specifying the constitutional levels at which its four kinds operate.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-009: T1's four kinds explain T3's most distinctive finding: that affect and moral action are structurally unified rather than sequential. In T1 terms, compassion-as-inner-event (splanchnizō) and compassion…
findings.finding_value: T1's four kinds explain T3's most distinctive finding: that affect and moral action are structurally unified rather than sequential. In T1 terms, compassion-as-inner-event (splanchnizō) and compassion-as-externalised-act are not two separate kinds but a continuous movement — the felt-movement is the beginning of the act. T3 confirms this: affect is the mechanism of movement, not its precursor. T1's finding that compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action (the unique position as motivational ground of conscientiousness) maps onto T3.10's finding of the same: the definitional claim (T1) that compassion is constitutively outward-facing explains T3's finding that it is the driving faculty between moral knowledge and moral action.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-010: T1's scope finding (compassion requires a suffering other; scope is determined by perceived need, not moral standing) is precisely confirmed in T4's relational analysis. The explicit crossing of coven…
findings.finding_value: T1's scope finding (compassion requires a suffering other; scope is determined by perceived need, not moral standing) is precisely confirmed in T4's relational analysis. The explicit crossing of covenantal boundaries (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) evidenced in T4 is the relational expression of T1's boundary-definition: compassion ends where the condition (pitiable need) is absent, not where covenantal membership ends. T1's four modes of operation (T1.4) — intra-covenantal, cross-boundary, anticipatory, Christological — map onto T4's chesed/splanchnizō distinction (within-bond sustaining vs across-distance extending) and the scope analysis (covenantal and transcovenantal registers). Definition and relational scope are structurally co-determining.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-001: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition of being in favour — charis as inhabited state), enabling capacity (the specific power given for specific tasks — 2Cor 12:9), and character quality (gracious speech, gracious conduct — chen in 889-003). No single English equivalent captures all four. The four modes of operation (sovereign bestowal, covenantal-relational sustaining, capacity-conferring, character-forming) correspond to the four kinds without collapsing them. Two structural opposites are identified: pride (the self-elevation that refuses the favour of the greater, active and willed) and ingratitude/gracelessness (acharistos — the failure to register and respond to grace received, which T3 confirms as image-impairment). The immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle) is a T1.5 finding confirming that grace does not bypass creaturely recognition but requires and produces it as a transitional state. The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed throughout: grace is constitutively directional — it flows from the greater to the lesser and requires the receptor's inner-being engagement to complete its operation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-008: T1's four-kind structure (disposition, standing, capacity, character quality) maps onto T2's constitutional levels. The divine-disposition kind operates at the level of grace's origin (T2.9 — God's ow…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure (disposition, standing, capacity, character quality) maps onto T2's constitutional levels. The divine-disposition kind operates at the level of grace's origin (T2.9 — God's own disposition; not a human constitutional level). The standing kind operates at the soul level (T2.2 — Rom 5:2 "this grace in which we stand"). The capacity kind operates at the spirit-soul interface — the specific enabling for specific tasks (2Cor 12:9) is received at the deepest level and expressed through specific faculties. The character-quality kind operates at the soul-to-body level (T2.7 — gracious conduct and speech expressing the received inner character outward). T1's constitutional movement finding (SD021 four-faces sequence) is the longitudinal form of T2's spatial map: T2 identifies the constitutional levels; T1 identifies the movement between them.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-010: T1's four modes of operation map onto T4's four relational directions. The sovereign-bestowal mode corresponds to the God-to-human direction (T4.1 — primary and dominant). The covenantal-relational-su…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes of operation map onto T4's four relational directions. The sovereign-bestowal mode corresponds to the God-to-human direction (T4.1 — primary and dominant). The covenantal-relational-sustaining mode corresponds to the relational scope (T4.5 — grace operating within and across covenantal boundaries). The capacity-conferring mode corresponds to the human-to-God direction in its supplication register (T4.2 — SD026: grace giving even the capacity to appeal). The character-forming mode corresponds to the human-giving direction (T4.3 — gracious conduct and speech as the horizontal expression of received grace-character). The vocabulary's structural insight (T4 synthesis: giving-side and receiving-side built from the same root, chen/tachanum) explains T1's finding that grace requires the receptor's inner engagement to complete its operation — the vocabulary encodes the two-sidedness because grace is constitutively a two-sided circuit.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — prominently. The oath (H0423, H7650 — OBS-034-007, OBS-034-017) is inherently speech-based: an oath is a spoken self-commitment before witnesses. The covenant curse (alah — OBS-034-036) is also speech-based: it is pronounced upon the covenant-breaker. Covenant operates through word: spoken oath (entry), spoken curse (sanction), spoken declaration (institution). The communicative mode is not secondary but constitutive — covenants come into being through speech.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — three paradoxes are documented: (1) Peace through suffering: Isa 53:5 ("the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed") — peace is purchased through suffering, not despite it (OBS-117-147). The mechanism of peace is its opposite (pain, punishment); (2) Peace through bitterness: Isa 38:17 ("it was for my welfare [shalom] that I had great bitterness") — Hezekiah's retrospective: his suffering was the path to his welfare. The paradox: shalom-welfare arrived via its experiential opposite; (3) Complacent ease as false peace: H7600 group 413-001 (Amo 6:1) and group 413-002 (Isa 32:18) — the same experiential condition of ease is either vice (self-generated) or blessing (divinely given). Peace and its counterfeit may be phenomenologically indistinguishable. The paradoxes converge on a single insight: authentic shalom is not produced by the absence of suffering or difficulty but by the presence of the peace-giver. Its opposite conditions (suffering, bitterness, difficulty) can be the means by which it arrives.

Yes — the gospel proclamation creates koinōnia (1Jo 1:3 — Group 1055); the message of reconciliation is entrusted as a speech act (2Cor 5:19 — Group 2069). Both the creation of fellowship and the restoration of broken fellowship are mediated through proclamation.

**BOUNDARY characterisation — Category 5: Demonstrative and expressive acts.** Terms: G1731 endeiknumi (to show/demonstrate), G1517 eirēnopoieō (to make peace), G1433 dōreō (to give/grant). Endeiknumi (Group 3218): the act of showing or demonstrating love (2Cor 8:24), divine power (Rom 9:17), patience and wrath (Rom 9:22), and the work of the law on hearts (Rom 2:15). The act of showing reveals the characteristic; it is not the characteristic. Eirēnopoieō (Group 1712, Col 1:20): Christ's reconciling work that restores the broken relationship — the means to fellowship, not fellowship itself. Dōreō (Group 2597, 2Pe 1:3): God's granting of all things needed for inner transformation; the giving act enables M05-G participation but is not itself the participation. Why BOUNDARY: these acts demonstrate, express, or enable the cluster's characteristics without being them. What this reveals: the cluster's characteristics need to be shown, enacted, and enabled before they are fully real in the human community. Love must be demonstrated; fellowship requires the peace-making that removes enmity; participation in divine life requires the divine granting act.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes — God's righteousness operates through proclamation. The psalmist's tongue declares it all day (Psa 35:28; 71:24; 145:7, VSG M26-A1-005); future generations shall proclaim it (Psa 22:31); God's righteous word goes out (Isa 45:23); revealed through the gospel (Rom 1:17). The proclamation of God's righteousness is not merely informational — it participates in the reality it declares.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — speech and discernment are named as expressions of righteousness in VSG M26-A2-011. The righteous person speaks justly. Speech is not merely expressive of righteousness — it is one of the primary modes through which righteousness in the person becomes visible.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Yes — this is the central mode of B's communicative operation. "He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly" (Isa 33:15, VSG 1212-002). The term me.shar specifically names the quality of speech (Pro 8:6; Pro 23:16: "my inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right"). Uprightness in speech is a defining mode of the B vocabulary.

**[C — Justification]** Yes — "by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned" (Mat 12:37, VSG 3201-001, adjacent to C). Justification is declared — it is a speech act of God, a verdict pronounced. The receiving person confesses faith.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — the cry for justice is the primary communicative mode of D. "Give me justice against my adversary" (Luk 18:3, VSG 944-001) is speech directed toward God. The cry is not mere complaint — it is an inner act of faith directed toward the God who will answer.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — "by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned" (Mat 12:37, VSG 3201-001). Condemnation operates through speech — both the external verdict declared by the judge and the inner speech of the condemning conscience.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — the reckoning faculty is associated with deliberation and inner speech. Logizomai in Mar 11:31 names a deliberative conversation. The inner act of counting (Rom 6:11) is a form of self-addressed speech: "consider yourselves dead to sin." The reckoning faculty operates through internal deliberation that functions as a speech act directed at the self.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Yes — wickedness has a communicative mode: it speaks falsehood, demands smooth things instead of truth (Isa 30:10, VSG 1214-001). The speech of the wicked is named as a marker of their condition throughout the Psalms.

**[CLUSTER]** The speech-based mode of operation is present in every sub-group — from God's proclamation (A1) to the human cry for justice (D) to self-addressed inner counting (F) to the condemning verdict (E) to upright speech (B). The cluster consistently shows that righteousness is not merely an inner state but one that seeks expression through speech — and that speech is both an expression of and a mode of operation of righteousness.
Pro 16:23 (VCG03 anchor): wisdom governs speech. 1Cor 2:13 (VCG07 corpus): speech either taught by human wisdom or by the Spirit. Wisdom has a speech mode.

findings.finding_value: M01-A has a significant speech-based dimension. Fear of God shapes testimony: Psa 66:16 ("those who fear God are qualified to hear testimony"), Psa 118:4 ("their inner reverence becomes the source of public proclamation"), Mal 3:16 (God records those who fear his name as they speak to one another). The 1Pe 3:15 material (reverence/fobos as the "inner manner in which believers are to give reasoned account of their hope") shows fear-of-God shaping even apologetic speech.

M01-B has a prominent speech-inhibiting mode: social fear (B-VCG-04) governs what people will say publicly — Joh 7:13 ("fear of the Jews suppresses open speech"), Gal 2:12 (Peter's social fear drives withdrawal from table fellowship), Mar 9:32 (disciples afraid to ask Jesus). Also 2Sa 3:11 (Ish-bosheth's fear shutting down his capacity to speak entirely). Fear silences.

M01-C terror does not have a primary communicative mode. It is imposed, not communicated. The one possible exception is the "terror on every side" (ma.gor) formula (Jer 20:10) used by enemies against Jeremiah — speech as a terror-weapon — but this is marginal.

M01-D has a speech-collapse mode: Job 32:15 (friends "dismayed into complete speechlessness"), Gen 45:3 (brothers "cannot answer" Joseph), Job 23:15 (standing in God's presence produces an "overpowering inner upheaval" that collapses speech). Dismay systematically shuts down verbal capacity.
M01-E trembling does not have a primary communicative mode, though the E-VCG-02 tradition (trembling at God's word) involves receiving communication rather than generating it.

M01-F anxiety has some speech-shaping effects: Pro 12:25 ("anxiety weighs down a man's heart — relieved only by an encouraging word") implies that speech is one mechanism through which anxiety is addressed. The pastoral anxiety material (2Cor 12:20; 2Cor 11:3) involves Paul's communicative concern for his churches.

M01-G has a speech-suppression mode analogous to B: Mat 25:25 (servant's fear producing hiding rather than investing) and the Rev 21:8 apostasy context both involve the failure to testify under pressure.

Fear has a consistent speech-shaping effect across M01: reverential fear shapes testimony (M01-A), acute fear and timidity suppress honest speech (M01-B, G), dismay collapses verbal capacity (M01-D). The pattern is that fear governs what can and cannot be said — ordered fear (M01-A) enables testimony; disordered fear (M01-B's social register, M01-G) silences it.

Yes, the pouring-and-spending corpus evidences a speech-mode: Isa 30:27 (M02-C-VCG-01) states God's indignation is expressed through burning anger and fury filling his very lips and tongue — judgment expressed as consuming speech. Jer 6:11 (M02-B-VCG-03) shows the prophet filled with wrath until it must be poured out in speech — the rage presses from within, demanding verbal release.

Divine indignation uses Assyria's sword as speech (Isa 10:5 — the staff of God's indignation). The communicative mode of indignation is prophetic declaration and enacted judgment, both of which function as speech-acts.
Strife and quarrel are explicitly speech-based (M02-F-VCG-01): logomachia (1Ti 6:4) is word-quarrels; the dispute-loving disposition (1Cor 11:16) is named in the context of community speech patterns.

The characteristic has a significant speech-based mode: anger presses toward verbal expression; divine indignation is often expressed through prophetic speech or enacted-judgment as communicative act; word-quarrels are the quintessential speech-form of M02-F.

Yes, prominently. The complaint vocabulary (si.ach — M03-BOUNDARY) is primarily speech-based — Job's complaint as vocal expression of inner anguish before God (Job 10:1). The groaning and sighing vocabulary (M03-E) has a vocal-somatic expression dimension: groaning is heard by others (Lam 1:21 — M03-E-VCG-01); the Spirit's groanings are too deep for words (Rom 8:26 — M03-E-VCG-02) — which paradoxically names the communicative mode as pre-verbal. The prophet's lament-speech (Jer 9:1 — M03-A-VCG-04) and the spoken lament cry "Alas, my brother!" (1Ki 13:30 — M03-B-VCG-01) are explicitly speech-based grief forms. In M03-D, distress is poured out before God as "trouble told" (Psa 142:2 — M03-D-VCG-01) — grief as verbal prayer. The cluster therefore has robust speech-based operation, particularly in its lament, prayer, and groan registers.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, strongly evidenced. re.na.nah (H7445) is the triumphing cry or joyful shout — an explicitly sonic-expressive form of exultation (Psa 63:5; 100:2; Job 3:7 by negation; Job 20:5; 23:582). Psa 32:11 commands "shout for joy, all you upright in heart." Psa 100:2 instructs "Come into his presence with singing." Zep 3:17 shows God himself "exulting over you with loud singing." Isa 49:13 calls the mountains to "break forth into singing." Zec 9:9 parallels "rejoice" with "shout aloud." The evidence shows exultation as constitutively expressive — its natural movement is from inner state to voiced proclamation, making the shout of joy and the triumphing song intrinsic to the characteristic rather than optional additions.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, prominently. The sim.chah/sa.mach register consistently moves into voice: Neh 12:27–43 (gladness expressed through singing, cymbals, harps, lyres); 1Ch 15:16 (David appointing Levites to "raise sounds of joy"); Jer 31:7 (singing aloud with gladness for Jacob); Joel 2:21–23 (rejoicing paired with praise). In the NT: chairo naturally moves into thanksgiving and praise (Act 13:48 — "began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord"); Phili 4:4's commanded rejoicing is paired with prayer (4:6). In M04-E-VCG-02: Mary's spirit rejoices and her mouth proclaims (Luk 1:47 → 1:46 Magnificat); Act 2:26 — "my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced." Joy is inherently communicative — it moves from inner state to voiced expression as its natural overflow.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes: Act 2:26 ("my tongue rejoiced" — agalliao) — the tongue as the expressive organ of inner Spirit-joy; Luk 1:47 (Mary's Magnificat is the vocal expression of her spirit's rejoicing); Luk 10:21 (Jesus' Spirit-rejoicing immediately moves into voiced prayer — "I thank you, Father"); Act 16:34 (the jailer's communal rejoicing presumably involved voiced expression). The communicative mode is prayer and praise, not merely verbal declaration — Suffering-Joy in its Spirit-enabled form consistently moves into worshipful, Godward speech.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, in two forms: (1) **Doxological declaration** — the ki-tov praise formulas (Psa 100:5; 106:1; 107:1; 118:1, 29; 135:3; 136:1) are verbal declarations of divine goodness that simultaneously express and reinforce inner gladness; the "give thanks" command consistently paired with the "for he is good" formula shows that gladness-declaration is intrinsic to worship; (2) **Good word/news** — M04-O-VCG-01 (Pro 12:25 — "a good word makes him glad"; Pro 15:23 — "a word in season, how good it is!"; Pro 15:30 — "good news refreshes the bones"; Isa 52:7 — the good-news herald; Zec 1:13 — gracious comforting words) — speech is the medium through which gladness is communicated and received; the apt, timely word is itself an instance of Gladness reaching the inner person through the channel of speech.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, in two forms: (1) **Divine speech declaring delight** — the baptism/transfiguration declarations (Mat 3:17; 17:5; Mar 1:11; Luk 3:22; 2Pe 1:17) — "this is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" — are the most programmatic speech-acts of Delight in Scripture; the Father's eudokeo is declared by a voice from heaven; (2) **Diplomatic and practical speech** — the M04-H-VCG-03 "as it seems good to you" / "if it please the king" idiom throughout the historical books (Esther, Nehemiah, Samuel, Kings) is a speech-mode of Delight: the speaker verbally defers to or invokes the other's inner pleasure as the governing standard; this is communicative Delight in the relational-volitional sense. The communicative mode is thus both the highest divine declaration and the most ordinary human relational deference.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes, in the speech-Pleasure register: (1) **Pro 16:24** — "gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body" — speech as the medium through which Pleasure is communicated and received; the gracious word is itself an instance of pleasantness reaching the inner person; (2) **Pro 15:26** — "gracious words are pure" — pleasantness characterising speech as morally wholesome; (3) **Psa 45:1** — "my heart overflows with a pleasing theme" — the inner pleasantness expressing through speech in the form of praise poetry; (4) **Pro 22:18** — "it will be pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips" — wisdom's pleasantness residing within and ready to flow through speech. The speech-Pleasure link is the most distinctive communicative mode for this characteristic: genuinely pleasant speech is itself an inner-being state of pleasantness expressed outward and received inward.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes, extensively — proclamation is the dominant expressive mode of VCG-01: (1) **"Tell of"** — 1Ch 16:9 ("tell of all his wondrous works"); Psa 9:1 ("I will recount all of your wonderful deeds"); 1Ch 16:24; Psa 26:7; 71:17; 78:4; 96:3; 105:2 — proclamation as the characteristic speech-act of Wonder; (2) **"Remember" + speech** — "remember the wondrous works" implies both inner memorial and outward declaration; (3) **"Meditate"** — Psa 119:27; 145:5 — the inner speech of contemplative Wonder; (4) **Questions** — the rhetorical "is anything too hard for the Lord?" (Gen 18:14; Jer 32:17, 27) and "who is like you?" (Exo 15:11) — Wonder expressed through the questioning mode that acknowledges God's incomparability. Wonder is uniquely the M04 characteristic that most consistently moves from inner response to outward vocal declaration.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All seven characteristics have communicative modes, but with different characteristic expressions: (1) **Proclamatory/declaratory** — Wonder (Char 6) is the most consistently proclamatory of the seven; its primary expressive mode is Tell-Remember-Declare (1Ch 16:9, 24; Psa 96:3; Psa 78:4 — generational transmission). Exultation (Char 1) is second through the triumphing cry (re.na.nah); (2) **Communal/shared** — Joy (Char 2) is the most communally-communicative: feast-joy is inherently social; sunchairo (Char 2's M04-D) is by definition shared rejoicing. The Pauline joy-over-communities (1Th 2:19; Phili 4:1) shows joy as a relational-speech act; (3) **Divine declaration** — Delight (Char 4) has the most theologically-weighty speech-mode: the Father's "this is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Mat 3:17; 17:5) is the highest possible communicative instance of Delight; (4) **Good word as Pleasure-medium** — Pleasure (Char 5) has the most distinctive speech-Pleasure link: Pro 16:24 ("gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul") names speech itself as the primary medium through which Pleasure is extended and received; (5) **Worshipful-prayer mode** — Suffering-Joy (Char 7): Luk 10:21 (Jesus' Spirit-rejoicing → voiced prayer to the Father); Mary's Magnificat (Luk 1:47) — the characteristic consistently moves toward worshipful vocal expression; (6) **Evaluative declaration** — Gladness (Char 3): the ki-tov "for he is good" declaration is simultaneously an inner recognition and a verbal act; the declaration reinforces the inner state it expresses.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, with a striking characteristic: shame's primary communicative expression is *silence*. Eze 16:63 (vc=65575) — "never open your mouth again because of your shame" — names this directly. The sinner before atonement is silenced by shame. Job 10:15 (vc=37502) — "I cannot lift up my head" — evidences the non-verbal, postural form of shame's expression. The head-covering gestures (Jer 14:3; Eze 7:18) are communicative but nonverbal. The M07-A-VCG-03 evidence (Act 8:32, vc=28925) — the lamb silent before the shearer — presents silence as the appropriate inner-outer expression of bearing unjust shame with willed stillness. Conversely, bold speech is what shame suppresses: the psalmist who speaks of God's testimonies before kings "shall not be put to shame" (Psa 119:46) — trust enables speech; shame removes it.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, through silencing. The fimoō evidence (Mat 22:12 — man rendered speechless; Mat 22:34 — Sadducees publicly silenced) shows humiliation enacted through the withdrawal of the capacity to speak. The humiliated nation becomes the object of others' speech (Jer 48:39 — "Moab has become a derision") while losing its own voice.

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 has a communicative mode through symbolic bodily acts (1Cor 11:4-5 — the covered and uncovered heads carrying messages of disrespect toward divinely ordered authority) and through explicit verbal declaration (Joh 8:49 — "you dishonor me" — the accusers' verbal engagement being itself the dishonouring act).

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 has a communicative mode: the conscience that has recognised shamefulness can articulate it. 1Cor 14:35 ("it is shameful for a woman to speak in church") is the articulated moral evaluation. 2Cor 4:2's renunciation of shameful ways is the public declaration of the conscience's finding. The inverted conscience of Phili 3:19 "glories in their shame" — it communicates its corrupted evaluation as honour.

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 has a specific speech-based mode: VCG-03 is constituted by verbal contempt. The reviling (loidoria) is the speech-act; the reputation-attack is the effect. 1Pe 3:9 (vc=37632) — "do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary bless" — shows the speech-based form of CHAR-5 and the appropriate speech-based counter-response. The inner will is directed away from retaliatory verbal attack toward blessing.

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 has a communicative mode through the gesture of hand-washing (Psa 26:6): the ritual washing of hands before approaching God's altar is the public declaration of the conscience's claim to innocence. This is CHAR-6 communicated symbolically through a bodily act that the community and God can observe. **[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics evidence a communicative or speech-based mode, but with vastly different centralities. Char 6 is constitutively speech-based — speech is the defining instrument (blasfēmeō, kakopoios). Char 1 has a substantial speech-expression VCG (VCG-08, speech of the wicked in Proverbs — Pro 10:6/11/32; 12:6; 15:28; 19:28) where speech reveals and enacts the inner wickedness. Char 5 has speech as a prominent expressive mode — Psa 10:7 (under the tongue: mischief and iniquity) and Pro 6:12 (crooked speech). Char 2 has the mouth as the overflow of the heart-treasury (Mat 12:34; Luk 6:45) — the constitutional evil's most natural expressive channel. Chars 3 and 4 have speech-based elements (Char 3: lying lips as abomination — Pro 12:22; prophetic naming — Eze 16:2; Char 4: prophetic declaration of abominations — Eze 22:2). The cluster reveals that evil expressed through speech (Char 6) is not an isolated phenomenon but the expressive surface of the five other characteristics — what Chars 1-5 produce in the inner person is what Char 6 delivers through speech. CHAR-6 is thus the speech-expression layer of the entire cluster.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, at two points. First, the public self-declaration of the unclean state: Lev 13:45 (M10c-B-VCG-03) — the person bearing skin disease "shall cry out 'Unclean, unclean.'" The inner reality of contamination is verbalized outward through ritual cry. The speech act is not merely announcement; it is the socially constitutive declaration that activates the community's protective response (maintaining distance). Second, the priestly pronouncement of the verdict: throughout M10c-B-VCG-02, "the priest shall pronounce him unclean" (Lev 13:3, 13:8, 13:11, 13:14, 13:15, 13:20, 13:22, 13:25, 13:27, 13:30, 13:44). The priestly speech act establishes the condition officially — it is not merely descriptive but performative. The condition exists objectively but is socially activated by the authoritative pronouncement.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, at two evidenced points. First, Isa 6:5 (VCG-01): the prophet names his own defilement in speech — "I am a man of unclean lips" — the conscience's recognition of the moral-inner defilement-state is expressed in first-person verbal declaration. The speech is the moment the inner condition is named and acknowledged before God. Second, Mat 23:27 (VCG-04): the Woe pronouncement is the authoritative naming of the defilement that is hidden within — Jesus's speech act makes the inner defilement visible and declares its incompatibility with the name "holy." The communicative mode here is prophetic/judicial: the external word exposes what the inner condition has concealed. Third, by negative implication: Eph 5:3 (VCG-04) — impurity "must not even be named among you" — naming the condition within the community of saints is itself a violation; the word-act of naming defilement where it should not be named is forbidden.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, at three evidenced points. (1) Public declaration of the corporate defiled condition: Lam 4:15 (VCG-05) — "Unclean! Away!" directed at the exiles — the community's defilement is proclaimed publicly by those who encounter them; the speech act activates social expulsion. (2) Divine naming of the defiled condition: Eze 22:5 (VCG-05) — "your name is defiled" — God's speech act declares the corporate defilement as a public moral identity. (3) The ordeal law's verbal self-declaration: Num 5:13-29 (VCG-01) — the woman is brought before God; the word of the ordeal names the defilement as either present or absent; the divine verdict through the ordeal water either confirms or denies the defilement. (4) The prophetic challenge: Jer 2:23 (VCG-02) — "how can you say, 'I am not unclean'?" — prophetic speech confronts the community's self-deceptive denial of their defilement-state.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, prominently — the speech operates through the inhabited person, not as the person's own speech. Mar 1:23 (VCG-01): "he cried out" — the man cries out through the spirit's prompting. Mar 3:11 (VCG-03): "they fell down before him and cried out, 'You are the Son of God'" — the spirits use the person's voice to confess divine identity. Mar 1:26 (VCG-02): "crying out with a loud voice" at departure. Act 8:7 (VCG-02): "crying out with a loud voice, came out of many." The spirit appropriates the person's voice as its own instrument of declaration, resistance, and departure — the human voice becomes the medium of adversarial spiritual speech.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics have a speech-based mode of operation, but the form and direction of the speech differs dramatically across them — revealing the cluster's range of communicative theology. Characteristic 1: (a) the public self-declaration of the unclean ("Unclean, unclean" — Lev 13:45, a socially constitutive speech act); (b) the priestly pronouncement of verdict (performative — "the priest shall pronounce him unclean"). Characteristic 2: (a) the prophet's first-person naming of his own defilement before God (Isa 6:5 — conscience expressed verbally); (b) the Woe pronouncement exposing hidden inner defilement (Mat 23:27 — prophetic speech making the condition visible); (c) the prohibition of naming (Eph 5:3 — naming defilement where it should not be named is itself a violation). Characteristic 3: (a) public declaration at exiles ("Unclean! Away!" — Lam 4:15); (b) divine naming of the corporate condition ("your name is defiled" — Eze 22:5); (c) prophetic challenge to self-deceptive denial (Jer 2:23). Characteristic 4: the spirit's appropriation of the person's voice as its instrument — the inhabited person's voice becomes the medium of adversarial speech (Mar 3:11 — confessing divine identity; Mar 1:26 — crying out at departure). The cluster's communicative theology moves from self-declaration (Char 1) to prophetic-judicial naming (Chars 2, 3) to voice-appropriation by an alien agent (Char 4) — a striking progression showing defilement's relationship to speech.

questions.question_text: What first or most immediate inner-being response does this verse show following the characteristic? Record it, or record none.

findings.session_b_note:
The data provides partial evidence — Q041 (partial answer) and Q046 address this:

**What is evidenced:**
- **Love-orientation:** Luk 7:47 — the woman who was forgiven much loved much. The immediate inner response named most explicitly is love — a relational orientation toward the one who forgave. OBS-064-029 establishes this as a causal chain: forgiveness received → love produced.
- **Fear/reverence:** Psa 130:4 — "that you may be feared." The knowledge of forgiveness available with God produces not presumption but awe. Q046 names this as "counterintuitive" — the expected response (relief or joy) is displaced by reverential fear.
- **Blessed state:** Rom 4:7 — "blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven." The makarios (blessed) term names a condition of well-being. Q041 (partial) notes this as indirect joy/blessing language.

**What is not evidenced:** Q041 notes the data does not provide a direct causal chain from forgiveness to joy as a named response, unlike the love-chain or fear-chain. The immediate response is not uniformly identified — it varies (love, fear, blessedness) depending on context.

findings.session_b_note:
The data surfaces multiple immediate responses — and they are counterintuitive. SD031 (Luk 1:28-30): the first response to grace-announcement is **fear**, not joy. SD038 (Zec 12:10): at the eschatological outpouring the first response is **mourning** — grief at the cost of what has been given. SD039 (Ruth 2:10): the first response to unexpected grace is **prostration** — the body enacting humility before articulation is possible. Fear, mourning, and prostration are the three documented immediate responses in the anchor evidence — all preceding joy, peace, or thanksgiving.

*New finding as a consolidated observation: prior analysis noted these responses in individual SD pointers but did not draw them together as a T1 pattern. The pattern is analytically significant: the immediate inner response to grace is consistently creaturely recognition (fear, grief, prostration) before positive states settle.*

findings.session_b_note:
The data is most explicit about the immediate response of the *giver* (the inner movement that precedes compassionate action) rather than the receiver. What follows is drawn from the available evidence:

**In the giver:** The most immediate inner-being response in the one from whom compassion flows is the gut-stirring of splanchnizō — an involuntary somatic event prior to volitional engagement. This is the pre-reflective, body-prior movement that the vocabulary captures. In Hos 11:8, the ni.chum (compassionate warmth) is named at the moment it contends with judgment — it is the first inner movement before deliberation resolves.

**In the receiver:** The data is largely silent on this point directly. Gen 19:16 (chem.lah — God's mercy toward Lot) shows the receiver of compassion being physically acted upon — taken by the hand and led out of danger. The compassion-act produces a rescue; the internal response of the recipient is not named. Luke 7:13-15 — Jesus, moved with compassion toward the widow, raises her son. The widow's immediate inner response is not stated.

**Partial evidence from the pitiable condition:** The eleeinos (pitiful) evidence implies that the person who cannot recognise their own pitiable condition cannot receive compassion. The first response to receiving compassion may therefore require a prior inner movement: the recognition of need.

**What is missing (P):** The data does not contain an explicit account of the receiver's immediate inner-being response to receiving compassion. This is a genuine gap; no SD pointer covers it directly. It is a new gap for Session D.

findings.session_b_note:
The framing of this question — "receiving" contrition — is imprecise for this characteristic. Contrition is not typically received from another; it is a condition that arises in the person. Adjusting the question to the more appropriate framing: what is the immediate inner-being response to the crushing/encounter that produces contrition?

The data evidences: the immediate response to the crushing is **lowliness and open need**. The crushed/contrite person is immediately characterised by an absence of self-claim and a posture of disclosed need before God. Psa 38:8 adds **groaning** as an immediate expression. The sequence (Q015 answer) begins with crushing → contrite posture: the contrite posture is the immediate state.

*Partial: the immediate response to the producing encounter is identifiable (lowliness, open need, groaning); the question of what contrition produces as an immediate response in another person who "receives" it is not evidenced in the data — the vocabulary is not configured that way.*

findings.session_b_note:
The data addresses inner responses to fellowship, but not uniformly at the level of *immediacy* — what happens first in the inner person upon encountering fellowship.

**What the data names:**
- **Hope:** Ecc 9:4 — being joined with the living produces hope. The joining and the hope are presented together, but the data does not sequence them at the level of "first response."
- **Desire to extend:** 1Jo 1:3 — the one who has received fellowship proclamation becomes part of a chain that extends further. The natural response is fellowship-extending.
- **Moral responsibility:** Mat 23:30 — those who claim they would not have participated in their fathers' evil. The relational alignment creates a moral awareness/response even in retrospect.

**Gap:** The data does not systematically identify the *first* inner-being response at the moment of fellowship encounter. The findings address what fellowship produces over time (finding 062-INNER-001) and what fellowship generates as natural response (finding 062-RESPO-001), but the question of the immediate first response is not precisely answered.

findings.session_b_note: Three immediate responses are named in the verse evidence: (1) Trust and refuge-taking — Psa 34:8 ("taste and see that the Lord is good; blessed is the man who takes refuge in him"). findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-001: T1 as a whole reveals that goodness is constitutively multi-modal but unified in origin. The characteristic's 12 distinct operational modes (Q&A-022) span quality, disposition, condition, and evaluati…
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that goodness is constitutively multi-modal but unified in origin. The characteristic's 12 distinct operational modes (Q&A-022) span quality, disposition, condition, and evaluative act — and yet all share a single definitional structure: goodness is what proceeds from and returns to God. The immediate response varies by encounter type (Q&A-025-026), the sustained effect is constitutive rather than reactive (Q&A-030), and the dimension structure is bipartite — Moral Character for human-subject goodness, Divine-Human Correspondence for divine-subject (Q&A-034). What the tier as a whole reveals is that the apparent definitional complexity of goodness (12 modes, multiple dimensions, varied immediate responses) resolves into a coherent characterological portrait: goodness is the quality of alignment with the character of the one who is Good — variable in its expression but unified in its source and standard.

findings.session_b_note:
The data evidences three immediate response patterns, each associated with a primary love-encounter type:
(1) **Responsive love** — 1Jo 4:19: the immediate response to receiving divine love is love in return. Love received generates love given — the response is the same characteristic activated in the receiver.
(2) **Rest/stillness** — Zep 3:17 (OBS-103-094): God's love toward Israel produces quieting — the immediate inner response to the experience of being loved is rest, not striving. Psa 127:2 (OBS-103-084): being-beloved produces effortless sleep (rest as divine love-gift).
(3) **Grief as love-evidence** — Joh 11:36 (OBS-103-149), 2Sa 1:26 (OBS-103-095), Joh 21:17 (OBS-103-153): the immediate response to love's loss or to love's cost is grief — the inner collapse or distress that reveals the depth of the prior love. This is not a response to love per se but to love's absence or cost, and it is consistently love's most visible immediate evidence.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-111-001: Mercy's definition is irreducibly complex — it cannot be reduced to a single act, disposition, or condition. Reading T1 as a whole reveals a four-element structure (Q&A-017: felt disposition, institut…
findings.finding_value: Mercy's definition is irreducibly complex — it cannot be reduced to a single act, disposition, or condition. Reading T1 as a whole reveals a four-element structure (Q&A-017: felt disposition, institutional mechanism, petition-response, spatial locus) operating across four distinct modes (Q&A-022: dispositional, mechanical, dialogic, institutional) with a two-pole boundary structure (mercy as character quality / mercilessness as constitutional collapse). The definitional synthesis is: mercy is the compassionate inner orientation of the greater toward the lesser in need or guilt, expressed through a structured range of mechanisms (atoning, supplicatory, dialogic, institutional), received through specific enabling inner postures (guilt-awareness, humility, persistence), and producing specific inner-state sequences (joy, shame, identity, belonging). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition primary, Transformation/GOD secondary) holds the two poles of the definition together: mercy is a disposition that is also a transforming mechanism.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-011: T1 identifies mercy as both disposition and act (Q&A-016), with immediate responses (joy, shame) and sustained effects (extension capacity, pastoral capacity, identity). T5 reveals that these sustaine…
findings.finding_value: T1 identifies mercy as both disposition and act (Q&A-016), with immediate responses (joy, shame) and sustained effects (extension capacity, pastoral capacity, identity). T5 reveals that these sustained effects are not automatic but developmental — they represent the formative arc that mercy initiates. Reading T1 and T5 together: mercy's definitional character (the distinction between disposition and act, immediate response and sustained effect in T1) is explained by T5's developmental logic — the immediate response (T1) is the first movement of the formative sequence (T5) that mercy initiates. Mercy is definitionally both a received event and a developmental process.

findings.session_b_note: The most immediate response named in the verse evidence is longing for joy — Psa 51:8: "let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones that you have broken rejoice." The contrite person's first named inner movement is not further grief but desire for restoration. The broken bones that produced the crushed condition are the same bones invited to rejoice — the physical-metaphorical continuity is striking. The immediate response is the turning of the inner longing from the weight of contrition toward hoped-for divine reviving. OBS-030-055.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-030-001: T1 as a whole reveals that contrition is a definitionally complex inner-being condition whose structure is determined by its origin (passive, produced by encounter), its constitutional location (spiri…
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that contrition is a definitionally complex inner-being condition whose structure is determined by its origin (passive, produced by encounter), its constitutional location (spirit and heart), and its directional logic (downward into brokenness, then threshold toward divine response). The three-mode structure (penitential, anguish, substitutionary) is unified by the crushing metaphor but differentiated by the agent and relational context of the crushing. The definition tier establishes contrition's primary asymmetry: the person is not the author of their own contrition — they receive it from encounter with reality they cannot deflect — and this passivity is precisely what positions them for divine nearness. The structural opposite (inner self-enclosure) and the blocking condition (merit-claiming) together define contrition negatively as the absence of self-sufficiency before God.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-064-001: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act (not primarily a feeling or condition) whose definitional core is the release of a legitimate claim — the cancellation of a debt that was real, by a creditor who c…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act (not primarily a feeling or condition) whose definitional core is the release of a legitimate claim — the cancellation of a debt that was real, by a creditor who could have retained it. The four-mode structure (covenantal-objective, divine relational-personal, human horizontal, intercessory) is layered: each mode assumes the prior modes are operative. The structural negative (retained claim producing inner torment) is as analytically significant as the positive: forgiveness withheld damages the withholder. The two downstream inner states (love — Luk 7:47; reverence — Psa 130:4) are named with precision: they arise in different contexts (love from having personally received; reverence from encountering the quality as divine attribute) and constitute the immediate inner-being consequences of the act. The definition tier's single most important structural claim: forgiveness is not a terminal state but a transitional act producing further inner states.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-009: T1's four modes explain T3's faculty engagement pattern. The covenantal-objective mode (no inner-being prerequisite) corresponds to T3's absence of any faculty requirement for that mode. The divine re…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes explain T3's faculty engagement pattern. The covenantal-objective mode (no inner-being prerequisite) corresponds to T3's absence of any faculty requirement for that mode. The divine relational-personal mode (faith, repentance, confession as access-postures) engages volition, conscience, and cognition. The human horizontal mode ("from your heart") requires volition, conscience, and moral evaluation. The intercessory mode requires the dependence-posture that engages cognition (accurate assessment of the grounds of the plea — God's character, not human merit) and volition. T1's definition of forgiveness as transitional (not terminal) is confirmed by T3's finding that every faculty engaged by forgiveness is deepened toward further engagement — not closed by the act but opened by it.
