findings.finding_value: T1's definitional structure explains T6's co-occurrence pattern with precision. Guilt-073 (51 shared verses) is the definitional counterpart (T1 — forgiveness releases guilt; they are structurally inseparable). Mercy-111 (15 shared) is the generating disposition (T1 — God's mercy is what produces the forgiving act). Repentance-135 (12 shared) is the access-posture (T1 — human side receiving condition). Love-103 (8 shared) is the named downstream state (T1 — Luk 7:47). Faith-059 (9 shared) is the receiving instrument (T1). Every major co-occurrence registry corresponds to a logical role in T1's definitional structure. T6's co-occurrence data is therefore a reading of the complete forgiveness transaction from the outside — each co-registry names one element of the transaction that T1 defines from the inside.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-001: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanch…
findings.finding_value: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanchnizō — the moment of being-moved), condition of its object (eleeinos — the pitiable state that calls compassion forth), and externalised act (almsgiving, mercy-act). No other characteristic in the programme review set operates across all four kinds simultaneously. The four root families (RACHAM, CHASAD, SPLANCHN, OIKTIROM) identify four constituent dimensions of the single characteristic, each naming a distinct register — somatic-maternal, covenantal-relational, visceral-immediate, and deliberative-pitying respectively. The structural opposites are two distinct kinds: willed judicial hardness (the hardened heart that refuses compassion) and unwilled prosperity-blindness (Eze 16:49 — the one who does not see the need because they are satiated). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed by the consistent outward-facing structure: compassion cannot exist without a suffering other. The definitional tier's most critical gap — the receiver's inner-being experience — is entirely absent from the data, affecting T1.5, T1.6, and T1.7 throughout. This gap is the single most significant analytical absence in the registry.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-001: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition of being in favour — charis as inhabited state), enabling capacity (the specific power given for specific tasks — 2Cor 12:9), and character quality (gracious speech, gracious conduct — chen in 889-003). No single English equivalent captures all four. The four modes of operation (sovereign bestowal, covenantal-relational sustaining, capacity-conferring, character-forming) correspond to the four kinds without collapsing them. Two structural opposites are identified: pride (the self-elevation that refuses the favour of the greater, active and willed) and ingratitude/gracelessness (acharistos — the failure to register and respond to grace received, which T3 confirms as image-impairment). The immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle) is a T1.5 finding confirming that grace does not bypass creaturely recognition but requires and produces it as a transitional state. The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed throughout: grace is constitutively directional — it flows from the greater to the lesser and requires the receptor's inner-being engagement to complete its operation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-009: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3…
findings.finding_value: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3.4 (affect is the first named faculty engaged by grace) and T3.6 (the agency-constituting paradox of 1Cor 15:10) together explain why T1.5 finds the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle: grace first produces the affective recognition (fear, mourning) before constituting the agency through which the person responds (prostration as the body enacting the inner posture that grace has produced). T1's finding that grace requires creaturely recognition to complete its operation (T1.7) is T3.1's finding at the faculty level: grace requires and enables perception simultaneously.

findings.session_b_note: The data shows varied immediate responses depending on the mode of encounter. (1) To God's covenant initiative: the immediate response is the volitional act of entering — joining, committing, taking the oath (Neh 10:29 — OBS-034-035). The text does not isolate a prior inner response before the entry act. (2) To the new covenant promise: Heb 8:10 and Jer 31:33 present the response as receiving — the inner person is written upon by God, not the reverse. The immediate response is being acted upon, not acting. (3) To covenantal exclusion (Eph 2:12 — OBS-034-060): the response is desolation — hopelessness, alienation, godlessness. (4) To covenant breach (Dan 9:11 — OBS-034-036): the experience of the activated curse — judgment as the immediate consequence. Gap: the data does not consistently present a single, uniform immediate inner response. The response depends heavily on which dimension of covenant is encountered (invitation, writing, exclusion, breach-consequence). This diversity is itself a finding: covenant is encountered differently by different inner-being subjects in different relational positions.

findings.session_b_note: The most consistently evidenced immediate response to receiving divine inner-being giving is worship — specifically the altar-building response in Gen 12:7 (OBS-060-035: "he built there an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him") immediately following the covenantal giving. Job 1:21 (OBS-060-044) shows the immediate response to divine giving and taking as blessing: "blessed be the name of the Lord." Hos 2:15 (OBS-060-050) shows inner responsiveness restored — "she shall answer" — as the immediate sign of received eschatological giving. The pattern across these instances: receiving divine inner-being giving produces immediate inner-being reorientation toward God — worship, blessing, responsive answering. The receiving of endowed inner capacity (Neh 9:20, OBS-060-040) does not show an explicit immediate response in the verse itself, but the purpose given (to instruct) implies the response is formation and obedience.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-001: T1 as a whole reveals that faithfulness in this registry is structurally composite and directional. The name ("faithfulness") promises a character quality; the OWNER term (na.tan) delivers an action. …
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that faithfulness in this registry is structurally composite and directional. The name ("faithfulness") promises a character quality; the OWNER term (na.tan) delivers an action. These are not contradictory — they are complementary aspects of the same inner-being reality: the dispositional quality only becomes faithfulness when it enacts itself (Q&A-016, Q&A-018). The triadic architecture (inner-being source → act → object given) is the definitional shape of this characteristic: it cannot be reduced to disposition alone or act alone (Q&A-017). The five operational modes (Q&A-022) show that this single definitional structure produces radically different expressions depending on what is given and from what inner state — the characteristic is definitionally unified but expressionally plural. The primary dimension (Moral Character) grounds this — it is the character quality that makes the giving faithful rather than merely generous. The definition's most distinctive feature is its disposition-in-action structure: faithfulness is a verb that must be enacted to be real, not a noun that can be possessed without expression.

From the person who is hated: Psa 69:20: "reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none." The immediate inner response to being hated is a shattering of the inner self — heart-breaking — followed by the cry for pity. Gen 37:4: the person who is hated finds that peaceful speech becomes impossible ("could not speak peacefully to him") — relational closure is immediate. From the one who receives a triggering injury and begins to hate: settlement of a hostile inner posture (Gen 37:4 — hatred immediate upon perceiving favouritism).

For the recipient: Psa 123:3-4: "our soul has had more than enough of the scorn...of the contempt of the proud" — the soul registers saturation and cries for relief. Job 31:34: "the contempt of families terrified me" — fear is the immediate affective response to received contempt. For the holder: the inner verdict is rendered — a private assessment of worthlessness applied to the object.

The immediate response is the recoil itself — the inner being pulling away from the object. Deu 7:26: "you shall utterly detest and abhor it" — the commanded abhorrence is a commanded pulling-away, a maintained distance. Job 30:10: "they abhor me; they keep aloof from me" — the immediate bodily and relational consequence of abhorrence in the holder is distance-keeping.

From the recipient (group 1775-002): Job 6:23: "deliver me from the adversary's hand...redeem me from the hand of the ruthless" — the immediate inner response of those under ruthless domination is appeal to God as the only power that can counteract the ruthless. Isa 25:4: God is the stronghold and shelter — the immediate response to ruthlessness in the victim is the cry for refuge. For the perpetrator: no immediate inner response is described.

Psa 69:20: "reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair." The immediate response is heart-breaking — a shattering of the inner self. The secondary immediate response: "I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none" — the reaching out for relational support, and the compounding of the condition when that support is absent.

Appeal. Psa 35:1: "contend, O Lord, with those who contend with me." Luk 18:3: "give me justice against my adversary." Jer 18:19: "hear me, O Lord, and listen to the voice of my adversaries." The immediate inner response to the adversary relationship is the turning to God for advocacy and justice.

Bodily expression: Eze 25:6 — "you have clapped your hands and stamped your feet." The soul's malice immediately produces celebratory bodily expression. The inner soul-level pleasure immediately expresses through physical celebration — the most somatic immediate expression in M06.

**BOUNDARY characterisation — Category 2: Qualities of objects that direct inner attention.** Terms: H5000 na.eh (lovely / fitting / becoming), G4375 prosfilēs (lovely / commendable / praiseworthy). These terms name the quality in an object or act that makes it fitting, beautiful, or praiseworthy — the attractiveness that draws the inner person's attention and evaluation toward it. Na.eh appears in aesthetic-evaluative contexts (Psa 33:1 — Group 1591; Song 2:14, 4:3, 6:4 — Group 1591; Pro 17:7, 19:10, 26:1 — Group 1591). Prosfilēs appears in Phili 4:8 (Group 1552): 'whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable... think about these things' — directing the mind's moral attentiveness. Why BOUNDARY: these terms name the quality of the object that elicits inner-being response — they describe what calls forth the love, admiration, or attention, not the love itself. What this reveals: the cluster's characteristics are always responsive to something that is genuinely lovely, fitting, or commendable. Love is constitutively directional, defined by its object.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** A double movement: humbling and acknowledgment. The pattern in A1-006 verses is the immediate acknowledgment of human guilt: "the Lord is righteous; we have acted wickedly" (Exo 9:27; Neh 9:33; Ezr 9:15; Lam 1:18; Dan 9:7). Pharaoh's acknowledgment, Israel's confession, and the prophet's lament all show the same immediate inner response. A secondary immediate response is alarm: Felix was alarmed (Act 24:25, VSG M26-A1-006) — conviction without conversion; recognition without submission.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** The immediate response to being in the state of righteousness is gladness, exultation, and praise — VSG 3246-003. The righteous person who encounters their own state or God's action toward them responds with joy. The righteous also respond to opposition with trust in God rather than panic (M26-A2-016).

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** The verse evidence in B does not specifically address the immediate response to receiving or encountering uprightness. The material describes uprightness as a path and disposition rather than a stimulus producing a response. Silence noted.

**[C — Justification]** The immediate response to justification is trust and hope: "being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life" (Tit 3:7). The justified person receives a new standing that produces hope as its immediate inner orientation.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** The immediate response to the cry for divine justice being answered is relief and perseverance. The parable of the widow (Luk 18:3–8) shows persistent appeal, not despair. The answer to the cry — "he will give justice to them speedily" (Luk 18:8) — produces hope and continued faithfulness.

**[E — Condemnation]** The immediate response to receiving the verdict of condemnation is weight. The immediate response to freedom from condemnation is release: "has no one condemned you? ... Neither do I condemn you" (Joh 8:10–11, VSG 4846-002). The release of being freed from the expected verdict.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The immediate response to the reckoning act is action: "count yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus... therefore do not let sin reign" (Rom 6:11–12). The reckoning act is immediately followed by a command to act from the conclusion.
**[G — Structural Opposites]** The verse evidence for G does not specifically address the immediate response of the person encountering wickedness or being in the wicked condition. Silence noted.

findings.finding_value: Multiple structural opposites are named across M39-A's verse landscape: (1) Cursing (the inverse of blessing): ba.rakh group 1299-004 contains the clearest inversions — Job 1:11; 2:5; 2:9 (cursing God), Gen 12:3 (cursing vs. blessing). The anti-structure is lexically encoded: the same word is used euphemistically for its opposite. (2) Mercilessness/ungrace: Rom 11:6 ("if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works — otherwise grace would no longer be grace") names the opposite as works-based merit-claim. (3) Rejection/non-acceptance: ra.tsah in the negative (Mal 1:10; Jer 14:10; Amo 5:22) — "I will not accept them" is the structural opposite of ra.tsah. (4) Corrupted grace: Nah 3:4 (chen as deadly charm); Psa 62:4 (ra.tsah directed at falsehood); the Acts political-favour texts (888-003) — grace weaponised or transactionalised.

findings.finding_value: The immediate inner response to ordered wealth received through character is enjoyment and gratitude. Ecc 5:19 names it: "God gives wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them" — the immediate response to rightly-ordered wealth is the capacity to enjoy it. Pro 13:4 (the soul of the diligent richly supplied) implies the immediate satisfaction of supply meeting the soul's need.

findings.finding_value: The immediate response to the encounter with Jesus that produces M46-D's voluntary release is joy and resolution: Zacchaeus stood and announced his giving immediately after Jesus came to his house (Luk 19:6-8). The immediate response to giving from poverty is joy: the Macedonian churches gave "with abundance of joy" even in "extreme poverty" (2Cor 8:2). The immediate response of poverty of spirit to the kingdom-word is blessing: Mat 5:3 declares the present tense (theirs is the kingdom).

findings.finding_value: The immediate inner response to fear-of-God in M01-A is obedience and worship. Hag 1:12 (anchor A-VCG-04 context: "after hearing the prophetic word, the remnant obeyed and the people feared the Lord") shows fear issuing immediately in obedience. Exo 14:31 ("feared the Lord and believed") shows fear immediately producing faith. Mat 9:8 ("the crowds' fear moves inward immediately into glorifying God") shows fear as gateway to worship.

The most immediate response to acute fear in M01-B is the will's impulse toward flight or protection: Gen 32:7 (fear immediately drives strategic action — splitting the camp), Gen 3:10 (Adam's fear immediately drives him to hide), 1Sa 17:24 (all men of Israel flee "without deliberation, driven by overwhelming dread"). The immediacy is extreme — fear produces action before deliberation.

The immediate response to M01-C terror is paralysis or melting: Gen 35:5 (terror "paralyzing the will to pursue"), Exo 15:16 ("rendering enemies motionless as stone"), Jos 2:9 ("causes the people to melt inwardly, dissolving capacity to resist"). The will collapses immediately.

The immediate response to M01-D dismay is inner speechlessness or cognitive shutdown: Gen 45:3 (brothers "cannot answer"), Isa 21:3 ("cannot see"), Job 32:15 (friends in "complete speechlessness"). The cognitive and verbal faculties are the first to fail.

The immediate response to M01-E terror-trembling is involuntary bodily trembling that precedes conscious processing: Exo 19:16 (the trembling is the direct response to the overwhelming sensory phenomena at Sinai — there is no gap between encounter and trembling).

M01-F anxiety does not have a single "immediate first response" — it is a sustained condition. But when anticipatory dread materializes (F-VCG-02, Job 3:25), the immediate experience is the correspondence between feared event and actual event.

The immediate response to the situation that provokes timidity (M01-G) is passive inaction: Mat 25:25 (servant buries the talent rather than acts), Joh 14:27 (heart yields to cowardly shrinking). Timidity's first response is the suppression of action.

Across M01, fear's most immediate inner-being responses are: flight/action (M01-B), paralysis (M01-C), speechlessness (M01-D), involuntary trembling (M01-E), and passive inaction (M01-G). In the ordered register (M01-A), the immediate response is obedience and worship. The immediate responses confirm that fear's primary operating theatre is the volitional faculty — it governs what the person does or fails to do in the first instance.

The recipient-experience corpus (M02-B-VCG-07) directly addresses this: Job 6:4 names it as inner spiritual poisoning — a toxic assault on the self that mirrors God's fury. Psa 88:16 names it as a sweeping, destroying force assaulting from within. Mic 7:9 shows a posture of willingly bearing the rage as consequence, trusting for shift to vindication. The most immediate inner response to encountering wrath is a sense of being overwhelmed and undone.

For the one who receives provocation that kindles their own anger: Est 3:5 (Haman filled with fury when Mordecai refuses to bow) shows the most immediate response is the filling of the inner being, taking possession.

For an observer of anger: Gen 44:18 (Judah entreating Joseph not to let anger burn against him) shows the immediate response to another's anger is apprehension and the protective petition to deflect it.

The most immediate response evidenced in M03's corpus is the outward overflow of the inner state. When grief arrives, it breaks through: Joseph turns away to weep privately (Gen 42:24 — M03-A-VCG-01); the friends raise their voices and weep (Job 2:12 — M03-A-VCG-01); Nehemiah immediately sits down and weeps (Neh 1:4 — M03-A-VCG-03). The immediacy is consistent — the corpus does not evidence a delay between the occasion of grief and its inner arrival. The secondary immediate response is the cry or movement toward God: distress drives prayer immediately (Psa 18:6 — M03-D-VCG-01; Jon 2:2 — M03-D-VCG-01). In the case of godly grief, the immediate response is self-examination (Mat 26:22, Mar 14:19 — M03-C-VCG-02) and ultimately action (Mat 18:31 — M03-C-VCG-02).

**[CHAR-1]** E — Where the evidence names an occasion for exultation, the immediate response is the surging of the inner state itself: Exo 18:9 (Jethro hears of God's acts → he rejoiced); Isa 25:9 (God's salvation arrives → "let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation"); Dan 6:23 (king sees Daniel unharmed → "was exceedingly glad"). The immediacy is notable — exultation is not described as arising after reflection but as the direct inner response to the encounter with divine reality. Where exultation is commanded rather than spontaneous (Psa 32:11; Zec 9:9), the command implies the will can initiate the state rather than merely waiting for it.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence across the corpus shows the immediate inner response to the occasion of joy is the arising of gladness in the heart before its expression outward: Exo 4:14 (Aaron "will be glad in his heart" — gladness in the heart is the immediate response); 1Ki 8:66 (people go home "joyful and glad of heart" — the gladness is located in the heart as the first response to what they experienced); Psa 4:7 (God has "put more joy in my heart" — the inner reception is the primary event); Act 12:14 (Rhoda's "joy" at recognising Peter's voice is so immediate it overrides action — she runs in without opening the gate). The heart's gladness is the first movement, before voice or action.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The evidence shows varied immediate responses: (1) **Spirit-gift form**: immediate Spirit-produced exultation — Luk 1:47 (Mary's spirit immediately exults upon the angel's announcement, despite her vulnerable situation); Act 16:34 (the jailer's rejoicing is immediate upon coming to faith); Act 2:26 (Peter quotes David's immediate heart-gladness at the resurrection promise); (2) **Fragile-sought form**: the immediate response is desire and attempt that may or may not succeed — Job 9:27 (considers attempting cheerfulness but the context makes clear he cannot sustain it); (3) **Commanded form**: the immediate response is volitional reorientation — Jas 1:2 ("count it all joy when you meet trials") — the command assumes the immediate response will not be joy but the will can redirect the inner state.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The immediate responses vary by mode: (1) **Good news register**: Pro 12:25 — "a good word makes him glad" — the immediate inner shift from anxiety to brightness; Pro 15:30 — good news "refreshes the bones" — physiological-inner penetration; Zec 1:13 — gracious words bring inner reassurance; Gen 40:16 — the baker's immediate inner opening to disclosure when he perceives the interpretation as "favorable"; (2) **Evaluative register**: no strong immediate-response language; the moral appraisals of M04-L-VCG-02 are deliberative rather than immediate; (3) **Wellbeing register**: 1Sa 16:23 — Saul "was refreshed and was well" — the immediate inner calm produced by music when the harmful spirit departed; (4) **Covenantal register**: Neh 2:18 — the people's resolve strengthened when they heard of God's good hand — immediate motivational response to gladness-testimony.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Varies significantly by mode: (1) **Affective-receptive mode** (M04-G): immediate inner animation and sustained orientation — Psa 94:19 ("your consolations cheer my soul" — sha.a producing immediate inner brightening when cares overwhelm); (2) **Volitional mode** (M04-H): immediate action — Gen 34:19 ("the young man did not delay to do the thing, because he delighted in Jacob's daughter") — the most immediate response: delight translating directly and instantly into action; (3) **Relational-delight mode** (M04-H-VCG-02): immediate rescue and action — Psa 18:19 ("he rescued me, because he delighted in me") — divine delight in the person produces immediate saving action; (4) **Obedience mode** (M04-M): immediate appropriate action — Joh 8:29 ("I always do the things that are pleasing to him") — the person oriented toward what pleases God acts immediately in alignment with that pleasure.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The immediate responses differ by mode: (1) **Relational pleasantness** — an immediate inner recognition and warm reception: 2Sa 1:26 (David immediately experiencing Jonathan's companionship as pleasant); Song 1:16; 7:6 (the lover's immediate appreciative response to the beloved's beauty); (2) **Good words/speech** — immediate inner animation: Pro 12:25 (good word making glad); Pro 16:24 (gracious words providing immediate nourishment — honey simile implies instant effect); (3) **Worship-Pleasure (ni.cho.ach)** — Gen 8:21 (God's immediate responsive resolve in his heart upon smelling Noah's offering); the divine response to the pleasing aroma is immediate and decisive; (4) **Divine beauty** — Psa 27:4's longing to gaze on God's beauty is an aspiration rather than an immediate response, but the assumption is that the encounter with divine no.am produces immediate worshipful reception.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The immediate responses differ by register: (1) **VCG-01 positive Wonder**: immediate arrested attention — Job 37:14 ("stop and consider the wondrous works of God") — the first response is to stop; Mar 1:27 ("they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves") — thambeō seized them immediately; Psa 118:23 ("this is the Lord's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes") — immediate recognition of divine agency; (2) **VCG-02 incomprehensibility**: immediate epistemological humility — Job 42:3 ("things too wonderful for me, which I did not know") — immediate recognition of the limit of one's knowledge; (3) **VCG-03 dark Wonder**: immediately unsettled and disturbed — Mar 10:32 ("they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid") — astonishment mixed with fear; Rev 17:6 ("I marvelled greatly") — overwhelmed inner seizure.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The immediate responses across the seven reveal a consistent structural pattern and a clear differentiation: (1) **Consistent pattern**: all seven show a movement from inner state to outer expression as the natural overflow; none of the seven remains purely internal — the immediate response always tends outward. This is the cluster's signature: positive inner-being states characteristically move toward expression; (2) **Differentiated primary response** — Exultation (Char 1): immediate inner surge, immediate outer cry; Joy (Char 2): immediate heart-gladness, then expression; Gladness (Char 3): in its good-news register, immediate inner brightening (Pro 12:25 — anxiety to gladness); Delight (Char 4): varies by mode — in the volitional mode, immediate action (Gen 34:19 — "did not delay"); in the affective mode, immediate inner orientation; Pleasure (Char 5): immediate warm inner reception; Wonder (Char 6): immediate arrested inner attention ("stop and consider" — Job 37:14); Suffering-Joy (Char 7): in Spirit-mode, immediate intense exultation (Luk 1:47; Act 16:34); in ba.lag mode, desired but uncertain brightening; (3) **Most agentively-immediate**: Delight (Char 4) in its volitional mode produces the most immediately-agentive response — Gen 34:19's "did not delay" and God's sovereign cha.phets in Psa 115:3 produce immediate action without intermediate steps; this makes Delight the most agentively-direct characteristic in the cluster.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence points to three closely related immediate responses: (1) **Collapse** — the inner state of confidence and standing falls. The psalmist's honour "turned into shame" (Psa 4:2, vc=37469); shame fills Job's inner being so completely that he cannot lift his head (Job 10:15, vc=37502). (2) **Concealment** — the face is covered, the head lowered: servants covering their heads (Jer 14:3, vc=38535/65555), horror covering bodies alongside shame (Eze 7:18, vc=34978), Jerusalem groaning and turning her face away (Lam 1:8, vc=21682). (3) **Turmoil** — enemies' confident opposition collapsing into "sudden, disorienting disgrace" (Psa 6:10, vc=34839 — "ashamed and greatly troubled"). These three are facets of the same immediate response: the inner collapse of standing expressed in bodily posture and inner agitation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The most immediate response to enforced humiliation is inner collapse of standing and confidence paired with withdrawal or retreat. The shaved envoys cannot return to public life (2Sa 10:5, vc=38517). The people "stole into the city... like those ashamed of fleeing battle" (2Sa 19:3, vc=38518). The withered-grass image (2Ki 19:26, vc=65493; Isa 37:27, vc=65537) — "shorn of strength, dismayed and confounded" — captures the total-collapse quality of the immediate response.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The most immediate inner response to receiving CHAR-3 depends on the worth-denial mode. In the active-willful mode (VCG-01), the focus in most verses is on the dishonorer's inner disposition rather than the dishonoured's immediate response. Joh 8:49 — Jesus responding to dishonour by redirecting to the honoring of his Father — shows the possibility of a response that does not absorb the worth-denial but deflects it. In the structural mode (VCG-02), Paul endures dishonour "through honor and dishonor" (2Cor 6:8, vc=34963) without his inner integrity being altered.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The immediate response to genuine recognition of shamefulness (functioning CHAR-4) is recoil and renunciation: Paul renounces disgraceful, underhanded ways (2Cor 4:2). The conscience that recognises Eph 5:12's deeds as shameful will not name them — the immediate response is avoidance of speech and act. In the inverted mode (VCG-03), the immediate response is glorying — the conscience, having inverted its evaluative standard, embraces what it should recoil from.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The most immediate inner response to CHAR-5 is wounded worth — the inner experience of having one's worth cancelled. Psa 14:6 (vc=65498) — "shame the plans of the poor" — shows CHAR-5 targeting the inner confidence and hope of the poor. Bartimaeus's beggar-identity (Mar 10:50) shows the accumulated inner-being effect of long-sustained contempt-shame: his identity has been formed around the shame-condition produced by society's contempt. 1Pe 3:9's call to bless rather than retaliate shows the acute immediate pull toward retaliatory speech when verbal contempt is received.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The most immediate inner response associated with functioning CHAR-6 (VCG-01) is confidence for approach — the person who has clean hands and a blameless heart can go around God's altar (Psa 26:6) without the collapse of confidence that guilt-shame would produce. The immediate response to the loss of CHAR-6 (Hos 8:5) is the inability to attain the inner purity that would enable approach — the question "how long will they be incapable?" names a state of persistent inner incapacity that bars the approach CHAR-6 would enable.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Reading the six immediate responses together, a threefold cluster-level pattern emerges. (1) Collapse and withdrawal — the most common across Chars 1, 2, and 5. The immediate impact of shame, humiliation, or contempt is an inward collapse of confidence paired with outward retreat (face-covering, backward-turning, inability to re-enter public space). (2) Recoil and renunciation — Char 4's immediate response to recognising the shameful: the functioning conscience recoils and the will renounces (2Cor 4:2). (3) Confidence for approach — Char 6's immediate response to maintained innocence: the clean-handed person moves toward God's altar without the hesitation that guilt would produce (Psa 26:6). These three responses map the cluster's inner-being range from collapse-and-withdrawal at one pole to confidence-for-approach at the other.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence distinguishes by direction. When CHAR-1 is encountered as its victim: the immediate response is crushing inner experience — Psa 123:4 (vc=33953, M08-A4-VCG-03): "our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud" — overwhelming inner saturation under contempt; Psa 13:2 (vc=34241, M08-A4-VCG-03): "how long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?" — inner sorrow and helplessness as the immediate response. When CHAR-1 is one's own inner state: the evidence is largely silent on any immediate internal recognition or discomfort in the proud person. 2Ch 26:16 (vc=34044, M08-A1-VCG-01) shows Uzziah acting from his pride without recorded inner resistance; Jer 49:16 (vc=34054, M08-A1-VCG-03) names "the horror you inspire has deceived you" — the proud person is deceived, not alarmed, by their own state. CHAR-1 appears to generate no immediate internal counter-signal in its possessor.

**[CHAR-2]** E — From the perspective of those who encounter CHAR-2 from another: the psalmist's response in the Psa 119 corpus is sustained anguish and the turn to God for rescue. Psa 119:122 (vc=34103, M08-B-VCG-02): "be a pledge for your servant for good; let not the insolent oppress me" — the victim's immediate response is appeal to God for protection. Psa 86:14 (vc=34097, M08-B-VCG-02): "a band of ruthless men seek my life" — the immediate experience is one of threat and vulnerability. From within the person exercising CHAR-2: the evidence suggests the will's assertion carries its own internal momentum — Deu 1:43 (vc=34123) evidences the people going up "presumptuously" without recorded inner hesitation after God's prohibition.

**[CHAR-3]** E — From the perspective of those who encounter CHAR-3: the Pauline discourse evidences the complexity of reception. 2Cor 11:1 (context of VCG-02 corpus): Paul asks the Corinthians to "bear with him in a little foolishness" — the audience's immediate response to boasting is to perceive it as foolish or socially uncomfortable; 2Cor 11:16 (vc=33893, M08-C-VCG-02): Paul anticipates that even legitimate examined boasting will be received as foolishness. 1Cor 5:6 (vc=33903, M08-C-VCG-01): "your boasting is not good" — the community's internal boasting produces a discomfort addressed directly.

**[CHAR-4]** E — 1Cor 5:2 (vc=33940, M08-D-VCG-01) provides the most direct evidence: the Corinthians are puffed up (CHAR-4 active) instead of mourning — implying that the appropriate immediate response to a community's moral failure is grief, not the self-inflating confidence they are displaying. The inflation specifically prevents the grief response. 1Cor 4:18 (vc=33938, M08-D-VCG-01): some are puffed up presuming Paul will not return — the immediate inner state is contemptuous confidence, not anxiety or appropriate humility.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The verse evidence in §3.D is largely silent on the immediate inner-being response of those who encounter CHAR-5 from another. The evidence focuses on God's response (breaking the pride — Lev 26:19, vc=33982) and the structural consequences (desolation — Eze 33:28, vc=33999), not on the victim's immediate inner experience.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster comparison reveals a pattern in what the immediate inner-being response evidence shows and conceals. CHAR-2 provides the clearest victim-response evidence: the psalmist's sustained anguish and appeal to God (Psa 119:122, M08-B-VCG-02). CHAR-3's VCG-03 evidences immediate joy as the response to community-boasting (2Cor 7:4, M08-C-VCG-03). CHAR-1 evidences the crushing experience of contempt received (Psa 123:4, M08-A4-VCG-03). CHAR-4 evidences displaced grief — the puffed-up community that should be mourning (1Cor 5:2, M08-D-VCG-01). CHAR-5 is largely silent. The cluster-synthesis: the most consistent immediate response across the cluster is the victim's appeal to God (CHAR-1 and CHAR-2) — the experience of pride from the receiving end drives the person toward divine appeal, not direct resistance.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Where the corpus addresses immediate response, two distinct patterns emerge by sub-group. In M09-C (inner disposition), the immediate inner response is a cognitive-volitional repositioning: the person arrives at an inner assessment that determines their self-understanding and allegiance — Luk17:10 ("we are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty") is the self-assessment that immediately follows doing what was commanded; Rom6:17 ("obedience from the heart") names the immediate inner state of genuine transformation. In M09-D (relational pattern), the immediate relational response is the visible obedient act: Act6:7 — priests becoming obedient to the faith as a decisive reorientation; 2Cor7:15 — the Corinthians' receptive welcome of Titus with fear and trembling as the immediate expression of their inner obedience.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The immediate inner-being response evidenced is God's response to the contrite state: Psa34:18 — "the Lord is near" and "saves the crushed in spirit"; Isa57:15 — "I dwell with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite." The immediate divine response is drawing near, saving, dwelling, and reviving. From the human side, the immediate response that the corpus evidences is the opening of the inner person toward God's action — the crushed spirit is one that does not resist God's nearness but is open to receive it. The corpus does not evidence an immediate human-experienced feeling that precedes or follows the state; the focus is on the divine response to the state.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The immediate responses are different for the two elements. Metriopatheō (Heb5:2) — the immediate inner response evidenced is the *engaged compassionate modulation* of one's manner toward the erring; the characteristic immediately shapes how the person responds to the erring person's condition. The erring person who encounters the high priest's metriopatheō receives a measured compassionate dealing rather than severity. Okneō (Act9:38) — the immediate inner response is *prompt movement without friction*: the person responding without hesitation immediately begins moving toward the caller's need. The characteristic is evidenced at the moment of call-and-response.

**[CHAR-5]** E — 1Ti3:4 evidences the most direct immediate response: the overseer's dignity produces "orderly, respectful compliance in his children" — the immediate response of those who encounter semnotēs is a form of ordered respect rather than defiance or casual dismissal. The characteristic naturally evokes the response of appropriate regard in those who encounter it. This is not a demanded response (the dignity does not assert its claim) but an evoked one — the settled moral gravity of the person naturally generates the corresponding response of respect.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The most immediate response evidenced is *the act of bringing/giving* — the freely-moved heart immediately issues in the outward act of offering. Exo35:5 — "whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring" — the willing heart and the bringing are directly connected without intervening friction. Exo35:22 — "all who were of a willing heart brought" — the aorist verb confirms the immediacy: the willing-hearted ones brought. 1Ch28:21 — "every willing man who has skill for any kind of service" — the willingness directly enables participation. The characteristic is its own immediate activation — no further inner preparation is required; the willing heart simply brings.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Where the corpus describes an immediate response, it is typically a relational opening toward God: in the ka.na narrative, the immediate correlate of humbling is God *hearing* the person — "I also have heard you" (2Ki22:19; 2Ch34:27). The inner movement is toward receptivity: the heart that was hardened or self-asserting becomes open to God's word, mercy, and address. In the NT register, the immediate relational opening is toward others: Eph4:2 positions humility as the disposition that enables bearing with one another; the tax collector in Luk18:14 goes home justified immediately following his posture of self-lowering before God. The characteristic thus produces an immediate relational opening — toward God in the OT register, toward divine justification/mercy in the NT. There is no evidence of delayed or deferred immediate response; the opening appears to be structurally immediate.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The immediate responses cluster into two families. *Divine-toward-person responses* (God's immediate response to the human state): CHAR-3 Contrition — God draws near and saves (Psa34:18); CHAR-1 Humility — God hears and extends mercy (2Ch12:7; Luk18:14). *Human-toward-world responses* (the characteristic's own immediate expression outward): CHAR-6 Willing-heartedness — immediate act of bringing (Exo35:22 — "brought"); CHAR-2 Submission — inner repositioning of will (cognitive-volitional self-assessment in Luk17:10); CHAR-4 Meekness — prompt responsive movement (Act9:38 — the expected unimpeded response); CHAR-5 Dignity — evoked ordered respect in others (1Ti3:4 — orderly compliance). CHAR-1's immediate response is the most multi-register: relational opening toward God (divine direction) and genuine regard toward others (horizontal direction). Cluster-level: the characteristic with the most immediate outward expression is CHAR-6 (willing heart → immediate bringing without friction); the characteristic with the most immediate divine response is CHAR-3 (crushed spirit → Lord draws near). The two poles illustrate the cluster's span: spontaneous outward-moving (CHAR-6) and inward-opened-toward-God (CHAR-3).

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The corpus reveals two divergent immediate responses to encountering wilful sinning. (1) *Conscience-activation and moral recognition*: Gen 42:22 — Reuben's immediate response to the brothers' sinning against Joseph is to invoke the reckoning that follows: "so now there comes a reckoning for his blood." The guilty party's immediate response is awareness of consequence. Gen 20:9 — Abimelech's immediate response to learning of the sin brought upon him is protest and confrontation: "you have brought on me and my kingdom a great sin." (2) *Moral refusal and naming*: Gen 39:9 — Joseph's immediate response to the temptation is to name it as "great wickedness and sin against God" — conscience-active refusal before the act is committed. The pattern suggests that the most immediate inner-being response to encountering wilful sinning (whether in oneself or from another) is moral recognition — the conscience registering the moral quality of the act.

**[CHAR-10]** E — Different response patterns across the three mechanisms. (1) *Enticement*: Jam 1:14 — the immediate response is "lured" — the person is drawn toward the temptation through their desire; the luring is the immediate inner-being effect of encountering the enticement. 2Pe 2:18 — the "barely escaping" persons are the susceptible targets whose immediate response to enticement is toward re-capture. (2) *Collective hypocrisy*: Gal 2:13 — Barnabas's "led astray" — the immediate response of the susceptible community member is to follow the collective performance rather than maintaining independent authentic identity. (3) *Apostasy*: Act 21:21 — the immediate response within the accusing community is alarm at the perceived defection from the covenantal framework.

**[CHAR-11]** E — Different responses across the VCG registers. (1) *VCG-01 response*: the condition of wickedness as identity produces judgment — Mal 4:1 — "shall set them ablaze"; Mal 1:4 — "I will tear down" — the response of God to the condition of settled wickedness is judicial destruction. (2) *VCG-02 response*: the condition encountered in the context of Jesus's ministry produces wonder and resistance — Luk 7:49 — "who is this, who even forgives sins?" — bystanders cannot categorise the one who addresses the condition; Mar 2:7 — "who can forgive sins but God alone?" — the scribes resist the implication of Jesus's authority over the condition. (3) *VCG-03 response*: awareness of the condition under the law produces inner conflict — Rom 7:9 — "when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died" — the inner response is a death-experience as the condition's full weight becomes known.

**[CHAR-12]** E — Two response patterns. (1) *The enslaved person's non-response*: the enslaved person continues in sin — Rom 6:1 — "continue in sin" is the rhetorical form of the question about what the enslaved might do; the enslaved state is characterised by continued sinning. (2) *The born-of-God person's structural non-response to the enslavement*: 1Jo 3:9 — "he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God" — the born-of-God person encounters the enslaving power but the God's-seed-indwelling constitutionally prevents it from gaining its typical hold. The protective dimension (1Jo 5:18 — "the evil one does not touch him") names the specific absence of the enslaving power's grip for the born-of-God person.

**[CHAR-13]** E — Multiple response patterns across the corpus. (1) *Confession*: Num 5:7 — "he shall confess his sin that he has committed" — the encounter with the record that "is made known" (Lev 4:23/28) triggers the confession-response; Psa 32:5 — "I acknowledged my sin to you... I said, 'I will confess my transgressions to the Lord'" — the immediate response to facing the record is acknowledgment. (2) *Sorrow*: Psa 38:18 — "I am sorry for my sin" — the encounter produces grief as an immediate affective response. (3) *Plea for pardon*: Exo 10:17 — Pharaoh's "forgive my sin, please, only this once" — the record encountered produces an urgent appeal for its cancellation.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Luk 7:47 — "she loved much" — the woman's love is the most immediate inner-being response to received forgiveness: the magnitude of forgiveness received produces a proportional love-response. Col 2:13 — "made alive" — the immediate inner response to forgiveness received is new life displacing prior death. Lev 16:30 — "you shall be clean before the Lord from all your sins" — the purity-status is the immediate declared condition following the atonement's completion. The immediate inner response thus ranges from the affective (love — Luk 7:47), through the vital (alive — Col 2:13), to the relational-status (clean — Lev 16:30).

**[CHAR-15]** E — Corporate confession. 1Ki 8:47 — "they turn their heart in the land... and repent and plead with you... saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly'" — the immediate inner response to encountering the generational condition in exile is heart-turning, repentance, and verbal confession. Jer 8:14 — "we have sinned against the Lord" — the corporate recognition produces a speech-act of acknowledgment. The most immediate response is thus the collective recognition and naming of the condition before God.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Two contrasting immediate responses. (1) *Prostration and plea*: Luk 5:8 — "he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man'" — the immediate inner response to recognising the sinner-identity in the presence of holiness is prostration, awe-dread, and the impulse to distance Jesus from the defiled self; Luk 18:13 — "stood far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner'" — the immediate inner response is physical self-abasement and penitential appeal; (2) *Dread*: Isa 33:14 — "sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless" — the sinner's immediate inner response to God's consuming presence is terror.

**[CHAR-17]** E — The immediate response pattern across VCG-01 is: recognition → shame or distress → remedial action. Gen 42:21 — "in truth we are guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul... that is why this distress has come upon us" — the immediate inner response is interpretive: the brothers connect their current suffering to their past guilty act; Ezr 9:6 — "I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you" — shame is the immediate inner-affective response to guilt-recognition; Gen 4:13 — Cain's "my punishment is greater than I can bear" — the immediate inner response to the punitive guilt-dimension is despair.

**[CHAR-18]** E — The immediate responses vary across the corpus. (1) *Conscience-strike*: 2Sa 24:10 — "David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people" — the immediate inner response to the iniquity is conscience activation; (2) *Shame and face-avoidance*: Ezr 9:6 — "I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads" — shame and the inability to face God are immediate; (3) *Request for removal*: 2Sa 24:10 — David immediately says "please take away the iniquity of your servant" — the immediate movement is toward plea for divine removal; (4) *Despair*: Psa 40:12 — "my iniquities have overtaken me, and I cannot see; they are more than the hairs of my head; my heart fails me" — the crushing weight produces immediate inner collapse.

**[CHAR-19]** E — The immediate responses vary significantly. (1) *Shame and exposure*: Lam 1:22 — "because of all my transgressions; for my groans are many, and my heart is faint" — the immediate response is grief and inner collapse; Ezr 10:13 — "we have greatly transgressed in this matter" — corporate acknowledgment; (2) *Dominion over the will*: Psa 19:13 — "let them not have dominion over me!" — the immediate threat is enslavement; (3) *Self-justification and denial*: Pro 28:24 — "Whoever robs his father... says, 'That is no transgression'" — the immediate response in hardened conscience is denial; (4) *Despairing awareness*: Eze 33:10 — "surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?" — despairing recognition.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The immediate inner-being response, once the sin surfaces to awareness, is *guilt-recognition and its confessional expression*. Lev 5:5 — "when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed" — names realisation-plus-confession as the immediate sequence. Balaam (Num 22:34) responds immediately to the angel's disclosure with: "I have sinned, for I did not know... if it is evil in your sight, I will turn back" — the immediate inner response is acknowledgment plus readiness to reverse. This immediate response distinguishes CHAR-2 from CHAR-4 (Conscience suppression): the person who suppresses awareness is not exhibiting CHAR-2 but its failure mode. The normative immediate response evidenced in the corpus is conscience engaging promptly once awareness arrives.

**[CHAR-20]** E — The immediate responses vary. (1) *Grief and mourning in the witness*: Ezr 9:4 — "those who trembled at the words of the God of Israel... gathered around me while I sat appalled until the evening sacrifice" — the spiritually aware person's immediate response to witnessing faithlessness is appalled grief; Ezr 10:6 — Ezra "mourning over the faithlessness of the exiles," fasting and drinking nothing; (2) *Shame*: Dan 9:7 — "to us open shame" — the immediate experiential consequence; Psa 25:3 — "they shall be ashamed who are wantonly treacherous" — shame; (3) *Hardening*: 2Ch 28:22 — "in time of his distress he became yet more faithless" — the perverse response of deepened unfaithfulness; (4) *Despair and desolation*: Lam 1:2 — "all her friends have dealt treacherously with her" producing weeping bitterly.

**[CHAR-21]** E — The immediate responses include confession and self-indictment. 1Ki 8:47 — "we have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly" — immediate communal confession naming perversity specifically; Dan 9:5 — "we have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled" — the comprehensive confessional self-indictment; 2Sa 24:17 — "I have sinned, and I have done wickedly" — David's immediate self-indictment upon seeing the plague; Job 33:27 — "I sinned and perverted what was right" — confessional first-person recognition.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Varied across positions. (1) *Response of the one suffering injustice*: Job 6:29 — "please turn; let no injustice be done. Turn now; my vindication is at stake" — urgent plea for relief; Psa 43:1 — "vindicate me, O God, and defend my cause against an ungodly people, from the deceitful and unjust man deliver me" — immediate appeal to God for deliverance; (2) *Response of the righteous observer*: Psa 37:1 — "fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers" — the warning against fretful envy; (3) *Non-response of the unjust*: Zep 3:5 — "the unjust knows no shame" — no inner response at all.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The corpus evidences varied immediate responses when one person confesses to another. (1) *Forgiveness/mercy offered*: Luk 15:20 (context — the father runs and embraces before the prodigal has completed his confession speech); 1Sa 26:21 — Saul promises "I will no more do you harm" in response to David's mercy that prompted his confession. (2) *Indifference or dismissal*: Mat 27:4 — the priests' response to Judas's confession is "What is that to us? See to it yourself" — the confession is heard but the recipients are unmoved. (3) *God's response*: Eze 33:16 — sins not remembered. The immediate response from the human side is not uniform; from the divine side the corpus points toward reception and cancellation.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The corpus evidences two divine responses to conscience suppression in others. (1) *Prophetic declaration of judgment*: Jer 2:35 — God responds to Israel's false innocence claim with "Behold, I will bring you to judgment" — the immediate response to the denial of sin is the announcement of accountability. (2) *Call to awakening and shame*: 1Cor 15:34 — "Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning... I say this to your shame" — Paul's response to conscience suppression in the community is an appeal to shame and alertness. Both responses treat conscience suppression as a condition requiring external correction, since the person's inner conscience is not performing its corrective function.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The corpus shows two patterns of response when refusal to repent is confronted externally. (1) *Continued non-departure*: the Kings corpus shows that prophetic and covenantal warnings did not break the pattern — the formula "did not depart from" applies even to kings who received divine word. Neh 9:29 — "you warned them... yet they acted presumptuously" — the warning met by presumptuousness is the inner response. (2) *Public rebuke required*: 1Ti 5:20 — "those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear" — the persistent refuser's response is not changed by normal correction; only public confrontation aimed at producing communal fear addresses it. The immediate inner response of the person who refuses to repent is continued refusal — the characteristic is by definition one that does not yield to normal correction.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Two response patterns. (1) *Continued hardening*: Exo 9:34 — Pharaoh "sinned yet again and hardened his heart" immediately upon the plague ceasing — the response to the relief from external pressure is to sin again and harden further. The confrontation (plague) produces temporary cessation, then resumed sinning with increased hardening. (2) *Non-response to correction*: 1Sa 2:25 — Eli's sons "would not listen to the voice of their father" — the habitual defector's characteristic response to correction is non-listening. The habitual pattern has become sufficiently entrenched that the father's voice produces no corrective effect.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The corpus evidences two responses when the community encounters the leader's transmitted sin. (1) *Compliance and adoption*: the dominant pattern in the Kings corpus — Israel/Judah follows the leader's sinning path; 1Ki 15:26 — "walked in the way of his father, and in his sin which he made Israel to sin" — the community walks in the transmitted path. The immediate response is alignment with the leader's sinning direction. (2) *Escalation*: 1Ki 14:22 — "Judah did what was evil... more than all that their fathers had done" — the community does not merely replicate the transmitted sin but escalates beyond it. The immediate response to contagious sin from a prior generation can be to exceed the transmitted level.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Two response patterns. (1) *Military response sought*: 2Ki 3:7 — Jehoram's immediate response to Moab's revolt is to summon Jehoshaphat for military alliance against Moab; the response is military-political engagement. (2) *Permanent fracture accepted*: 1Ki 12:19 / 2Ch 10:19 — "to this day" — the narrator's assessment implies that the response to Israel's revolt from the Davidic house was not immediate restoration but the acceptance of a permanent division. The responses differ: revolt against a vassal nation triggers military response; revolt against the governing authority within the covenant community produces lasting fracture.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Two response patterns. (1) *Judicial/legal response*: VCG-02 — the immediate response to the charge of blasphemy is judicial verdict: Mat 26:65 — the high priest tears his robes and calls for witnesses; Mar 14:64 — "they all condemned him as deserving death" — the immediate response is escalation to capital punishment. (2) *Community correction*: VCG-01 — Eph 4:31; Col 3:8 — the immediate response prescribed is renunciation and replacement with edifying speech. The responses differ by context: blasphemy against God in the judicial context produces a death-verdict; slander in the community context produces a call to put it away.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence addresses the response to encountering the wicked person from the outside rather than the inner experience of adopting the characteristic from within. From the outside: the evidence shows immediate moral recoil and avoidance as the appropriate response. Psa 26:5 (VCG-03): "I hate the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked" — deliberate moral separation as the will's first response. Psa 1:1 (VCG-04): the blessed person "walks not in the counsel of the wicked" — avoidance of the wicked person's counsel-register as the first step. Gen 18:25 (VCG-04) and Exo 23:7 (VCG-01) show the first response of the just judge: separation between wicked and righteous (the judicial impulse to name and distinguish). The response from the wicked person's own inner life to correction is the opposite: Pro 9:7 shows the immediate response is injury and abuse — wickedness resists its own naming.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence addresses two types of encounter: encountering the command to abhor evil, and encountering the wicked person who embodies it. For the righteous community encountering the constitutionally evil: Rom 12:9 (vc=14417 — VCG-06) calls for "abhorring" evil — a deep moral revulsion as the first inner response. 1Pe 2:1 (vc=14369 — VCG-05) calls for immediately "putting away" malice as the first act of the community that receives the word. Jam 1:21 (vc=14368 — VCG-05) calls for stripping away rampant wickedness. The immediate response to the characteristic's presence is therefore a call to active repugnance and removal. For the constitutionally evil person encountering truth or testimony: Joh 7:7 (vc=14449 — VCG-04) shows the world hating the one who testifies that its works are evil — the immediate response of the constitutionally evil to exposure is hatred of the witness.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The evidence addresses two distinct immediate-response patterns. From the perspective of the one who perceives abomination in another: Eze 9:4 (vc=1698 — VCG-04) shows the immediate response as sighing and groaning — a conscience-driven, grief-laden inner recoil at encountered abomination. Pro 29:27 (vc=65959 — VCG-01): "an unjust man is an abomination to the righteous" — the righteous person's immediate inner response is moral revulsion mirroring the divine response. From the perspective of the person who has committed abomination without conscience engagement: Jer 6:15 (vc=1680 — VCG-04) and Jer 8:12 (vc=1696 — VCG-04) show no immediate response — the conscience is wholly silenced and produces no shame or blushing. The immediate response therefore varies radically depending on whether conscience is functional (grief and recoil) or silenced (complete inner non-response).

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence shows two distinct immediate-response patterns. From the outside (the reforming king or the prophet): the immediate response to encountering idolatrous abomination is an act of will to remove it — 2Ch 15:8 (vc=65902 — VCG-03): Asa "took courage and put away the detestable idols from all the land"; 2Ki 23:24 (vc=65901 — VCG-03): Josiah "put away the mediums and necromancers and the household gods and the idols and all the abominations." The immediate response of the reforming agent is decisive volitional removal. From inside the characteristic (the community already practising it): the immediate response to prophetic warning is stubborn continuation — Eze 20:8 (vc=65911 — VCG-05): "they rebelled against me and were not willing to listen to me. None of them cast away the detestable things their eyes feasted on" — the immediate inner response to the call to remove is refusal.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Two distinct immediate-response patterns emerge. From the perspective of the victim encountering iniquity from another: Psa 55:3 (vc=38188 — VCG-01): "they drop trouble upon me, and in anger they bear a grudge against me" — the immediate experience of iniquity directed at the victim is crushing pressure and sustained anger from the oppressor. Psa 64:2 (vc=38244 — VCG-03): the psalmist prays for protection from "the secret plots of the wicked" — the immediate response to encountering scheming iniquity is the need for divine covering. From the perspective of the prayer not to receive iniquity's dominion: Psa 119:133 (vc=38227 — VCG-04): "let no iniquity get dominion over me" — the immediate concern is volitional resistance against the characteristic's pull. The evidence shows two distinct encounter-types: the victim's crushing experience and the pray-er's self-protective resistance.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The evidence reveals two distinct immediate-response patterns depending on the position of the encountering person. For the one targeted by false accusation (VCG-03 and VCG-02): 1Cor 4:13 (vc=14351 — VCG-02): "when slandered, we entreat" — the immediate response to receiving slander is non-retaliatory appeal; 1Pe 3:16 (vc=14380 — VCG-03): good conscience maintained amid slander — the immediate response is inner-integrity maintenance. For the recipient of blasphemous speech directed at God: the evidence does not directly document the inner response of the observer who hears blasphemy — the focus is on the blasphemer and the effect. What is evidenced is the non-response of the blasphemer under judgment: Rev 16:9 (VCG-01): no repentance — the characteristic has foreclosed the corrective inner response.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster reveals distinct immediate-response patterns for victims vs. witnesses vs. practitioners of inner evil. For victims: Char 5's VCG-01 (trouble/distress dropped on the psalmist — Psa 55:3) and Char 6's slandered apostle (1Cor 4:13 — entreat rather than retaliate) both show the victim's immediate response as bearing pressure with non-retaliatory constrained response. For witnesses of inner evil: Char 3 (Eze 9:4 — those who grieve over abominations respond with sighing and groaning — conscience-driven grief) and Char 6 (third-party witnesses to blasphemy — not directly evidenced). For practitioners of the characteristic under divine pressure: Char 6 shows the most extreme response — Rev 16:9/11/21: escalating defiance under judgment. The cluster's most distinctive immediate-response finding across all six is Char 6's VCG-01 — the only characteristic showing escalation rather than any form of arrest in the immediate response to external corrective pressure.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The most immediate response evidenced in the corpus is conscience awakening — the moment of recognition that the condition has been incurred. Lev 5:2-3 (M10c-A-VCG-01) describes this precisely: "it is hidden from him and he has become unclean, and he realises his guilt." The defilement precedes awareness; the awakening of guilt is the immediate inner response when the person "comes to know it." A second immediate response is grief at the prospect of exclusion: Num 9:7 (M10c-A-VCG-07) — the men approach Moses immediately upon recognising their condition and express the grief of being "kept from bringing the Lord's offering." The immediacy is notable — they do not wait; the exclusion motivates immediate approach to leadership. These two immediate responses — conscience awakening and grief-driven seeking — characterise the well-formed inner response to the defilement-state in the evidence.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The most immediate inner response evidenced is the recognition of moral collapse in the presence of divine holiness. Isa 6:5 (VCG-01): upon seeing divine holiness the prophet's immediate response is "woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips" — the encounter with holiness triggers immediate conscience-activated self-recognition of the defilement-state. The response is a cry of distress and lostness. A second immediate response is shown at 2Cor 7:1 (VCG-03): "let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit" — the recognition of defilement in the context of divine promises triggers an active first-response of self-purification. These two immediate responses (self-recognition in distress and active cleansing) represent the two poles of the characteristic's immediate register.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Three immediate inner responses are evidenced, varying by register. (1) Restrained grief and simmering awareness (VCG-01 — Gen 34:5): Jacob's immediate response to the violation of Dinah is restrained, simmering awareness — "Jacob held his peace until they came"; the inner impact is named as felt violation. (2) Jealousy as immediate affective response (VCG-01 — Num 5:14): the spirit of jealousy comes over the husband when he suspects his wife has defiled herself — jealousy is the immediate inner response to suspected covenantal betrayal. (3) Self-loathing as future eschatological response (VCG-02 — Eze 20:43): in the restoration, the community will remember its defilements and loathe itself — this is a prospective immediate response named as the desired future inner state when the community finally perceives what it has done.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Two immediate response patterns are evidenced — in observers and in proxies, not in the affected person. For observers: Mar 1:27 (VCG-03) — amazement ("they were all amazed... 'What is this?'"); Luk 4:36 (VCG-03) — "they were all amazed" at Jesus's authority. For proxies seeking help: Mar 7:25 (VCG-01) — "immediately a woman... came and fell down at his feet" — urgent supplication. For the divine response: Mar 5:8 (VCG-01) — "Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!" is the immediate divine response to encountering the condition.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The four characteristics reveal different primary actors and different forms of immediate response, converging on a cluster-level taxonomy. Characteristic 1's paradigmatic immediate responses are: conscience awakening (Lev 5:2-3 — "comes to know it and realises his guilt") and grief-driven seeking (Num 9:7 — the men approach Moses immediately). Characteristic 2's paradigmatic responses are: conscience-activated distress (Isa 6:5 — "woe is me!") and active self-purification (2Cor 7:1). Characteristic 3's responses vary by perceiver: denial by the defiled community (Jer 2:23), simmering grief within the victim's family (Gen 34:5), jealousy in the betrayed spouse (Num 5:14), self-loathing as eschatological response (Eze 20:43). Characteristic 4's responses are the community's amazement (Mar 1:27, Luk 4:36) and the proxy's urgent prostrate seeking (Mar 7:25) — the affected person cannot narrate their own response. The cluster pattern reveals: the well-formed immediate response to defilement is recognition, grief, and active seeking of resolution. The deviant responses are denial (Char 3 — corporate self-deception) and hardened non-response (Char 2 — conscience suppressed). Characteristic 4 is uniquely marked by the absence of the person's own response — the only characteristic where the primary actor's immediate inner response is structurally inaccessible.

questions.question_text: Across the verses, is that immediate response consistent or varied?

findings.session_b_note:
The immediate response **varies** — and the variation is itself analytically significant:

- **Luk 7:47** → love (relational orientation toward the forgiver)
- **Psa 130:4** → fear/reverence (awe at the depth of God's forgiveness-capacity)
- **Rom 4:7** → blessedness (a condition of well-being)
- **Mat 18:35 logic** → the expected response to receiving forgiveness is the extension of it to others — the commanded response is horizontal generosity

The variation appears to follow the context and the specific aspect of forgiveness encountered:
- When received in the context of personal guilt and love (Luk 7:47), the response is relational love
- When encountered as a divine attribute in the context of depth (Psa 130), the response is reverence
- When named as a declared status (Rom 4:7), the response is blessedness

The variation does not indicate inconsistency but **contextual differentiation** — the inner response tracks the specific aspect of forgiveness encountered. This has not been assembled as an observation in the existing analysis.

The somatic stirring is the invariant first event. This consistency is confirmed across diverse contexts: healing, feeding, teaching, consoling. The movement is the same; only its occasion differs.

**What is missing (P):** Consistency of the receiver's immediate response remains unaddressed in the data.

findings.session_b_note:
The immediate inner-being response varies across the three modes:

- **Penitential-relational mode**: Lowliness, open need, and orientation toward God are the immediate states (Psa 34:18; Isa 57:15; Psa 51:17).
- **Experiential-anguish mode**: Dismay, anguish, and groaning are the immediate responses (Psa 143:3; Psa 38:8; Jer 46:5 — terror).
- **Substitutionary mode**: The Servant's bearing produces peace and healing in the community — the immediate response is in the recipients, not the one bearing the crushing.

Variation is therefore intrinsic to the vocabulary's semantic range: the three modes produce different immediate states because they arise in different contexts and through different mechanisms.

findings.session_b_note: The immediate response varies by context and subject. When the human encounters divine goodness: trust, praise, and receptive desire (as above). When the person encounters not-goodness (their own — Eze 36:31): the immediate response is self-loathing and moral awareness — the recognition of deeds as not-good immediately produces self-directed revulsion. When the person encounters divine chrēstotēs (Rom 2:4): the immediate inner movement is toward repentance — the goodness of God produces a first response of conviction and turning. The variation is structured: different registers of goodness encounter produce different first responses, but each response is coherent with the register. Divine goodness in its fullness produces trust; divine goodness as conviction produces repentance; human not-goodness recognised produces loathing. (OBS-067-OBS-035, OBS-067-OBS-025, SBF-067-Q031)

findings.session_b_note: The response varies by the type of love-encounter. When divine love is received: the immediate response is love-in-return (1Jo 4:19) or rest (Zep 3:17, Psa 127:2). When love is expressed at cost (forgiveness-love, enemy-love): the immediate response in the giver is not named directly. When love is lost: the immediate response is grief (Song 5:6, OBS-103-062; 2Sa 1:26, OBS-103-095). When the beloved is encountered: the immediate response is delight and longing (Song 2:16, OBS-103-061; Luk 15:20 — the father's compassion-movement at sight of the returning son, OBS-103-057). The variation is systematic, not random: the type of encounter determines the response type. There is no single invariant immediate response to love — the response depends on the direction of the encounter (giving vs receiving vs losing vs encountering).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-001: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanch…
findings.finding_value: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanchnizō — the moment of being-moved), condition of its object (eleeinos — the pitiable state that calls compassion forth), and externalised act (almsgiving, mercy-act). No other characteristic in the programme review set operates across all four kinds simultaneously. The four root families (RACHAM, CHASAD, SPLANCHN, OIKTIROM) identify four constituent dimensions of the single characteristic, each naming a distinct register — somatic-maternal, covenantal-relational, visceral-immediate, and deliberative-pitying respectively. The structural opposites are two distinct kinds: willed judicial hardness (the hardened heart that refuses compassion) and unwilled prosperity-blindness (Eze 16:49 — the one who does not see the need because they are satiated). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed by the consistent outward-facing structure: compassion cannot exist without a suffering other. The definitional tier's most critical gap — the receiver's inner-being experience — is entirely absent from the data, affecting T1.5, T1.6, and T1.7 throughout. This gap is the single most significant analytical absence in the registry.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-001: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition of being in favour — charis as inhabited state), enabling capacity (the specific power given for specific tasks — 2Cor 12:9), and character quality (gracious speech, gracious conduct — chen in 889-003). No single English equivalent captures all four. The four modes of operation (sovereign bestowal, covenantal-relational sustaining, capacity-conferring, character-forming) correspond to the four kinds without collapsing them. Two structural opposites are identified: pride (the self-elevation that refuses the favour of the greater, active and willed) and ingratitude/gracelessness (acharistos — the failure to register and respond to grace received, which T3 confirms as image-impairment). The immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle) is a T1.5 finding confirming that grace does not bypass creaturely recognition but requires and produces it as a transitional state. The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed throughout: grace is constitutively directional — it flows from the greater to the lesser and requires the receptor's inner-being engagement to complete its operation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-009: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3…
findings.finding_value: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3.4 (affect is the first named faculty engaged by grace) and T3.6 (the agency-constituting paradox of 1Cor 15:10) together explain why T1.5 finds the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle: grace first produces the affective recognition (fear, mourning) before constituting the agency through which the person responds (prostration as the body enacting the inner posture that grace has produced). T1's finding that grace requires creaturely recognition to complete its operation (T1.7) is T3.1's finding at the faculty level: grace requires and enables perception simultaneously.

findings.session_b_note: It varies — and the variation is structured rather than random. The immediate response tracks the relational position of the subject: (a) covenantal invitee who receives → volitional commitment and entry; (b) new covenant recipient → constitutional reception (being written upon); (c) covenantal outsider → inner desolation; (d) covenant-breaker → inner moral failure + activated curse. The variation confirms the finding in Q&A-016 (covenant operates in four modes) and Q&A-025. The data does not support a single uniform immediate response; it supports a spectrum of responses structured by the person's relational position relative to the covenant. This is not a gap — it is a structural finding about covenant's positional character.

findings.session_b_note: The immediate response varies by the mode of giving received. (1) Covenantal giving → worship/altar-building (Gen 12:7). (2) Compassionate giving (child given to Leah) → naming/attribution of divine hearing (Gen 29:33, OBS-060-037) — the name Simeon memorialises the inner act of divine hearing and giving. (3) Judicial giving-over → no inner-being response recorded in the anchor verses — the judicial act proceeds without a recorded human response in the primary texts. (4) Eschatological giving → restored responsiveness/praise (Hos 2:15, Isa 61:3). (5) Divine giving-and-taking → blessing-under-loss (Job 1:21). The variation is directionally consistent: where receiving is welcome, the response is worship/praise/gratitude; where receiving is judicial, there is silence on response (suggesting the human is the object, not the agent). The variation is meaningful, not random.
