The immediate responses across M05 consistently name positive inner movements — joy, relief, rest, cheer, heart-refreshment, responsive love — as the experiential consequence of receiving these characteristics. The cluster produces affective-relational inner states of well-being in those who receive it. The one exception is compassion (M05-B), whose immediate response is the inner movement in the giver rather than in the receiver — compassion's immediate response is the stirring of the one who perceives suffering, not the relief of the one who suffers.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Varies systematically. The unrighteous person encountering God's righteousness responds with humbling and guilt-acknowledgment. The righteous person appealing to God's righteousness responds with confident petition (Psa 31:1; 71:2; 143:1). Felix responds with alarm (Act 24:25). The variation is systematic — the response depends on the moral standing of the one encountering the standard.
**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Varies between the response to being in the righteous state (gladness — 3246-003) and the response to opposition or threat (continued trust, A2-013; A2-016).
**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Silent on immediate response.

**[C — Justification]** Consistently oriented toward hope and relationship (Tit 3:7). The variation in the Job material (947-001) is notable: Job's sense of being in the right before God but unable to answer him (Job 9:15–20) shows the complexity — rightness before God does not necessarily produce peace when the legal-relational framework feels hostile.
**[D — Avenging Justice]** Consistent: the wronged person cries out and persists; God promises to answer speedily. The consistency of the widow parable reinforced by the martyr cry (Rev 6:10).

**[E — Condemnation]** Varies: the woman freed from condemnation (Joh 8:11) is instructed to go and sin no more. The self-condemned person (Tit 3:11) is described as warped and sinful — no immediate repentance evident. The Ninevites who generate the condemnation of Israel repented — in response to preaching, not condemnation.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Consistent: the correct reckoning produces action (Rom 6:11–12). The incorrect reckoning (doubt-based, Rom 14:23) produces condemnation. Variation between right reckoning (freedom and right action) and wrong reckoning (condemned state).
**[G — Structural Opposites]** Silent on immediate response.
Consistent in structure (cognitive opening, orientation toward God) but varies by mode of encounter (receiving endowment vs encountering wisdom in another vs meeting self-attributed substitute).

findings.finding_value: The immediate response in M01-A varies by context: in ethical contexts the response is restraint from wrongdoing (Lev 19:14); in wisdom contexts it is the opening of the cognitive faculty to knowledge (Pro 1:7); in worship contexts it is approach to God (Psa 5:7; Heb 12:28); in the corporate miracle context it is glorifying God (Mat 9:8). There is variation, but all responses are characterised by alignment with God's reality rather than resistance to it.

M01-B's immediate response varies significantly: theophany fear produces prostration (Mat 17:6; Luk 24:5); Jesus-miracle fear produces wonder and questioning (Mar 4:41); military threat fear produces flight (Gen 32:7; 1Sa 17:24); social fear produces speech-suppression (Joh 7:13). The variation is a function of the object of fear.
M01-C terror is consistently paralyzing or melting in its immediate effect — less variation than M01-B.

M01-D varies between speechlessness (Job 32:15; Gen 45:3) and violent agitation (Dan 11:44: "alarming news converting inward alarm into violent external action"). The ba.hal root spans both responses.

The immediate response is not consistent across the cluster — it varies by object, sub-group, and context. This variation is itself a finding: fear is a highly context-sensitive characteristic whose immediate expression is governed by what triggered it and toward what it is directed.

The immediate response varies by position: the one under divine wrath is overwhelmed and undone (Psa 88:7; 90:7 / M02-B-VCG-06); the one in whom anger erupts is taken possession of and driven to action (Dan 3:19; Exo 32:19 / M02-B-VCG-02/03); the one provoked is stirred and galvanised (Act 17:16 / M02-D-VCG-03); the one who witnesses another's anger is apprehensive and seeks appeasement (Gen 44:18; Pro 16:14 / M02-B-VCG-05). The character of the immediate response is shaped by the person's position relative to the anger.

The immediacy of the inner arrival is consistent. Grief comes suddenly, without gradual onset: anguish seizes (Jer 49:24 — M03-D-VCG-04), mourning arrives in a single day (Rev 18:8 — M03-B-VCG-04), distress presses in (Psa 22:11 — M03-D-VCG-01). The form of the immediate response, however, varies by context and character: some weep (M03-A), some groan (M03-E), some pray (M03-D-VCG-01), some go silent (Job 2:13 — M03-F-VCG-02). Two outlier cases are worth noting: Mal 2:13 (M03-A-VCG-02) shows performative weeping where the outward expression does not match the inner condition, demonstrating that the outward response can be decoupled from the genuine inner state. And Herod's grief (Mar 6:26 — M03-C-VCG-01) shows grief that is genuine but weak — a real inner response that fails to govern the will.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The spontaneous pattern is consistent: when God acts in salvation or deliverance, the immediate inner response is exultation (Psa 9:14; 35:9; Isa 25:9; Hab 3:18). The volitional-initiated pattern is also consistent: when commanded, the command addresses the will directly. No evidence shows exultation arising from a slow reflective process — it is presented throughout as a direct inner-state response.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Consistent in kind, varied in intensity and occasion. The heart-gladness response is universal across the corpus. What varies is: (1) Intensity — from the overwhelming joy that causes Rhoda to forget to open the gate (Act 12:14) to the quiet gladness of Solomon's people eating and drinking (1Ki 4:20); (2) Occasion — from cosmic events (the Lord's reign calling the earth to rejoice) to personal moments (Aaron's heart glad at seeing his brother); (3) Presence of volition — some responses are spontaneous (Exo 4:14) and others are commanded and require volitional engagement (Deu 16:11; Phili 4:4).

**[CHAR-7]** E — The immediate response varies by mode: Spirit-enabled agalliao produces immediate intense exultation (Luk 1:47; Act 16:34); ba.lag is explicitly an attempted state that may fail (Job 9:27); the commanded forms (Mat 5:12; Jas 1:2) presuppose that the immediate natural response is grief/complaint rather than joy, requiring deliberate volitional redirection. The inconsistency is itself analytically significant: this is the one M04 characteristic where the immediate response is explicitly not guaranteed to be the characteristic itself — it requires either the Spirit's production or the will's deliberate act.

For those praying against the characteristic's grip: Psa 141:4 (vc=38230 — VCG-04): "do not let my heart incline to any evil" — the immediate response is the prayer for inner resistance. Variation is consistent with the person's relational position to the characteristic: the victim suffers; the witness protests; the person who has not yet been captured prays for protection.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The response varies by position. For the slandered/falsely accused (VCG-02/03): 1Cor 4:13 (VCG-02): immediate non-retaliatory entreaty; 1Pe 3:16 (VCG-03): maintained good conscience. For the blasphemer encountering divine judgment (VCG-01): no repentance — the immediate response is further defiance: Rev 16:11 (vc=14350 — VCG-01): "in pain and sores they cursed God rather than repent" — suffering deepens the defiance rather than breaking it. The variation is between the victim's non-retaliatory resilience and the perpetrator's escalated defiance when confronted. The VCG-03 false-accusation context (Joh 18:30 — VCG-03: Jesus delivered over) does not document an immediate inner response of the falsely accused in this corpus.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster shows systematic variation across positions. For those within the characteristic (practitioners): Char 6 VCG-01 shows the most extreme and consistent inner response — sustained defiance that intensifies under judgment. Chars 1 and 2 show the inner response as the absence of conscience-engagement (the wicked person's "practical atheism" — Psa 10:4). Char 4 shows the soul delighting in abominations (Isa 66:3 — VCG-04) as the inverted affective response. For those opposing or resisting the characteristic: Char 3 (VCG-04 — Eze 9:4: grieving conscience) and Char 6 VCG-03 (1Pe 3:16 — good conscience under slander) both show conscience-driven resilience. The cluster's most consistent pattern across all six is the absence of repentance or corrective inner response in those fully in the characteristic's hold — this absence of arrest is the cluster's defining behavioural signature.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The immediate response varies, and the variation itself is significant. The well-formed response is conscience awakening, grief at exclusion, and active pursuit of remedy — as at Lev 5:2-3 and Num 9:7. But Num 19:20 (M10c-A-VCG-07) shows the deviant response: "if the man who is unclean does not cleanse himself, that person shall be cut off from the midst of the assembly." The will can refuse remedy rather than pursue it. The willful non-cleansing is treated as the decisive moral fault — not the defilement itself but the failure to respond to it through the appointed remedy. This contrast between the grief-driven seeking of Num 9:7 and the willful refusal of Num 19:20 shows the characteristic as a diagnostic of the inner person: the same condition produces either conscience-awakened pursuit or will-hardened resistance, revealing the inner orientation of the person.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The immediate response varies significantly across the 26-verse corpus. Three distinct immediate response patterns are evidenced. (1) Conscience-activated distress and recognition (Isa 6:5, VCG-01 — "woe is me"); (2) Active self-purification (2Cor 7:1, VCG-03 — "let us cleanse ourselves"); (3) Hardened non-response — the opposite of recognition — in the cases where the defilement has advanced far enough that the conscience is silenced: Eph 4:19 (VCG-02) — "become callous," giving themselves up to impurity; 2Cor 12:21 (VCG-02) — those who "have not repented." The variation reveals that the characteristic does not produce a uniform response — it produces recognition and distress in those whose conscience remains active, and entrenched non-response in those whose conscience has been suppressed.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The immediate response varies significantly. The corporate idolatry register (VCG-02) shows self-deception as the dominant immediate inner response: Jer 2:23 — "how can you say, 'I am not unclean'?" — the community's immediate inner response is denial and self-justification rather than recognition. The exile register (VCG-05) shows shame and expulsion as the immediate social response: Lam 1:17 — Jerusalem becomes "a filthy thing among them"; Lam 4:15 — "Unclean! Away!" The ordeal register (VCG-01) shows the social mechanism of judgment as the immediate outcome. The variation shows that immediate response depends on who is perceiving the defilement: the community in the defilement-state denies it; God perceives it clearly (Eze 23:13); the surrounding nations expel the defiled community; prophetic speech confronts the self-deception.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The immediate response varies by actor. (1) Divine response: consistently authoritative command — Mar 5:8, Mar 9:25, Luk 9:42. (2) Observer response: consistently amazement at the authority (Mar 1:27, Luk 4:36). (3) Spirit response: consistently submission despite resistance (Mar 1:26 — departing; Act 8:7 — crying out but departing). (4) Family/proxy response: immediate seeking of help (Mar 7:25 — the mother; Luk 9:42 — father receiving son back). (5) The affected person's own immediate response: not narrated — the condition suppresses the person's capacity for self-expression.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Variation is consistent across all four characteristics, but the form of variation differs. Characteristic 1's variation diagnoses the inner person: the same defilement-state produces either grief-driven remedy-seeking (Num 9:7 — well-formed response) or willful non-cleansing (Num 19:20 — the decisive moral fault), revealing the characteristic as a diagnostic of the person's inner orientation. Characteristic 2's variation reveals the conscience's state: recognition-and-distress (Isa 6:5 — active conscience) vs hardened non-response (Eph 4:19, 2Cor 12:21 — suppressed conscience). Characteristic 3's variation reveals which actor is perceiving: denial (the defiled community — Jer 2:23), clear perception (God — Eze 23:13), shame/expulsion (surrounding nations — Lam 4:15). Characteristic 4's variation reveals the actor's role in the response network: amazement (observers — Mar 1:27), authority (divine — Mar 5:8, Mar 9:25), submission (spirits — Mar 1:26), urgent seeking (proxies — Mar 7:25), silence (the possessed person). Cluster pattern: the variation in immediate response is not random but structured by (a) the integrity of the person's conscience (Chars 1, 2), (b) the perceiver's relationship to the condition (Chars 3, 4), and (c) the degree to which the characteristic has suppressed the person's own inner access to the condition (Chars 2, 4).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-001: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanch…
findings.finding_value: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanchnizō — the moment of being-moved), condition of its object (eleeinos — the pitiable state that calls compassion forth), and externalised act (almsgiving, mercy-act). No other characteristic in the programme review set operates across all four kinds simultaneously. The four root families (RACHAM, CHASAD, SPLANCHN, OIKTIROM) identify four constituent dimensions of the single characteristic, each naming a distinct register — somatic-maternal, covenantal-relational, visceral-immediate, and deliberative-pitying respectively. The structural opposites are two distinct kinds: willed judicial hardness (the hardened heart that refuses compassion) and unwilled prosperity-blindness (Eze 16:49 — the one who does not see the need because they are satiated). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed by the consistent outward-facing structure: compassion cannot exist without a suffering other. The definitional tier's most critical gap — the receiver's inner-being experience — is entirely absent from the data, affecting T1.5, T1.6, and T1.7 throughout. This gap is the single most significant analytical absence in the registry.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-001: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition of being in favour — charis as inhabited state), enabling capacity (the specific power given for specific tasks — 2Cor 12:9), and character quality (gracious speech, gracious conduct — chen in 889-003). No single English equivalent captures all four. The four modes of operation (sovereign bestowal, covenantal-relational sustaining, capacity-conferring, character-forming) correspond to the four kinds without collapsing them. Two structural opposites are identified: pride (the self-elevation that refuses the favour of the greater, active and willed) and ingratitude/gracelessness (acharistos — the failure to register and respond to grace received, which T3 confirms as image-impairment). The immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle) is a T1.5 finding confirming that grace does not bypass creaturely recognition but requires and produces it as a transitional state. The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed throughout: grace is constitutively directional — it flows from the greater to the lesser and requires the receptor's inner-being engagement to complete its operation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-009: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3…
findings.finding_value: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3.4 (affect is the first named faculty engaged by grace) and T3.6 (the agency-constituting paradox of 1Cor 15:10) together explain why T1.5 finds the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle: grace first produces the affective recognition (fear, mourning) before constituting the agency through which the person responds (prostration as the body enacting the inner posture that grace has produced). T1's finding that grace requires creaturely recognition to complete its operation (T1.7) is T3.1's finding at the faculty level: grace requires and enables perception simultaneously.

findings.finding_value: Three contour-revealing findings from the structural opposite: (1) Grace is genuine personal engagement, not mechanical — the fact that divine acceptance (ra.tsah) can be withheld (Mal 1:10) reveals that when it is given, it is truly given from a personal inner disposition, not automatically dispensed. (2) Grace is logically exclusive of merit — Rom 11:6 shows that the opposite of grace is not merely its absence but its categorical replacement by works; the two cannot coexist in the same soteriological frame. (3) The grace-characteristic can be corrupted from within — the same vocabulary serves both grace and its distortion (1299-004; Nah 3:4), revealing that the characteristic's corruption is not external attack but internal inversion.

findings.finding_value: M01-F-VCG-01 (chronic pervasive anxiety) and M01-F-VCG-03 (covenantal curse-dread) are silent on immediate response because they describe sustained conditions rather than acute events. By definition they lack a first response — they are the condition the person is already in.

The indignation corpus (M02-C-VCG-01) is largely silent on the immediate response to encountering divine indignation from the recipient's perspective. Most verses describe the indignation from the side of God's maintenance of it, not from the recipient's immediate inner experience. This contrasts with the burning-rage corpus where recipient-experience is explicitly evidenced.

The M03-G bitterness corpus (8 verses) does not describe an immediate response to the arrival of bitterness. The bitterness texts describe the condition already settled within the person (Pro 14:10 — sealed in the heart; Job 9:18 — God filling the person with bitterness) but do not narrate the moment of its arrival.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The VCG-02 (inverted/absent exultation) and VCG-03 (relational and natural) verses are largely silent on the immediate response pattern — they address the object or absence of exultation rather than its mechanism of arising.

**[CHAR-2]** E — M04-E's sa.s.von corpus is largely future-oriented and thus describes promised joy rather than immediate inner response. Similarly, the VCG-06 (inverted/absent joy) corpus by definition describes the absence or distortion of the immediate response rather than its presence. The inverted joy passages (Pro 2:14; Eze 25:6) do show the immediate inner response to wrong objects — but they are morally condemned precisely because of the wrongness of the object rather than the wrongness of the inner response mechanism itself.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Joh 8:56 (Abraham's anticipatory rejoicing at seeing Christ's day) and 1Pe 1:8 (inexpressible joy in the unseen Christ) describe a sustained inner state rather than an immediate response to a specific moment. The ongoing-state form of Suffering-Joy is not captured by the "immediate response" framework.

**[CHAR-3]** E — M04-L-VCG-02's moral appraisals and M04-L-VCG-03's wisdom-comparative evaluations are largely silent on immediate inner response; they describe the cognitive judgment rather than the felt first reaction to encountering the characteristic. The Eze 36:31 recognition of "not good" deeds produces self-loathing (an immediate negative response), but this is the inverted register.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The M04-P corpus (corrupt delight) is silent on immediate response in the formal sense — it describes the corrupt inner state but does not trace an immediate response sequence. The beast-captivation (Rev 13:3; 17:8) shows collective astonishment-following as the immediate response to the beast's apparent resurrection, but this is the immediate response to the stimulus, not an unpacking of the inner sequence of Delight itself. M04-M's obedience-orientation (ni.cho.ach aroma) is similarly silent on the sequence of inner response.

**[CHAR-5]** S — M04-K-VCG-03 (the wisdom better-than comparatives) does not evidence an immediate response to Pleasure — these are evaluative verdicts about what is more genuinely pleasant, not descriptions of a felt immediate response. Similarly, M04-K-VCG-01 on the human side (the person offering the sacrifice) is silent on the person's immediate inner state — the focus is on the divine reception. The luxury register (M04-K-VCG-02) is also largely silent on the immediate experiential response of the person enjoying luxury, focusing instead on the curse (Deu 28) or the catalogue (Ecc 2:8).

**[CHAR-6]** S — The dominant VCG-01 corpus (61 verses of "tell of his wondrous works," "remember his wonders," "his wondrous works in the deep") largely describes Wonder in its retrospective-proclamatory mode rather than tracing the immediate inner response at the moment of encounter. The immediate encounter-response is most visible in the Mark thambeō instances (Mar 1:27; 10:24; 10:32) and in the negative cases (Neh 9:17 — failure to respond) rather than in the Psalmic proclamatory corpus.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The most analytically significant silences: (1) Gladness's evaluative mode (M04-L-VCG-02) is largely silent on immediate inner response — the moral appraisals describe the conclusion of deliberation, not the felt first reaction; (2) Wonder's proclamatory corpus (VCG-01's 61 verses) describes Wonder in its retrospective-memorial mode rather than at the moment of encounter — the immediate response is most visible in the thambeō instances (Mark) rather than the Psalmic tradition; (3) Delight's M04-P corrupt register is silent on immediate response sequence; (4) Pleasure's wisdom-comparative register (M04-K-VCG-03) gives evaluative verdicts, not felt immediate responses.

**[CHAR-1]** S — The evidence is relatively complete on immediate response; the verse corpus is unusually rich in phenomenological detail about the experience of shame. No significant silence on this prompt.

**[CHAR-2]** S — Judg 18:7 (vc=38529): Pass A notes the term may not be active; no clear inner-being immediate response evidenced. Mar 4:39 (vc=30401) and Mar 1:25/Luk 4:35 fimoō verses apply to demons and the storm — no human inner-being immediate response evidenced.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The evidence is substantially silent on the immediate inner-being response of the one who receives dishonour. The corpus is focused on the dishonorer's inner disposition. Silent on this specific area.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The evidence is substantially focused on the evaluator's conscience rather than the experience of those whose conduct is evaluated. Silent on an extensive immediate-response description.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The evidence is largely silent on the sustained inner-being response of the despised person — the focus is often on the contempt-er's inner disposition rather than the recipient's experience. The beggar-identity of Bartimaeus (Mar 10:50) is the most sustained description of how contempt-shaped shame forms a person's inner self-understanding over time. Silent on many verses' depiction of the recipient's full inner response.

**[CHAR-6]** S — The 8-verse corpus is compact and does not provide extensive description of the range of immediate responses to CHAR-6's presence or absence. Silent on more extensive immediate-response description.

**[CLUSTER]** S — Primary areas of silence on immediate response: Char 3 focuses on the dishonorer's disposition rather than the dishonoured's immediate response; Char 6's compact 8-verse corpus does not elaborate the full range of immediate responses.

**[CHAR-1]** S — The verse evidence is silent on the proud person's immediate internal recognition of their own pride in the moment of its exercise. No verse in §3 evidences the proud person perceiving or being disturbed by their own CHAR-1 as it operates. This silence is analytically significant: it suggests CHAR-1 is phenomenologically self-concealing in its possessor, operating without generating the internal signals that would alert the person to its presence. The wisdom corpus's emphasis on external consequences (Pro 16:18, vc=34073: "pride goes before destruction") as the primary corrective signal is consistent with this absence — if internal recognition occurred, external catastrophe would not need to serve as the sole correction mechanism.

**[CHAR-2]** S — The verse evidence is silent on the immediate internal experience of the presumptuous person during the act of CHAR-2. No verse in §3.A describes the inner phenomenology of the will in the moment of its boiling-over transgression. The evidence focuses on the external act, its characterisation, and its consequences rather than the felt inner experience.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The verse evidence is largely silent on the inner phenomenology of the person exercising VCG-01 condemned boasting in the moment of its execution. The evidence focuses on what is boasted about and why it is wrong, not the felt inner experience of the boasting act.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The verse evidence is silent on the immediate internal experience of the person exercising CHAR-4. What is named is the cognitive state (inflated self-picture) and external consequence (controversy, blindness, communal disorder), not the felt inner experience. Confirmed.
**[CHAR-5]** S — The verse evidence is silent on the immediate inner-being response of those who encounter CHAR-5 from another. Confirmed.

**[CLUSTER]** S — All five characteristics are silent on the immediate internal experience of the person exercising the characteristic (as distinguished from the victim's response or the external consequence). The cluster-wide silence on the inner phenomenology of the pride-possessor is analytically significant: the evidence consistently describes pride from outside (its acts, its characterisation, its consequences) rather than from inside (the felt experience of self-elevation in the moment). This may reflect the evidence's consistently third-person or second-person address to pride rather than first-person description by the person in its grip.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence is not broadly silent on immediate response (see T1.5.1 and T1.5.2). However, the eschatological instances (Gen49:10 — future gathering of nations; 1Pe1:2 — goal of the Spirit's sanctifying work) describe the characteristic as a future telos rather than an immediate response to present encounter; their immediate-response profile is implied rather than named.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The corpus addresses the divine immediate response extensively (see T1.5.1 and T1.5.2) but is silent on the human-experienced immediate inner response *to* the state of contrition — what it feels like to be in the state, or what immediately precedes or accompanies it from the human experiential side. The two-verse corpus focuses on what God does in response rather than on the human experiential phenomenology of the state itself.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The inner experiential response of the person who possesses the characteristic (what meekness/gentleness feels like from the inside) is not directly addressed in the two-verse corpus. The evidence names the characteristic's outward quality (dealing gently with the erring; coming without delay) rather than the phenomenological inner experience of the person who has it.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The immediate response of the bearer of the characteristic (what it feels like to have semnotēs) is not directly addressed — the evidence describes the effect on others (orderly compliance, authenticated teaching, peaceable life) rather than the inner phenomenology of possessing the characteristic.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The inner phenomenology of the person exercising the characteristic (what willing-heartedness feels like from the inside) is not directly addressed. The evidence describes the outer acts produced by the inner disposition rather than the felt inner experience of the person who is willing-hearted.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence addresses immediate response extensively. The M09-B register (experienced lowliness — 2Cor7:6; 2Ch28:19; Psa107:12) is the partial exception: the imposed-lowering verses describe the state of being brought low but do not always record an immediate inner response from the person who is lowered. 2Cor7:6 ("God who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus") names God's response to the state but the person's immediate inner response is implicit rather than named. This partial silence is analytically significant: in the imposed-lowering register, the inner response is not automatically generated — the person may experience the lowered state without the relational opening that characterises the voluntary register. The two registers thus differ in their immediate response profile.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The inner phenomenology of *having* the characteristic (what it feels like from the inside) is universally silent across all six characteristics in this cluster. All six evidence the outward expressions or divine responses but not the first-person phenomenological experience of the person who has the characteristic. This cluster-wide silence is itself a finding: M09 is a cluster of *other-directed* characteristics whose evidence is primarily about effects on others and divine responses rather than about the subjective experience of the person possessing them. This distinguishes M09 from clusters (such as grief or joy clusters) where the phenomenology is directly addressed. The silence is consistent across all six and suggests that the characteristic of truly non-self-assertive existence is precisely that it does not call attention to itself, even in Scripture's description.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence is not globally silent on immediate response (see T1.5.1 and T1.5.2), but the corpus is notably sparse on the immediate inner response of the sinning agent in the God-directed register (VCG-01). The verses in VCG-01 primarily record the fact of sinning and its consequences (national disaster, exile) rather than the sinning person's immediate inner experience of committing the act. Eze 18:4/20 declare outcome (death) without describing the sinner's immediate inner response at the moment of sinning. This silence may reflect the prophetic genre's interest in consequence over phenomenology.

**[CHAR-10]** S — The inner phenomenological experience of the person in the moment of being enticed, joining in hypocrisy, or departing from covenantal standing — what these mechanisms feel like from within — is not described in the corpus. The corpus describes the mechanisms and their consequences, not the inner subjective experience of undergoing them.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The inner phenomenological experience of the person who has not yet encountered the good news of the condition's remedy — what it feels like to live under sin's dominion without awareness of the gospel — is not directly described in the corpus. The corpus describes the condition (VCG-01/03), its remedy-announcement (VCG-02), and specific responses to the remedy-announcement, but not the raw subjective experience of living under the condition without reference to its remedy.

**[CHAR-12]** S — The inner phenomenological experience of the person in the moment of sin's enslaving power taking hold — what it feels like from within to move from free practice to constituted slavery — is not described in the corpus. The corpus describes the structural state (slavery — Joh 8:34) and its prevention (new birth — 1Jo 3:9) but not the subjective experience of the enslavement process itself.

**[CHAR-13]** E — For the many persons described as carrying the Jeroboam-sin legacy (VCG-04 — 46 verses of kings who "walked in the sins of Jeroboam and did not depart"), the immediate inner response to the record is not described. The corpus characterises their conduct and its consequences but not the moment-by-moment subjective experience of carrying the recorded sin-pattern.

**[CHAR-14]** E — For the kip.pu.rim atonement passages (VCG-01 — Exo 29:36; 30:10/16; Lev 23:27/28; 25:9; Num 5:8; 29:11; 2Ch 29:23/24), the immediate inner response of the individual receiving the atonement's benefit is not described. The corpus characterises the ritual mechanism and its purpose but not the individual worshipper's moment-by-moment inner experience of the atonement's completion.

**[CHAR-15]** E — For the prophetic passages (Isa 43:27; Isa 64:5; Isa 65:20; Eze 37:23), the immediate inner response of the person who hears the naming of the generational pattern is not directly described. The naming of the first father's sin (Isa 43:27) and the prolonged-sin condition (Isa 64:5) describe the condition without specifying the hearer's immediate inner response.

**[CHAR-16]** E — For the social-stigma sinner-category (VCG-01 — Mat 9:10; Luk 15:1/2; Luk 7:37) — the sinners who draw near to Jesus, recline at table, or approach with ointment — the immediate inner response of receiving the sinner-label from others is not directly described. The corpus characterises their behaviour (drawing near, reclining, approaching) but not the moment-by-moment inner experience of bearing the externally assigned sinner-identity.

**[CHAR-17]** E — For the communal accumulated guilt contexts (VCG-02 — 2Ch 24:18; 2Ch 28:10/13; 1Ch 21:3), the immediate inner response of the individual community-members to the collectively incurred guilt is not described. The corpus names the guilt and its communal consequences (divine wrath) but not the individual's moment-by-moment inner experience of bearing the community's accumulated guilt-weight.

**[CHAR-18]** E — For the generational-transmission register (VCG-02 — Exo 20:5; Deu 5:9; Lev 26:39-43), the immediate inner response of individual community members to inherited iniquity from ancestors is not described. The corpus names the transmission and its consequences (rotting in exile — Lev 26:39) but not the moment-by-moment inner experience of the person discovering they bear their fathers' iniquity as a personal burden.

**[CHAR-19]** E — For the threshold-accumulation register (VCG-03 — Amos 1:3/6/9 — nations whose transgressions are counted toward judgment), the immediate inner response of the transgressing nations to their own accumulation is not described. The corpus names the transgressions and the divine judgment-threshold but not the moment-by-moment inner experience of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Judah, and Israel as they commit and accumulate their counted transgressions.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The VCG-02 cultic-purification verses (Exo 29:36; Lev 8:15; Lev 9:15; Eze 43:20/22; Eze 45:18) are silent on inner personal response — because in this register no personal moral act is in view; the cha.ta verb applies to the cleansing of objects. This silence is expected given the register, not a gap in the evidence.

**[CHAR-20]** E — For VCG-03's constitutional-character register (Isa 24:16; Isa 33:1; Isa 48:8; Jer 3:8/11), the immediate inner response of the person who has been characterised by treachery from before birth (Isa 48:8) to their own constitutional unfaithfulness is not described. The corpus names the identity and its divine foreknowledge but not the moment-by-moment inner experience of the person constitutionally given over to faithlessness.

**[CHAR-21]** E — For VCG-04's sexual perversion (Lev 18:23/20:12 — bestiality and incest named "perversion"), the immediate inner experience of the person committing these acts is not described. The corpus names the acts and their classification as perversion and their penalty (death) but not the inner recognition or response of the one committing them.

**[CHAR-22]** E — For VCG-01's judicial context (Eze 18:8 — "withholds his hand from injustice") and commercial context (Lev 19:35 — "do no wrong in judgment, in measures"), the immediate inner experience of the person who is actively withholding their hand is described in the negative (what they don't do) rather than the positive inner-experience dimension. The corpus names the restrained act but not the inner sensation of restraining.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The corpus is not globally silent on immediate response (T1.5.1 and T1.5.2 show the range). The specific silence is on the confessor's immediate inner-being experience at the moment of speaking the confession — the corpus describes what comes before (conscience activated) and what comes after (plea, forgiveness, dismissal), but the moment of speaking itself is not described phenomenologically. The inner experience of the act of naming one's own sin is present in 2Sa 24:10 (heart-struck) but the moment of actual speech is not described separately from the surrounding conscience-activation.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The Ecclesiastes verses (Ecc 2:26; 8:12) and Job 35:6 do not evidence immediate response scenarios — they describe the state of conscience suppression as an observed condition (the sinner defined by not-pleasing-God, doing evil a hundred times) rather than as an encounter. The corpus is silent on the inner immediate response of the conscience-suppressed person themselves — they do not appear to experience an immediate internal response because the conscience that would generate it is suppressed.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The corpus is not silent on immediate response — the response is consistently continued refusal (T1.5.1 and T1.5.2). However, the inner phenomenological experience of the person who is refusing to repent — what it feels like from within — is not evidenced. The corpus describes the condition and its external expression (non-departure) but not the person's inner experience of the moment of confrontation.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The inner phenomenological experience of the person within habitual defection — what the pattern feels like from within — is not evidenced in the corpus. The corpus describes the condition (settled direction toward sin) and its external markers (altars multiplied, non-listening, sinning yet again) but does not describe the inner subjective experience of being habitually oriented toward sin.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The inner phenomenological experience of the community members receiving the transmitted sin — what it feels like from within to be formed toward sin by a leader's authority — is not described in the corpus. The corpus describes the outcomes (Israel sinning, following the Lord being abandoned) but not the subjective inner experience of the transmission.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The inner phenomenological experience of the revolting party — what the inner person experiences in the moment of revolt — is not described in the corpus. The corpus describes the political-military facts and consequences of revolt, not the inner subjective experience of the decision to revolt.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The inner phenomenological experience of the person who commits sinful speech — what they experience in the moment of blasphemy or slander — is not described in the corpus. The corpus describes the acts, their origins (the heart — Mat 15:19; conceit — 1Ti 6:4), and the responses they provoke, but not the inner experience of the speaker in the moment of sinful speech.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence is not silent; it is addressed above (T1.5.1–T1.5.2). The evidence does not address the inner phenomenology of initially adopting wickedness (the transition moment) — that is silent. What the evidence richly documents is the response of the established wicked person when encountered, corrected, or threatened.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence is not silent on immediate response; it is addressed in T1.5.1–T1.5.2. What remains unaddressed is the phenomenology of first-person inner experience of the characteristic in the moment of its formation or initial adoption — the evidence does not describe what it feels like to become constitutionally evil. The evidence addresses the established state and responses to it, not the process of its initial emergence. This silence is noted.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The evidence is not silent on immediate response — it is richly documented in VCG-04 (T1.5.1–T1.5.2 above). What is silent is the phenomenological description of the inner experience of the abominable person who is aware of their condition. The evidence describes consequences, verdicts, and responses but not the first-person inner phenomenology of recognition. This silence is noted.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence is not silent on immediate response; it is documented above (T1.5.1–T1.5.2). What is silent is the phenomenological description of the moment of first attachment — the inner experience of first turning the heart toward an idol-object. The evidence documents the established state and responses to it, not the initiation phenomenology. This is noted.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The evidence is not globally silent on immediate response; specific patterns are documented (T1.5.1–T1.5.2). What is silent is the phenomenological description of the immediate inner experience of the person who has just begun scheming iniquity — the first-person experiential account of what it feels like to conceive evil for the first time. The evidence documents the practitioner's established state and the responses of those around them, not the initiation phenomenology. This silence is noted.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The immediate inner response of the observer who witnesses blasphemy is silent in this corpus. The evidence documents the blasphemer's response (further defiance — VCG-01) and the falsely accused's response (non-retaliatory maintenance — VCG-02/03), but not the inner experience of third-party witnesses to blasphemous speech. This silence is noted.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The evidence is not uniformly silent; Chars 3, 5, and 6 all evidence immediate-response patterns. The cluster's silence is specific: no characteristic documents the immediate phenomenological inner experience of the person who first encounters the characteristic as attractive or tempting — the evidence addresses established conditions rather than initial entry phenomenology. Additionally, the third-party observer's immediate inner response to witnessing evil (other than grief and sighing — Eze 9:4, Char 3) is generally silent across the cluster.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence is not silent. Both varieties of immediate response (conscience-awakening/grief-seeking and willful non-response) are directly evidenced. However, the large majority of the 133 verses describe the condition and its prescribed remedy without narrating the person's inner response — they are normative/legal rather than narrative. Immediate response is directly evidenced at Lev 5:2-3, Num 9:6-7, Num 19:20, and Lev 13:45 (the self-declaration cry). The remaining verses provide structural information about the condition but leave the inner response implicit.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence is not uniformly silent — three patterns of immediate response are evidenced (T1.5.2 above). However, the majority of the 26 verses (particularly the legal-didactic VCG-02 corpus: Gal 5:19, Col 3:5, 1Th 2:3/4:7) describe the condition without narrating the person's immediate inner response to recognising it. In these cases the verse evidence is silent on the immediate response and focuses instead on the condition's nature and the calling away from it.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The evidence is not uniformly silent — immediate responses are evidenced across VCGs (Gen 34:5, Num 5:14, Jer 2:23, Lam 4:15, Eze 23:13, Eze 20:43). However, the large majority of the prophetic-legal corpus (Lev 18, Num 35, Deu 21/24, Eze 5/7/9/22/36/43, Hos, Mic) describes the condition and its consequences without narrating a specific immediate inner response. The evidence base is substantially normative/prophetic rather than narrative.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence is silent on the immediate inner-being response of the affected person from within the condition. In all 21 verses, the person in the defilement-state does not narrate or express their own immediate inner response — they are under the spirit's domination. This silence is analytically significant: Characteristic 4 is the only M10c characteristic where the affected person's own inner response to being in the condition is structurally inaccessible — the domination that constitutes the characteristic is what prevents the person from narrating their response to it.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's silence pattern on immediate response is analytically revealing. Characteristic 1: the 133 normative/legal verses largely describe the condition and its prescribed remedy without narrating immediate inner response; Lev 5:2-3, Num 9:7, 19:20 and Lev 13:45 are the direct evidence points. Characteristic 2: the legal-didactic corpus (Gal 5:19, Col 3:5, 1Th 2:3/4:7) describes the condition without narrating the person's immediate inner response. Characteristic 3: the prophetic-legal corpus (Lev 18, Num 35, Deu, Eze, Hos, Mic) is substantially silent on immediate inner response. Characteristic 4: structurally silent on the affected person's own response — the most analytically significant silence in the cluster, because the domination that constitutes the characteristic is what prevents the person from narrating their response to it. Cluster-level pattern: the primary form of silence across the cluster is the normative corpus's silence (Chars 1, 2, 3) — these verses describe the condition without narrating the response. Characteristic 4's silence is qualitatively different — it is structural, not merely the result of the text's genre. The cluster's combined silence profile shows that most of the evidence is about what the condition is, not about how the person experiences it from within.

questions.question_text: What does the characteristic produce in the inner being over time in this verse — what states, qualities, capacities, or orientations does it establish? Record it, or record none.

findings.session_b_note:
The data establishes several sustained effects across the corpus:

1. **Love-orientation (sustained relational disposition):** Luk 7:47 — "she loved much." OBS-064-029 names this as an inner-being generator: forgiveness received produces love-orientation as a downstream inner state. The love produced is not a passing emotion but an orientation of the inner being.

2. **Reverential fear (sustained awe):** Psa 130:4-7 — the Psalmist's discovery that forgiveness belongs to God produces a sustained posture of waiting and hope: "I wait for the Lord... his steadfast love, with him is plentiful redemption." The immediate fear becomes a sustained orientation of expectant trust.

3. **Hope (sustained forward orientation):** Q040 answer draws from Psa 130 — forgiveness as the ground of hope. The person who knows forgiveness is available does not despair at the depth of their guilt but waits in hope. This is a sustained inner-being orientation produced by the knowledge that forgiveness exists.

4. **Release from guilt-state (sustained condition change):** Afesis (G0859) names the condition of release. The person is no longer in the guilt-state but in the release-state — a permanent condition change, not a temporary relief.

5. **Capacity for horizontal forgiveness (sustained enabling):** F-003 — the vertical reception structurally enables horizontal extension. This is a sustained inner-being transformation: the person who has received becomes capable of giving in a way they were not before.

findings.session_b_note:
The data addresses sustained effect more through the chesed/channum vocabulary than through the splanchnizō/ra.cham vocabulary.

**Chesed as sustained constitutional state:** The chesed vocabulary (H2617B, H2617A as XREF) names God's compassion-love as *everlasting* (Lam 3:22 — "his mercies never come to an end"; Isa 54:8 — "everlasting chesed"). In the human person, cha.sad (2 Sam 22:26) names the settled character quality of covenantal mercy-faithfulness that defines the person's inner orientation. Over time, chesed produces the character type of the chasid (devoted/loyal person, H2623 XREF) — the one whose inner life is constitutively shaped by covenantal loyalty.

**Sumpatheō and community formation:** The 1 Pet 3:8 community portrait (unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, tender heart, humble mind) suggests that sustained operation of the sumpathēs quality produces an inner fabric of community solidarity — a person shaped for genuine relational presence.

**What is missing (P):** The data does not directly address what sustained *reception* of divine compassion produces in the inner being over time. What does a person become, constitutionally, as the sustained object of divine ra.cham and chesed? This is implied by the supplication vocabulary and the covenantal frame but not stated. This is a gap; no SD pointer addresses it directly.

findings.session_b_note:
The verse evidence describes what divine response to contrition produces (revival, nearness, salvation) rather than what contrition itself produces over time as a sustained inner-being state. Contrition is not typically described as a long-duration condition whose effects accumulate — it is presented as a posture that draws divine response, after which the revival/restoration changes the inner-being condition.

What can be said from the data: sustained contrition (as a settled orientation of lowliness) produces the quality of **humility** as a character disposition. Isa 57:15 pairs contrite spirit with lowly spirit as simultaneous characteristics. Isa 66:2 presents humble + contrite + trembling as a settled three-fold orientation. The sustained effect of the contrite orientation appears to be a character formation in the direction of lowliness, genuine self-knowledge, and receptivity to God's word.

*Partial: character formation toward lowliness and receptivity is a reasonable inference from the data; the data does not directly address sustained effects over time.*

findings.session_b_note:
Finding 062-INNER-001 addresses this directly. The sustained effects named in the data:

- **Capacity for divine nature participation** (2Pe 1:4): over time, fellowship with divine nature enables ontological transformation — escape from corruption, growing participation in what God is.
- **Hope** (Ecc 9:4): sustained fellowship with the living maintains hope as an inner-being orientation.
- **Moral formation** (Psa 119:63, Isa 1:23, Job 34:8): fellowship with the righteous produces righteous character alignment; fellowship with wickedness produces wicked character conformity. Finding 062-CHAR-001 establishes this comprehensively.
- **Inner purification** (Pro 20:30): fellowship through disciplinary wounding, sustained through the corrective process, produces cleansing of evil from the innermost parts.
- **Healing** (Isa 53:5): fellowship through redemptive wounding produces inner restoration.
- **Enabling capacity** (finding 062-ENABLE-001): fellowship with Christ produces capacity for mutual support (Ecc 4:10) and shared suffering that leads to resurrection power (Phili 3:10).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-001: T1 as a whole reveals that goodness is constitutively multi-modal but unified in origin. The characteristic's 12 distinct operational modes (Q&A-022) span quality, disposition, condition, and evaluati…
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that goodness is constitutively multi-modal but unified in origin. The characteristic's 12 distinct operational modes (Q&A-022) span quality, disposition, condition, and evaluative act — and yet all share a single definitional structure: goodness is what proceeds from and returns to God. The immediate response varies by encounter type (Q&A-025-026), the sustained effect is constitutive rather than reactive (Q&A-030), and the dimension structure is bipartite — Moral Character for human-subject goodness, Divine-Human Correspondence for divine-subject (Q&A-034). What the tier as a whole reveals is that the apparent definitional complexity of goodness (12 modes, multiple dimensions, varied immediate responses) resolves into a coherent characterological portrait: goodness is the quality of alignment with the character of the one who is Good — variable in its expression but unified in its source and standard.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-011: T1's distinction between immediate response and sustained effect (Q&A-030) maps precisely onto T5's two transformation sequences (Q&A-126). The immediate response pattern (trust, praise, receptive des…
findings.finding_value: T1's distinction between immediate response and sustained effect (Q&A-030) maps precisely onto T5's two transformation sequences (Q&A-126). The immediate response pattern (trust, praise, receptive desire) corresponds to the initial stages of T5's positive arc (encounter → trust → refuge). The sustained effect (stable orientation, community capacity, settled disposition) corresponds to T5's later stages (reorientation → overflow → formation-agent capacity). Furthermore, T1's "sustained effect" (Q&A-028) identified stable inner orientation as the primary sustained product — T5 confirms this through the transformation to orientation change (Q&A-123) and the formation-agent role (Q&A-136). The two tiers read together reveal a temporal architecture for goodness: immediate contact produces first responses; sustained formation produces constitutive character; and the character-formed person becomes a formative resource for others.

(5) **Obedience pattern** — Joh 14:15 (OBS-103-140): sustained love of Christ produces a sustained pattern of commandment-keeping. The inner orientation produces an enduring behavioural pattern.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-062-001: T1 establishes fellowship as a structurally complex characteristic whose definitional core (genuine participation-in, determined by its object) is expressed through five distinct modes and whose susta…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes fellowship as a structurally complex characteristic whose definitional core (genuine participation-in, determined by its object) is expressed through five distinct modes and whose sustained operation produces constitutional character formation. The definition tier's key insight: fellowship is formally unified by the object-determines-character logic but materially diverse across five modes (existential, companionship, moral complicity, transformative suffering, ontological). The structural negative (misdirected fellowship) is more dangerous than absence of fellowship — Hos 4:17 and Mat 23:30 present the active wrong-direction as the primary threat, not non-participation. The definitional complexity of fellowship explains why the single English word is analytically inadequate: it covers a range from minimal existential participation (Ecc 9:4) to maximal ontological transformation (2Pe 1:4) under the same label.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-011: T1 establishes that habitual fellowship produces constitutional character formation; T5 maps this as the primary formation mechanism and identifies the sequence (volitional alignment → habituation → c…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes that habitual fellowship produces constitutional character formation; T5 maps this as the primary formation mechanism and identifies the sequence (volitional alignment → habituation → constitutional fixing). Together T1 and T5 reveal the full arc: the definitional claim that fellowship's object determines character (T1) is the endpoint of a formation process that moves through distinct phases (T5). The five-mode structure (T1) generates two distinct formation mechanisms in T5: participatory-transfer (companionship → habituation → character) and wound-as-cleansing (suffering → inner purification). T1's most radical mode (ontological, 2Pe 1:4) is T5's eschatological telos (divine nature participation as the formation endpoint).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-064-001: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act (not primarily a feeling or condition) whose definitional core is the release of a legitimate claim — the cancellation of a debt that was real, by a creditor who c…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes forgiveness as an act (not primarily a feeling or condition) whose definitional core is the release of a legitimate claim — the cancellation of a debt that was real, by a creditor who could have retained it. The four-mode structure (covenantal-objective, divine relational-personal, human horizontal, intercessory) is layered: each mode assumes the prior modes are operative. The structural negative (retained claim producing inner torment) is as analytically significant as the positive: forgiveness withheld damages the withholder. The two downstream inner states (love — Luk 7:47; reverence — Psa 130:4) are named with precision: they arise in different contexts (love from having personally received; reverence from encountering the quality as divine attribute) and constitute the immediate inner-being consequences of the act. The definition tier's single most important structural claim: forgiveness is not a terminal state but a transitional act producing further inner states.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-001: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanch…
findings.finding_value: T1 reveals compassion as a definitionally complex characteristic that simultaneously operates as character quality (ra.chum — the settled disposition of the compassionate person), inner event (splanchnizō — the moment of being-moved), condition of its object (eleeinos — the pitiable state that calls compassion forth), and externalised act (almsgiving, mercy-act). No other characteristic in the programme review set operates across all four kinds simultaneously. The four root families (RACHAM, CHASAD, SPLANCHN, OIKTIROM) identify four constituent dimensions of the single characteristic, each naming a distinct register — somatic-maternal, covenantal-relational, visceral-immediate, and deliberative-pitying respectively. The structural opposites are two distinct kinds: willed judicial hardness (the hardened heart that refuses compassion) and unwilled prosperity-blindness (Eze 16:49 — the one who does not see the need because they are satiated). The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed by the consistent outward-facing structure: compassion cannot exist without a suffering other. The definitional tier's most critical gap — the receiver's inner-being experience — is entirely absent from the data, affecting T1.5, T1.6, and T1.7 throughout. This gap is the single most significant analytical absence in the registry.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-011: T1's sustained-effect analysis (largely P-rated because the receiver's inner-being experience is absent) and T5's formation arc together reveal a gap that is structurally significant: the formation pr…
findings.finding_value: T1's sustained-effect analysis (largely P-rated because the receiver's inner-being experience is absent) and T5's formation arc together reveal a gap that is structurally significant: the formation process from single compassion-event to compassion-character is the most important untraced developmental relationship in the registry. T5 provides the directional finding (the formative cycle feeds back from after-state to before-state) and names the three mechanisms (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological). T1 provides the definitional starting point (compassion as character quality is the endpoint of formation). Together they frame an arc that is identified but not filled: how does the moment of splanchnizō (T1 inner-event) accumulate into the settled character of ra.chum (T1 character quality)? T5's mechanisms suggest the answer but the data does not trace the path explicitly — a gap confirmed by both tiers.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-001: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes grace as a definitionally multi-kind characteristic: simultaneously divine disposition (the inclination of the greater toward the lesser — chen root), relational standing (the condition of being in favour — charis as inhabited state), enabling capacity (the specific power given for specific tasks — 2Cor 12:9), and character quality (gracious speech, gracious conduct — chen in 889-003). No single English equivalent captures all four. The four modes of operation (sovereign bestowal, covenantal-relational sustaining, capacity-conferring, character-forming) correspond to the four kinds without collapsing them. Two structural opposites are identified: pride (the self-elevation that refuses the favour of the greater, active and willed) and ingratitude/gracelessness (acharistos — the failure to register and respond to grace received, which T3 confirms as image-impairment). The immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle) is a T1.5 finding confirming that grace does not bypass creaturely recognition but requires and produces it as a transitional state. The dimension classification (Relational Disposition as primary) is confirmed throughout: grace is constitutively directional — it flows from the greater to the lesser and requires the receptor's inner-being engagement to complete its operation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-011: T1's sustained-effect finding (immediate/sustained contrast as qualitative, not merely temporal — what grace does immediately is creaturely recognition; what it does over time is constitution of ident…
findings.finding_value: T1's sustained-effect finding (immediate/sustained contrast as qualitative, not merely temporal — what grace does immediately is creaturely recognition; what it does over time is constitution of identity and character) maps onto T5's formation mechanisms. The encounter mechanism (T5) produces the immediate effects named in T1.5; the word, inference, and mediated-transformation mechanisms (T5) produce the sustained effects of T1.6. T5's five mechanisms collectively explain how the four kinds named in T1.2 are produced across different temporal and contextual registers: disposition-receipt is the encounter mechanism; standing is the spirit-outpouring mechanism; capacity is the mediated-transformation mechanism; character quality is the sustained word-and-inference mechanism. T1 names what is produced; T5 names how each kind is produced.

(4) Inner transformation — the new covenant's sustained effect is progressive inner renewal: law written on the heart is not a one-time event but an ongoing constitutive reality (OBS-034-059, OBS-034-061).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-034-001: T1 as a whole reveals that covenant is constitutively architectural — it is not a characteristic that exists on its own terms but one that structures the conditions within which other inner-being char…
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that covenant is constitutively architectural — it is not a characteristic that exists on its own terms but one that structures the conditions within which other inner-being characteristics operate. Its working description (Q&A-018) names it as "the solemn, binding relational bond... the structured architecture of faithful relationship." Its primary dimension is Relational Disposition (Q&A-034), but its four modes of operation (disposition, act, quality, condition — Q&A-016) and its composite structure (five constituent elements — Q&A-017) reveal that covenant is genuinely multi-modal. No other characteristic in the programme is described as simultaneously a disposition, an act, a quality, and a condition — this four-modal nature is unique to covenant and is what makes it architecturally prior to other C17 characteristics. T1 establishes that covenant is not one inner-being characteristic among equals but the structural framework within which the relational-grace vocabulary of C17 operates.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-099-001: T1 reveals that kindness is a structurally composite, other-oriented disposition — not a simple quality. Its essential character is loyal goodwill (chesed = faithfulness + kindness in a single concept…
findings.finding_value: T1 reveals that kindness is a structurally composite, other-oriented disposition — not a simple quality. Its essential character is loyal goodwill (chesed = faithfulness + kindness in a single concept), constituted internally by faithfulness, justice, compassion, and forgiveness. It operates in three distinct modes — dispositional orientation, deliberate volitional act, and Spirit-produced formation — and these are not alternatives but layers of a single integrated phenomenon. The immediate and sustained effects are distinct in kind: the immediate response to received kindness is receptive and affective (praise, relief, petition); the sustained effect is formative and dispositional (the person becomes the chasid — one whose character is shaped by chesed over time). The structural opposite is the self-enclosed inward orientation; the counterfeit (chrēstologia) is not merely an absence but an active imposture. T1's most significant intra-tier finding: kindness is primarily dispositional, but the disposition is itself composite — removing any one of its constituent elements (faithfulness, compassion, justice) changes what remains into something that is no longer fully kindness.

findings.session_b_note: The sustained effects of shalom documented in the data: (1) Stumble-proof stability — Psa 119:165 ("great peace have those who love your law; nothing can make them stumble") — sustained shalom produces inner stability resistant to external shocks; (2) Wisdom reception — Isa 32:17 ("the effect of righteousness will be peace, and the result of righteousness, quietness and trust forever") — sustained peace is the condition in which trust is formed and wisdom operates; (3) Turning many from iniquity — Mal 2:6 — Levi's sustained walk in peace produced transformative effects in others; (4) Righteousness harvest — Jam 3:18 ("a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace") — peace-orientation produces righteousness as its long-term fruit; (5) Strength — Isa 30:15 ("in quietness and in trust shall be your strength") — the sustained inner posture of quiet trust produces strength. The sustained profile: shalom is not only an experienced condition but a formative one — it produces stability, trust, strength, and the capacity to impact others.

findings.session_b_note: The sustained inner-being effects of divine giving in this registry cluster around three outcomes. (1) Identity formation: God's covenantal giving over generations produces a people who know themselves as recipients of promise — the land-giving texts (Gen 12:7 through Jer 17:4 in group 872-001) address communities who inherit a narrative of divine faithfulness accumulated across generations. (2) Inner-being capacity: the endowing giving (872-003) deposits Spirit, wisdom, and understanding that shape the person's cognitive and formative capacities over time (Neh 9:20, OBS-060-040). (3) Transformed inner states: the eschatological giving (872-007) produces lasting new inner-being orientations — not momentary experience but stable conditions: "oaks of righteousness" (Isa 61:3, OBS-060-049) names a durable identity, not a passing moment.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-001: T1 as a whole reveals that faithfulness in this registry is structurally composite and directional. The name ("faithfulness") promises a character quality; the OWNER term (na.tan) delivers an action. …
findings.finding_value: T1 as a whole reveals that faithfulness in this registry is structurally composite and directional. The name ("faithfulness") promises a character quality; the OWNER term (na.tan) delivers an action. These are not contradictory — they are complementary aspects of the same inner-being reality: the dispositional quality only becomes faithfulness when it enacts itself (Q&A-016, Q&A-018). The triadic architecture (inner-being source → act → object given) is the definitional shape of this characteristic: it cannot be reduced to disposition alone or act alone (Q&A-017). The five operational modes (Q&A-022) show that this single definitional structure produces radically different expressions depending on what is given and from what inner state — the characteristic is definitionally unified but expressionally plural. The primary dimension (Moral Character) grounds this — it is the character quality that makes the giving faithful rather than merely generous. The definition's most distinctive feature is its disposition-in-action structure: faithfulness is a verb that must be enacted to be real, not a noun that can be possessed without expression.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-004: The working description of the characteristic (T1.2.3, Q&A-018) — faithfulness as an inner-being quality that enacts commitments, orientations, and compassions through giving — is directly illuminated…
findings.finding_value: The working description of the characteristic (T1.2.3, Q&A-018) — faithfulness as an inner-being quality that enacts commitments, orientations, and compassions through giving — is directly illuminated by T5's formation account. The working description names a state of the person; T5 reveals how that state is produced and where it is oriented. Specifically: the sustained inner-being effects (T1.6: trust, praise orientation, responsiveness, cognitive formation) are precisely the formation arc outcomes of T5. Sustained covenantal giving produces identity as recipients of promise (T5.5); endowing giving constitutes cognitive capacity (T5.3); eschatological giving produces the endpoint state of "oaks of righteousness" (T5.6). What this pair reveals: the working definition of the characteristic is not a static description but an arc description — it names the person being formed toward a fullness that is not yet complete. The characteristic is definitionally developmental.

In the hater: progressive narrowing of the inner life around the object of hatred. Pro 10:18: concealed hatred requires lies — the person becomes complicit in self-deception. Hos 9:7: accumulated communal hatred produces "the prophet is a fool; the man of the spirit is mad" — the spiritual perceptive capacity is obliterated by the accumulated inner climate. In the hated: sustained hatred from others produces despair (Psa 69:20), fear of abandonment (Gen 50:15), and the chronic condition of disfavour (group 550-NEW-01 — the unloved wife across Deuteronomy and Genesis).

Progressive estrangement from the object of contempt. Isa 1:4: "they have despised the Holy One of Israel, they are utterly estranged" — the estrangement is the sustained effect. In group 172-002 (contempt of reproof): the sustained effect is the closure of the formation pathway — the person becomes permanently closed to correction. In the communal register (Jer 23:17): the community that despises God's word becomes receptive to false prophets — the contempt has corrupted the capacity to distinguish true from false.

In the righteous form (group 252-001): sustained abhorrence of evil produces stable moral orientation — the person is constitutionally set against what God opposes. In divine form (group 252-003): sustained divine abhorrence toward covenant violators produces judgment and exclusion. In the eschatological terminus (group 1283-001): the sustained effect of being abhorrent becomes permanent — "everlasting contempt" (Dan 12:2) and "they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh" (Isa 66:24).

In the perpetrator: Pro 11:17 — "a cruel man hurts himself." Job 15:20: "the wicked man writhes in pain all his days, through all the years that are laid up for the ruthless." The sustained effect of cruelty on the cruel person is their own undoing. In the victim (group 1775-002): sustained exposure to ruthless domination strips all relational and social shelter, producing the ongoing experience described in Isa 25:4 — those under the ruthless seek shelter as from a storm.

In the individual: sustained reproach restructures the person's inner life — their perception of themselves (Psa 22:6: "I am a worm and not a man"), their relation to others (Psa 31:11: "those who see me in the street flee from me"), and their volitional capacity (Job 31:34: "I kept silence, and did not go out of doors"). In the corporate register: sustained reproach produces communal shame that becomes a defining identity (Jer 24:9 — "a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse in all the places where I shall drive them"). Isa 54:4 shows that restoration from deep reproach requires active forgetting — the reproach has been laid down in memory so deeply that removal is not automatic.

Sustained operation of the adversary relationship produces vigilance (1Pe 5:8: "be sober-minded; be watchful") and sustained appeal (Luk 18:3 — "kept coming to him"). The sustained effect is a heightened inner alertness and persistent orientation toward the advocate.

Eze 25:15: "never-ending enmity" — malice is self-perpetuating. The pleasure in destruction renews itself with each new occasion of the other's suffering. The sustained effect is a deepening inner orientation toward the other's destruction as the source of the soul's pleasure — the characteristic does not cycle down but intensifies.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Increasing confidence in appeal (the psalmists return to it repeatedly — Psa 31:1; 71:2; 143:1; 143:11, VSG M26-A1-004) and deepening capacity for proclamation (declaring God's righteousness "all day" — Psa 35:28; 71:24). Sustained encounter with God's righteousness generates ongoing testimony.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** The sustained effect of righteousness in the human person is: rootedness and stability (M26-A2-013: "the roots of the righteous will never be moved"), increasing capacity for outward orientation (A2-012), and the development of a recognisable life path (M26-A2-017). The image of the palm tree (Psa 92:12, VSG M26-A2-001) implies growth over time.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Uprightness sustained produces the capacity for moral discernment — "then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path" (Pro 2:9, VSG 1212-002). The sustained orientation toward what is straight produces increasing capacity to recognise what is right. The Preacher's uprightness in writing (Ecc 12:10, VSG 1211-003) suggests that sustained uprightness produces reliable, truthful expression over time.

**[C — Justification]** Justification sustained as a received condition produces an heir-status that grows in the person's identity and expectation: "heirs according to the hope of eternal life" (Tit 3:7). The sustained effect is the development of hope — not as a mood but as an orientation toward promised future reality.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** The sustained entrusting of vengeance to God (6841-002) produces the inner capacity to bless rather than curse — Rom 12:14–19 shows the entrusting of vengeance as part of a sustained posture of non-retaliation and active goodwill.

**[E — Condemnation]** The sustained freedom from condemnation (4846-002: Rom 8:34) produces increasing security before God — the person who lives in the knowledge that Christ intercedes is established in a condition that nothing can overthrow.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The sustained exercise of the reckoning faculty produces increasing clarity about moral reality. Rom 8:18 — the sustained reckoning of present suffering against future glory — produces the capacity to endure suffering without being crushed by it.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Sustained wickedness produces increasing hardness and insensitivity to divine righteousness. Rom 2:5 (VSG 3207-001) names the "hard and impenitent heart" that is "storing up wrath" — sustained wickedness accumulates a weight of future judgment.
